DETAILED ACTION
The text of those sections of Title 35, U.S. Code not included in this section can be found in a prior Office Action.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
Claims 1, 4, 6, and 9 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by USPN 2005/ to Aufderheide et al.
Regarding claims 1 and 6, Aufderheide teaches an input device for a man-machine interface (patterned conductor touch screen, title) comprising an upper board providing a first plastic based resistant film structure (Fig. 6, see the upper half of the touch screen construction 670 and all the parts above second substrate 610). The structure also comprises a lower board corresponding to said upper board and providing a second plastic resistant film structure opposite to said first plastic based resistant film structure (Fig. 6, see the lower half of the touch screen construction 670 and all parts below second substrate 610). The boards are plastic based because they may have plastic supporting substrates (PET, paragraph [0025]), and resistant because of the included materials (desired sheet resistance, paragraph [0020]). The first and second plastic based resistant film structures are respectively composed of an ITO based conductive film (paragraph [0027]), a printed silver conductor layer (paragraph [0045]), a carbon layer (paragraph [0048]), an insulation layer (solvent-based epoxy insulator ink, paragraph [0046]), and an adhesive layer (filler, paragraph [0029]). Note that claim 6 is identical to claim 1, but instead recites that the upper and lower boards are glass based; because the substrates (110, 210, 410, 550, and 690) of Aufderheide may be either plastic or glass based (paragraph [0025]), claim 6 is also anticipated. Aufderheide also teaches that the carbon layer is arranged to overlay the insulation layer (carbon conductive ink printed over a further silver ink layer, paragraph [0048], which itself overlays the solvent-based epoxy insulator ink of paragraph [0046]). Although it is not explicitly disclosed, the structure of Aufderheide avoids dissociation of silver ions from the printed silver layer, because the silver is no longer directly exposed to oxidation (air). Furthermore, the carbon layer is arranged to overlay of Aufderheide is arranged to overlay the insulation layer (carbon conductive ink printed over a further silver ink layer, paragraph [0048]), which avoids the dissociation of silver ions from the printed silver layer.
For claims 4 and 9 Aufderheide teaches that the layer of ITO conductive film is printed on the base substrate, which is either polymeric or glass as above (paragraph [0043]). A silver conductor layer was overlaid on the surface of the ITO layer (paragraph [0045]). An insulator (solvent-based epoxy insulator ink) was overlaid on the printed silver conductor layer (paragraph [0046]). A carbon layer was overlaid the insulation layer (carbon conductive ink printed over a further silver ink layer, paragraph [0048]). An adhesive layer was overlaid the carbon layer (filler, paragraph [0037], note that the filler may be adhesive as disclosed in paragraph [0036]).
This structure is repeated for both the upper and lower resistant film structures (best shown by Fig. 6), and the base substrate may be either plastic or glass as above.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
Claims 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, and 9 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over USPA 2005/ to Aufderheide et al.
Regarding claims 1 and 6, Aufderheide teaches an input device for a man-machine interface (patterned conductor touch screen, title) comprising an upper board providing a first plastic based resistant film structure (Fig. 6, see the upper half of the touch screen construction 670 and all the parts above second substrate 610). The structure also comprises a lower board corresponding to said upper board and providing a second plastic resistant film structure opposite to said first plastic based resistant film structure (Fig. 6, see the lower half of the touch screen construction 670 and all parts below second substrate 610). The boards are plastic based because they may have plastic supporting substrates (PET, paragraph [0025]), and resistant because of the included materials (desired sheet resistance, paragraph [0020]). The first and second plastic based resistant film structures are respectively composed of an ITO based conductive film (paragraph [0027]), a printed silver conductor layer (paragraph [0045]), a carbon layer (paragraph [0048]), an insulation layer (solvent-based epoxy insulator ink, paragraph [0046]), and an adhesive layer (filler, paragraph [0029]). Note that claim 6 is identical to claim 1, but instead recites that the upper and lower boards are glass based; because the substrates (110, 210, 410, 550, and 690) of Aufderheide may be either plastic or glass based (paragraph [0025]). Aufderheide also teaches that the carbon layer is arranged to overlay the insulation layer (carbon conductive ink printed over a further silver ink layer, paragraph [0048], which itself overlays the solvent-based epoxy insulator ink of paragraph [0046]). Although it is not explicitly disclosed, the structure of Aufderheide avoids dissociation of silver ions from the printed silver layer, because the silver is no longer directly exposed to oxidation (air).
Aufderheide does not explicitly teach that alternatively, the carbon layer is arranged to overlay the printed silver conductive layer.
However, Aufderheide does discuss that carbon conductive ink may be screen printed over silver ink traces in areas where corrosion protection is required (paragraph [0048]). Performing this preventative measure on the silver ink pattern under the epoxy insulating ink would form the recited structure, because the carbon layer would now be overlaid the printed silver conductor layer. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention to insert protective carbon layers are needed junctures in order to protect silver layers from corrosion, especially in light of potentially oxidizing (corrosive) nature of epoxy-based polymers.
For claims 4 and 9, Aufderheide teaches that the layer of ITO conductive film is printed on the base substrate, which is either polymeric or glass as above (paragraph [0043]). A silver conductor layer was overlaid on the surface of the ITO layer (paragraph [0045]). An insulator (solvent-based epoxy insulator ink) was overlaid on the printed silver conductor layer (paragraph [0046]). A carbon layer was overlaid the insulation layer (carbon conductive ink printed over a further silver ink layer, paragraph [0048]). An adhesive layer was overlaid the carbon layer (filler, paragraph [0037], note that the filler may be adhesive as disclosed in paragraph [0036]).
This structure is repeated for both the upper and lower resistant film structures (best shown by Fig. 6), and the base substrate may be either plastic or glass as above.
Claims 2 and 7 are identical to claims 4 and 9, but instead recite that the carbon layer is overlaid the printed silver conductor layer. This structure is obviated by Aufderheide for the reasons discussed in the rejection of claims 1 and 6.
Response to Arguments
Receipt of the response to the previous Office Action, dated 25 January 2010, is acknowledged.
The objections to the drawings and specification are withdrawn in light of applicant's submitted amendments.
Regarding the rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, applicant's arguments have been fully considered but are not persuasive.
For the rejections of claims 1 and 6, applicant argues that amended claim 1 does not recite the transparent conductor patters taught by Aufderheide. However, it is the examiner's position that the Aufderheide reference still obviates the claims due to the open, "comprising" language, which has been interpreted consistent with MPEP § .
Applicant further argues that Aufderheide teaches that the carbon layer is printed over the silver layer to protect the traces for corrosion and abrasion, but that the claims recite that the carbon layer is printed over the silver in order to prevent the dissociation of silver ions. This argument is not persuasive for two reasons. First, in relation to the question of whether the prior art anticipates the claims under 35 U.S.C. 102, MPEP § states that the fact that the prior art is not recognized as solving the problem solved by the claimed invention is not germane to an inherency rejection. Twin Disc, Inc. v. United States, 231 USPQ 417, 424 (Cl. Ct. 1986) (quoting In re Self, 671 F.2d 1344, 213 USPQ 1, 7 (CCPA 1982)). Second, in relation to the question of whether the prior art obviates the claims under 35 U.S.C. 103, MPEP § 2145; the fact that applicant has recognized another advantage which would flow naturally from following the suggestion of the prior art cannot be the basis for patentability when the differences would otherwise be obvious. See Ex parte Obiaya, 227 USPQ 58, 60 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1985).
The arguments directed to claims 2, 4, 7, and 9 are also on the grounds that the features of amended claim 1 is not taught by the Aufderheide reference. However, as discussed above, these features are indeed present.
Because it has been determined that Aufderheide still teaches the claimed invention as currently presented, the rejections of the previous office actions have been modified to meet the amended claim features and reapplied.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).
A shortened statutory period for reply to this final action is set to expire THREE MONTHS from the mailing date of this action. In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action. In no event, however, will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the date of this final action.

DETAILED ACTION
Response to Amendment
The amendment filed December 13, 2011 has been entered, correcting the deficient parts of the amendment filed November 29, 2011, the claims and remarks of which are the subject of this Office Action.
Drawings
The drawings are objected to under 37 CFR 1.83(a). The drawings must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims. Therefore, the “single playback button which can operate each of the plurality of channels” of claim 14 must be shown or the feature(s) canceled from the claim(s). No new matter should be entered.
Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. The figure or figure number of an amended drawing should not be labeled as “amended.” If a drawing figure is to be canceled, the appropriate figure must be removed from the replacement sheet, and where necessary, the remaining figures must be renumbered and appropriate changes made to the brief description of the several views of the drawings for consistency. Additional replacement sheets may be necessary to show the renumbering of the remaining figures. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claim 14 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over “Multi Message Recorder” (MMR) (as supported by “TERS Electronic Ltd” (TERS) and “China Trader Online” (CTO)) (already of record) in view of Pawlowski et al. (US Patent 6,038,199 ('199)) (already of record).
Regarding claim 14, MMR teaches a personal reminder digital voice recorder (“Multi Message Recorder”; TERS and CTO title) comprising: a) a battery operated (“3pcs 1.5volt cells are required”; TERS and CTO “Product Description” #3) audio microchip system for recording, storing and reproducing a single personal audio recording (“Flash Memory preserves the digital recordings”; TERS and CTO “Product Description” #2) on each of a plurality of channels (“the recorded messages can be preserved as five paragraphs...”; TERS and CTO “Product Description”); c) a single LED corresponding to each of the channels (“LED indicator upon ‘P1’ is on’; TERS "Operating Guide” #2; wherein " ‘P1’ button means anyone button of father, mother, boy1, boy2 and girl"; TERS “Remark”), each LED having a means to turn the LED on when the channel has an active message recorded (“The LED indicator upon P1 button will be blink until pressing ‘P1' button”; TERS “Operating Guide” #6); and d) a means to turn each LED off when a corresponding channel has a message that is inactive (“...will be blink until pressing ‘P1’ button”; TERS “Operating Guide” #6).
MMR does not explicitly teach “b) a single playback button which can operate each of the plurality of channels”.
In the same field of endeavor, Pawlowski teaches selecting among a plurality of channels (‘199 Figs. 5 and 9) and a single playback button which can operate each of the plurality of channels (“the selected voice file may be played back or edited by the user by means of the control switches...”; ‘199 col. 5 lines 50-52) for the benefit of expanding the total number of recording channels without having to expand the number of interface buttons accordingly.
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to modify the personal voice recorder taught by MMR with the display interface for selecting a recording and playing said recording back with a single button as taught by Pawlowski for the benefit of expanding the total number of recording channels without having to expand the number of interface buttons accordingly.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed November 29, 2011 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Applicant argues that “the reference does not teach a single playback button with lights corresponding to each channel“ (p. 3 middle of second paragraph). Examiner respectfully disagrees as MMR clearly illustrates a single LED per recording channel, while Pawlowski teaches selecting among several recordings (i.e. channels), then using a single switch to select a playback mode. Pawlowski figure 5 illustrates selecting “entry 132” (by indicating it with mark #140). When a particular entry is selected, the "playback" can be selected with a single switch (i.e. Fig. 2 #34). While Pawlowski teaches selecting a playback mode with a single “switch” instead of a “button” as claimed, MMR teaches playback and selecting a channel exclusively through use of “buttons”. As “buttons” and "switches” are well-known obvious variants, Pawlowski’s teaching of a single “switch” still renders a single “button” obvious.
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure.

14 is
“Multi Message Recorder” (MMR) (as supported by “TERS Electronic Ltd” (TERS) and “China Trader Online” (CTO)) (already of record) in view of Pawlowski et al. (US Patent 6,038,199 ('199)) (already of record).
Regarding claim 14, MMR teaches a personal reminder digital voice recorder (“Multi Message Recorder”; TERS and CTO title) comprising: a) a battery operated (“3pcs 1.5volt cells are required”; TERS and CTO “Product Description” #3) audio microchip system for recording, storing and reproducing a single personal audio recording (“Flash Memory preserves the digital recordings”; TERS and CTO “Product Description” #2) on each of a plurality of channels (“the recorded messages can be preserved as five paragraphs...”; TERS and CTO “Product Description”); c) a single LED corresponding to each of the channels (“LED indicator upon ‘P1’ is on’; TERS "Operating Guide” #2; wherein " ‘P1’ button means anyone button of father, mother, boy1, boy2 and girl"; TERS “Remark”), each LED having a means to turn the LED on when the channel has an active message recorded (“The LED indicator upon P1 button will be blink until pressing ‘P1' button”; TERS “Operating Guide” #6); and d) a means to turn each LED off when a corresponding channel has a message that is inactive (“...will be blink until pressing ‘P1’ button”; TERS “Operating Guide” #6).
MMR does not explicitly teach “b) a single playback button which can operate each of the plurality of channels”.
In the same field of endeavor, Pawlowski teaches selecting among a plurality of channels (‘199 Figs. 5 and 9) and a single playback button which can operate each of the plurality of channels (“the selected voice file may be played back or edited by the user by means of the control switches...”; ‘199 col. 5 lines 50-52) for the benefit of expanding the total number of recording channels without having to expand the number of interface buttons accordingly.
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to modify the personal voice recorder taught by MMR with the display interface for selecting a recording and playing said recording back with a single button as taught by Pawlowski for the benefit of expanding the total number of recording channels without having to expand the number of interface buttons accordingly
Applicant's arguments filed November 29, 2011 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Applicant argues that “the reference does not teach a single playback button with lights corresponding to each channel“ (p. 3 middle of second paragraph). Examiner respectfully disagrees as MMR clearly illustrates a single LED per recording channel, while Pawlowski teaches selecting among several recordings (i.e. channels), then using a single switch to select a playback mode. Pawlowski figure 5 illustrates selecting “entry 132” (by indicating it with mark #140). When a particular entry is selected, the "playback" can be selected with a single switch (i.e. Fig. 2 #34). While Pawlowski teaches selecting a playback mode with a single “switch” instead of a “button” as claimed, MMR teaches playback and selecting a channel exclusively through use of “buttons”. As “buttons” and "switches” are well-known obvious variants, Pawlowski’s teaching of a single “switch” still renders a single “button” obvious.
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure.

Claims 19 and 20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which applicant regards as the invention. Claims 19 and 20 are confusing because there is no antecedent basis for the expression "said spring” on the last line of claim 19. Apparently, claim 19 should depend from claim 14, not claim 1.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102/103
s 1, 2, 5, 6, 14, 15, 18, and 19 are
b
Aihara et al. Aihara et al (note Figure 1) show a carburetor vacuum accelerator module 14 with a diaphragm 34 and compression spring 42 (note col. 3, lines 20-52) as claimed (35 USC 102b). It would appear that Aihara et al may not explicitly state that a vacuum is created in the operation of the acceleration module. However, Aihara et al do describe the production of a negative pressure in col. 3, lines 5-19 in the operation of the module 14 which would indicate the creation of a vacuum. Consequently, it is inherent or at least would have been readily obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art (35 USC 103a) that Aihara et al’s acceleration module is a vacuum operated module
s 3, 4, 7-13, 16, 17, and 20 are
Aihara et al in view of Ogishi. Aihara et al, as described above in paragraph 5, disclose a carburetor vacuum acceleration module substantially as claimed. Apparently, Aihara et al may not explicitly disclose housing attachment clips and cavities and a spring retainer. In any case, Ogishi (note ref. characters P, 7c, 20, 22, 31, Figures 1, 4) teaches the well-known uses of housing attachment clips and cavities and a spring retainer in a carburetor vacuum acceleration module for the purpose of ensuring proper negative pressure actuation (note col. 2, lines 36-49). Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to employ housing attachment clips and cavities and a spring retainer in the Aihara et al carburetor vacuum acceleration module in order to facilitate negative pressure actuation as taught by Ogishi

DETAILED ACTION
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Response to Amendment
Applicant has amended claims 1, 3, 9, and 10 and added claims 12-20.
The amendments to the claims have overcome the 112, second paragraph rejections of record.
The amendments to the claims have overcome the prior art rejections of record. However, after further search and consideration, new grounds of rejection, necessitated by amendment are submitted in view of newly cited references Strauss (US 2006/0147634), Yundt (US 4,119,649), and Lambourne et al. (US 2011/0147219). See 102 and 103 rejections below.
Response to Arguments

A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –

With regard to claims 1 and 2: Strauss teaches method for fabricating a superhydrophobic surface (abstract), comprising:
Preparing a metal base material, i.e. titanium substrate 26 (abstract, Figures 2A and 2B, Paragraphs [0016] and [0017]).
Anodizing the titanium metal base 26 to form a ceramic layer (titanium oxide layer) 30 having a complex structure of mountain range-shaped microstructures (microscopic sharp points and valleys) made up of nano-fiber (nanotube) structures 38 on a surface of the titanium base metal 26 (Figures 2A and 2B, Paragraphs [0017]-[0019]). And applying a hydrophobic polymer material on the complex structure, i.e. the ceramic, titanium oxide layer 30, to form an even polymer layer (hydrophobic coating) across the complex structure (Figures 2A and 2B, Paragraph [0021]). DETAILED ACTION
Claims 1-7 and 11-19 are pending as amended on 9 September 2016, claims 8-10 and 20-21 are withdrawn from consideration.
The text of those sections of Title 35, U.S. Code not included in this action can be found in a prior Office action.
Applicant’s amendments to the claims and the remarks/arguments, as well as the declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 by Kenneth Oglesby have been entered and fully considered.
Response to Amendment and Arguments
Applicant’s amendment overcomes the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(d) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, 4th paragraph of claim 19. The rejection has been withdrawn.
Applicant’s amendment does not distinguish from US Patent 5268112 (Hutchins).
Applicant's arguments in light of amendment and the declaration under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Applicant argues that Hutchins does not teach plugging and sealing of fluid flow channels. The examiner disagrees. Although Hutchins discloses generation of flow pathways, Hutchins expressly teaches, before forming such pathways, injecting the gellable composition into a subterranean formation to occupy a portion of the pores, reduce permeability (col.11, line 50-55,col. 12, line 5- 25) or form a more permanent selective plug (col. 12, line 55-65).
Applicant argues that Hutchins does not teach non-crosslinked polymers. The examiner disagrees. Hutchins teaches the gel-forming composition need only contain water soluble crosslinkable polymers including polyacrylamide and cellulose(col.5, line 60-68) without a crosslinking agent (col. 5, line 30-35), thus the crosslinkable polymers meet the limitation of non-crosslinked polymers.
Applicant argues in view of the declaration that a crosslinked polyacrylamide provide inferior results to non-crosslinked polymer. First, the examiner notes the chart attached to the declaration is not legible. Secondly, as set forth above, Hutchins the crosslinkable polymer of Hutchins is not crosslinked prior to the injection of crosslinking agent (col. 5, line 30-35).
In view of the foregoing, when all of the evidence is considered, the totality of the rebuttal evidence of nonobviousness fails to outweigh the evidence of obviousness.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
Claims 1-7 stand rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by US Patent 5268112 (Hutchins).
Regarding claims 1 and 7, Hutchins teaches a method comprises mixing in aqueous media a gel-forming ingredient with a gas precursor such as urea and a delayed acting substance such as esters, anhydrides to form a gellable composition ( col.4, line 10-23 and col.6, line 29-40 and 65-68), both of which meet the claimed initiator, and the gellable composition meets the single stage alkaline fluid; and injecting the gellable composition into a subterranean formation (col.6, line 35-40,col. 7, line 40-50 and col.11, line 50-55) to occupy a portion of the pores, which meets the fluid flow channels, and reduce permeability (col. 12, line 5-15 and 25) or form a more permanent selective plug (col. 12, line 55-65), wherein the gel-forming ingredients comprises one or more ingredients selected from the group consisting of alkali metal salts of silicates and crosslinkable polymers, etc. (col.4, line 60-69, col.5, line 3-5, 30-45 and 68, and claims 1 and 4).
Regarding claims 2-4, Hutchins teaches the amount of polymer is selected to assure gel stability at reservoir and gelation time frame (col. 6, line 35-40), the amount of the ester/anhydride is preferably to transform some or all of the gas precursors into the gas (col. 7, line 15-20), and the amount of the gas precursor is selected to supersaturate the gel with the gas thus the gel properties (col. 4, line 30-35). Since ratio is a term relative to the amount of other ingredient, selecting the amount of any one ingredient meets the limitation of selecting a ratio of other ingredient.
Regarding claim 5, Hutchins further teaches utilizing temperature of the subterranean formation to control the gas formation thus the gel properties (col. 4, line 35-55).
Regarding claim 6, Hutchins teaches the delayed acting substances, i.e., the esters or anhydrides can also be injected into the formation as a separate slug (col. 6, line 60-62), wherein the delayed acting substance is transformed to its active specie after the gelation period, which anticipates injecting the delayed acting substance after the placement of the gellable composition.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
Claims 11-18 stand and claim 19 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hutchins.
The teachings of Hutchins are set forth above.
Regarding claims 11-14 and 18-19, Hutchins teaches alternate sequentially injection of one or more slugs of the gel-forming composition and one or more slugs of a gas such as carbon dioxide (col.7, line 40-50 and col. 8, line 5).
Hutchins does not teach pumping a first portion of gas precursor /delayed acting substance, pumping a gel-forming ingredient and pumping a second portion of precursor /delayed acting substance.
However, it would be obvious for one of ordinary skill at the time of the invention to sequentially pumping gas precursor/ester/anhydride and the gel-forming ingredients since it has been held that selection of any order of performing process steps or selection of any order of mixing ingredients is prima facie obvious in the absence of new or unexpected results. In re Burhans, 154 F.2d 690, 69 USPQ330 (CCPA 1946) and In re Gibson, 39 F.2d 975, 5USPQ 230 (CCPA 1930).
See MPEP 2144.04[R-6]IV.
Regarding claim 15, Hutchins teaches alkali metal salts silicates (col. 5,line 3-5), which one of ordinary skill in the art would at once envisage sodium and potassium silicates. It is further noted that Hutchins teaches adding potassium chloride to the water employed in making the gel-forming composition (col. 11, line 15-16), thus the solution comprises potassium ion therefore potassium silicate.
Regarding claim 16, Hutchins teaches the pH is 3 to 11 (col. 4,line 5-10), which overlaps with the claimed range of pH 10 to13 thus a prima facie case of obviousness exists. In re Wertheim, 541 f. 2d 257,191 USPQ 90(CCPA 1976). See MPEP 2144.05.I.
Generally, differences in ranges will not support the patentability of subject matter encompassed by the prior art unless there is evidence indicating such ranges is critical. See MPEP 2144.05, In re Boesch, 617 F2d 272, 205 USPQ 215 (CCPA 1980); In re Aller, 220 F2d 454, 456, 105 USPQ 233, 235 (CCPA 1955) and In re Hoeschele, 406 F2d 1403, 160 USPQ 809 (CCPA 1969).
Regarding claim 17, Hutchins teaches the polymer includes polyacrylamide and cellulose(col.5, line 60-68).
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
6. The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
7. Claims 1-6, 8-11, 13, 15, 18-19, and 22-23 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over DE 34 36 089 to Kronseder (Machine Translation provided).
Regarding claims 1-3 and 15,
Kronseder discloses a transport device for upright bottles comprising:
a housing (7) in which at least one transport element (2) comprising bottle carriers (not labelled) conveys the bottles (1) through different system zones [Fig. 1; page 6, lines 23-28];
at least one metal wall (8) is provided in the housing (7) as a boundary of the bottle transport path, which the metal wall can be contacted on a bottle contact side by bottles at least in at least one locally defined wear portion along the bottle transport path [Fig. 1-2; page 6, lines 28-35];
at least one exchangeably arranged wear plate (11) which in the wear portion defines the bottle contact side of the wall is provided in the wear portion of the metal wall (8) [Fig. 1-2; page 7, lines 7-16];
wherein the sheet-metal wear plate (i.e. slide member) is provided with a recess in the bottom in which a screw (16) or locking pin (21) can then intervene, allowing for releasable mounting [page 8, lines 12-16]; and
wherein the wall (8) comprises a local recess matched to a thickness of the wear plate (11) and configured to receive the wear plate such that an upper surface of the wear plate is flush with an upper surface of the wall [Fig. 2; page 7, lines 7-18].
Kronseder does not explicitly teach that the wall (8) or the wear plate (11) are made from sheet-metal. However, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention to make said wall (8) and wear plate (11) from sheet-metal for the known benefit of providing a durable, low-cost, easily replaceable material, since it has been held to be within the general skill of a worker in the art to select a known material on the basis of its suitability for the intended use as a matter of obvious design choice. In re Leshin, 125 USPQ 416. See MPEP 2144.07. Furthermore, Kronseder suggests that it is old and well known within the art for a wall and wear plate to comprise sheet-metal, or similarly, metal strips [page 5, lines 14-25].
Regarding the recitation “the bottles are conveyed in transverse rows, and wherein the bottles in each transverse row are conveyed spaced apart from one another with gaps along given bottle paths”, this recitation is a statement of intended use which does not patentably distinguish over the prior art since Kronseder meets all the structural elements of the claim(s) and is capable of performing said recitation of intended use if so desired. See MPEP 2114.
Regarding claims 4 and 13,
Kronseder discloses the system of claim 1, wherein a plurality of sheet-metal wear plates (i.e. slide members) are provided side by side with one end having a recess (19) and the other end having a mating projection (18), forming a butt joint next to the bottle paths [Fig. 5; page 4, claim 14].
Regarding claims 5-6 and 18-19,
Kronseder discloses the system of claim 1, wherein the sheet-metal wear plate (i.e. slide member) is made of a wear-resistant hard material, such as sheet-metal [page 2, lines 8-12], with a rectangular outer contour [page 4, claims 16-17]. Furthermore, the outer contour of each wear plate may have recesses (i.e. anchoring points) on its bottom surface for engagement to a support member (10) with screws (16) or locking pins (21) [page 8, lines 12-16].
Regarding claim 8,
Kronseder discloses the system of claim 1, wherein the wear plate (11) is made of a durable wear-resistant material having a hardness of at least 7 on the Mohs scale [page 5, claim 22]. Kronseder does not, however, explicitly teach that the sheet-metal wear plate is more wear-resistant than portions of the sheet-metal wall adjacent to the wear plate. However it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention to make the wear plate of a more wear-resistant material than the portions of the sheet-metal wall adjacent to the wear plate to durably support bottles, since it has been held to be within the general skill of a worker in the art to select a known material on the basis of its suitability for the intended use as a matter of obvious design choice. In re Leshin, 125 USPQ 416. See MPEP 2144.07. Furthermore, it can be seen from Fig. 2 that the wear plate (11) consists of more wear-resistant sheet-metal material than the portion of sheet-metal wall (8) [page 7, lines 7-10].
Regarding claim 9,
Kronseder discloses the system of claim 1, wherein the wear plate (11) is made of a wear-resistant hard material such as sheet-metal [page 2, lines 8-12], and that its height may exceed that of the longitudinal groove it is placed in [page 7, lines 7-10], but does not teach that the bottle contact side has a convex or concave curvature. However it would have been obvious for a person having ordinary skill in the art at time of invention to provide a convex or concave bottle contact side since it has been held that a change in shape was a matter of choice which a person of ordinary skill in the art would have found obvious absent persuasive evidence that the claimed configuration was significant .In re Dailey, 357 F.2d 669, 149 USPQ 47 (CCPA 1966). See MPEP 2144.04.
Regarding claim 10,
Kronseder discloses the system of claim 1, wherein the sheet-metal wear plate (11) is arranged in a wear portion of the bottle transport path that is at least substantially flat [Fig. 1; page 6, lines 23-27].
Regarding claim 11,
Kronseder discloses the system of claim 9, wherein the dome- or depression-shaped bottle deflection zone extends in a direction transverse to a transport direction of bottles conveyed in transverse rows [Fig. 1; page 6, lines 34-35], and that in the wear portion a plurality of sheet-metal wear plates (11) of the same width in a direction transverse to the transport direction with the same lengths are arranged in a direction transverse to the transport direction one after the other and in an individually exchangeable way [Fig. 1; page 7, line 39- page 8, line 2].
Regarding claim 22,
Kronseder discloses the system of claim 1, but does not teach that the upper surface of the sheet-metal wall has a convex curvature corresponding to the curvature of the sheet-metal wear plate. However it would have been obvious for a person having ordinary skill in the art at time of invention to provide a convex curvature for said sheet-metal wall/wear plate configuration for desirably allowing support of the bottles by the wear plate since it has been held that a change in shape was a matter of choice which a person of ordinary skill in the art would have found obvious absent persuasive evidence that the claimed configuration was significant. In re Dailey, 357 F.2d 669, 149 USPQ 47 (CCPA 1966). See MPEP 2144.04.
Regarding claim 23,
Kronseder discloses the system of claim 1, wherein it is noted that the recitation “the sheet-metal wear plate is wider than an underside of each of the bottles transported along the bottle transport path” is a statement of intended use which does not patentably distinguish over the prior art since Kronseder meets all the structural elements of the claim(s) and is capable of performing said intended use if so desired. See MPEP 2114. Claims directed to apparatus must be distinguished from prior art in terms of structure rather than function. In re Danly, 263 F.2d 844, 847, 120 USPQ 528, 531 (CCPA). “[A]pparatus claims cover what a devices is not what a device does” Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Bausch & Lomb Inc., 909 F.2d 1464, 1469, 15 USPQ2d 1525, 1528 (Fed. Cir. 1990). It is fundamental that an apparatus claim defines the structure of the invention and not how the structure is used in a process, or what materials the structure houses in carrying out the process. Ex parte Masham, 2 USPQ2d 1647, 1648 (BPAI 1987). See also In re Yanush, 477 F.2d 958, 959, 177 USPQ 705,706 (CCPA 1973); In re Finsterwalder, 436 F.2d 1028, 1032, 168 USPQ 530, 534 (CCPA 1971); In re Casey, 370 F.2d 576, 580, 152 USPQ 235,238 (CCPA 1967). The apparatus of Kronseder is capable of processing a bottle less than a width of the sheet-metal wear plate; therefore the prior art meets the claim.
Furthermore, it would have been an obvious matter of design choice to modify the size of the sheet-metal wear plate/wall such that the width of the wear plate is greater than that of the bottles in order to provide added support, since such a modification would have involved a mere change in the size of a component. A change in size is generally recognized as being within the level of ordinary skill in the art. In re rose, 105 USPQ 237 (CCPA 1955). See MPEP 2144.04.

(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 1-12 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Takahashi (2006/0143418) and Nakajima (US 20080244139 A1).
As per claim 1, Takahashi discloses a management apparatus for managing a computer system including a plurality of storage apparatuses disposed in a plurality of sites, for virtually providing a virtual storage apparatus to a host system over the plurality of storage apparatuses, each of the plurality of storage apparatuses having a logical volume as a virtual volume of the virtual storage apparatus, [Abstract; Fig. 4], the management apparatus comprising: a storage apparatus grouping unit for grouping the respective storage apparatuses constituting the virtual storage apparatus into a plurality of storage groups in accordance with a designated grouping policy and assigning a group ID specific to the storage group, to which the relevant storage apparatus belongs, to each storage apparatus [Figs. 9; claim 23]; and a copy pair setting unit used when setting a copy pair, for switching a part or whole of each of the logical volumes, which are associated with the respective virtual volumes designated as a copy source and a copy designation of the copy pair, to an appropriate logical volume as necessary based on the group ID assigned to each storage apparatus and in accordance with a designated copy pair setting policy related to a relationship between the copy source virtual volume and the copy destination virtual volume [Figs. 11, 12; Abstract; claim 24], wherein the copy pair setting policy includes information on local copy or remote copy of the respective logical volumes associated with designated as the copy source virtual volume and the copy destination virtual volume [Figs. 13-15; par. 198; claim 16].
Takahashi, however, does not explicitly disclose the storage apparatus is configured to group storage apparatuses disposed at an identical site as an identical storage group and assign to each of the plurality of storage apparatuses a group ID. Nakajima discloses the storage apparatus is configured to group storage apparatuses disposed at an identical site as an identical storage group and assign to each of the plurality of storage apparatuses a group ID [¶0054, 0051, 0094].
Thus, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to have storage apparatus configured to group storage apparatuses disposed at an identical site as an identical storage group and assign to each of the plurality of storage apparatuses a group ID because doing such would have optimized the processing performance of a plurality of storage apparatuses storing data (¶0002) as taught by Nakajima.
As per claim 2, Takahashi discloses the management apparatus according to claim 1, wherein the grouping policy includes at least one of a first grouping policy to group the storage apparatuses based on product information, a second grouping policy to group the storage apparatuses based on access information retained by each storage apparatus about access from the host system, a third grouping policy to group the storage apparatuses based on network information, and a fourth grouping policy to group the storage apparatuses manually [Figs. 12, 17; Abstract; claim 16, 24]. As per claim 3, Takahashi discloses the management apparatus according to claim 2, wherein the storage apparatus grouping unit is configured to: display a grouping policy selection screen for selecting one grouping policy from selectable grouping policies among the first to fourth grouping policies [Fig. 17]; and group the storage apparatuses in accordance with the grouping policy selected by using the grouping policy selection screen [Figs. 17, 20]. As per claim 5, Takahashi discloses the management apparatus according to claim 4, wherein the copy pair setting unit is configured to: display a copy pair setting screen for designating the respective virtual volumes which are the copy source and the copy destination virtual volume constituting the copy pair, and the copy pair setting policy [Figs. 14, 16; claims 17, 23]; and switches a part or whole of each of the logical volumes, which are associated with the respective virtual volumes designated as the copy source and the copy destination of the copy pair on the copy pair setting screen, to an appropriate logical volume as necessary in accordance with the copy pair setting policy designated by using the copy pair setting screen [Figs. 4, 9; Abstract; par. 198]. As per claim 6, Takahashi discloses the management apparatus according to claim 1, wherein the copy pair setting policy further includes designation of a copy type of replication copying to be executed by the copy pair [Figs. 13, 15; Abstract]. Applicant's arguments filed 02/16/2017 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.

Examiner disagrees. Tamura teaches and shows in par. 0030 and figs.1 and 3: “This system includes a base station 1, a mobile station 2 connectable to this base station 1 by wireless, and a terminal device 3 connectable to this mobile station 2 by wireless through short-distance wireless communication.”
It is clear that the mobile station 2 of Tamura comprising 2 modules, a second module is use to communicate with a base station using wireless mobile communication network or long range network, a first module is used to communicate with the terminal device 3 using Bluetooth network or short-distance wireless communication network.
Therefore, Tamura teaches a “first communication module” and “a second communication module, as claimed.
Applicant also argues on page 3 of Remarks: “Tamura fails to expressly or impliedly teach a control module configured to obtain a communication profile required for operating the second communication module using the external electronic device connected through the first communication module.”
Examiner disagrees. Par. 0032 of Tamura: “The mobile station 2 is specifically a mobile phone, and executes data communication or audio communication with the base station 1 through mobile communication. DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
Status of Claims
The amendment filed on 4/14/2017 has been entered. In the amendment, Applicant amended claims 1-6. Currently claims 1-6 are pending.
Claim Objections
Claim 1 is objected to because of the following informalities: “An apparatus […] comprising at least one processor to implement:
a gesture recognizer configured to recognize […];
a controller configured to control […]; and
a display configured to display […],”
is suggested to be changed to:
“An apparatus […] comprising:
at least one processor to implement:
recognizing […]; and
controlling […];
a display configured to display […],”
It is noted that Applicant clearly indicates no intention of invoking 35 USC § 112(f) interpretation in the Remarks filed on 4/14/2017 but that the amendment made to the claim filed on 4/14/2017 fails to carry that out. The suggested change by Examiner would revoke the unintended treatment of claim limitations “a gesture recognizer” and “a controller” under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, which would otherwise be invoked.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 1, 2, 4 and 5 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention.
Regarding claim 1, an essential operative relationship of “a starting point”, recited in ll. 9, with a hand gesture for inputting a character is omitted. Without the essential relationship, the descriptive term “starting" is meaningless and does not positively limit the so called “starting point” positioned in a central area of the character pad interface to a starting point of a hand gesture.
Claim 2 is rejected because it depends on claim 1 and does not add the essential operative relationship that is missed in claim 1.
Claim 4 is rejected for the same rationale as applied to claim 1.
Claim 5 is rejected for the same rationale as applied to claim 2.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
Claims 1, 2, 4 and 5 is/are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Kornev et al. (US 2010/0333011) in view of Park et al. (US 8799779).
Regarding claim 1, Kornev teaches an apparatus (Fig. 1: device 100; Para. [0001]) for inputting a character based on a hand gesture (Fig. 2B), the apparatus comprising at least one processor to implement:
a gesture recognizer (Fig. 1: processor 116) configured to recognize hand gestures of a user corresponding to diagonal directions (Fig. 2B; Paras. [0025] and [0028]; Examiner’s Note: hand gestures corresponding to slide paths 248, i.e., four diagonal directions, are recognized for determining secondary characters 244);
a controller (Fig. 1: processor 116) configured to control character input according to directions of the recognized hand gestures (Fig. 2B; Para. [0025]: last two sentences; Para. [0029]: 4th-6th sentences); and
a display (Fig. 1: touch screen 104) configured to display a character pad (Fig. 2B: touch screen including a plurality of keys 208) for the character input,
wherein the character pad comprise a character pad interface (Fig. 2B: character menu 240) in which a starting point (Fig. 2B: center of menu 240; Para. [0028]: last two sentences) is positioned in a central area of the character pad interface.
Kornev does not further teach
In this embodiment, Kornev does not teach:
(1) the gesture recognition unit configured to recognize hand gestures corresponding to horizontal directions and vertical directions,
(2) the display unit displays a character input according to the directions of the hand gestures recognized on the character pad, and
(3) the starting point indicating a type of characteristics that is enabled to be input through a currently activated interface.
The multi-character key 208 in Fig. 2B of Kornev has four characters located at the four corners of character menu 240 and accordingly needs only hand gestures corresponding to four diagonal directions to select the four characters on the multi-character key. For applying Kornev’s technique to a multi-character key including more than four characters, hand gestures corresponding to other directions are required to be recognized. It is not new arranging more characters to a multi-character key.
Kornev, for instance, teaches in Fig. 3 each key 308 has eight characters surround a character located in the center.
At the effective filing date of the invention, it would have been obvious for one ordinary skill in the art to modify Kornev’s technique in Fig. 2B by substituting the multi-character key arrangement in Fig. 3 of Kornev for the multi-character key arrangement in Fig. 2B of Kornev and applying the same concept/technique of sliding a finger to select one of eight characters on the edge of the multi-character key, which would necessarily require the differentiating feature (1), i.e., the gesture recognition unit configured to recognize hand gestures corresponding to two horizontal directions and two vertical directions, in addition to the four diagonal directions.
The motivation/suggestion would have been to allow less keys in a small touch screen.
In the above modified apparatus, Kornev does not further teach differentiating feature (2), i.e., the display unit displaying a character input according to the directions of the hand gestures recognized on the character pad.
In another embodiment, Kornev, however, teaches: the display unit display a character input according to the directions of the hand gestures recognized on the character pad (Fig. 8: highlight 816 for selection of the “A” character).
At the effective filing date of the invention, it would have been obvious for one ordinary skill in the art to further modify the above modified apparatus of Kornev with Kornev’s another technique, enabling the display unit to display a character input according to the directions of the hand gestures recognized on the character pad.
The motivation/suggestion would have been to provide confirmation to the user on selection of a character input, which would obviously enhance a user's experience.
Kornev does not further teach differentiating feature (3), i.e.,
the starting point indicating a type of characteristics that is enabled to be input through a currently activated interface.
Kornev’s menu 240 in Fig. 2B is a multi-character key and its starting point is a central area corresponds to a character. However, the character does not indicate a type of characteristics. The differentiating feature would appear if a multifunctional button/menu whose central area correspond to selecting a type of characters.
Park teaches in Col. 9, ll. 14-15 a multifunctional key for selecting a consonant, a vowel, a double consonant, and a space.
At the time of the invention, it would have been obvious for one ordinary skill in the art to combine Park’s technique with Kornev’s technique making a spatial arrangement of the functions of selecting a consonant, a vowel, a double consonant, and a space associated with Park’s first key in a manner as shown in Kornev’s menu 240 in Fig. 2B and assigning to the central area of the key one of functions of selecting a consonant, a vowel, a double consonant. The modification would have resulted in the differentiating feature (3), i.e., the starting point (i.e., the central area) indicating a type of characteristics that is enabled to be input through a currently activated interface (Examiner’s Note: According to Park’s disclosure in Col. 9, ll. 10-21 and with a consideration of its context, a character pad interface is activated upon a selection of a consonant, a vowel, a double consonant is made).
The motivation/suggestion would have been to applying Kornev’s technique for efficient selection of a function, which is obviously desirable for enhancing a user's experience.
Regarding claim 2, Kornev/Park teaches the apparatus of claim 1. Kornev further teaches the apparatus of claim 1, wherein the gesture recognition unit recognizes the hand gesture of the user corresponding to one among a total of eight directions including two horizontal directions, two vertical directions, and four diagonal directions. (Figs. 2-3; Examiner’s Note: in view of the modification applied to claim 1 substituting the character arrangement in Fig. 3 for the character arrangement in Fig. 2 and using eight slide gestures to select eight characters, respectively, on the edge of a key 308, the eight hand gestures of the user correspond to eight directions including two horizontal directions, two vertical directions, and four diagonal directions).
Claim 4 is rejected for substantially the same rationale as applied to claim 1.
Claim 5 is rejected for substantially the same rationale as applied to claim 2.
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 3 and 6 objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments with respect to claims 1 and 4 have been considered but are moot because the arguments do not apply to a new combination of the references being used in the current rejection (see detailed rejection above).
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

DETAILED ACTION
AIA
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
Claims 1-7, 10-13, and 16-18 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Choi et al. (US 2014/0179093 A1)(hereinafter referred to as Choi) in view of Lin et al. (US 2014/0264911 A1)(hereinafter referred to as Lin), further in view of Cheng et al. (US 2011/0287600 A1)(hereinafter referred to as Cheng).
Regarding claim 1, Choi teaches a method for fabricating an integrated circuit, the method comprising:
providing a partially fabricated integrated circuit (structure in Fig. 4C of Choi) including a dielectric layer (sacrificial layer 420 in Fig. 4B) formed with a trench (gate openings 430 in Fig. 4B of Choi) bound by a trench surface (reverse sidewall-spacer 440 in Fig. 4C of Choi);
depositing metal (gate material 460 in Fig. 4D of Choi may include a metal such as tungsten, as disclosed in paragraph [0033] of Choi reference, lines 30-31 of the column to the right) in the trench and forming an overburden portion of metal overlying the dielectric layer (gate material 460 is form and an overburden portion is overlying the sacrificial layer 420, as seen in Fig. 4D of Choi).
However, Choi does not teach selectively etching the metal with a chemical etchant and removing the overburden portion of metal.
Lin teaches a method of forming a TSV which is filled with a conductive material (Fig. 3e of Lin). The excess conductive material (#472 in Fig. 3e of Lin) is removed using a planarization process such as etch-back (paragraph [0032] lines 6-7), which is an etching process that is not only selective spatially, via the use of masks, but also chemically (for example, in Figs 6-7 of Cheng, the SiGe stressor 220 is removed using an etch-back process which selective to only SiGe while other parts/materials of the structure remained unaffected by the etch-back process). Thus, Lin teaches selectively etching the metal with a chemical etchant and removing the overburden portion of metal.
It would have been obvious at the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to have used the etch-back process disclosed in Lin to remove the excess gate material (in Fig. 4D of Choi) in order to improve control of the planarizing process (line 13 of [0032] of Lin).
Regarding claim 2, the combination of Choi-Lin-Cheng teaches all the limitations of claim 1. The method disclosed in Choi further comprising: selectively etching the metal within the trench to form a recessed surface (see Fig. 4F and paragraph [0036] of Choi reference, the gate material 460 inside the gate structure 465 is recessed using an anisotropic dry-etching process, which is a selective etching process); and depositing a dielectric material over the recessed surface to form dielectric gate cap (see Fig. 4G and paragraph [0036] capping material 480 is deposited into the gate recesses 470; the capping material 480 can be any nitride material, which includes dielectric material).
Regarding claim 3, the combination of Choi-Lin-Cheng teaches all the limitations of claim 1 and also discloses such method further comprising planarizing a portion of the dielectric layer and the metal. But the combination does not teach wherein the portion is less than about 25 nm thick.
It would have been obvious at the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to have stopped the deposition of the dielectric and the metal (gate liner 450 and gate material 460 in Fig. 4D of Choi) before the thickness of these materials outside the trench (gate openings 430 in Figs. 4B & 4D of Choi) reaches 25 nm, since it has been held that where the general conditions of a claim are disclosed in the prior art, discovering the optimum or working ranges involves only routine skill in the art (In re Aller, 105 USPQ 233). An advantage of stopping depositing before such thickness reaches 25 nm is to save cost.
Regarding claim 4, the combination of Choi-Lin-Cheng teaches all the limitations of claim 3, but does not discloses wherein planarizing a portion of the dielectric layer and the metal comprises planarizing a portion having a thickness from about 5 nm to about 20 nm.

Regarding the argument that the planarizing process disclosed by Lin (lines 6-7 of paragraph [0032] in Lin) is “an additional etching process may be paired with the mechanical planarizing process”, the Examiner respectfully disagrees. Lines 6-7 of paragraph [0032] of Lin reference recites “the planarizing process may also be performed with etch-back techniques” which does not contain or implies the word “additional”. As written, the sentence means the etch-back process is a planarizing process, not an additional process to a planarizing process.
Regarding the argument that the Cheng reference does not teach “selectively etching the metal with a chemical etchant and removing the overburden portion of metal”, and hence cannot be combined with the Choi and Lin combination, the Examiner respectfully disagrees. The limitation “selectively etching the metal with a chemical etchant and removing the overburden portion of metal” is taught by the Lin reference (as stated in the rejection of claims 1 and 10). The Cheng reference is used to show that the etch-back process is a selective process, both spatially and chemically. Another example illustrating that the etch-back process is a selective process is provided by Cleeves (US 5652182) (as can be seen in Fig. 5(g) of Cleeves, the tungsten material 570 is deposited by a blanket CVD process and is planarized using an etch-back process, as stated in lines 34-39 of column 10 of Cleeves). Response to Arguments
02/27/2015
Regarding the argument that the planarizing process disclosed by Lin (lines 6-7 of paragraph [0032] in Lin) is “an additional etching process may be paired with the mechanical planarizing process”, the Examiner respectfully disagrees. Lines 6-7 of paragraph [0032] of Lin reference recites “the planarizing process may also be performed with etch-back techniques” which does not contain or implies the word “additional”. As written, the sentence means the etch-back process is a planarizing process, not an additional process to a planarizing process.
Regarding the argument that the Cheng reference does not teach “selectively etching the metal with a chemical etchant and removing the overburden portion of metal”, and hence cannot be combined with the Choi and Lin combination, the Examiner respectfully disagrees. The limitation “selectively etching the metal with a chemical etchant and removing the overburden portion of metal” is taught by the Lin reference (as stated in the rejection of claims 1 and 10). The Cheng reference is used to show that the etch-back process is a selective process, both spatially and chemically. Another example illustrating that the etch-back process is a selective process is provided by Cleeves (US 5652182) (as can be seen in Fig. 5(g) of Cleeves, the tungsten material 570 is deposited by a blanket CVD process and is planarized using an etch-back process, as stated in lines 34-39 of column 10 of Cleeves). Both Cheng and Cleeves references show the capability of etch-back technique at the filing date of the invention
