AIA
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
DETAILED ACTION
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statements (IDS) submitted on 8/10/2016, 10/5/2016, 11/30/2016 and 12/28/2016 was filed after the mailing date of the non-final office action on 7/29/2016. The submission is in compliance with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97. Accordingly, the information disclosure statement has been considered by the examiner.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 10/31/2016 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive. In response to Applicant’s argument that the Office Action fails to explain why the lock surface could only be at the top or bottom of the cartridge. The Examiner made that finding in keeping with the scope of Applicant’s invention. The Examiner merely moved a claimed surface to a different location opposite the claimed surface. Furthermore, one skilled in the art understands finite to be measurable, able to be counted. A polygon has a finite number of sides. Thus, the Examiner maintains that there are a finite number of locations for the lock surface. Additionally, if Applicant is suggesting that claimed lock surface can be put at any of an infinite number of locations along either of the sides, or along the back surface depending on the structure of the corresponding device receiving the cartridge, then it would appear that the placement is arbitrary or obvious "depending on the structure of the corresponding device receiving the cartridge."
In response to Applicant’s argument that the lock surface provided at the upper surface provides better visibility for the user operating the lock, as evidence of expected or superior results. The Examiner finds that that particular reason is neither unexpected nor superior. One skilled in the art, would expect better visibility having the lock surface closer to where the user can see it.
In response to Applicant’s argument that the application explains that placing the lock surface at the upper surface provides an improved location for placing reinforcing surfaces for the lock surface. The Examiner notes that the reinforcing surfaces are not claimed in the instant claim. Additionally, one skilled in the art would expect that by relocating the lock surface, for better visibility for the user operating the lock, that any reinforcing surfaces associated with the lock surface would also be beneficial (and expected) for the same reason.
In response to Applicant’s argument that Gilson fails to disclose “the operation surface faces the upward direction and the second direction” as recited in claim 1. The Examiner maintains the Gilson’s figures depict what is being claimed. Gilson's operation panel is slanted upward. It is also in the second direction, which is opposite the Z direction. The Examiner made a typographical error in that instance. The rejection refers to “the second direction” in three other instances, prior to this fourth instance. In each of those instances, “the second direction” was referred to as opposite the Z direction (see pages 9-10 of the non-final rejection).
Terminal Disclaimer
The terminal disclaimer filed on 10/31/2016 disclaiming the terminal portion of any patent granted on this application which would extend beyond the expiration date of US Patent Application 14/838,438 has been reviewed and is accepted. The terminal disclaimer has been recorded.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
Claims 1, 3, 6-7 and 11-13 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over USP 5,949,459 Gasvoda et al. “Gasvoda” as modified by USP 8,272,704 Gilson et al. “Gilson.”
With regard to Claim 1, Gasvoda teaches a liquid cartridge (12 - ink container) configured to be inserted into a liquid consuming apparatus (10 - printing system and 72 - ink receiving station) in a first direction (Z direction, shown in fig. 5) along a horizontal direction against an urging force (bias from a urging member 98 - spring, 108 - spring, fig. 7) directed in a second direction (opposite Z direction) opposite the first direction (Z direction), and thereby to be mounted to the liquid consuming apparatus( 10/72), comprising:
a liquid chamber (22 - fluid reservoir) configured to store liquid (19 - ink) therein; a front face (50 - leading edge) facing the first direction (Z direction) when the liquid cartridge (12) is inserted into the liquid consuming apparatus (10/72) (col. 4, lines 37-42);
a liquid supply portion (30 - fluid outlet) positioned at the front face 50);
an upper face (top of 12, fig. 8A) facing an upward direction (Y direction) when the liquid cartridge is inserted into the liquid consuming apparatus (10/72);
wherein the liquid cartridge (12) is configured to pivot between a first attitude (figs. 8B, 8C) and a second attitude (8D) when the liquid cartridge (12) is inserted into the liquid consuming apparatus (10/72),
wherein when the liquid cartridge (12) is in the first attitude (figs. 8B and 8C), the lock surface (62 - latch features) contacts the lock portion (76 - latching features) in the second direction (opposite Z direction).
Gasvoda does not expressly teach a lock surface positioned at the upper face and configured to contact a lock portion of the liquid consuming apparatus in the second direction and wherein when the liquid cartridge is in the second attitude, the lock surface is positioned further in a downward direction than the lock portion.
Gasvoda teaches a lock surface (62 -latch features) positioned at the lower (see edited fig. 8D below) face and configured to contact a lock portion (76) of the liquid consuming apparatus (72) in the second direction (opposite Z direction) wherein when the liquid cartridge is in the second attitude, the lock surface is positioned further in a downward direction than the lock portion (col. 5, lines 57- 60).
The Examiner notes that there are a finite number of possibilities for placement of the lock surface (i.e. one of two likely surfaces). As stated in the MPEP 2143, choosing from a finite number of identified predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success is indicia of obviousness. Here, there are two likely placement locations for the lock surface, the lower face, as taught by Gasvoda or the upper face, as claimed. In the absence of the Applicant providing unexpected or superior results from its chosen placement of the lock surface, the Examiner sees no patentable distinction between any of these two likely options.
As such, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Gasvoda to have the lock surface positioned at the upper face as a design choice because the location of surface does not affect the function (i.e. contacting the lock portion) as claimed.
PNG media_image1.png 361 571 media_image1.png Greyscale
Gasvoda doesn't teach an operation surface faces the upward direction and the second direction, and positioned at the upper face and positioned further in the second direction than the lock surface.
However, Gilson teaches (figs. 1 and 2) an operation surface (17) positioned at the upper face and positioned further in the second direction. As depicted in the figures the operation surface (17) is extended from furthest point on the sidewall (12). Therefore it would not interfere with Gasvoda’s upper face. Furthermore, Gilson teaches (figs. 1 and 2) wherein the operation surface (17) faces the upward direction and the second direction (opposite the Y direction).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Gasvoda with the operation surface as taught by Gilson for the purpose of providing a means for grasping the cartridge for facilitating insertion and removal of the cartridge.
With regard to Claim 3, the combination of Gasvoda and Gilson teach wherein when the liquid cartridge is in the first attitude (fig. 8B and 8C of Gasvoda), at least a portion of the operation surface (figs. 1 and 2 of Gilson) protrudes further than the lock surface in the upward direction.
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Gasvoda with the operation surface as taught by Gilson for the purpose of providing a means for grasping the cartridge for facilitating insertion and removal of the cartridge.
With regard to Claim 6, Gasvoda does not teach wherein the operation surface comprises a plurality of protrusions formed thereon.
However, Gilson teaches (figs. 1 and 2) the operation surface (17) comprises a plurality of protrusions formed thereon (shown below).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Gasvoda with the operation surface as taught by Gilson for the purpose of providing a means for grasping the cartridge for facilitating insertion and removal of the cartridge.
With regard to Claim 7, Gasvoda does not teach wherein the plurality of protrusions is a plurality of elongated protrusions.
However, Gilson teaches (figs. 1 and 2) the operation surface (17) comprises a plurality of elongated protrusions. The operation surface (fig. 1, enlarged below) shows a rigid surface with a plurality of elongated protrusions.
The motivation is the same for this claim as discussed above in Claim 6.
PNG media_image2.png 678 706 media_image2.png Greyscale
With regard to Claim 11, Gasvoda teaches further comprising a seal member (120 - compliant septum) positioned at the liquid supply portion and having a liquid supply opening (30) formed therethrough, wherein the seal member (120) is configured to contact an outer surface of a liquid supply tube (92) while being elastically deformed when the liquid supply tube (92) is inserted through the liquid supply opening (fig. 7), wherein the liquid cartridge (12) is configured to pivot about a pivot center (shown above in edited fig. 8D above) which is a center of the liquid supply opening when the liquid cartridge (12) is inserted into the liquid consuming apparatus (10/72) and the liquid supply tube (92) is inserted through the liquid supply opening (col. 3, lines 42-43).
With regard to Claim 12, Gasvoda does not teach wherein the operation surface is fixed relative to the liquid chamber.
However, Gilson teaches (figs. 1 and 2) wherein the operation surface does not move relative to the liquid chamber. As depicted in the figures, the handle appears to be integrated with the sidewalls without movement.
The motivation is the same for this claim as discussed above in Claim 6.
With regard to Claim 13, Gasvoda teaches wherein the liquid cartridge (12) is configured to be inserted into a case (38 - printer chassis) of the liquid consuming apparatus (10/72), and the lock surface (62) is configured to contact the lock portion which is fixed relative to the case (38) (col. lines 63-67 and col. 8, lines 1-2 and 34-40).
AIA
Claim 24 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gasvoda as modified Gilson and further in view of US Pub. No. 2008/0259136 A1 Nishihara.
With regard to Claim 24, Gasvoda as modified by Gilson does not teach the liquid cartridge further comprising a liquid detection portion positioned farther than the locking surface in the first direction.
However Nishihara teaches (fig. 12) a liquid cartridge (CA) further comprising a liquid detection portion (51/53) positioned further than the locking surface in the first direction.
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Gasvoda as modified by Gilson to include the liquid detection portion as taught by Nishihara for the purpose of improving detection accuracy in the liquid detection device [0011].
AIA
Claim 25 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gasvoda as modified Gilson and further in view of US Pub. No. 2013/0050357 Kanbe et al. “Kanbe.”
With regard to Claim 25, Gasvoda as modified by Gilson does not teach the liquid cartridge further comprising a plurality of the electrodes positioned at the upper surface.
However Kanbe teaches (fig. 2) a liquid cartridge further comprising a plurality of the electrodes (75, 76 and 77) positioned at the upper surface.
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify Gasvoda as modified by Gilson to include the plurality of electrodes as taught by Kanbe for the purpose of aligning the cartridge in the direction perpendicular to the insertion/removal direction [0082].
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 2, 4, 5 and 8-10 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
The following is a statement of reasons for the indication of allowable subject matter: The primary reason for the allowance of Claims 2 and 5 is the inclusion of the limitations wherein the upper face comprises a sub upper face positioned further in the downward direction than the operation surface, wherein when the liquid cartridge is in the first attitude, the operation surface and the sub upper face at least partly overlap in the downward direction, and a space is formed between the operation surface and the sub upper face in the downward direction. It is these features found in the claim(s) which have not been found, taught or suggested by the prior art of record, which makes these claims allowable over the prior art.
The primary reason for the allowance of Claim 4 is the inclusion of the limitations wherein the operation surface and the first direction forms an angle therebetween, and the angle is greater than or equal to 10 degrees and less than or equal to 45 degrees. It is these features found in the claim(s) which have not been found, taught or suggested by the prior art of record, which makes this claim allowable over the prior art.
The primary reason for the allowance of Claim 8 is the inclusion of the limitations further comprising a first reinforcing surface and a second reinforcing surface, wherein the lock surface has an end in a third direction which is perpendicular to the first direction, the second direction, the upward direction, and the downward direction, and the first reinforcing surface is continuous and extends from the third-direction side end of the lock surface, wherein the first reinforcing surface extends from a virtual plane toward the first direction, forming an acute angle between the first reinforcing surface and the virtual plane, which virtual plane includes the lock surface and extends in the downward direction, the upward direction, the third direction, and a fourth direction opposite the third direction, wherein the lock surface has an end in the fourth direction, and the second reinforcing surface is continuous and extends from the fourth-direction side end of the lock surface, wherein the second reinforcing surface extends from the virtual plane toward the first direction, forming an acute angle between the second reinforcing surface and the virtual plane. It is these features found in the claim(s) which have not been found, taught or suggested by the prior art of record, which makes this claim allowable over the prior art.
The primary reason for the allowance of Claims 9 and 10 is the inclusion of the limitations further comprising an inclined surface, a third reinforcing surface, and a fourth reinforcing surface, wherein the inclined surface is positioned at the upper face and positioned further in the first direction than the lock surface, and the inclined surface faces the upward direction and the first direction when the liquid cartridge is in the first attitude, wherein the inclined surface has an end in a third direction which is perpendicular to the first direction, the second direction, the upward direction, and the downward direction, and the third reinforcing surface is continuous and extends from the third-direction side end of the inclined surface, wherein the third reinforcing surface extends from a virtual plane toward the downward direction, forming an acute angle between the third reinforcing surface and the virtual plane, which virtual plane includes the inclined surface and extends in the third direction and a fourth direction opposite the third direction, wherein the lock surface has an end in the fourth direction, and the fourth reinforcing surface is continuous and extends from the fourth-direction side end of the inclined surface, wherein the fourth reinforcing surface extends from the virtual plane toward the downward direction, forming an acute angle between the fourth reinforcing surface and the virtual plane. It is these features found in the claim(s) which have not been found, taught or suggested by the prior art of record, which makes these claims allowable over the prior art.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).
A shortened statutory period for reply to this final action is set to expire THREE MONTHS from the mailing date of this action. In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action. In no event, however, will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the date of this final action.

The nonstatutory double patenting rejection is based on a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy (a policy reflected in the statute) so as to prevent the unjustified or improper timewise extension of the “right to exclude” granted by a patent and to prevent possible harassment by multiple assignees. A nonstatutory double patenting rejection is appropriate where the conflicting claims are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s). See, e.g., In re Berg, 140 F.3d 1428, 46 USPQ2d 1226 (Fed. Cir. 1998); In re Goodman, 11 F.3d 1046, 29 USPQ2d 2010 (Fed. Cir. 1993); In re Longi, 759 F.2d 887, 225 USPQ 645 (Fed. Cir. 1985); In re Van Ornum, 686 F.2d 937, 214 USPQ 761 (CCPA 1982); In re Vogel, 422 F.2d 438, 164 USPQ 619 (CCPA 1970); In re Thorington, 418 F.2d 528, 163 USPQ 644 (CCPA 1969).

AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Drawings
The drawings were received on 05/08/2015. These drawings are acceptable.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(b) the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country, more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States.
Claims 21-27, 35, 36, and 39-41 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by Giorgio (EP 2,000,294).
Giorgio discloses an apparatus for making boxes with reinforced corners comprising; an input for receiving a sheet of material with predetermined fold lines defining panels (Figs. 1 & 2; via 16); a loader for loading reinforcement elements (Fig. 9; via loader 10 for reinforcement material 5); a gripper movable between a first gripping position and second position (Fig. 9; via gripper 20) to attach the reinforcement elements to the sheet in a predetermined positioning pattern to include elements at each junction of two fold lines, such that when the sheet of material folds into the box, portions of the reinforcement elements are disposed immediately adjacent to one another to form a reinforced inside corner, see for example (Figs. 1 & 2; via reinforcement materials 5); three reinforcement elements at each junction of two fold lines disposed immediately adjacent to or in contact with one fold line (Figs. 1-3); a marker to place a plurality of locators on the sheet for indication locations of the positioning pattern (Figs. 1 & 2; via the corners of the folded lines could be consider as markers); gluer for depositing an adhesive on the sheet (column 4, lines 45-55; via “layer of glue”), mechanical elements insertion member for attaching the reinforcement elements to the sheet at positions identified by the locator (column 4, lines 45-55); cutter for cutting the reinforcement elements to sizes (Fig. 7; via 11 cuts into sizes 5); a marker for depositing a plurality of visual locators on the sheet according to the predetermined positioning pattern (via the corner of the fold lines on the blank); the gripper includes a support bridge and head movable being movable between the first and second positions, the gripper includes an arm to move the gripper (Fig. 9; via movable gripper 20 with arm 21).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 28-34 and 37 rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Giorgio (EP 2,000,294).
Giorgio does not disclose the use of marker on the sheet to be visual locators made by printing or incisions, reader to identify the markers, a use of optical viewing in the gripper and image unit for forming an image of part of the sheet, nor a use of control unit. The office takes an official notice that a use of printed markers on a sheet to identify positions of further operations to be done, along with use of sensors or optical viewing to image the sheets and feeding the information to a control unit, is old and well known in the art.
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to have modified Giorgio’s apparatus by the use of printed markers on the sheet and further use of imaging and control unit as needed, in order to get more accurate locations of positioning the enforcement material on the blank.
Note, the amended claims rebeatedly using a broad terms, such as “defining", “such that”, “so as”, "configured to”, “in order”, etc. along with an intended use term “for”, which render the followed claimed limitations to be broad and not positively cited limitations. Therefore, whatever claimed limitations followed by the mentioned broad terms are not given much patentable weight.
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 38 and 42 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
In regard to claim 38: the prior art of record fails to disclose the combination of the claimed language of claim 37 along with claim 38, in particular moving the gripper to position the reinforcement elements according to commands received from the command and control unit to position the reinforcement elements on predetermined positioning pattern, (Fig. 5; via controller unit 101, gripper 17, reinforcement elements 15).
In regard to claim 42: the prior art of record fails to disclose the combination of the claimed language of claims 39-42, in particular acquiring images of the sheet and transmit them to a command and control unit, according to the images acquired, coordinates the marking step automatically.
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments with respect to claims 21-42 have been considered but are moot because the arguments do not apply to any of the references being used in the current rejection.
Conclusion

DETAILED ACTION
This action is in response to amendments received 4/4/2016. Claims 1-14 and 16 are pending in the application, with claims 1 and 16 currently amended, and claim 15 now cancelled.
AIA
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statement (IDS) with mailroom date 4/4/2016 was filed in compliance with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97-1.98. Accordingly, the Examiner has considered the information disclosure statement.
Priority/Specification Objection
Applicant’s claim for the benefit of a prior-filed application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) is acknowledged. The priority claim is deficient because the specification recites U.S. application No. 11/398,733 (par. 1) but should recite 11/938,733. The Examiner notes that a corrected ADS has been filed on 4/12/2016, along with a petition to correct the priority claim. The petition has not yet been acted upon by the Office of Petitions and as such the Examiner will monitor the future decision on whether the petition is granted. However, the specification remains objected to because it has not been amended to correct the priority data. Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Interpretations
The claim limitation of a “right of first refusal” (claim 1) is afforded a specific, narrow interpretation that is similar to the contractual right of the same name. This interpretation is in keeping with the one found in parent U.S. Application No. 11/938733 (see e.g., Applicant’s remarks submitted 10/23/2013 and Notice of Allowance mailed 10/30/2013).
Double Patenting
The nonstatutory double patenting rejection is based on a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy (a policy reflected in the statute) so as to prevent the unjustified or improper timewise extension of the “right to exclude” granted by a patent and to prevent possible harassment by multiple assignees. A nonstatutory double patenting rejection is appropriate where the claims at issue are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s). See, e.g., In re Berg, 140 F.3d 1428, 46 USPQ2d 1226 (Fed. Cir. 1998); In re Goodman, 11 F.3d 1046, 29 USPQ2d 2010 (Fed. Cir. 1993); In re Longi, 759 F.2d 887, 225 USPQ 645 (Fed. Cir. 1985); In re Van Ornum, 686 F.2d 937, 214 USPQ 761 (CCPA 1982); In re Vogel, 422 F.2d 438, 164 USPQ 619 (CCPA 1970); and In re Thorington, 418 F.2d 528, 163 USPQ 644 (CCPA 1969).
A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or 1.321(d) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on a nonstatutory double patenting ground provided the reference application or patent either is shown to be commonly owned with this application, or claims an invention made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement. See MPEP § 717.02 for applications subject to examination under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA as explained in MPEP § 2159. See MPEP §§ 706.02(l)(1) - 706.02(l)(3) for applications not subject to examination under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA. A terminal disclaimer must be signed in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(b).
The USPTO Internet website contains terminal disclaimer forms which may be used. Please visit www.uspto.gov/forms/. The filing date of the application in which the form is filed determines what form (e.g., PTO/SB/25, PTO/SB/26, PTO/AIA/25, or PTO/AIA/26) should be used. A web-based eTerminal Disclaimer may be filled out completely online using web-screens. An eTerminal Disclaimer that meets all requirements is auto-processed and approved immediately upon submission. For more information about eTerminal Disclaimers, refer to http://www.uspto.gov/patents/process/file/efs/guidance/eTD-info-I.jsp.
AIA
Claims 1-14 and 16 are rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claims 1-11 of U.S. Patent No. 8,668,564. Although the claims at issue are not identical, they are not patentably distinct from each other because the instant claims are encompassed by those of the ‘564 patent claims.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 101
35 U.S.C. 101 reads as follows:
Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
Claims 1-14 and 16 are directed to non-statutory subject matter because the claim(s) as a whole, considering all claim elements both individually and in combination, do not amount to significantly more than an abstract idea.
A patent may be obtained for “any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.” 35 U.S.C. § 101. The Supreme Court has held that this provision contains an important implicit exception: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable. Alice Corp. Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank Int’l, 134 S. Ct. 2347, 2354 (2014); Gottschalk v. Benson, 409 U.S. 63, 67 (1972) (“Phenomena of nature, though just discovered, mental processes, and abstract intellectual concepts are not patentable, as they are the basic tools of scientific and technological work.”). Notwithstanding that a law of nature or an abstract idea, by itself, is not patentable, the application of these concepts may be deserving of patent protection. Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus Labs., Inc., 132 S. Ct. 1289, 1293–94 (2012). In Mayo, the Court stated that “to transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent eligible application of such a law, one must do more than simply state the law of nature while adding the words ‘apply it.’” Mayo, 132 S. Ct. at 1294 (citation omitted).
In Alice, the Supreme Court reaffirmed the framework set forth previously in Mayo “for distinguishing patents that claim laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas from those that claim patent-eligible applications of these concepts.” Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2355. The first step in the analysis is to “determine whether the claims at issue are directed to one of those patent-ineligible concepts.” Id. If the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept, then the second step in the analysis is to consider the elements of the claims “individually and ‘as an ordered combination”’ to determine whether there are additional elements that “‘transform the nature of the claim’ into a patent-eligible application.” Id. (quoting Mayo, 132 S. Ct. at 1298, 1297). In other words, the second step is to “search for an ‘inventive concept’‒ i.e., an element or combination of elements that is ‘sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.’” Id. (brackets in original) (quoting Mayo, 132 S. Ct. at 1294). The prohibition against patenting an abstract idea “cannot be circumvented by attempting to limit the use of the formula to a particular technological environment or adding insignificant post-solution activity.” Bilski v. Kappos, 561 U.S. 593, 610–11 (2010) (citation and internal quotation marks omitted). The Court in Alice noted that “‘[s]imply appending conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality,’ was not ‘enough’ [in Mayo] to supply an ‘inventive concept.’” Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357 (quoting Mayo, 132 S. Ct. at 1300, 1297, 1294).
As summarized in the 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility, examiners must perform a Two-Part Analysis for Judicial Exceptions. In Step 1, it must be determined whether the claims fall into one of the four statutory categories of invention. Claims 1-14 are directed to methods of playing a game (i.e., processes) and claim 16 is directed to an electronic device or entertainment gaming machine (i.e., an apparatus), both of which fall into statutory categories of invention.
In Step 2A, it must be determined whether the claimed invention is ‘directed to’ a judicially recognized exception. Claims 1-14 and 16 are directed to the abstract idea of playing a conventional casino table game with the granting of a right of first refusal to place a bet on a jackpot. Dependent claims 3-14 further define the types of games, such as roulette, Las Vegas baccarat, and various jackpot payout rules (e.g., Rules (I), (II), and (III) in claims 12, 13, and 14, respectively). The abstract idea may be viewed, for example as:
a method of exchanging financial obligations (e.g., a wagering game, which is effectively a method of exchanging and resolving financial obligations based on probabilities created during the game) as discussed in Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank and In re Smith (CAFC 2016),
a fundamental economic practice (e.g., rules for conducting a wagering game) as discussed in Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank and In re Smith,
a method of managing a game (e.g., a slot machine game) similar to that of managing a game of bingo in Planet Bingo, LLC v. VKGS LLC (CAFC 2014); and/or
a method of organizing human activities (e.g., accepting wagers from a human player and allowing the human player to play the game according to rules of the game method) as discussed in Bilski v. Kappos and Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank.
The claimed abstract idea reproduced above is effectively a method of exchanging and resolving financial obligations between a player and an operator of the gaming machine based on probabilities created during the game (see Smith and Alice). Based on the reasoning in Smith, the recited steps of conducting a wagering game in the instant claims relate to the “fundamental economic practice” of wagering. The abstract idea is also similar to that of Planet Bingo, in which a method of managing a bingo game was found to be an abstract idea. Though the instant claims are not limited to bingo games, they encompass the management of an analogous wagering game. Finally, the claimed steps require a player to make a wager, which is a financial transaction, in order to play a wagering game, which may result in an award being paid to the player, which is another financial transaction, based on the rules of the game (e.g., “an award in response to the outcome meeting a predetermined award criterion defined by symbol combinations in a paytable” in claim 22). Such financial transactions are akin to the sort of organizing of human activities, i.e., risk hedging, discussed in Bilski (and shadow accounts in Alice).
Therefore, the claims are directed to the judicially recognized exception of an abstract idea.
Step 2B requires that if the claim encompasses a judicially recognized exception, it must be determined whether the claimed invention recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Claims 1-14 and 16 encompass the following additional element(s) or combination of elements in the claim(s) other than the abstract idea per se: cards or dice (claim 1), a betting terminal (claims 1-14 and 16), a non-transitory computer readable medium (claims 1-14 and 16), and an electronic device or entertainment gaming machine (claim 16). Viewed as a whole, these additional claim element(s) do not provide meaningful limitation(s) to transform the abstract idea into a patent eligible application of the abstract idea such that the claim(s) amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea itself. These features do not meaningfully limit the abstract idea because they constitute generic, conventional, and well-known computer components.
The Supreme Court found that claim recitations of a “data processing system” with a “communications controller” and “data storage unit” are purely functional and generic (Alice at 16). The Court further stated, “Put another way, the system claims are no different from the method claims in substance...The method claims recite the abstract idea implemented on a generic computer; the system claims recite a handful of generic computer components configured to implement the same idea” (Alice at 16). The Court concluded that “[b]ecause petitioner's system and media claims add nothing of substance to the underlying abstract idea, we hold that they too are patent ineligible under §101” (Alice at 17). The same conclusion is reached with respect to the claims of the instant invention. Therefore, the claim(s) are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as being directed to non-statutory subject matter. See Alice Corporation Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank International, et al., 573 U.S. __ (2014).
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 4/4/2016 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Applicant addresses the rejection of claims under §101 on pages 10-11 of the Remarks section. Applicant refers to Example 21 of the July 2015 Update on Subject Matter Eligibility, which includes two example claims directed to stock quote transmission, one that is found to be ineligible and one that is found to be eligible. Applicant states on page 11 of the Remarks that the present invention “solves the problem of limited numbers of conventional casino table games and allowing for additional jackpot bets by second players at a betting terminal that is apart from the table game after granting a right of refusal.” Applicant also states on page 11 that casinos benefit by filling their game tables and players benefit by being incentivized to sit at a game table.
While the instant invention may provide some benefit to casinos or players of table games, this is not the sort of technological improvement sought by the courts or the USPTO guidance to demonstrate patent eligibility. Looking to the stock quote example, the USPTO guidance states that the claimed invention “addresses the Internet-centric challenge of alerting a subscriber with time sensitive information when the subscriber’s computer is offline… by transmitting the alert over a wireless communication channel to activate the stock viewer application, which causes the alert to display and enables the connection of the remote subscriber computer to the data source over the Internet when the remote subscriber computer comes online” (cited in Remarks, p. 10-11). The stock quote example therefore solves a technological problem of delivering time-sensitive data to a user who is not currently online. The instant invention, by contrast, merely provides for table games to be played by various players using terminals according to predefined rules. The claimed invention does not address any need to alert offline players of time-sensitive stock quote information. The claimed invention also does not mention the use of the Internet or solve any Internet-centric challenge. As such, the claimed invention does not comport with the fact pattern of the proffered USPTO example.
Moreover, the use of the Internet alone is not sufficient to save an otherwise patent-ineligible claim to a judicial exception. For instance, the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (CAFC) found in Cybersource Corp. v. Retail Decisions, Inc. that “a method for verifying the validity of a credit card transaction over the Internet” was directed to an abstract idea or unpatentable mental process. Furthermore, the solving of an Internet-centric challenge as defined in DDR Holdings was clarified by the CAFC in Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One Financial. The Court stated that “[t]he patent at issue in DDR provided an Internet-based solution to solve a problem unique to the Internet that (1) did not foreclose other ways of solving the problem, and (2) recited a specific series of steps that resulted in a departure from the routine and conventional sequence of events after the click of a hyperlink advertisement” but the “patent claims here do not address problems unique to the Internet, so DDR has no applicability” (p. 15). The stock quote example found that the eligible claim addresses features unique to the Internet. However, because the instant claims do not address problems unique to the Internet, the CAFC instructs that DDR is not applicable here. As such, the findings of the stock quote example are similarly not applicable here.
Finally, the CAFC recently found in In re Smith that steps of conducting a wagering game relate to the “fundamental economic practice” of wagering, as well as a method of exchanging financial obligations. The fact pattern in Smith is similar to the one here, in that both claimed inventions relate to rules for playing a wagering game coupled with routine and conventional steps. The CAFC ultimately found that such steps were ineligible for patenting.
In light of the above analysis, the claimed invention fails to demonstrate patent-eligibility.
Conclusion

a fundamental economic practice (e.g., rules for conducting a wagering game) as discussed in Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank and In re Smith,
a method of managing a game (e.g., a slot machine game) similar to that of managing a game of bingo in Planet Bingo, LLC v. VKGS LLC (CAFC 2014); and/or
a method of organizing human activities (e.g., accepting wagers from a human player and allowing the human player to play the game according to rules of the game method) as discussed in Bilski v. Kappos and Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank.
The claimed abstract idea reproduced above is effectively a method of exchanging and resolving financial obligations between a player and an operator of the gaming machine based on probabilities created during the game (see Smith and Alice). Based on the reasoning in Smith, the recited steps of conducting a wagering game in the instant claims relate to the “fundamental economic practice” of wagering. The abstract idea is also similar to that of Planet Bingo, in which a method of managing a bingo game was found to be an abstract idea. Though the instant claims are not limited to bingo games, they encompass the management of an analogous wagering game. Finally, the claimed steps require a player to make a wager, which is a financial transaction, in order to play a wagering game, which may result in an award being paid to the player, which is another financial transaction, based on the rules of the game (e.g., “an award in response to the outcome meeting a predetermined award criterion defined by symbol combinations in a paytable” in claim 22). Such financial transactions are akin to the sort of organizing of human activities, i.e., risk hedging, discussed in Bilski (and shadow accounts in Alice).
Therefore, the claims are directed to the judicially recognized exception of an abstract idea.
Step 2B requires that if the claim encompasses a judicially recognized exception, it must be determined whether the claimed invention recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Claims 1-14 and 16 encompass the following additional element(s) or combination of elements in the claim(s) other than the abstract idea per se: cards or dice (claim 1), a betting terminal (claims 1-14 and 16), a non-transitory computer readable medium (claims 1-14 and 16), and an electronic device or entertainment gaming machine (claim 16). Viewed as a whole, these additional claim element(s) do not provide meaningful limitation(s) to transform the abstract idea into a patent eligible application of the abstract idea such that the claim(s) amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea itself. These features do not meaningfully limit the abstract idea because they constitute generic, conventional, and well-known computer components.
The Supreme Court found that claim recitations of a “data processing system” with a “communications controller” and “data storage unit” are purely functional and generic (Alice at 16). The Court further stated, “Put another way, the system claims are no different from the method claims in substance...The method claims recite the abstract idea implemented on a generic computer; the system claims recite a handful of generic computer components configured to implement the same idea” (Alice at 16). The Court concluded that “[b]ecause petitioner's system and media claims add nothing of substance to the underlying abstract idea, we hold that they too are patent ineligible under §101” (Alice at 17). The same conclusion is reached with respect to the claims of the instant invention. Therefore, the claim(s) are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as being directed to non-statutory subject matter. See Alice Corporation Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank International, et al., 573 U.S. __ (2014).
Applicant's arguments filed 4/4/2016 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Applicant addresses the rejection of claims under §101 on pages 10-11 of the Remarks section. Applicant refers to Example 21 of the July 2015 Update on Subject Matter Eligibility, which includes two example claims directed to stock quote transmission, one that is found to be ineligible and one that is found to be eligible. Applicant states on page 11 of the Remarks that the present invention “solves the problem of limited numbers of conventional casino table games and allowing for additional jackpot bets by second players at a betting terminal that is apart from the table game after granting a right of refusal.” Applicant also states on page 11 that casinos benefit by filling their game tables and players benefit by being incentivized to sit at a game table.
While the instant invention may provide some benefit to casinos or players of table games, this is not the sort of technological improvement sought by the courts or the USPTO guidance to demonstrate patent eligibility. Looking to the stock quote example, the USPTO guidance states that the claimed invention “addresses the Internet-centric challenge of alerting a subscriber with time sensitive information when the subscriber’s computer is offline… by transmitting the alert over a wireless communication channel to activate the stock viewer application, which causes the alert to display and enables the connection of the remote subscriber computer to the data source over the Internet when the remote subscriber computer comes online” (cited in Remarks, p. 10-11). The stock quote example therefore solves a technological problem of delivering time-sensitive data to a user who is not currently online. The instant invention, by contrast, merely provides for table games to be played by various players using terminals according to predefined rules. The claimed invention does not address any need to alert offline players of time-sensitive stock quote information. The claimed invention also does not mention the use of the Internet or solve any Internet-centric challenge. As such, the claimed invention does not comport with the fact pattern of the proffered USPTO example.
Moreover, the use of the Internet alone is not sufficient to save an otherwise patent-ineligible claim to a judicial exception. For instance, the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (CAFC) found in Cybersource Corp. v. Retail Decisions, Inc. that “a method for verifying the validity of a credit card transaction over the Internet” was directed to an abstract idea or unpatentable mental process. Furthermore, the solving of an Internet-centric challenge as defined in DDR Holdings was clarified by the CAFC in Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One Financial. The Court stated that “[t]he patent at issue in DDR provided an Internet-based solution to solve a problem unique to the Internet that (1) did not foreclose other ways of solving the problem, and (2) recited a specific series of steps that resulted in a departure from the routine and conventional sequence of events after the click of a hyperlink advertisement” but the “patent claims here do not address problems unique to the Internet, so DDR has no applicability” (p. 15). The stock quote example found that the eligible claim addresses features unique to the Internet. However, because the instant claims do not address problems unique to the Internet, the CAFC instructs that DDR is not applicable here. As such, the findings of the stock quote example are similarly not applicable here.
Finally, the CAFC recently found in In re Smith that steps of conducting a wagering game relate to the “fundamental economic practice” of wagering, as well as a method of exchanging financial obligations. The fact pattern in Smith is similar to the one here, in that both claimed inventions relate to rules for playing a wagering game coupled with routine and conventional steps. The CAFC ultimately found that such steps were ineligible for patenting.
In light of the above analysis, the claimed invention fails to demonstrate patent-eligibility.

A patent may be obtained for “any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.” 35 U.S.C. § 101. The Supreme Court has held that this provision contains an important implicit exception: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable. Alice Corp. Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank Int’l, 134 S. Ct. 2347, 2354 (2014); Gottschalk v. Benson, 409 U.S. 63, 67 (1972) (“Phenomena of nature, though just discovered, mental processes, and abstract intellectual concepts are not patentable, as they are the basic tools of scientific and technological work.”). Notwithstanding that a law of nature or an abstract idea, by itself, is not patentable, the application of these concepts may be deserving of patent protection. Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus Labs., Inc., 132 S. Ct. 1289, 1293–94 (2012). In Mayo, the Court stated that “to transform an unpatentable law of nature into a patent eligible application of such a law, one must do more than simply state the law of nature while adding the words ‘apply it.’” Mayo, 132 S. Ct. at 1294 (citation omitted).
In Alice, the Supreme Court reaffirmed the framework set forth previously in Mayo “for distinguishing patents that claim laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas from those that claim patent-eligible applications of these concepts.” Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2355. The first step in the analysis is to “determine whether the claims at issue are directed to one of those patent-ineligible concepts.” Id. If the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept, then the second step in the analysis is to consider the elements of the claims “individually and ‘as an ordered combination”’ to determine whether there are additional elements that “‘transform the nature of the claim’ into a patent-eligible application.” Id. (quoting Mayo, 132 S. Ct. at 1298, 1297). In other words, the second step is to “search for an ‘inventive concept’‒ i.e., an element or combination of elements that is ‘sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself.’” Id. (brackets in original) (quoting Mayo, 132 S. Ct. at 1294). The prohibition against patenting an abstract idea “cannot be circumvented by attempting to limit the use of the formula to a particular technological environment or adding insignificant post-solution activity.” Bilski v. Kappos, 561 U.S. 593, 610–11 (2010) (citation and internal quotation marks omitted). The Court in Alice noted that “‘[s]imply appending conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality,’ was not ‘enough’ [in Mayo] to supply an ‘inventive concept.’” Alice, 134 S. Ct. at 2357 (quoting Mayo, 132 S. Ct. at 1300, 1297, 1294).
As summarized in the 2014 Interim Guidance on Patent Subject Matter Eligibility, examiners must perform a Two-Part Analysis for Judicial Exceptions. In Step 1, it must be determined whether the claims fall into one of the four statutory categories of invention. Claim 15 does not fall into a statutory category because it recites software per se, as discussed above. Claims 1-14 are directed to methods of playing a game (i.e., processes) and claim 16 is directed to an electronic device or entertainment gaming machine (i.e., an apparatus), both of which fall into statutory categories of invention.
In Step 2A, it must be determined whether the claimed invention is ‘directed to’ a judicially recognized exception. Claims 1-16 are directed to the abstract idea of playing a conventional casino table game with the granting of a right of first refusal to place a bet on a jackpot. Dependent claims 3-14 further define the types of games, such as roulette, Las Vegas baccarat, and various jackpot payout rules. The abstract idea may be viewed, for instance, as a method of exchanging financial obligations, a method of organizing human activities, a method of managing a game, and/or a method of creating a contractual relationship. Therefore, the claims are directed to the judicially recognized exception of an abstract idea.
Step 2B requires that if the claim encompasses a judicially recognized exception, it must be determined whether the claimed invention recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Claims 1-16 encompass the following additional element(s) or combination of elements in the claim(s) other than the abstract idea per se: cards or dice (claim 1), a betting terminal (claims 1-16), one or more software programs (claim 15), and an electronic device or entertainment gaming machine (claim 16). Viewed as a whole, these additional claim element(s) do not provide meaningful limitation(s) to transform the abstract idea into a patent eligible application of the abstract idea such that the claim(s) amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea itself. These features do not meaningfully limit the abstract idea because they constitute generic, conventional, and well-known computer components.
The Supreme Court found that claim recitations of a “data processing system” with a “communications controller” and “data storage unit” are purely functional and generic (Alice at 16). The Court further stated, “Put another way, the system claims are no different from the method claims in substance...The method claims recite the abstract idea implemented on a generic computer; the system claims recite a handful of generic computer components configured to implement the same idea” (Alice at 16). The Court concluded that “[b]ecause petitioner's system and media claims add nothing of substance to the underlying abstract idea, we hold that they too are patent ineligible under §101” (Alice at 17). The same conclusion is reached with respect to the claims of the instant invention. Therefore, the claim(s) are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as being directed to non-statutory subject matter. DETAILED ACTION
Note: The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions. This action is responsive to the amendments received after a Non-Final Rejection on 19 September 2016. Claims 21-40 are currently pending.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 25, 31-32 and 38 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the applicant regards as the invention.
Regarding claim 25, There exits an inconsistency between the language of claim 21 and that of claim 25 dependent thereon, thus making the scope of the claim unclear. In lines 2-3 of claim 21, the applicant recites “an implantable first base part” with an implantable second base part being only functionally recited (i.e. “configured to be separable from an implantable second base part”, thus indicating that the claim is directed to the subcombination, “an implantable first base part.” However, in lines 1-2 of claim 25, the applicant positively recites the second base part as part of the invention (i.e. a pin located in the aperture in the first and second base parts”), thus indicating that the combination (i.e. first base part and second base part), is being claimed. As such, it is unclear whether the applicant intends to claim the subcombination or combination. The applicant is hereby required to indicate to which, combination or subcombination, the claims are intended to be directed, and amend the claim such that the language thereof is consistent with this intent. For examination purposes claims 21-28 will be considered as being drawn to the combination (i.e. first base part and second base part).
Note: For example, amending lines 2-3 of claim 21 to read “first and second base parts configured to be separable and defining a channel therebetween” would be acceptable as language directing the claims to the combination.
Regarding claims 31 and 32, There exits an inconsistency between the language of claim 29 and that of claim 31 dependent thereon, thus making the scope of the claim unclear. In lines 2-3 of claim 29, the applicant recites “an implantable first base part” with an implantable second base part being only functionally recited (i.e. “configured to be separable from an implantable second base part”, thus indicating that the claim is directed to the subcombination, “an implantable first base part.” However, in lines 2-3 of claim 31, the applicant positively recites the second base part as part of the invention (i.e. at least a portion of the aperture in the channel being formed in each of the first and second base parts, the stopping member extending into the aperture in the channel”), thus indicating that the combination (i.e. first base part and second base part), is being claimed. As such, it is unclear whether the applicant intends to claim the subcombination or combination. The applicant is hereby required to indicate to which, combination or subcombination, the claims are intended to be directed, and amend the claim such that the language thereof is consistent with this intent. For examination purposes claims 29-34 will be considered as being drawn to the combination (i.e. first base part and second base part).
Note: For example, amending lines 2-3 of claim 29 to read “first and second base parts configured to be separable, the first and second base parts positioned together and defining a channel…” would be acceptable as language directing the claims to the combination.
Claim 38 recites the limitation "the retainer assembly" in line 1. There is insufficient antecedent basis for this limitation in the claim.
Note: It appears that amending line 2 of claim 35 to read “an implantable stabilizer member having a base and a retainer assembly including a first retainer member…" would overcome this rejection.
Double Patenting
AIA
The nonstatutory double patenting rejection is based on a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy (a policy reflected in the statute) so as to prevent the unjustified or improper timewise extension of the “right to exclude” granted by a patent and to prevent possible harassment by multiple assignees. A nonstatutory double patenting rejection is appropriate where the conflicting claims are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s). See, e.g., In re Berg, 140 F.3d 1428, 46 USPQ2d 1226 (Fed. Cir. 1998); In re Goodman, 11 F.3d 1046, 29 USPQ2d 2010 (Fed. Cir. 1993); In re Longi, 759 F.2d 887, 225 USPQ 645 (Fed. Cir. 1985); In re Van Ornum, 686 F.2d 937, 214 USPQ 761 (CCPA 1982); In re Vogel, 422 F.2d 438, 164 USPQ 619 (CCPA 1970); In re Thorington, 418 F.2d 528, 163 USPQ 644 (CCPA 1969).
A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) or 1.321(d) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on nonstatutory double patenting provided the reference application or patent either is shown to be commonly owned with the examined application, or claims an invention made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement. See MPEP § 717.02 for applications subject to examination under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA as explained in MPEP § 2159. See MPEP §§ 706.02(l)(1) - 706.02(l)(3) for applications not subject to examination under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA. A terminal disclaimer must be signed in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(b).
The USPTO Internet website contains terminal disclaimer forms which may be used. Please visit www.uspto.gov/patent/patents-forms. The filing date of the application in which the form is filed determines what form (e.g., PTO/SB/25, PTO/SB/26, PTO/AIA/25, or PTO/AIA/26) should be used. A web-based eTerminal Disclaimer may be filled out completely online using web-screens. An eTerminal Disclaimer that meets all requirements is auto-processed and approved immediately upon submission. For more information about eTerminal Disclaimers, refer to www.uspto.gov/patents/process/file/efs/guidance/eTD-info-I.jsp.
Claim 29 is rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claim 5 of U.S. Patent 9,138,272. Although the claims at issue are not identical, they are not patentably distinct from each other because the application claim is merely broader than the patent claim.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(b) the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country, more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States.
Claim 35 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by Nuss et al. (U.S. Patent 6,024,759).
Nuss et al. disclose a pectus bar stabilizer assembly (i.e. assembly defined by 10 and 80) comprising an implantable stabilizer member (80) having a base (56) and a first retaining member (62), the base including a channel (82) and capable of being attached to (i.e. via 64 and 66) a patient’s tissue, the first retaining member capable of traversing (i.e. moving along, see Note below regarding the term “traverse”) the channel; an implantable pectus bar (10) capable of being received by the channel between the base and the first retaining member (reception as best seen in Figure 12); and an implantable stopping member (90) capable of being fixed to the pectus bar after the pectus bar is inserted into the channel to restrict movement of the pectus bar relative to the tissue, wherein the pectus bar is capable of being removed from (i.e. via the removal of 90) the channel while the base is attached to the patient’s tissue (see Figures 9-12 and column 6, line 64 – column 8, line 6).
Note: For examination purposes and in keeping with the broadest reasonable interpretation, the term “traverse” is being treated as to pass or move over, along, or through; cross (definition taken from http://www.thefreedictionary.com/traverse).
With regard to the statements of intended use and other functional statements, such as “configured to,” they do not impose any structural limitations on the claims distinguishable over the invention of Nuss et al. which is capable of being used as claimed if one so desires to do so. In re Casey, 152 USPQ 235 (CCPA 1967) and In re Otto, 136 USPQ 458, 459 (CCPA 1963). Furthermore, the law of anticipation does not require that the reference “teach” what the subject patent teaches, but rather it is only necessary that the claims under attack “read on” something in the reference. Kalman v. Kimberly Clark Corp., 218 USPQ 781 (CCPA 1983). Furthermore, the manner in which a device is intended to be employed does not differentiate the claimed apparatus from the prior art apparatus satisfying the claimed structural limitations. Ex parte Masham, 2 USPQ2d 1647 (1987).
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 21-24 and 26-28 are allowed.
Claims 21-28 in the instant application have not been rejected using prior art because no references, or reasonable combination thereof, could be found which disclose, or suggest, in combination with the underlined limitations below, a pectus bar stabilizer assembly comprising an implantable first base part configured to be separable from an implantable second base part and defining a channel therebetween; an implantable pectus bar capable of being received by the channel; and an implantable retainer assembly including a stopping member and a first rib, the stopping member capable of being fixed to the pectus bar and the first rib capable of extending across the channel and preventing displacement of the stopping member past the first rib to retain the pectus bar in the channel, wherein the pectus bar is capable of being removed from the channel with the stopping member fixed to the pectus bar while the first and second base parts are within a patient's anatomy.
Claim 25, 31-32 and 38 would be allowable if rewritten to overcome the rejection(s) under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), 2nd paragraph, set forth in this Office action and to include all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Claims 30, 33-34, 36-37 and 39-40 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure.

Claim Objections

Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
AIA
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112:
The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.
Claims 1-15 18-20 and 22-23 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement. The claim(s) contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the relevant art that the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the inventor(s), at the time the application was filed, had possession of the claimed invention.
On the bottom of page 9 of the remarks filed February 2, 2016, Applicant incorrectly expands the written description coverage to include the combination of distinct species. Specifically, applicant has added “at least one” to independent claim 1 and similarly to new independent claim 22 seemingly for limiting the number of claims. However, there is no original disclosure of the combination of the two species into one embodiment. Applicant has not cited any support for the combination of species. Applicant failed to claim the distinct species as alternatives. All of the dependent claims must also have support for the claimed embodiment where the distinct species are both claimed. Applicant has fails to cite any support for the combination of the distinct species of the independent claim 1 and also for each of the dependent claims dependent therefrom.
In other words, Applicant's claims 1 and 22 are not written as generic claims reading on either of the distinct species. Applicant’s remarks on the bottom of page 9 evidence such a conclusion. Therefore, Applicant should cite specific support from the original disclosure for each claim which embodies the combination of species. Otherwise, the claims fail to meet the written description requirement of 35 USC §112, first paragraph.
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f):
(f) Element in Claim for a Combination. – An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph:
An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
Claim 16 limitation “charging device part” and “another charging device part” has/have been interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, because it uses/they use a generic placeholder “part” coupled with functional language “charging” without reciting sufficient structure to achieve the function. Furthermore, the generic placeholder is not preceded by a structural modifier.
Since the claim limitation(s) invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, claim(s) 16 has/have been interpreted to cover the corresponding structure described in the specification that achieves the claimed function, and equivalents thereof.
A review of the specification shows that the following appears to be the corresponding structure described in the specification for the 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph limitation: actuator and turbine housing, respectively.
If applicant wishes to provide further explanation or dispute the examiner’s interpretation of the corresponding structure, applicant must identify the corresponding structure with reference to the specification by page and line number, and to the drawing, if any, by reference characters in response to this Office action.
If applicant does not intend to have the claim limitation(s) treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 , sixth paragraph, applicant may amend the claim(s) so that it/they will clearly not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, or present a sufficient showing that the claim recites/recite sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function to preclude application of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
For more information, see MPEP § 2173 et seq. and Supplementary Examination Guidelines for Determining Compliance With 35 U.S.C. 112 and for Treatment of Related Issues in Patent Applications, 76 FR 7162, 7167 (Feb. 9, 2011).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(b) the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country, more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States.
Claims 1-3, 6, 10-12, 16 and 19 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by United States Patent No. 4,708,552 (Bustos et al. hereinafter).
For claim 1, Bustos et al. teach a limit stop device for limiting an adjustment path of a mobile component (picture for example) relative to a stationary component, comprising: a sleeve body 18 configured to be inserted into an opening formed in the stationary component 24, the sleeve body including a retaining segment 46, 48 disposed in the interior of the opening, a core body 34 disposed in the interior of the sleeve body 18 for radially bracing the retaining segment against an inner wall of the stationary component thereby axially fixing the sleeve body on the stationary component, a stop surface 14 protruding into the adjustment path of the mobile component configured to limit the adjustment path of the mobile component.
For claim 2, the core body 34 is axially fixed in the sleeve body 18 by way of radially bracing the core body 34 against the sleeve body 18 (see tabs 52, 54).
For claim 3, the stop surface 14 is formed on the sleeve body 18, 16 or disposed on the sleeve body 16, 18.
For claim 6, the sleeve 18 has protrusions 50 on the radially outer surface, extending radially outward around the circumference of the sleeve 18.
For claim 10, the sleeve body 18 includes a radially projecting collar section 40 axially braced against an enclosure 16 trimming the opening and wherein, the core body 34 in the insertion direction of the sleeve body is axially pressed into the sleeve body 18 for radially bracing the retaining segment 46, 48.
For claim 11, the sleeve 18 has a stop section 16 protruding from the opening and comprising the stop surface 14, and wherein the stop surface 14 is formed at least from any surface of the section 16 and surface 14 which prevents anything from moving.
As to claim 12, the stop surface 14 is formed on a limit stop body 16 disposed on a stop section 40 of the sleeve body 18 protruding from the opening.
For claim 19, the core body 34 head could function as a stop surface of a hanger wire for example, and thus meets the functional limitations of claim 19.
Claims 16 and 17 differ only from respective claims 1 and 2 in that the preamble of claims 16 and 17 recite a charging device. The preamble is not structurally limiting however, since it is not necessarily to give any meaning to the body of the claim.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed February 2, 2016 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive. The presentation of claims 1 and 22 covering an embodiment of the combination of distinct species is not support by the original disclosure. Applicant failed to claim the distinct species as alternatives.
Claim 16 hasn’t incorporated any inherent structure. What is implied by a charging device part? Nothing. See 35 USC §112, sixth paragraph rejection of claim 16 above.
Allowable Subject Matter
Claim 21 is objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).
