DETAILED ACTION
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a), the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered therein were made absent any evidence to the contrary. Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and invention dates of each claim that was not commonly owned at the time a later invention was made in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
Claims 17, and 19-23 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Mayer, Jr. (herein “Mayer”; US Pub. No. 2008/0009371 A1).
Regarding claim 17, Mayer discloses a golf ball comprising, an inner core layer (Fig. 1, item 12); an outer core layer enclosing the inner core layer (Fig. item 14); an inner cover layer enclosing the outer core layer (Fig. 1, item 17), the inner cover layer having a first flexural modulus (par. [0056]); an outer cover layer enclosing the inner cover layer (Fig. 1, item 18), the outer cover layer having a second flexural modulus (par. [0057]; noting a flexural modulus would be inherent). It is noted that Mayer does not specifically disclose wherein the first flexural modulus is at least about 45,000 psi greater than the second flexural modulus. However, Mayer discloses using a hard inner cover layer and a soft outer cover layer (par. [0055]), an inner cover layer having a flexural modulus between 70,000 to 120,000 psi (par. [0056]), and an outer cover layer having a flexural modulus between 1,000 to 30,000 (par. [0038]; noting the inner cover can be 80,000 psi and the outer cover can be 10,000 psi, so 70,000 – 10,000 = 60,000 psi which satisfies the limitation). Thus, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to modify Mayer to make the first flexural modulus is at least about 45,000 psi greater than the second flexural modulus as taught and suggested by both Mayer because doing so would using known technique (using an outer cover having a soft feel and low flexural modulus) to improve a similar product (a golf ball having a hard and high modulus inner cover surrounded by a soft cover) in the same way (the continued ability to use a soft and durable cover layer and a hard inner cover layer to provide high COR at high club head speeds, and good feel at lower club head speeds - see Mayer: pars. [0058] and [0055]).
Regarding claim 19, Mayer discloses that the first flexural modulus is between about 60,000 psi and about 95,000 psi greater than the second flexural modulus (pars. [0038] and [0056]; noting the inner cover can be 80,000 psi and the outer cover can be 10,000 psi, so 70,000 – 10,000 = 60,000 psi which satisfies the limitation).
Regarding claim 20, Mayer discloses that the inner core layer includes a third flexural modulus and the third flexural modulus is between about 15,000 psi to 65,000 psi greater than the second flexural modulus (pars. [0049] and [0038]; noting the outer cover can be 10,000 psi and the inner core can be 75,000 psi, so that 75,000 - 10,000 = 65,000 psi which satisfies the limitation).
Regarding claim 21, Mayer discloses that the first flexural modulus is about 50,000 psi to about 100,000 psi (par. [0056]; noting 70,000 to 120,000 psi anticipates the claimed range).
Regarding claim 22, Mayer discloses that the second flexural modulus is about 200 psi to about 3,000 psi (par. [0038]; noting it can be as low as 1,000 psi).
Regarding claim 23, Mayer discloses that the first flexural modulus is about 77,000 psi (par. [0056]; noting 70,000 to 120,000 psi anticipates the claimed value) and the second flexural modulus is about 1,000 psi (par. [0038]). It is noted that Mayer does not specifically disclose that the second flexural modulus is about 550 psi (noting the fact that applicant uses the word “about” means that the 550 psi can actually be closer in value to the 1,000 psi). However, regarding using 550 psi over that of 1,000 psi, it has been held that applicant must show that the particular range is critical, generally by showing that the claimed range achieves unexpected results relative to the prior art range. In re Woodruff, 919 F.2d 1575, 16 USPQ2d 1934 (Fed. Cir.1990) (see MPEP 2144.05 (I) where Titanium Metals Corp. of America v. Banner states “a prima case of obviousness exists where the claimed ranges and the prior art ranges do not overlap but are close enough that one in the art would have expected them to have the same properties") (see applicant’s spec, page 22; applicant giving no criticality to lesser value of 550 psi). Thus, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to modify Mayer to use a lower flexural modulus value of 550 psi because the lower value would not achieve unexpected results: that is, the cover would still be soft and durable regardless of its exact flexural modulus value.
Claims 17, 19-23 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Sullivan et al. (herein “Sullivan”; US Pub. No. 2004/0214661 A1; as cited in applicant’s IDS).
As cited in applicant’s IDS and by way of applicant's PCT International search report, Sullivan also makes obvious claims 17, 19 and 20. Regarding claim 17, Sullivan discloses the four piece ball (Fig. 1), the ability to make the inner cover layer a high modulus material of 70,000 to 120,000 psi (par. [0062]) and the outer cover layer a low modulus material of less than 30,000 psi (par. [0009]). As such, it would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to select values consistent with the Mayer rejection above to arrive at the claimed difference (noting the disclosed Sullivan ranges are similar to the disclosed Mayer ranges). The same is true for claim 19. As for claim 20, Sullivan discloses flexural modulus for the inner core (par. [0055]). Again, it would have been obvious for one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to select values consistent with the Mayer rejection above to arrive at the claimed difference (noting the disclosed Sullivan ranges are similar to the disclosed Mayer ranges).
Regarding claim 21, Sullivan discloses that the first flexural modulus is about 50,000 psi to about 100,000 psi (par. [0062]; noting 65,000 to 120,000 psi anticipates the claimed range).
Regarding claim 22, Sullivan discloses that the second flexural modulus is about 200 psi to about 3,000 psi (par. [0009]; noting 30,000 psi or less anticipates the claimed range).
Regarding claim 23, Sullivan discloses that the first flexural modulus is about 77,000 psi (par. [0062]; noting 65,000 to 120,000 psi anticipates the claimed range) and the second flexural modulus is about 550 psi (par. [0009]; noting 30,000 psi or less anticipates the claimed range).
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 12/17/14 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Applicant essentially argues that the Examiner has no rationale for his obviousness statement. The Examiner respectfully believes applicant is incorrect.
Par. [0055] specifically envisions using a hard inner cover and a soft outer cover. This particular harder inner cover and softer outer cover produces a ball with “low spin and long distance benefits of a hard cover ball when struck with a driver club and high spin and soft feel characteristics of a traditional soft cover all when struck with short irons” (see also pars. DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1-6, 8-11 and 13-20 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Whitman et al. 20090101693 in view of Green et al. 5,449,365.
Whitman et al. discloses in at least Figs. 6a-6d and 17a-17c a shaft assembly for interconnecting an end effector 811a and an electromechanical power source 8103 comprising an outer tube 523; a rotatable drive shaft 527, a proximal neck housing 503, a distal neck housing 543 pivotally connected to the proximal neck housing; a pivot pin 551, and a gear train including a proximal gear 505a coupled to the drive shaft, an intermediate gear 549a supported on the pivot pin, a distal gear 5413 and a pair of output gears 5412/539, the gears all in operative engagement and wherein the output gears define a socked to receive drive axle 537 and a release assembly (Fig. 2b, 713a/b are quick connects with 1664 of Fig. 10) disposed at a distal end of the shaft assembly configured for selective engagement with the end effector. Whitman et al. further discloses a rotation of the drive shaft rotates both output gears (Fig. 6C). Whitman et al. further discloses the shaft assembly having straight and angled configurations between about 0 and about 90 degrees (Fig. 17A). Whitman et al. further discloses the gear train transmits rotation from the drive shaft to both output gears when the shaft is in either configuration (Fig. 6C). Whitman et al. further discloses the axis of rotation of the proximal and distal gears are coaxial with the drive shaft and the output gears are parallel with that of the distal gear (Fig. 6C). Whitman et al. further discloses the axis of rotation of the distal gear is orthogonal to the axis of the pivot pin (Fig. 6C). Whitman et al. further discloses the end effector including an upper jaw 850 and a lower jaw 880 movable with respect to one another between open and closed positions and wherein the end effector is connectable to the distal neck housing of the shaft assembly (Fig. 17A) and is movable between the straight and angles configurations. Whitman et al. further discloses a pair of holes 553 offset by 90 degrees from a second pair of holes 552 for attaching the end effector and able to receive attachment pins (Fig. 4C).
However, Whitman et al. does not disclose the release assembly being actuatable from a proximal end of the shaft assembly.
Green et al. discloses a clamp assembly having a detachable end effector 30 and a release assembly 40 on the distal and of the shaft 24 actuatable by trigger 50 on the proximal end of the shaft assembly. Green et al. further discloses the release assembly comprising a pair of diametrically opposed connection pins 182/184 which have an inward (actuated in that it must be compressed to be in this state) and outward projection condition (non-actuated in that the arms expand in their relaxed state). Green et al. further discloses a release cable 92 attached to release button 50.
It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to modify the device of Whitman et al. with the release assembly of Green et al. in order to facilitate the surgeon holding the device handle in one hand and releasing the end effector with the same hand, thus enabling the surgeon to replace the end effector with the free hand.
Claim 12 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Whitman et al. in view of Green et al. as applied to claim 1 above and further in view of Racenet et al. 20080105730.
Whitman et al. in view of Green et al. discloses the invention essentially as claimed as discussed above. Whitman et al. further discloses an articulation rod 525 connected to a rotatable drive shaft and offset from the central axis of the device, wherein actuation of the rotatable drive shaft causes the rod to translate (Fig. 6B).
However, Whitman et al. in view of Green et al. does not disclose the articulation rod/link system claimed.
Racenet et al. discloses a shaft assembly essentially as claimed including an articulation rod 50 and an articulation link 52, wherein axial translation of the articulation rod causes the distal neck housing to pivot off axis relative to the proximal neck housing.
It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to modify the device of Whitman et al. in view of Green et al. by substituting the rod/gear system of Whitman et al. for the rod/link system of Racenet et al. since the two are known to be equivalent systems in the art.
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments with respect to claims 1-6 and 8-20 have been considered but are in view of the new grounds of rejection.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

AIA
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
AIA
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
DETAILED ACTION
The amendment to Application # 14/483,153 was filed with the written response received on April 17, 2017 have been considered and an action on the merits follows. As directed by the amendment, claims 1, 3-6, 14, and 17 have been amended; claims 18-20 have been canceled; claim 21 has been added; and claims 2, 7-13, 15, and 16 stand as originally filed. Accordingly, claims 1-17 and 21 are pending in this application.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments, filed on April 17, 2017, have been considered but are moot in view of the new grounds of rejection as seen below. Applicant’s arguments with respect to the claims have been considered but are moot because the arguments do not apply to any of the references being used in the current rejection.
Drawings
The drawings are objected to because the terminology used to refer to the various brackets in the Specification and Drawings (submitted September 10th, 2014) do not align with the new amended claims, submitted April 17th, 2017. In newly amended Claims 1, 17 and 21, the Applicant recites wherein “a first bracket being movable relative to the safety hat once the face-shield bracket assembly is fixedly installed to the safety hat, and the face-shield bracket assembly including a second bracket being fixedly installable to the front hat section of the safety hat;” However, it should be noted that the claim limitations appear to be the reverse of what is shown in the Figures and the Specification.
Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. The figure or figure number of an amended drawing should not be labeled as “amended.” If a drawing figure is to be canceled, the appropriate figure must be removed from the replacement sheet, and where necessary, the remaining figures must be renumbered and appropriate changes made to the brief description of the several views of the drawings for consistency. Additional replacement sheets may be necessary to show the renumbering of the remaining figures. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Claim Objections
The claim 14 is objected to because the claim include reference characters which are not enclosed within parentheses.
Reference characters corresponding to elements recited in the detailed description of the drawings and used in conjunction with the recitation of the same element or group of elements in the claims should be enclosed within parentheses so as to avoid confusion with other numbers or characters which may appear in the claims. See MPEP § 608.01(m).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
Claims 1-17 and 21 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention.
Regarding Claims 1, 17, and 21, the applicant recites “the face-shield bracket assembly including a first bracket being movable relative to the safety hat once the face-shield bracket assembly is fixedly installed to the safety hat; and the face-shield bracket assembly including a second bracket being fixedly installable to the front hat section of the safety hat.” However, such a limitation is unclear and confusing, because in the Applicant’s Figures and Specification, it appears that the second bracket is movable and that the first bracket fixedly installed to the front hat section. By virtue of their dependency on independent Claim 1, all subsequent dependent claims are likewise rejected.
Regarding Claims 1 and 11, the Applicant recites the use of “a second bracket” in claim. The Applicant later goes on to recite the use of a visor attachment bracket in Claim 11. However, it should be noted that, in the Applicants Specification (paragraph 0033), it appears that the Applicant has support stating that the second bracket is also called the visor attachment bracket. It is unclear if the Applicant is the visor attachment bracket of Claim 11 as the second bracket as previously claimed or if this is a new structure entirely. Such limitation renders the claim indefinite since it is not clear what structural limitation applicant intends to cover. For the purpose of Examination, the Examiner will treat the second bracket as recited in claim 1 and the visor attachment bracket as recited in Claim 11 as being the same structural item. By virtue of their dependency on Claim 1, all subsequent dependent claims are likewise rejected.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
AIA
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary. Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.
AIA
Claims 1-13, 15, 17, and 21, as best understood by the Examiner, are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Bay (US 4,117,553) in view of Gyorfy (US 3,026,525).
Regarding the limitations following the term “configured to…,” it is noted that applicant is hereby noted language such as "configured to.." or “adapted to…” is nothing more than functional implications and statements of intended use which deemed not to impose any structural limitations distinguishable over the cited prior art. Therefore no patentable weight is given to such functional language, see Superior Industries v. Masaba (Fed. Cir. 2014) (in this instant the court clearly indicate that no patentable weight should be given to claim terms focusing on how a device is “configured to” perform a particular task).
Regarding Claim 1, Bay substantially discloses an apparatus for a safety hat (As shown in Bay Figures 1 and 3) having a front hat section and a rear hat section (See the front and rear hat sections in Bay Annotated Figure 3 Below), and the safety hat also having a hat brim (Bay Fig 3, 21) that extends from the front hat section and shields the eyes of a user from debris, and a face-shield bracket assembly (As shown in Bay Figures 1 and 3, wherein the face-shield bracket comprises the three brackets listed below) being configured to be fixedly installed to the safety hat, the face-shield bracket assembly including a first bracket (Bay Fig 3, 24) being movable relative to the safety hat once the face-shield bracket assembly is fixedly installed to the safety hat; a second bracket (See Bay Annotated Figure 3) being fixedly installable to the front hat section of the safety hat; and a third bracket (Bay Fig 3, 31) being fixedly installable to the rear hat section of the safety hat, and a safety visor (Bay Fig 3, 15) being configured to extend from the first bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly once the second bracket (See Bay Annotated Figure 1) of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the front hat section of the safety hat (As shown in Bay Figure 3), and the third bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the rear hat section of the safety hat (See Bay Annotated Figure 3, wherein the third bracket is installed to the rear hat section, inasmuch as the applicant has claimed), and the face-shield bracket assembly being configured to selectively position the safety visor between a visor deployed position and a visor retracted position (As shown in Bay Figure 3).
However, the Bay reference is silent to use of a cover assembly. Nevertheless, Gyorfy does teach the use of a cover assembly (Gyorfy Fig 1, 10) including a connector assembly (As shown in Gyorfy Figures 1-4, wherein the connector assembly comprises a plurality of snap buttons, 33) is fully capable of connecting the cover assembly to the first bracket (Bay Fig 3, 24) of the face-shield bracket assembly, so that a front cover section (See Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3 Below) of the cover assembly is positioned proximate to the front hat section of the safety hat once the second bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the front hat section of the safety hat, and the cover assembly also including a connectable section (As shown in Gyorfy Figure 2, wherein an individual snap button could be considered a connectable section, inasmuch as the applicant has claimed) extending rearward from the cover assembly, and the connectable section being configured to connect a rear section (See Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3) of the cover assembly to the third bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly, so that the connectable section is positioned proximate to the rear hat section of the safety hat once the third bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the rear hat section of the safety hat, inasmuch as the applicant has claimed.
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art prior to the effective filing date to have incorporated the cover assembly, as taught by Gyorfy; because Gyorfy teaches that this structure is well-known in the helmet art and protecting the user’s head in an industrial setting (Gyorfy Col 1, lns 7-41).

Regarding Claim 5, Bay and Gyorfy as combined above in claim 1 discloses the invention as claimed. The combined reference of Bay and Gyorfy teaches wherein the connector assembly (As shown in Gyorfy Figures 1-4, wherein the connector assembly comprises a plurality of snap buttons, 33) is configured to connect the cover assembly (Gyorfy Fig 1, 10) to the face-shield bracket assembly (As shown in Bay Figures 1 and 3), so that the cover assembly is retracted, at least in part, from the front hat section (See Bay Annotated Figure 3 Above) and from the hat brim (Bay Fig 3, 21) while the face-shield bracket assembly (As shown in Bay Figures 1 and 3), in use, positions the safety visor (Bay Fig 3, 15) in the visor retracted position (As shown in Bay Figure 3).
Regarding Claim 6, Bay and Gyorfy as combined above in claim 1 discloses the invention as claimed. The combined reference further teaches wherein the connector assembly (As shown in Gyorfy Figures 1-4, wherein the connector assembly comprises a plurality of snap buttons, 33) is configured to connect the cover assembly (Gyorfy Fig 1, 10) to the face-shield bracket assembly (As shown in Bay Figures 1 and 3), so that the cover assembly is retracted (As shown in Gyorfy Figure 4), at least in part, from the front hat section (See Bay Annotated Figure 3 Above) and from the hat brim (Bay Fig 3, 21) while the face-shield bracket assembly, in use, positions the safety visor in the visor retracted position (As shown in Bay Figures 3); and the debris received by and positioned on the cover assembly, in use, falls away from the hat brim thereby preventing inadvertent injury to the eyes of the user of the safety hat, inasmuch as the applicant has claimed.

Regarding Claim 17, Bay substantially discloses an apparatus for a user having eyes and for a safety hat (As shown in Bay Figures 1 and 3) having a front hat section and a rear hat section (See the front and rear hat sections in Bay Annotated Figure 3 Above), the safety hat also having a hat brim (Bay Fig 3, 21) extending from the front hat section, and the hat brim for shielding, at least in part, eyes of the user from debris, the apparatus comprising a face-shield bracket assembly (As shown in Bay Figures 1 and 3, wherein the face-shield bracket comprises the three brackets listed below) being configured to be fixedly installed to the safety hat; and the face-shield bracket assembly including a first bracket (Bay Fig 3, 24) being movable relative to the safety hat once the face-shield bracket assembly is fixedly installed to the safety hat; a second bracket (See Bay Annotated Figure 3) being fixedly installable to the front hat section of the safety hat; and a third bracket (Bay Fig 3, 31) being fixedly installable to the rear hat section of the safety hat; and a safety visor (Bay Fig 3, 15) being configured to extend from the first bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly once the second bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the front hat section of the safety hat (As shown in Bay Figure 3), and the third bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the rear hat section of the safety hat (See Bay Annotated Figure 3, wherein the third bracket is installed to the rear hat section, inasmuch as the applicant has claimed); and the face-shield bracket assembly being configured to selectively position the safety visor between a visor deployed position and a visor retracted position(As shown in Bay Figure 3).

Regarding Claim 21, Bay substantially discloses an apparatus, comprising a safety hat (As shown in Bay Figures 1 and 3) having a front hat section and a rear hat section (See the front and rear hat sections in Bay Annotated Figure 3 Above); and the safety hat also having a hat brim (Bay Fig 3, 21) extending from the front hat section, and the hat brim for shielding, at least in part, eyes of a user from debris; and a face-shield bracket assembly (As shown in Bay Figures 1 and 3, wherein the face-shield bracket comprises the three brackets listed below) being configured to be fixedly installed to the safety hat; and the face-shield bracket assembly including a first bracket (Bay Fig 3, 24) being movable relative to the safety hat once the face-shield bracket assembly is fixedly installed to the safety hat; a second bracket (See Bay Annotated Figure 3) being fixedly installable to the front hat section of the safety hat; and a third bracket (Bay Fig 3, 31) being fixedly installable to the rear hat section of the safety hat; and a safety visor (Bay Fig 3, 15) being configured to extend from the first bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly once the second bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the front hat section of the safety hat (As shown in Bay Figure 3), and the third bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the rear hat section of the safety hat (See Bay Annotated Figure 3, wherein the third bracket is installed to the rear hat section, inasmuch as the applicant has claimed); and the face-shield bracket assembly being configured to selectively position the safety visor between a visor deployed position and a visor retracted position (As shown in Bay Figure 3).
However, the Bay reference is silent to use of a cover assembly. Nevertheless, Gyorfy does teach the use of a cover assembly (Gyorfy Fig 1, 10) including a connector assembly (As shown in Gyorfy Figures 1-4, wherein the connector assembly comprises a plurality of snap buttons, 33), and the connector assembly is fully capable of connecting the cover assembly to the first bracket (Bay Fig 3, 24) of the face-shield bracket assembly, so that a front cover section (See Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3 Above) of the cover assembly is positioned proximate to the front hat section of the safety hat once the second bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the front hat section of the safety hat; and the cover assembly also including a connectable section (As shown in Gyorfy Figure 2, wherein an individual snap button could be considered a connectable section, inasmuch as the applicant has claimed) extending rearward from the cover assembly, and the connectable section being configured to connect a rear section (See Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3) of the cover assembly to the third bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly, so that the connectable section is positioned proximate to the rear hat section of the safety hat once the third bracket of the face-shield bracket assembly is installed to the rear hat section of the safety hat, inasmuch as the applicant has claimed.
AIA
Claim 14, as best understood by the Examiner, is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over the combination of Bay (US 4,117,553) and Gyorfy (US 3,026,525), as applied in Claim 1, and in further view of McGlasson et al (hereinafter McGlasson) (US 6,256,799 B1).
Regarding Claim 14, Bay and Gyorfy as combined above in claim 1 discloses the invention as claimed. Gyorfy teaches wherein the cover assembly (Gyorfy Fig 1, 10) includes a plurality of connectable sections, including a first connectable section, a second connectable section, a third connectable section, a fourth connectable section, a fifth connectable section, and a connector section (See the connector sections in Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3), wherein the end sections of the fourth connectable section and the fifth connectable section are connected together so as to form the rear section of the cover assembly (See Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3), the connector section is connected to an end portion of the fourth connectable section and the fifth connectable section, the fourth connectable section and the fifth connectable section are connected to an end portion of the first connectable section (See Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3 via the third connector section), the second connectable section is connected to an edge portion of the first connectable section so as to form a first side section of the cover assembly (See Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3), the third connectable section is connected to an edge portion of the first connectable section so as to form a second side section of the cover assembly (See Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3), and the second connectable section and the third connectable section are positioned on opposite lateral sides of the first connectable section (See Gyorfy Annotated Figure 3). It should be noted that while Gyorfy is silent to the various pieces of material being sewn together, McGlasson does teach that is well-known to sew various pieces of material together to make a helmet cover (McGlasson Figure 4, 32).
Furthermore, it should be noted that “the fourth connectable section and the fifth connectable section are sewn to an end portion of the first connectable section, the second connectable section is sewn to an edge portion of the first connectable section so as to form a first side section of the cover assembly, the third connectable section is sewn to an edge portion of the first connectable section so as to form a second side section of the cover assembly” is a product-by-process limitation. Even though product-by-process claims are limited by and defined by the process, determination of patentability is based on the product itself. The patentability of a product does not depend on its method of production. See MPEP 2113. Patentability shall not be given for the process by which the claimed product was made. The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
DETAILED ACTION
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments, see pages 5-6, filed 3/4/2014, with respect to the rejection(s) of claim(s) 1-9 under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) have been fully considered and are persuasive. Therefore, the rejection has been withdrawn. However, upon further consideration, a new ground(s) of rejection is made in view of Cumming.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1-6, and 8-9 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Blake (US 2006/0064161) in view of Cumming (US 2001/0016771). Referring to claims 1 and 5, Blake discloses an accommodating intraocular lens (AIOL) comprising: an optic (312); and at least one haptic plate (314) coupled to the optic by at least one connector (flexible or resilient arm portions, 316), the at least one haptic plate surrounding the optic (Fig. 9). Blake lacks a detailed description of the optic and haptic plate having a combined surface area between 70 mm2 and 100 mm2 and the at least one haptic plate has a width in a radial dimension of 1.0 - 3.5 mm across its entire angular extent and the connector being less rigid than the haptic portion. However, Blake discloses that the lens is designed to be placed in the capsular bag of the eye (paragraph 1) and that the device can be customized to take into account the interior of the eye of the patient (paragraph 19). Also, the plate haptic portion can be harder or softer than the lens portion (paragraph 53). Therefore it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to modify the dimensions of the lens of Blake, and to construct the connecting regions of a more resilient material than the haptic plate to allow for the haptic plate to move relative to the lens portion in order to accommodate each patient's particular vision and to fit in the eye. Additionally, Blake lacks a detailed description of at least one filament being coupled to the haptic plate extending from a periphery of the haptic plate. Cumming teaches an AIOL in the same field of endeavor with a haptic plate and with a filament coupled to the haptic plate extending from the periphery of the haptic plate for the purpose of providing support for and stabilizing the optic (Fig. 44 haptic plate 604, filament 602). Therefore it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to modify the haptic plate of Blake to have a filament extending from the periphery of the haptic plate as taught in Cumming in order to support and stabilize the optic in the eye.
Referring to claim 2, Blake discloses wherein the at least one haptic plate forms a continuous 360 degree boundary around the optic (Fig. 9).
Referring to claim 3, Blake discloses wherein the at least one haptic plate comprises at least two haptic plates (Fig. 14, two haptic plate portions, 814 that surround the optic).
Referring to claim 4, Blake discloses wherein the at least one haptic plate has an area of at least 60mm2 (paragraph 85).
Referring to claim 6, Blake discloses wherein the at least one connector comprises at least two connectors (Fig. 9 items 316).
Referring to claim 8, Blake discloses wherein the at least one haptic plate has a conical shape (paragraph 16, plate changes shaped to a cup or bowed configuration and is being interpreted as a conical shape).
Referring to claim 9, Blake discloses wherein the AIOL does not have a hinge between the optic and the at least one haptic plate (the embodiments of the haptic plate and between the optic and haptic plate do not contain hinges).
Claims 7 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Blake in view of Cumming as applied to claim 1, and further in view of Richardson (US 2008/0021550). Referring to claim 7, Blake discloses the thickness of the haptic plate can be varied (paragraph 85). Blake lacks a detailed description of the haptic plate thickness that is greater than any portion of the connector. Richardson teaches an accommodative lens in the same field of endeavor where the connectors (arms) are thinner than the haptic plate (Fig. 9). Therefore it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art to modify the connectors of Blake to be thinner than the haptic plate in order to provide increased flexibility to increase accommodation.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
1. The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
2. The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
3. Claims 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17, 19 and 20 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over by Lee et al. (US Publication Number 2007/0271424, hereinafter “Lee”) in view of Hampel et al. (US Publication Number 2007/0260841, hereinafter "Hampel").
4. As per claims 1, 11 and 20, Lee teaches a method and memory control component of controlling a memory module having memory components disposed thereon (figure 11), the method comprising: outputting first and second memory read commands to the memory module at respective times (multiple read commands are outputted to the memory module based at timing, paragraphs 85 and 86); receiving first read data concurrently (concurrent reception of data in memory for command operation) from a first plurality of the memory components via a first plurality of data paths, respectively, in response to the first memory read command (commands associated with a first memory m1, paragraph 86); and receiving second read data concurrently from a second plurality of the memory components via a second plurality of data paths, respectively, in response to the second memory read command (commands associated with the second memory m2, paragraph 86), the first plurality of the memory components including at least one memory component not included in the second plurality of the memory components and vice-versa (concurrent yet separate handling of the commands with respect to the memory where the first particularly when dealing with MG1 versus MG2 and the memory structure therein).
Lee does not explicitly disclose the first plurality of the memory components including at least one other memory component that is also included in the second plurality of memory components.
Hampel teaches a first plurality of the memory components including at least one other memory component that is also included in the second plurality of memory components (609, figure 9, paragraph 46).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of Applicant’s invention to modify Lee with the above teachings of Hampel. One of ordinary skill would be motivated to make such modification in order to enhance data transfer utilization (paragraph 2).5. Lee modified by the teachings of Hampel as seen in claim 1 above, as per claims 2 and 12, Lee teaches a method and memory control component further comprising outputting a maintenance command to the at least one memory component included in the first plurality of the memory components but not included in the second plurality of the memory components, the maintenance command instructing the at least one memory component to execute a maintenance operation during an interval that transpires concurrently with receiving the second read data from the second plurality of the memory components (control signal is the maintenance command instructing the memory component to handle a particular operation concurrently with the pending memory operations, paragraph 46). 6. Lee modified by the teachings of Hampel as seen in claim 1 above, as per claims 4 and 14, Lee teaches a method and memory control component wherein outputting the first and second memory read commands to the memory module at respective times comprises outputting the first and second memory read commands to first and second pluralities of nonvolatile memory components (time difference in outputting, paragraph 15). 7. Lee modified by the teachings of Hampel as seen in claim 1 above, as per claims 6 and 16, Lee teaches a method and memory control component wherein outputting the first and second memory read commands to the memory module at respective times comprises, at a first time, outputting chip-select signals (chip selection signal line, paragraph 44) exclusively to the first plurality the components while outputting first command signals on a command signaling path coupled to each of the memory components of the first and second pluralities, and, at a second time outputting chip-select signals exclusively to the second plurality of the memory components while outputting second command signals on the command signaling path (paragraph 45, where each MG1 and MG2 have independent CS lines). 8. Lee modified by the teachings of Hampel as seen in claim 1 above, as per claims 7 and 17, Lee teaches a method and memory control component further comprising outputting a third memory read command to the memory module after outputting the first and second memory read commands, and receiving third read data from the third plurality of memory components via a third plurality of data paths, respectively, in response to the third memory read command, the third plurality of memory components including (i) at least one memory component not included in the first plurality of memory components and (ii) at least one other memory component not included in the second plurality of memory components (MG3, third memory component with respective data path and memory components with read concurrent mechanism in place, figure 11).
9. Lee modified by the teachings of Hampel as seen in claim 1 above, as per claims 9 and 19, Lee teaches a method and memory control component wherein outputting the first memory command to the memory module comprises receiving a request to read data from the memory module, obtaining a value that indicates the first plurality of memory components and outputting chip-select signals exclusively to the first plurality of the memory components (paragraph 45, where each MG1 and MG2 have independent CS lines).
10. Claims 3, 5, 10, 13 and 15 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Lee in view of Hampel further in view of Tsern et al. (US Publication Number 2007/0088995, hereinafter "Tsern").
11. As per claims 3 and 13, Lee teaches a method and memory control component wherein outputting the first and second memory read commands to the memory module at respective times comprises outputting the first and second memory read commands (figure 11, paragraph 86), however does not explicitly disclose teachings of a dual inline memory module (DIMM).
Tsern teaches outputting the first and second memory read commands to the memory module at respective times comprises outputting the first and second memory read commands to a dual inline memory module (DIMM) (figure 9a, DIMM) at respective times via a command/address path coupled in common to all the memory components included in the first and second pluralities (paragraph 70).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of Applicant’s invention to modify Lee/Hampel with the above teachings of Tsern. One of ordinary skill would be motivated to make such modification in order to enhance memory module efficiency (paragraph 37).
12. Lee modified by the teachings of Hampel/Tsern as seen in claim 3 above, as per claims 5 and 15, Tsern teaches a method and memory control component wherein the nonvolatile memory components comprise Flash memory components (paragraph 53).

Applicant's arguments with respect to claim 1, 6, 11 and 16 have been considered but are moot in view of the new ground(s) of rejection. Applicant's amendments necessitated new grounds of rejection.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
AIA
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the claimed invention(s) absent any evidence to the contrary. Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and effective filing dates of each claim that was not commonly owned as of the effective filing date of the later invention in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) for any potential 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) prior art against the later invention.

transmitting an inter radio access technology (IRAT) measurement report for a plurality of neighbor cells (Fig. 2, Para. [0067], discloses IRAT measurement and reporting measurement data to the NW); and
prioritizing IRAT measurement scheduling for the plurality of neighbor cells triggering the IRAT measurement report until an IRAT handover command is received (Fig. 2, Para. [0072], [0067], discloses prioritizing IRAT measurement and reporting the measurement data to the NW and executes handover).
Nevertheless, Eerolainen does not explicitly teach prioritizing, by a user equipment (UE), IRAT measurement.
However, Martin explicitly teaches prioritizing, by a user equipment (UE), IRAT measurement (see Para. Para. [0032], “the UE will prioritize the members of its neighbor cell list and measure them according to those priorities, during its scheduled measurement opportunities”).

Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claim 22 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention. Specifically, it is unclear what is meant by “the two brake actuators include a first and a second brake actuator, the spring being connected with the first brake actuator, and the first brake actuator being further affixed with a pedal.” Specifically, it is not clear from the specification as filed what is meant by the two brake actuators include a first and a second brake actuator.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
Claims 1, 6, 14, 18, 21 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Solinski in view of Cheng et al. (US 5,765,665).
In re claim 1, 6, 14, 18, 21 Silonski discloses a brake mechanism for use in an infant stroller apparatus, comprising: two wheel supports (54) adapted to affix with two transversally spaced-apart legs (26) of the infant stroller apparatus; two wheels respectively assembled with the two wheel supports about a rotation axis (fig. 2) wherein each of the two wheels includes a hub portion (46); two latches (108) respectively assembled with the two wheel supports and operable to rotationally lock the two wheels; and including a brake actuator (88) respectively disposed adjacent to the two wheel supports, and a cable (116) having an end anchored with the brake actuators, the brake actuators having a cam surface (80), the cam surfaces of the brake actuators being respectively in sliding contact with latch (figs. 6-7), wherein the brake actuators is rotatable about the rotation axis to cause displacements of the latch parallel to the rotation axis to respectively engage and disengage the hub portions of the two wheels (figs. 6-7), the cable coupling each the brake actuator (fig. 4); wherein at least a first one of the two wheel supports includes a fixed part adapted to affix with one of the legs, and a pivotal part pivotally connected with the fixed part, the pivotal part has a first and a second side surface opposite to each other, the wheel and the brake actuator associated with the first wheel support are respectively assembled adjacent to first and second side surface (clear from fig. 4); wherein at least one of the two brake actuators is affixed with a pedal portion; further including two springs (134) operable to respectively bias the two latches into sliding contact with the two cam surfaces; a support frame having two rear legs; and the brake mechanism according to claim 1 assembled with the two rear legs (par. 40).
Solinski differs in that it does not disclose two brake actuators. Attention, however, is directed to Cheng which teaches two connected brake actuators, each connected to a wheel. It would be obvious to modify the stroller of Solinski to include two brake actuators, as taught by Cheng to allow for the user to use either foot.
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 13, 15-17, 23-28 are allowed.
Claims 2-5, 7, 14 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Response to Arguments
Applicants arguments are directed to the claims as amended. an examination of those amendments can be found above.

DETAILED ACTION
This action is in response to the filing of 1-30-2015. Claims 1 and 3-15 are pending and have been considered below:
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1-3, 5, 8-13 and 15 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Niwamoto et al. (“Niwamoto” 7631197 B2) in view of Arling et al. (“Arling” 20050097618 A1) and Nakajima (20030095211 A1).
Claim 1: Niwamoto discloses a slave relay station in communication with a personal communication device via a network, the slave relay station having a processing device and a non-transitory computer readable media on which are stored instructions which, when executed by the processing device, cause the slave relay station to perform steps for controlling a controllable device, comprising:
causing a graphical user interface page to be provided to the personal communication device (Claim 1; Figures 19 and 20; Column 22, Lines 40-57; graphical page provided);
the graphical user interface page having an activatable link (Figures 19 and 20; activatable links to control device);
receiving from the personal communication device via the network a request, the request containing data that functions to indicate that the activatable link of the graphical user interface page was selected (Column 23, Lines 42-66; provides links on the graphical user interface); and
Niwamoto discloses a user ID and apparatus ID (Column 23, Lines 20-29) and to further expound on a tag file, and the tag file comprising both a definition of the controllable device and a listing of one or more commands to be transmitted directly to the controllable device Arling is provided. Arling also discloses a system for controlling home appliances, while providing relay functionalities (Paragraph 41) and further discloses the linking of commands in addition to data elements and device definitions which are found in XML files (tag files)(Paragraph 30). Therefore it would have been obvious to of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to provide the functionality of providing the file providing device information as constructed by Arling. One would have been motivated to provide this functionality because it provides an established system of accessing information improving overall operability.
Niwamoto and Arling disclose in response to receiving the request, executing the tag file whereupon a communication protocol corresponding to the definition of the controllable device contained in the tag file associated with the activatable link is used to transmit directly to the controllable device (Arling: Figure 1, Paragraphs 29 and 30; tag file capability and direct transmission) the one or more commands contained in the tag file associated with the activatable link (Niwamoto: Column 23, Lines 42-66 and Column 24, Lines 23-46; provides links on the graphical user interface and takes request and transmits a command); Not explicitly disclosed is wherein the data that functions to indicate that the activatable link of the graphical user interface was selected comprises data that is usable by instructions to select from a plurality of tag files that have been associated with a corresponding plurality of activatable links of the graphical user interface page the tag file is to be executed. Nakajima is provided because it discloses a graphical user interface with activatable links (Figures 3A-C) and further provides functionality of selecting and providing XML language with content that corresponds to the page to be executed further the commands can be directly provided (Figure 8 and Paragraphs 31, 34 and 51). Therefore it would have been obvious to of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to provide the functionality of providing the file with device information as constructed by Nakajima. One would have been motivated to provide this functionality because it provides an established system of accessing information improving overall operability.
Claim 3: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 1, wherein the data that functions to identify the tag file associated with the activatable link comprises a file name of the tag file (Arling: Paragraph 30; provides XML file).
Claim 5: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 1, wherein the graphical user interface page is stored in a memory of the slave relay station (Niwamoto: Column 18, Lines 50-67). The display information is found in the database of the gateway and transmitted to the communication device.
Claim 8: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 1, wherein the instructions cause the graphical user interface page to be placed into a form determined to be appropriate for capabilities of the personal communication device (Niwamoto: Column 23, Lines 30-37; provides appropriate application which will contain interface).
Claim 9: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 8, wherein the instructions use data indicative of the capabilities of the personal communication device to place the graphical user interface page into a form determined to be appropriate for capabilities of the personal communication device (Niwamoto: Column 18, Lines 60-67 and Column 23, Lines 30-37; provides appropriate application which will contain interface).
Claim 10: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 9, wherein the data indicative of the capabilities of the personal communication device comprises data indicative of a make and model of the personal communication device (Niwamoto: Column 12, Lines 1-14; database provides size performance of device).
Claim 11: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 9, wherein the data indicative of the capabilities of the personal communication device comprises data indicative of an identity and revision of software used in connection with the display (Niwamoto: Column 12, Lines 1-14 and Column 28, Lines 19-25; provides revisions/updates of application).
Claim 12: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 1, wherein the graphical user interface page caused to be provided to the personal communications device is selected from a plurality of preformatted graphical user interface pages as a function of capabilities of the personal communication device (Niwamoto: Column 18, Lines 60-67 and Column 23, Lines 30-51); selects application information that can be used, it is understood that applications are formatted previously.
Claim 13: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 1, wherein the slave relay station is preconfigured with communication protocol information for a plurality of controllable devices (Niwamoto: Column 9, Lines 19-22; Claim 1, section iii). Converts operation information previously saved to control the device.
Claim 15: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 1, wherein the tag file is XML encoded (Niwamoto: Column 22, Lines 40-46 and Arling: Paragraph 30).
Claim 4 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Niwamoto et al. (“Niwamoto” 7631197 B2), Arling et al. (“Arling” 20050097618 A1) and Nakajima (20030095211 A1) in further view of Kopf (20080294667 A1).
Claim 4: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 1, but do not explicitly disclose wherein the request comprises an HTTP protocol request which includes a file name of the tag file to be executed. Therefore Kopf is provided because it discloses a system for sending commands from a display device to a secondary device, which further uses the functionality of a relay (Paragraph 124) and also uses HTTP request protocols and XML file (Paragraphs 37 and 41). Therefore it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to provide the functionality of HTTP request protocols as taught by Kopf. One would have been motivated to provide this functionality because it provides an established system of accessing/sending information improving overall operability.
Claims 6, 7 and 14 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Niwamoto et al. (“Niwamoto” 7631197 B2), Arling et al. (“Arling” 20050097618 A1) and Nakajima (20030095211 A1) in further view of Yuh et al. (“Yuh” 7093003 B2).
Claim 6: Niwamoto, Arling and Nakajima disclose a slave relay station as recited in claim 1, wherein the graphical user interface page is stored in a memory of a server device in communication with the slave relay station and the personal communication device. Niwamoto discloses pulling information from the internet (web server) however does not disclose that graphical user interface is provided from the server. Therefore Yuh is provided because it discloses providing a graphical user interface through the server (Column 1, Lines 55-63). It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to provide a graphical user interface from a server to the gateway device of the modified Niwamoto. One would have been motivated to provide the information from a server because this provides the system with a vast resource to pull data and supply information about an appliance.

Applicant's arguments filed have been fully considered but they are not persuasive. Applicant argues that providing direct transmission in Niwamoto would change the principle by which the system is intended to operate. It is understood that the main operation of the system is to control the device. The operations of the system are provided to a device not capable of directly executing the commands transmitted. The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:

35 U.S.C. 101 reads as follows:
Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
Claims 1 and 16 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter. In view of the recent Supreme Court decision in Alice Corpora/ion Pty. Ltd. v. CLS Bank International, et al. ("Alice Corp. "), the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter because the claim(s) as a whole, considering all claim elements both individually and in combination, do not amount to significantly more than an abstract idea. The additional element(s) or combination of elements in the claim(s) other than the abstract idea per se amount(s) to no more than: methods and devices for gathering data and processing data which are needed to implement the abstract idea. Viewed as a whole, these additional claim element(s) do not provide meaningful limitation(s) to transform the abstract idea into a patent eligible application of the abstract idea such that the claim(s) amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea itself. Therefore, the claim(s) are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as being directed to non-statutory subject matter.

The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
AIA
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
AIA
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claims 1-3, 7 and 9 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Giglio et al U.S. Patent 5,765,314.
Giglio discloses an attraction facility comprising a plurality of sections (26, 28, 30, 32, 34), each of the sections including a stage (col. 4, lines 30-35), and all of the stages are located in the same building.
Regarding claim 9, Figs. 2 and 3 show the stages are walled off from the visitors in line (outside the building) to a stage in such way the visitors in line cannot hear what is being said on stage.
Regarding the limitations "a television game show, whereby the visitors of the said attraction facility can enter the recreated stages and try themselves out as participants of imitations of the said television game shows" and “whereby each of the attraction’s sections provides a TV game show participation imitation separately from that of another section” as in claim 1, "a television game show is recreated and exploited in an attraction section in multiple copies" in claim 2; "all the recreated stages of television game shows" in claim 3; “whereby the players’ stage of the said television game show is recreated and exploited in the said attraction facility in multiple copies…game show” in claim 7, and “unless provided with broadcast sound from the said stage” in claim 9; these limitations are considered intended uses of the claimed invention and they do not include any structural features of the facility. Accordingly, the stages of Giglio are more than capable of being used in the claimed manner.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
Claims 4-6 and 8 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Giglio et al.
It is noted that Giglio only show one building instead of more than one building as claimed. However, such difference is merely a matter of multiplication of the same part. Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill to duplicate the facility of Giglio to accommodate additional viewers and/or participants.
Response to Arguments
In response to applicant's argument that the prior art fails to teach the intended use “whereby each of the attraction’s sections provides a TV game show participation imitation separately from that of another section, a recitation of the intended use of the claimed invention must result in a structural difference between the claimed invention and the prior art in order to patentably distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art. If the prior art structure is capable of performing the intended use, then it meets the claim. In this case, applicant fails to recite any specific structural component to distinguish the claimed invention and the prior art of record.
Conclusion
