The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
DETAILED ACTION
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(d):
(d) REFERENCE IN DEPENDENT FORMS.—Subject to subsection (e), a claim in dependent form shall contain a reference to a claim previously set forth and then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed. A claim in dependent form shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), fourth paragraph:
Subject to the [fifth paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA)], a claim in dependent form shall contain a reference to a claim previously set forth and then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed. A claim in dependent form shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers.
AIA
Claims 36 and 40 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(d) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, 4th paragraph, as being of improper dependent form for failing to further limit the subject matter of the claim upon which it depends, or for failing to include all the limitations of the claim upon which it depends. Claims 36 and 40 do not further limit claims 1 and 11 on which they respectively depend because the dependent claims merely states limitations that have been recited in claim 1 (boiling point and surface tension limitations). Applicant may cancel the claim(s), amend the claim(s) to place the claim(s) in proper dependent form, rewrite the claim(s) in independent form, or present a sufficient showing that the dependent claim(s) complies with the statutory requirements.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
AIA
Claims 1-2, 5, 10, and 34-37 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Tregub WO 2013/040468.
Per claims 1-2, 5, 10, and 34-37, Tregub teaches a process for forming an OLED, including forming either the light-emitting layer [0018]. Regarding the light emitting layer, Tregub teaches steps comprising forming a layer of an ink composition in a pixel cell of an OLED pixel bank [0027], the organic EL material [0043] dissolved in an ester-based solvent [0033] (solvent blends including amyl octanoate and alkyl benzoate), both of which are ester based solvents. Tregub teaches selecting two solvents, and therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to have used these two solvents with a reasonable expectation for success and predictable results, since Tregub teaches that these two solvents are workable to create a blend, and therefore form an ester-based solvent consisting essentially of ester solvents.
Tregub teaches the solvent system with a surface tension lower than 40 dynes/cm, which overlaps with the claimed range [0018]. Tregub teaches a boiling point of about 300C or evaporation temperature to be from 250-500C [0081], which also overlaps with the claimed range. In the case where the claimed ranges “overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art” a prima facie case of obviousness exists. In re Wertheim, 541 F.2d 257, 191 USPQ 90 (CCPA 1976); In re Woodruff, 919 F.2d 1575, 16 USPQ2d 1934 (Fed. Cir. 1990). It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to have selected a boiling point/evaporation temperature and a surface tension of the deposition ink within the disclosed workable range with a reasonable expectation for success and predictable results to arrive at the claimed range. Tregub teaches allowing the solvent to evaporate to form the layer [0017]. Tregub teaches formation of a uniformly thick layer (see Tregub claim 1).
AIA
Claims 11-12, 16-18, and 38-41 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Tregub WO 2013/040468 in view of Yamauchi US 2012/0211729.
Per claims 11-12, 16-18, and 38-41, Tregub teaches a light emitting layer formed as claimed (see rejection of claim 1 discussed above). Furthermore, Tregub teaches a process for forming an OLED, including forming the hole transporting layer [0018]. Regarding the hole transporting layer, Tregub teaches forming the layer in a pixel bank area [0027], the HTL components dissolved in an ester-based solvent [0033] (solvent blends including amyl octanoate and alkyl benzoate), both of which are ester based solvents. Tregub teaches selecting two solvents, and therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to have used these two solvents with a reasonable expectation for success and predictable results, since Tregub teaches that these two solvents are workable to create a blend, and therefore form an ester-based solvent consisting essentially of ester solvents.
Tregub teaches the solvent system with a surface tension lower than 40 dynes/cm, which overlaps with the claimed range [0018]. Tregub teaches a boiling point of about 300C or evaporation temperature to be from 250-500C, which also overlaps with the claimed range. In the case where the claimed ranges “overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art” a prima facie case of obviousness exists. In re Wertheim, 541 F.2d 257, 191 USPQ 90 (CCPA 1976); In re Woodruff, 919 F.2d 1575, 16 USPQ2d 1934 (Fed. Cir. 1990). It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to have selected a boiling point/evaporation temperature and a surface tension of the deposition ink within the disclosed workable range with a reasonable expectation for success and predictable results to arrive at the claimed range. Tregub teaches allowing the solvent to evaporate to form the layer [0017]. Tregub teaches formation of a uniformly thick layer (see Tregub claim 1).
Tregub does not teach a crosslinking polymer in the HTL. Yamauchi teaches a process of forming an OLED (abstract), wherein crosslinking polymers can be included in the HTL [0092]. The crosslinking polymer would not be fully crosslinked at some point during the process. It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to have included crosslinking polymers in the HTL to form OLEDs because Yamauchi teaches crosslinking aids in lamination and adhesion in forming layers of an OLED device [0092].
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 6-9 and 13-15 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Claims 19 and 42-48 are allowed.
The following is a statement of reasons for the indication of allowable subject matter: The above mentioned claims (except for claim 13) all include a solvent comprising or consisting of octyl octanoate. A prior art search of octyl octanoate has not yielded any relevant results regarding the claimed solvent. Tregub is interpreted as the closest prior art of record. Tregub does not teach octyl octanoate and there would have been no apparent reason or motivation to have modified the prior art to arrive at the claimed invention to include octyl octanoate as a solvent. Regarding claim 13, none of the prior art teach using a solvent system comprising two or more alkyl octanoates.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 3/25/2016 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive. Applicant argues that amyl octanoate has a lower boiling point than 300C. However, Tregub teaches a solvent system of two or more solvents, where other solvents listed are also ester solvents. As such, Applicant's arguments are not persuasive (see rejection above regarding new claim limitations). Applicant's arguments regarding the claims indicated under allowable subject matter are persuasive, specifically claims 13 and 42-48 are persuasive and the claims are indicated as containing allowable subject matter.
Conclusion

s 1-2, 5, 10, and 34-37 are
Tregub WO 2013/040468
Per claims 1-2, 5, 10, and 34-37, Tregub teaches a process for forming an OLED, including forming either the light-emitting layer [0018]. Regarding the light emitting layer, Tregub teaches steps comprising forming a layer of an ink composition in a pixel cell of an OLED pixel bank [0027], the organic EL material [0043] dissolved in an ester-based solvent [0033] (solvent blends including amyl octanoate and alkyl benzoate), both of which are ester based solvents. Tregub teaches selecting two solvents, and therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to have used these two solvents with a reasonable expectation for success and predictable results, since Tregub teaches that these two solvents are workable to create a blend, and therefore form an ester-based solvent consisting essentially of ester solvents.
Tregub teaches the solvent system with a surface tension lower than 40 dynes/cm, which overlaps with the claimed range [0018]. Tregub teaches a boiling point of about 300C or evaporation temperature to be from 250-500C [0081], which also overlaps with the claimed range. In the case where the claimed ranges “overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art” a prima facie case of obviousness exists. In re Wertheim, 541 F.2d 257, 191 USPQ 90 (CCPA 1976); In re Woodruff, 919 F.2d 1575, 16 USPQ2d 1934 (Fed. Cir. 1990). AIA
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
DETAILED ACTION
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
AIA
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 1, 2, 7, 8, 11-13, 18, 19, 22-24, 29 and 30 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Tsuboi et al. (US. Pub. No. 2011/0021233 A1; hereinafter “Tsuboi”) in view of Uchida (US. Pub. No. 2015/0117186 A1)
Regarding claim 1, Tsuboi teaches a method for detecting dedicated short range communications (DSRC) transmissions to determine whether to use at least a portion of the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 107), comprising:
operating, by a multi-mode client device (see Tsuboi, fig. 1, 100, fig. 3, 107), outside of the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 101, WAVE spectrum outside DSRC spectrum, para. [0031, 33], 5.9 Ghz is outside of 5.8 Ghz and/or 700 Mhz); and
switching while operating outside of the DSRC spectrum to detect DSRC transmissions using the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 105, para. [0042]).
Tsuboi is silent to teaching that comprising:
operating using a first clock rate; and
switching to a second clock rate.
In the same field of endeavor, Uchida teaches a method comprising
operating using a first clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 115, 80 Mhz); and
switching to a second clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 116, 113, 20Mhz) to detect DSRC transmissions (see Uchida, fig. 8, interference power, para. [0079-80]).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi with the teaching of Uchida in order to improve transmission efficiency and implement bandwidth control and to implement an proper clock rate for the operating frequencies (see Uchida, para. [0007]).
Regarding claim 2, the combination of Tsuboi and Uchida teaches the method of claim 1, further comprising:
determining whether the detected DSRC transmissions exceed a threshold (see Uchida, fig. 9, para. [0080], -90, -70 dBm).
Regarding claim 7, the combination of Tsuboi and Uchida teaches the method of claim 1, further comprising:
monitoring at least one of a plurality of frequency bands within the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi , fig. 3, 105, para. [0042]) while operating at the second clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 8, fig. 5, 113).
Regarding claim 8, the combination of Tsuboi and Uchida teaches the method of claim 7, further comprising:
determining an activity level of transmissions on each of the monitored frequency bands (see Uchida, fig. 8, para. [0079-80]).
Regarding claim 11, the combination of Tsuboi and Uchida teaches the method of claim 1, wherein the second clock rate is half the first clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 113, 114, 115).
Regarding claim 12, Tsuboi teaches a multi-mode client device for detecting dedicated short range communications (DSRC) transmissions to determine whether to use at least a portion of the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 105), comprising:
a processor; memory in electronic communication with the processor (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 107); and
instructions stored in the memory, the instructions being executable by the processor to:
operating the multi-mode device (see Tsuboi, fig. 1, 100, fig. 3, 107), outside of the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 101, WAVE spectrum outside DSRC spectrum, para. [0031, 33], 5.9 Ghz is outside of 5.8 Ghz and/or 700 Mhz); and
switch while operating outside of the DSRC spectrum to detect DSRC transmissions using the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 105, para. [0042]).
Tsuboi is silent to teaching that configured to
operate using a first clock rate; and
switch to a second clock rate.
In the same field of endeavor, Uchida teaches apparatus configured to
operate using a first clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 115, 80 Mhz); and
switch to a second clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 116, 113, 20Mhz) to detect DSRC transmissions (see Uchida, fig. 8, interference power, para. [0079-80]).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi with the teaching of Uchida in order to improve transmission efficiency and implement bandwidth control and to implement an proper clock rate for the operating frequencies (see Uchida, para. [0007]).
Regarding claims 13, 18, 19 and 22, the dependent claims are interpreted and rejected for the same reasons as set forth above in claims 2, 7, 8 and 11, respectively.
Regarding claim 23, Tsuboi teaches a multi-mode client device for detecting dedicated short range communications (DSRC) transmissions to determine whether to use at least a portion of the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 105), comprising:
means for operating the multi-mode device (see Tsuboi, fig. 1, 100, fig. 3, 107), outside of the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 101, WAVE spectrum outside DSRC spectrum, para. [0031, 33], 5.9 Ghz is outside of 5.8 Ghz and/or 700 Mhz); and
means for switching while operating outside of the DSRC spectrum to detect DSRC transmissions using the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 105, para. [0042]).
Tsuboi is silent to teaching that comprising:
means for operating using a first clock rate; and
means for switching to a second clock rate.
In the same field of endeavor, Uchida teaches an apparatus comprising
means for operating using a first clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 115, 80 Mhz); and
means for switching to a second clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 116, 113, 20Mhz) to detect DSRC transmissions (see Uchida, fig. 8, interference power, para. [0079-80]).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi with the teaching of Uchida in order to improve transmission efficiency and implement bandwidth control and to implement an proper clock rate for the operating frequencies (see Uchida, para. [0007]).
Regarding claims 24 and 29, the dependent claims are interpreted and rejected for the same reasons as set forth above in claims 2 and 7, respectively.
Regarding claim 30, Tsuboi teaches a computer program product for detecting dedicated short range communications (DSRC) transmissions to determine whether to use at least a portion of the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 105, para. [0008]), the computer program product comprising a non-transitory computer-readable medium storing instructions executable by a processor to:
operate a multi-mode client device (see Tsuboi, fig. 1, 100, fig. 3, 107) outside of the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 101, WAVE spectrum outside DSRC spectrum, para. [0031, 33], 5.9 Ghz is outside of 5.8 Ghz and/or 700 Mhz); and
switch while operating outside of the DSRC spectrum to detect DSRC transmissions using the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 3, 105, para. [0042]).
Tsuboi is silent to teaching that configured to
operate using a first clock rate; and
switch to a second clock rate.
In the same field of endeavor, Uchida teaches apparatus configured to
operate using a first clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 115, 80 Mhz); and
switch to a second clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 116, 113, 20Mhz) to detect DSRC transmissions (see Uchida, fig. 8, interference power, para. [0079-80]).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi with the teaching of Uchida in order to improve transmission efficiency and implement bandwidth control (see Uchida, para. [0007]).
Claims 3, 9, 10, 14, 20, 21 and 25 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Tsuboi and Uchida as applied to claims 2, 8, 13, 19, and 24 above, and further in view of Park (US. Pub. No. 2012/0069746 A1)
Regarding claim 3, the combination of Tsuboi and Uchida teaches the method of claim 2, further comprising:
upon determining that the detected DSRC transmissions fails to exceed the threshold, switching to the first clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 116, 115, fig. 9).
The combination of Tsuboi and Uchida is silent to teaching that comprising
operating in at least a portion of the DSRC spectrum.
In the same field of endeavor, Park teaches a method comprising
operating in at least a portion of the DSRC spectrum (see Park, fig. 3, 4, 306; para. [0049-50]).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi and Uchida with the teaching of Park in order to improve wideband communication quality (see Park, para. [0004-5]).
Regarding claim 9, the combination of Tsuboi and Uchida teaches the method of claim 8, further comprising:
switching to the first clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 116, 115, fig. 9);
selecting at least one of the monitored frequency bands (see Uchida, fig. 8) ; and
operating using the at least one selected frequency band, the frequency band being selected based at least in part on the determined activity level (see Uchida, fig. 8, 9).
The combination of Tsuboi and Uchida is silent to teaching that comprising
operating in the DSRC spectrum.
In the same field of endeavor, Park teaches a method comprising
operating in the DSRC spectrum (see Park, fig. 3, 4, 306; para. [0049-50]).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi and Uchida with the teaching of Park in order to improve wideband communication quality (see Park, para. [0004-5]).
Regarding claim 10, the combination of Tsuboi, Uchida, and Park teaches the method of claim 9, wherein selecting at least one of the monitored frequency bands comprises:
avoiding the selection of frequency bands allocated for safety-related transmissions in the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 4, S205).
Regarding claims 14, 20, 21, and 25, the dependent claims are interpreted and rejected for the same reasons as set forth above in claims 3, 9, and 10, respectively.
Claims 4, 5, 15, 16, 26 and 27 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Tsuboi and Uchida as applied to claims 1, 2, 12, 13, 23, and 24 above, and further in view of Kasher et al. (US. Pub. No. 2007/0298810 A1; hereinafter “Kasher”)
Regarding claim 4, the combination of Tsuboi and Uchida teaches the method of claim 2, further comprising:
upon determining that the detected DSRC transmissions exceed the threshold (see Uchida, fig. 8, para. [0080]), switching to the first clock rate (see Uchida, fig. 2, 116, 113); and
continuing to operate outside of the DSRC spectrum (see Tsuboi, fig. 2, 313).
The combination of Tsuboi and Uchida is silent to teaching that comprising
continuing to operate for a predetermined period of time.
In the same field of endeavor, Kasher teaches a method comprising
continuing to operate for a predetermined period of time (see Kasher, fig. 3, 350, re-evaluate, para. [0040]).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi and Uchida with the teaching of Kasher in order to provide high throughput and improve communication quality (see Kasher, para. [0003-4]).
Regarding claim 5, the combination of Tsuboi and Uchida teaches the method of claim 1.
The combination of Tsuboi and Uchida is silent to teaching that further comprising:
operating at the second clock rate for a predetermined period of time; and
upon an expiration of the predetermined period of time, switching to the first clock rate.
In the same field of endeavor, Kasher teaches a method comprising
operating at the second clock rate for a predetermined period of time (see Kasher, fig. 3, 348, 350); and
upon an expiration of the predetermined period of time, switching to the first clock rate (see Kasher, fig. 3, 352).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi and Uchida with the teaching of Kasher in order to provide high throughput and improve communication quality (see Kasher, para. [0003-4]).
Regarding claims 15, 16, 26, and 27, the dependent claims are interpreted and rejected for the same reasons as set forth above in claims 4 and 5, respectively.
Claims 6, 17 and 28 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Tsuboi and Uchida as applied to claims 1, 12, and 23 above, and further in view of Kasher and Lv et al. (US. Pub. No. 2013/0195018 A1; hereainfter “Lv”)
Regarding claim 6, the combination of Tsuboi and Uchida teaches the method of claim 1, further comprising:
reporting an occurrence of one or more detected DSRC transmissions to an access point (AP);
receiving instructions from the AP, the instructions based at least in part on the reported occurrences of the DSRC transmissions; and
operating in at least a portion of the DSRC spectrum based at least in part on the instructions received from the AP.
In the same field of endeavor, Kasher teaches a method comprising
receiving instructions from the AP, the instructions based at least in part on the reported occurrences of the DSRC transmissions (see Kasher, fig. 3, 326, 344, 352); and
operating in at least a portion of the DSRC spectrum based at least in part on the instructions received from the AP (see Kasher, fig. 3, 328, 346, 354).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi and Uchida with the teaching of Kasher in order to provide high throughput and improve communication quality (see Kasher, para. [0003-4]).
The combination of Tsuboi, Uchida, and Kasher is silent to teaching that comprising
reporting an occurrence of one or more detected DSRC transmissions to an access point (AP).
In the same field of endeavor, Lv teaches a method comprising
reporting an occurrence of one or more detected DSRC transmissions to an access point (AP) (see Lv, para. [0068], fig. 4).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi, Uchida, and Kasher with the teaching of Lv in order to implement new channelization and reduce interference (see Lv, para/ [0007]).
Regarding claims 17 and 28, the dependent claims are interpreted and rejected for the same reasons as set forth above in claim 6.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 9/17/2015 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Applicant argues that Tsuboi teaches an AP. The examiner submits Tsuboi also teaches a client device 100, fig. 3.
Applicant argues that Tsuboi is silent to operating outside of DSRC spectrum. The examiner submits that Tsuboi,’s fig. 3, 101 operates in WAVE spectrum at 5.9 Ghz outside DSRC spectrum of 5.8 Ghz and/or 700 Mhz.
Applicant also argues that Uchida cannot be combined with Tsuboi. The examiner submits that Tsuboi is silent of the different clock rates needed for its various operating frequencies for WAVE, WiFi, and DSRC. Uchida teaches the proper clock rates for various frequencies.
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to combine the teaching of Tsuboi with the teaching of Uchida in order to improve transmission efficiency and implement bandwidth control and to implement an proper clock rate for the operating frequencies (see Uchida, para. [0007]).
Conclusion

AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
DETAILED ACTION
Applicant’s response to restriction requirement of 8/18/14 is entered.
Claim 21 is cancelled.
Claims 1-20 and 22-33 remain pending.
Election/Restrictions
Applicant’s election of the species of ECM, dermis, porcine, anti-inflammatory agent, NHS, IDA, Zinc, and lyphostatin species in the reply filed on 2/24/14 was previously acknowledged. Because applicant did not distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the restriction requirement, the election has been treated as an election without traverse (MPEP § 818.03(a)).
Due to the amended drawings, now providing support for the invention, and further consideration in light of such, the combination of species elected is found to overcome the rejections of record, and no further rejection could be had. Therefore, the Examiner has opened the species of Zinc, to consider all metals.
Claims 2-4, 13, 14, 23, 29, and 30 remain from further consideration pursuant to 37 CFR 1.142(b) as being drawn to a nonelected species, there being no allowable generic or linking claim. Election was made without traverse in the reply filed on 2/24/14.
Claims 1, 5-12, 15-20, 22, 24-28, and 31-33 are considered herein for the elected species.
Drawings
The drawings remain objected to.
While the objections to Figures 1A, 2, 3, and 4 are withdrawn, Figure 1B remains objected to.
Figure 1B remains grainy and will not be clear when compressed. The high-quality rendering provided by the office still portrays the lysostaphin, zinc, and crosslinker molecules, along with the scaffold, with very blurry definition. The lysostaphin will not compress and even be intelligible at all, much less differentiated from the zinc and crosslinker.
New corrected drawings in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in this application for the reasoning above. Applicant is advised to employ the services of a competent patent draftsperson outside the Office, as the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office no longer prepares new drawings. The corrected drawings are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. The requirement for corrected drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Double Patenting
For the record, it is noted that Application No. 13/777,153 was considered for purposes of obviousness-type double patenting, but the claims do not encompass, as part of their written description, the requirement for a chelator covalently bound to the matrix. Therefore, while the reverse may be true, the present Application is not obviousness-type double patenting over the other Application.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
AIA
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112:
The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.
In light of the amended drawings, and support found as Applicant has argued, the rejections of Claims 1, 5-12, 15-22, 24-28, and 31-33 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement, are withdrawn.
To wit, the new drawings make clear that the previous data was poorly rendered and did not provide a proper interpretation of the data, and therefore, it is now found possessed, and to be the proper data, as supported by the parent provisional Application.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 101
35 U.S.C. 101 reads as follows:
Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
In light of the amended drawings, the rejections of Claims 1, 5-12, 15-20, 22, 24-28, and 31-33 under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the disclosed invention is inoperative and therefore lacks utility, are withdrawn.
For the same reasoning as the rejections under possession, these rejections are withdrawn.

Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
AIA
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112:
The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.
Claims 1, 5-12, 15-20, 22, 24-28, and 31-33 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, because the specification, while being enabling for the porcine acellular matrix and levels of Zinc and IDA-Zinc utilized in Example 3, does not reasonably provide enablement for other embodiments. The specification does not enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and/or use the invention commensurate in scope with these claims.
Applicant’s claims are broad for scaffolds, chelating agents, and metals bound to the chelating agent.
The specification teaches that the structures are meant to inhibit growth of bacteria in the matricies.
Example 3 is vaguely described in paragraph 105, and is the most pertinent portion of the specification. In example 3, porcine dermal tissue are incubated with NHS-IDA, to allow crosslinking of the IDA to the matrix. Then the samples are washed with saline and incubated in 1mM ZnSO4 solution. Some of these samples were then washed overnight to remove excess/unbound zinc. Then the samples are innoculated with S. aureus, and incubated overnight. Then bacterial concentrations are determined (CFU) on each matrix and compared to IDA only controls, a control untreated matrix, and innoculum. In Figure 3, the results show that IDA alone produces high levels of S. aureus, with Zinc alone (although it is not reported as to the level of zinc present, nor how it was made) producing less, and Zinc-IDA producing the lowest levels of S. aureus.
These results conflict somewhat with the prior Art. To wit, it has been known for a long time that zinc chelation itself inhibits S. aureus growth. E.g., Corbin, et al. (2008) “Metal Chelation and Inhibition of Bacterial Growth in Tissue Abscesses”, Science, 319(5865): 962-65 demonstrates that calprotectin is a protein released by neutrophils into abscesses to chelate manganese and zinc, and thereby stop S. aureus growth. Given the chelation of IDA with zinc, by IDA here instead of calprotectin, the Artisan would not expect IDA itself to have no growth-curbing effects, but instead to inhibit the growth of S. aureus, as calprotectin does.
In addition, Zinc alone (again it is not clear how much zinc is present or how it was prepared) decreases growth. This makes no sense either, except if one considers that Zinc itself is known to block manganese influx in bacteria, but this occurs at much higher levels of zinc. E.g., Mc Devitt, et al. (2011) "A Molecular Mechanism for Bacterial Susceptibility to Zinc", PLoS Pathogens, 7(11): e1002357 (pp. 1-9) indicates, in the ABSTRACT, that it known that zinc in excess has significant toxicity to bacteria, and then goes on to discuss the mechanism of inhibition of manganese influx inhibition.
Given this knowledge, Applicant's disclosed experiments can only have hit upon something heretofore unknown, and therefore, it is impossible to extrapolate to the great many metals, matricies, and chelators encompassed by the claims. In addition, in order to determine if any particular combination would work, the Artisan would have to experiment to determine if that combination would work.
Such is undue experimentation as it is such experimentation as is required to enable the breadth of claims.
Due to the finding of undue experimentation, the claims are not enabled except for the embodiment of Figure 3.
Art Made of Record
The following appears to be the closest prior art and was previously made of record: Belyansky, et al. (December 2011) “The Addition of Lysostaphin Dramatically Improves Survival, Protects Porcine Biomesh from Infection, and Improves Graft Tensile Shear Strength”, Journal of Surgical Research, 171: 409-15.
Conclusion
No claim is allowed.

AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
DETAILED ACTION
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 22 DEC 14 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
In response to the assertion that the amendments to the claims being clearly not shown or taught by the prior art of record, examiner must respectfully disagree. As will be demonstrated, US 2010/0126054 to Daniel et al. (hereinafter Daniel) broadly yet reasonably reads on the claims.
Drawings
The drawings are objected to as failing to comply with 37 CFR 1.84(p)(4) because reference character “80” has been used to designate both forward tab members and a gap or opening. See Fig. 2, for example, as well as ¶¶ [0037] and [0039] of US 2014/0075804, the PG Pub of the instant application. Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The text of those sections of Title 35, U.S. Code not included in this action can be found in a prior Office action.
Claims 1, 7, 16, 18 – 28 and 30 – 32 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by Daniel.
Re – claims 1, 7 and 16, Daniel discloses the claimed invention including a firearm, Title, ¶ [0002], comprising: an upper receiver, 151 Fig. 1, for example; a bottom portion 102B configured to be removably secured to the upper receiver, ¶¶ [0019] – [0053], wherein the bottom portion has a forward portion located forward of a top rail 107, ¶ [0027], of the upper receiver, as shown; an upper portion (upper rail extension, claim 1) 102A configured to be removably secured to the forward portion of the bottom portion, wherein the upper rail extension has a rail portion (lower-right, topmost portion of 102A in Fig. 1, for example—see annotated drawing below, as well) and a pair of side members (longitudinal edges 110) defining an opening (port 113) proximate to an end of the rail portion of the upper rail extension, wherein the opening of the upper rail extension is located between the rail portion of the upper rail extension and the top rail of the upper receiver when the upper rail extension is secured to the bottom portion; and a release mechanism 104 for releasably securing the upper portion to the forward portion of the bottom portion. While not demonstrated in the drawings, the opening 113 of the upper rail extension would normally be located between the rail portion (the rail portion near callout 113) of the upper rail extension and the top rail 107 of the upper receiver when the upper rail extension is secured to the bottom portion. Evidence to the contrary is welcome.
PNG media_image1.png 352 506 media_image1.png Greyscale
Re – claim 18, Daniel further discloses wherein the upper portion further comprises an integrally formed top rail portion and wherein the bottom portion further comprises an integrally formed bottom rail portion. See relevant note above.
Re – claim 19, in light of the structure disclosed by Daniel, the method of manufacturing the device would have been inherent, since it is the normal and logical manner in which the device can be assembled.
Re – claim 20, 23, 26 and 30, Daniel further discloses wherein the opening of the upper rail extension is located forward of a sight opening in the upper receiver when the upper portion is secured to the bottom portion. This is asserted for two reasons: front sight base 152, being the kind usually part of the disclosed M-16 and AR-15 style weaponry, would inherently include an opening, such as wherein the front sight pin is disposed, and the opening 113 would be located forward thereof, at least in part; and, “a sight opening” can broadly yet reasonably be construed as any one of the many grooves of rail 107 extending perpendicularly to the longitudinal axis 154, such as an opening that would assist in mounting a telescope, for example.
Re – claims 21, 24, 27 and 31, Daniel further discloses wherein the pair of side members secures the upper rail extension to the bottom portion, via fasteners 112, for example.
Re – claim 22, 25, 28 and 32, Daniel further discloses wherein the pair of side members abuts a forward end of the upper receiver when the upper rail extension is secured to the bottom portion. This is asserted because at least one connector 118 is disclosed as being clamped about barrel nut 155, ¶ [0045], for example.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
Claim 6 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Daniel in view of US 2012/0036756 to Brown.
Anent the claims, Daniel discloses the claimed invention as applied above except for wherein the release mechanism further comprises a pair of members pivotally mounted to the bottom portion wherein each of the pair of members have a portion configured to be received within a feature of the upper rail extension.
Brown teaches a member 104, Fig. 3, for example, pivotally mounted to the upper portion, via 116, wherein the member has a portion 108 configured to be received within a feature 142 of the bottom portion for coupling purposes, except for there being a pair of members being mounted to the bottom portion received within a feature of the upper portion.
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to modify Daniel as taught by Brown in order to couple the components. Further rationale: All claimed elements were known in the prior art and one skilled in the art could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods with no change in their respective functions, and the combination would have yielded predictable results to a skilled artisan at the time the invention was made.
With respect to there being a pair, i.e., duplication, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to duplicate the pivotal member, since it has been held that mere duplication of the essential working parts of a device involves only routine skill in the art. St, Regis Paper Co. v. Bemis Co., 193 USPQ 8.
With respect to reversing, see above, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to reverse the coupling components from upper to lower portions and vice versa, since it has been held that a mere reversal of the essential working parts of a device involves only routine skill in the art. In re Einstein, 8 USPQ 167.
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 29 and 33 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Conclusion

DETAILED ACTION
The withdrawal of claims 1-2 and 4-9 and amendment to claim 16 in the response filed July 8, 2014 have been acknowledged.
AIA
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Response to arguments
3. Claim 16 was objected to in the previous action for a minor informality. The examiner thanks the applicant for amending claim 16 and thus withdraws the objection.
4. Applicant’s arguments, see pages 7-10 of applicant’s remarks, filed July 8, 2014, with respect to the rejection(s) of claim(s) 3 and 13 under 103(a) have been fully considered and are not persuasive. The argument that Walter does not teach a continuous process is not persuasive. Walter teaches that the object to be cleaned is placed in a vessel and then sequentially cleaning and rising fluid pass though the vessel [col 2 lines 13-17]. In addition, Walter teaches that the washing or rinsing liquid is returned to the tank after use for reuse [col 3 lines 3-6]. This sequential process of steps and returning the liquid back to the system for reuse of Walter reads on a continuous process. Please refer to the detailed discussion below.
The argument which is implied by the applicant is that Hayes does not teach separate tanks and that it is not obvious to combine Hayes with Walter is not persuasive. While Walter is being relied upon to teach a continuous process, Hayes also teaches cleaning using solvating and rinsing agents (col 10 lines 22-45). Hayes teaches a weir (13) or barrier to produce a section for solvating agent (14) and another section for rinsing agent (15), as seen from fig 1 of Hayes. These sections represent different containers or tanks. Please refer to the detailed discussion below.
The argument that it is not obvious to combine Donnelly for teaching distillation with the combined teaching of Walter and Hayes is not persuasive. In fact the combination of Walter and Hayes suggests that it is known to recycle the cleaning fluids for reuse in the system using distillation [col 10 lines 45-55 of Walter]. Donnelly teaches a method that utilizes distillation [col 3 lines 35-40] for recovering and recycling solvents in order to clean contaminated solvents and preparing them to be reused again [col 3 lines 35-50]. Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to utilize distillation for separating contaminants from the rinsing solvent of Donnelly with the method of cleaning electronic components of Walter in order to achieve the predictable result of separating contaminants from the rinsing solvent to recover the rinsing solvent and reusing the rinsing agent back in the rinse tank. Please refer to the detailed discussion below.
The argument that it is not obvious to combine Tonkovich for teaching a micro-still with the combination of Walter, Hayes, and Donnelly is not persuasive. However, the combination of Walter, Hayes, and Donnelly teach that it is known to utilize distillation for separating contaminants from the rinsing solvent [col 10 lines 45-55 of Walter and col 3 lines 35-40 of Donnelly]. Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention for the distillation tank of Donnelly to be a micro-still as taught by Tonkovich in order to achieve the predictable result of separating contaminants from the rinsing agent and to directing the residual solvating agent and contaminants to a waste disposal (as taught by bottoms product of micro-still of Tonkovich). Please refer to the detailed discussion below.
The argument that the examiner found it necessary to combine four references to reject the claims is not persuasive. In response to applicant's argument that the examiner has combined an excessive number of references, reliance on a large number of references in a rejection does not, without more, weigh against the obviousness of the claimed invention. See In re Gorman, 933 F.2d 982, 18 USPQ2d 1885 (Fed. Cir. 1991).
The argument that the combination of Walter, Hayes, Donnelly, and Tonkovich is based from hindsight and is improper is not persuasive. There is a motivation for the references to be combined with each other and that the combination is not based on hindsight. Walter provides a reasoning to combine with Hayes. The combination of Walter and Hayes provide a reasoning to combine with Donnelly, and the combination of Walter, Hayes, and Donnelly provide a reasoning to combine with Tonkovich. Furthermore, in response to applicant's argument that the examiner's conclusion of obviousness is based upon improper hindsight reasoning, it must be recognized that any judgment on obviousness is in a sense necessarily a reconstruction based upon hindsight reasoning. But so long as it takes into account only knowledge which was within the level of ordinary skill at the time the claimed invention was made, and does not include knowledge gleaned only from the applicant's disclosure, such a reconstruction is proper. See In re McLaughlin, 443 F.2d 1392, 170 USPQ 209 (CCPA 1971). Please refer to the arguments above and the detailed discussion below.
The argument that claims 10,12,14, and 16 are nonobvious since claim 3 upon which claims 10 and 12 depend and claims 13 upon which claim 14 and 16 depend is also nonobvious is not persuasive. Since the arguments related to why claims 3 and 13 are not obvious are not persuasive, the argument that claims 10,12,14, and 16 is not obvious is also not persuasive. Please refer to the detailed discussion below.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
5. The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
6. The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
7. Claims 3 and 10-16 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Walter (U.S Patent 6,348,101 B1) in view of Hayes (U.S Patent 5,716,457) and Donnelly et al. (U.S Patent 6,159,345) and Tonkovich (PG Pub 20060016215).
8. Regarding claims 3 and 13 Walter teaches a method for continuously separating contaminants
from rinse solvent in a system for cleaning electronic and other components comprising (col 2 lines 1-35,
col 3 lines 3-6): treating a contaminated substrate that has been subjected to treatment with a solvating
agent [terpene reads on solvating agent] with a rinsing solvent to remove any remaining contaminants
and solvating residual agent in a rinse tank whereby contaminants removed from said component collect
in said rinse tank; and removing contaminated rinsing solvent from said rinse tank (col 10 lines 10-55).
Walter fails to teach a separate rinse tank; and fails to teach removing contaminated rinsing solvent from
rinse tank to a micro-still to separate contaminants from the rinsing solvent, directing rinsing solvent agent
back to rinse tank, and directing residual solvating agent and contaminants to waste disposal.
However, Hayes teaches that it is known to apply solvating agents in one tank and the rinse fluid in
another tank in order to achieve the predictable result of removing contaminants and residual solvating
agents from electronic and other components wherein the use of a separate rinsing tank minimizes contamination of the rinsing liquid with the solvating agent and removed contaminants (col 11 lines 1-32). Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to clean components in another tank using solvating agents before cleaning them in the rinse tank of Walter using a rinsing agent in order to achieve the predictable result of cleaning contaminants and residual solvating agents from electronic and other components to minimize contamination of the rinsing liquid with the solvating agent and removed contaminants. Although Walter is aware of disposing, recycling, and reusing the rinse solvent using a distillation recovery system can be done (col 10 lines 35-55), the combination of Walter and Hayes fail to specifically teach separating contaminants from the rinsing solvent, directing rinsing agent back to the rinse tank, and directing residual solvating agent and contaminants to waste disposal. However, Donnelly teaches a method that utilizes distillation (col 3 lines 35-40) for recovering and recycling solvents in order to clean contaminated solvents and preparing them to be reused again (col 3 lines 35-50). Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to utilize distillation for separating contaminants from the rinsing solvent of Donnelly with the method of cleaning electronic components of Walter in order to achieve the predictable result of separating contaminants from the rinsing solvent to recover the rinsing solvent and reusing the rinsing agent back in the rinse tank. The combination of Walter, Hayes, and Donnelly fail to teach specifically that a micro-still is used to separate the contaminants from the rinsing solvent and that the residual solvating agents and contaminants are directed to a waste disposal. However, Tonkovich teaches that it is well known to use a micro-still for a distillation process for separating fluids (abstract and para 0051) and for withdrawing a bottoms product from the system (para 0052). Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention for the distillation tank of Donnelly to be a micro-still as taught by Tonkovich in order to achieve the predictable result of separating contaminants from the rinsing agent and to directing the residual solvating agent and contaminants to a waste disposal (as taught by bottoms product of micro-still of Tonkovich).
9. Regarding claims 10 and 14, the combination of Walter, Hayes, Donnelly, and Tonkovich teach
that the rinsing solvent is separated from said contaminants in said micro-still by distilling said rinsing
solvent, and then condensing the resulting vaporized rinsing solvent to be directed back to said rinse tank
[The micro-still of Tonkovich includes a condenser to obtain a distillate. (para 0051 of Tonkovich), which
reads on the system represented by Donnelly where a condenser eventually returns the cleaned solvent
(col 4 lines 35-65 of Donnelly) to be reused as stated by Walter (col 10 lines 45-55)].
10. Regarding claims 11 and 15, the combination of Walter, Hayes, Donnelly, and Tonkovich teach
that the contaminated rinsing solvent is passed to said micro-still by pumping (col 6 lines 30-60 of
Donnelly).
11. Regarding claims 12 and 16, the combination of Walter, Hayes, Donnelly, and Tonkovich teach
contaminated rinsing solvent is passed to said micro-still responsive to a still liquid level control (col 6
lines 50-60 of Donnelly) and that the pump is activated responsive to the liquid level in the still (col 12
lines 37-67 of Donnelly).
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action. In no event, however, will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the date of this final action.

If attempts to reach the examiner by telephone are unsuccessful, the examiner’s supervisor, Michael Kornakov can be reached on 571-272-20971303. The fax phone number for the organization where this application or proceeding is assigned is 571-273-8300.

DETAILED ACTION
This action is in response to the submission filed on 2/24/2015. Claims 1-20 are presented for examination. The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Response to Arguments- 35 USC § 103
Applicant's arguments filed 2/24/2015 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Argument 1:
Applicant argues on page 5 that Lee fails to disclose “modeling a drill string having a plurality of ranging device contact locations.”
The contact location of the ranging devices/magnets are shown in Kennedy, paras [0110-0112], “The magnets (142) are shown schematically on FIG. 6 in order to indicate possible locations for incorporating the magnets with the drilling motor, and not in order to depict a particular preferred configuration for the magnets (142)”. In response to applicant's arguments against the references individually, one cannot show nonobviousness by attacking references individually where the rejections are based on combinations of references. See In re Keller, 642 F.2d 413, 208 USPQ 871 (CCPA 1981); In re Merck & Co., 800 F.2d 1091, 231 USPQ 375 (Fed. Cir. 1986).
Argument 2:
Applicant argues on page 6 that Lee fails to teach “simulating the response of the modeled drill string…to create a drill string profile.
Paragraph [0368] of Lee states, "simulate downhole conditions as closely as possible" and para [0392] states, "modeling would be required to ensure that the coil could reach the borehole intersection". Applicant argues that a drill string profile is something that anticipates points of contact between the string and the walls of the wellbore. Paragraph [0028] states that the Lee invention “relates to drilling methods for connecting together at least two boreholes to provide or form at least one U-tube borehole.” Clearly, the entire point of simulating downhole conditions is to anticipate the behavior of the string as it drills/comes in contact with the walls of the wellbore.
Argument 3:
Applicant argues on page 6 that Lee fails to teach the determination of contact points.
Paragraph [0035] of Lee recites, “a U-tube borehole may be drilled as a first borehole extending from the first end at the first surface location and a second borehole extending from the second end at the second surface location. The first borehole and the second borehole may then intersect at a borehole intersection to provide the U-tube borehole.” While the term “contact point” is not explicitly used, clearly the drill string must come into contact with the borehole wall in order to drill the downhole path.
Argument 4:
Applicant argues on page 6 that Homan fails to teach an insulator member located between the ranging device contact locations.
This claim language is not found in the claims as written. The claim states that the insulator member is adjacent to one contact point. The magnetic ranging devices of Kennedy as shown in paras [0110-0112] were applied to the claims, not the transmitter/receivers of Homan. Even if the transmitter/receiver is applied, the insulator is still adjacent to the devices, even if the devices are located inside the insulator.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims under 35 U.S.C. 103(a), the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered therein were made absent any evidence to the contrary. Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and invention dates of each claim that was not commonly owned at the time a later invention was made in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).

Lee as modified by Kennedy discloses a method for simulating a ranging system on a drill string. However Lee as modified by Kennedy does not explicitly disclose insulator members/sleeves/tubes. Homan does teach this.

DETAILED ACTION
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
The communication dated Sept. 02, 2015 has been entered and fully considered. Claims 1-16 are currently pending. Claims 1-2, 4-5, 7-9, 11-12, and 14 were amended. Claims 15-16 are new.
Claim Objections
Claims 15 and 16 are objected to because of the following informalities:
The term “absorbant” should be spelled “absorbent”.
Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(b) the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country, more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States.
Claims 1, 4, 7-8, 11, and 14 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by US Patent No. 5,145,658 to Chao (hereinafter referred to as Chao).
In regard to claim 1, Chao teaches in Fig. 2 a recovery apparatus of carbon dioxide comprising:
an absorption column 124 configured to bring a gas containing carbon dioxide S-4 (in line 126) into contact with an absorbing liquid S-6, S-7 (in lines 130 and 194, respectively) and to allow the absorbing liquid to absorb carbon dioxide (col. 13 lines 38-46, col. 12 lines 13-18);
a regeneration column 144 for regenerating the absorbing liquid, configured to cause the absorbing liquid having carbon dioxide absorbed in the absorption column to release carbon dioxide by heat (released carbon dioxide exits the regeneration column 144 in line 156; heat is provided through steam generators 138,140 and reboiler 116) (col. 10 line 62 – col. 11 line 15);
a circulation system (represented by lines 130, 136, 142, 146, 150, 152, 156, 164, 168, 172, 174, 176, 178, 180, 184, 188, 190, 192, 194, 198, 200; and the pumps, valves, and heat exchangers/coolers on those lines) configured to circulate the absorbing liquid in such a manner that the absorbing liquid flows from the absorption column 124 and returns to the absorption column 124 through the regeneration column 144 (See Fig. 2); and
a steam supply system (reboilers 138, 140) configured to supply to the regeneration column steam available for a heat source that regenerates the absorbing liquid, the steam supply system comprising: a steam generator 138, 140 configured to generate steam (col. 13 lines 58-60, col. 14 lines 49-51), using at least one of the absorbing liquid that returns to the absorption column 124 by the circulation system and the absorbing liquid in the absorption column 124, and a compression device (steam jet 186) configured to compress the generated steam S-12 to raise a temperature of the steam S-12 to be higher (stream S-11 at 298°C and 43738 lb/h, S-12 at 223.3°F and 33311 lb/h, and S-13 at 234.3°F and 27937 lb/h gives a temperature for the stream in line 188 of ~257.01°F and a higher pressure than that of streams S-12 and S-13; Example 2 table) than a regeneration temperature of the absorbing liquid (S-24: 243.6°F; Example 2 table) (col. 13 line 49 – col. 14 line 45).
In regard to claim 4, Chao teaches the recovery apparatus of carbon dioxide according to claim 1, wherein the steam generator 140 comprises a tank configured to depressurize the absorbing liquid to generate steam S-12 (see the table for Example 2 in cols. 11-14: S-12 has a lower pressure at 15.5 psia than S-24 at 22.5 psia), and the absorbing liquid is decreased in a temperature by the generation of the steam in the tank (the absorbing liquid in S-24 has a temperature of 243.6°F before tank 140 and a temperature of 223.3°F after; Example 2 table).

Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 3, 5-6, 10, and 12-13 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Chao, as discussed above in regard to claims 4 and 11, respectively.
In regard to claims 3, 5, 10, and 12, Chao teaches the recovery apparatus of carbon dioxide and method for its use according to claims 1 and 8, respectively. Chao teaches the steam supply system/step comprises a first steam generator/generation step (in reboiler 140) configured to generate the steam from the absorbing liquid that returns to the absorption column/step 124. Chao does not disclose a second steam generator/generation step configured to generate the steam from the absorbing liquid in the absorption column/step. However, Chao does teach absorption of an acid gas by an alkaline scrubbing agent causes the rich scrubbing solution temperature to increase by virtue of the heat of reaction between the acid gas and the alkaline agent (col. 1 lines 21-24). It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to reclaim the heat from the absorption of an acid gas by an alkaline scrubbing agent by placing a steam generator having a tank and followed by the compression device 186 in the absorption column since this would supply heat for the steam production as well as remove heat from the absorption process. As is well known in the art, according to Henry’s Law, the absorption process becomes more efficient at lower temperatures.
In regard to claims 6 and 13, Chao teaches the recovery apparatus of carbon dioxide and method for its use according to claims 4 and 11. Chao does not disclose the apparatus is configured to include a plurality of the compression devices and to compress the steam stepwise, however, this is considered to be a duplication of parts and that by so duplicating the compression device and placing the duplicates in series, the steam would be compressed in a stepwise manner. The mere duplication of parts has no patentable significance unless a new and unexpected result is produced. See MPEP 2144.04 VI B.
Claims 14 and 15 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Chao, as discussed above in regard to claims 1 and 8, respectively, in view of US Patent No. 4,112,050 to Sartori et al. (hereinafter referred to as Sartori).
In regard to claims 14 and 15, Chao teaches the apparatus and method of claims 1 and 8, respectively. Chao teaches the absorbent comprises an alkaline solution such as K2CO3 and KHCO3. Chao does not disclose the absorbing liquid includes an amine absorbent.
Sartori teaches that carbon dioxide absorbents comprising potassium carbonate or potassium bicarbonate advantageously comprises an amine (col. 5 lines 60-68). The inclusion of an amine improves the efficiency, effectiveness and cyclic working capacity of the acid gas scrubbing processes (col. 4 lines 28-31).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to include in the absorbent as taught by Chao an amine as taught by Sartori in order to improve the efficiency, effectiveness and cyclic working capacity of the acid gas scrubbing processes.
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 2 and 9 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed Sept. 02, 2015 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
On pages 11-12 of the applicant remarks, applicant argue that “Turning now to the cited art, Chao describes steam generation from a lean scrubbing solution returning to the absorber. However, the teachings of Chao are different from the claimed invention. For example, as the scrubbing solution of Chao (potassium carbonate solution, etc.) is of a different type from the absorbing liquid of the present invention, the absorption-regeneration mechanism of Chao is different from that of the present invention.1”
In response to applicant's argument that the references fail to show certain features of applicant’s invention, it is noted that the features upon which applicant relies (i.e., the absorbing liquid composition) are not recited in the rejected claim(s) 1-14. Although the claims are interpreted in light of the specification, limitations from the specification are not read into the claims. See In re Van Geuns, 988 F.2d 1181, 26 USPQ2d 1057 (Fed. Cir. 1993). However, instant claims 15 and 16 teach the absorbent includes amine. Chao teaches a scrubbing liquid of K2CO3 and KHCO3. Sartori teaches it is known to include an amine in the absorbent of K2CO3 and KHCO3 in order to improve absorption efficiency (see the rejection of claims 15-16 under 35 USC 103 above).
On page 12 of the Applicant Remarks, Applicant argues "Specifically, in Example 2, the rich scrubbing solution of Chao is cooled from 254.9 °F (S-15) to 233 °F (S-8) before it is supplied to the regenerator, and it is regenerated by means of steam stripping. This is different from the present invention comprising regeneration by heat based on thermal equilibrium. Indeed, the liquid temperature of Chao is high (237.1-254.9 °F (see S-7 and S-15) in the absorber column 124,2 and near the temperature inside the regenerator. If an absorbing liquid with amine absorbent was used in Chao, absorption of carbon dioxide would have been difficult."
In response to applicant's argument that the references fail to show certain features of applicant’s invention, it is noted that the features upon which applicant relies (i.e., regeneration by heat based on thermal equilibrium) are not recited in the rejected claim(s). Although the claims are interpreted in light of the specification, limitations from the specification are not read into the claims. See In re Van Geuns, 988 F.2d 1181, 26 USPQ2d 1057 (Fed. Cir. 1993). Furthermore, Sartori teaches it is known to use amines in absorbent comprising K2CO3 and KHCO3 as discussed above in regard to claims 15 and 16 under the heading of 35 USC 103.
On page of the Applicant Remarks, Applicant argues "Accordingly, the steam temperature is not important for Chao, and Chao fails to disclose the final temperature and pressure of the steam that is supplied to the generator. In other words, Chao does not teach that the steam is heated by compression to be higher in temperature than the regeneration temperature. "
The Examiner notes that the steam in S-11 is at a temperature of 298°C, 65 psia, and 43,738 lb/h while the steam in S-12 is at a temperature of 223°C, 15.5 psia, and 33,311 lb/h. By calculations of simple thermodynamics, the temperature of the combined stream leaving steam jet 186 will be well over 260.5°C which is above the regeneration temperature of 243.6°C. This change in temperature happens at the same time as the pressure is raised for steam S-12, i.e., steam S-12 undergoes compression.
On page of the Applicant Remarks, Applicant argues " Moreover, the steam jet 186 of Chao is not a compression device. Instead, it is a vacuum inducing device to reduce the pressure on the shell side of the reboiler. In the table of Example 2, the pressure values of steam are 65.0 psia (S-11), 15.5 psia (S-12) and 22.5 psia (S-13). These values are not considered as such a condition that the steam jet 186 may compress the steam S-12. Even if the temperature of steam S-12 is raised, it must be raised by mixing with the steam S-11, and not due to compression. Therefore, the steam jet 186 is not a compression device to heat the steam to be higher than the regeneration temperature. Thus, Chao does not teach compression heating of the steam so as not to decrease the temperature in the regenerator.”
The Examiner respectfully disagrees as evidenced by at least US Publication No. 2011/0079504 to Govindan et al. [0045], US Patent No. 5,766,412 to Railey (col. 5 lines 57-60), and US Patent No. 5,435,977 to Chao (col. 2 lines 14-16) that a steam jet ejector is a compression device.
For at least the reasons given above, the Examiner maintains the rejections of claims 1, 3-8, and 10-16.
Conclusion

(b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.

The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.

3. Claims 1, 9 7, and claims depending therefrom are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter as the claims do not fall within one of the four categories of patent eligible subject matter because the claims are directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more.
The rejection rationale below is made in view of the following guidance provided to the examining corps, available to the public at the following world-wide web address: http://www.uspto.gov/patent/laws-and-regulations/examination-policy/2014-interim-guidance-subject-matter-eligibility-0 (Last visited September 15, 2015).
Independent claims 1,9 are directed towards a process, where claim 14 is directed towards a product. However, independent claims 1,9 and 14 are directed towards an abstract idea. Certain concepts have been judicially determined to be abstract ideas, including "fundamental economic practices," "ideas themselves," "certain methods of organizing human activity," and “mathematical relationships/formulae.” In this case, claims 1,9 and 14 recite the following limitations: “receiving a reference signal for channel state measurement; calculating a first value; calculating a second value; generating bit information;“ which are directed towards the abstract idea of "ideas themselves", in that the a reference signal for channel state measurement, a first value, and second value thereof, which are recited as being given certain values or comparing to a ratio, and then feedback, is essentially “using categories to organize, store and transmit information.” Claims directed towards the abstract idea of “mathematical relationships/formulae”, in that the “receiving a reference signal for channel state measurement; calculating a first value; calculating a second value; generating bit information;“ thereof, which are recited, is essentially " algorithm for calculating parameters indicating an abnormal condition’" Claims directed towards the abstract idea of " algorithm for calculating parameters indicating an abnormal condition’ " have been judicially determined to be ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. {}101. See (Digitech Image Technologies, LLC v. Electronics For Imaging, Inc., Case No. 13-1600 (Fed. Cir. July 14, 2014),).
Additionally, claims 1,9 and 14 as a whole do not amount to significantly more than the abstract idea in that additional limitations of claims 1,9 and 14, including the receiving from a base station, the transmitting from the base station, and feeding back to the base station merely append well-understood, routine and conventional activities previously known in the industry, which is also like generally linking the use of the abstract idea to the particular technological environment of a UE/eNB system and MIMO system. Therefore, claims 1,9 and 14, and claims depending therefrom, are interpreted herein as being subject matter ineligible under 35 U.S.C. §101.

A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains.
