With regards to claims 1 and 14, Li et al discloses in (fig.5), an operation method of a terminal in a multi-user multi-input multi-output (MIMO) system (wireless communication system shown in fig. 2), comprising:
receiving (RF module, UE,222 shown in fig. 3) a reference signal for channel state measurement from a base station (501);
calculating (processor, 710, a first value that is a ratio of a signal transmitted from the base station to the terminal and noise based on the reference signal( see step 502, The user equipment is comprised in a wireless communication system. The wireless communication system further comprises the first base station. The user equipment estimates a first Signal to Interference and Noise Ratio, SINR, based on reference signals for subframes of a first type)
calculating a second value that is a ratio of interference from the base station and noise based on the reference signal (see step 503, The user equipment further estimates a second SINR based on reference signals for subframes of a second type) and
feeding back the first value to the base station (see step 509, The user equipment further calculates channel state information based on said created compensated first SINR and said created compensated second SINR. The user equipment then transmits (feedback) the calculated channel state information to the first base station).
Li et al discloses all of the subject matter discussed above, but is not explicit about generating bit information by comparing a ratio of the second value and the first value with a predetermined threshold value; and feeding back the bit information to the base station.
However, Park et al discloses fig. 5, [0111], the UE2 acquires the interference-reflecting CQI due to the access of the UE2 according to the aforementioned second feedback scheme, compares the acquired interference-reflecting CQI with the required CQI, and then feeds back the MUI and the basic CQI or the interference-reflecting CQI. In [0120]-[0121], the UE determines whether a difference between the basic CQI value and the interference-reflecting CQI value is larger than the predetermined threshold (Th) in step S436. When the difference between the basic CQI value and the interference-reflecting CQI value is smaller than the threshold, it means that an effect of the access of the additional UE is low and thus the UE feeds back the interference-reflecting CQI value in step S440. In [0103], an MUI flag is set to "1" and then transmitted. When the additional UE is inaccessible, the MUI flag is set to "0" and then transmitted (feedback).
In claim 14, feeding back an MUI of an accessible flag (one bit) and the interference-reflecting CQI value when a required CQI corresponding to a minimum requirement for a currently accessed UE or a UE to be additionally accessed is set and the interference-reflecting CQI value is larger than a required CQI value, and feeding back an MUI of an inaccessible flag and the basic CQI value when the interference-reflecting CQI value is smaller than a required CQI value.
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before theeffective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the invention of Li et al astaught by Park et al for generating bit information by comparing a ratio of the second value and the first value with a predetermined threshold value; and feeding back the bit information to the base station.
Rationale: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art thatwould have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or tocombine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention

(1) a finding that there was some teaching, suggestion, or motivation, either inthe references themselves or in the knowledge generally available to one of ordinaryskill in the art, to modify the reference or to combine reference teachings;
(2) a finding that there was reasonable expectation of success; and
(3) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries may benecessary, in view of the facts of the case under consideration, to explain a conclusionof obviousness.
In this case:
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before theeffective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the invention of Li et al astaught by Park et al for generating bit information by comparing a ratio of the second value and the first value with a predetermined threshold value; and feeding back the bit information to the base station with a reasonable expectation of success, thusto transfer information on all interference between UEs to a BS for efficient MU-MIMO support (see Park et al , [0012]).

DETAILED ACTION
This Office Action is in response to the Applicant’s communication (Amendment) filed on 10 February 2014. In virtue of this communication, Claims 1-7 are currently pending in the instant application.
AIA
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 10 February 2014 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
With respect to Claim 1, Applicant asserts that Fujisawa is insufficient to teach “first, second, and third dichroic mirrors between the fluorescent members and the prism” (see Page 3 of Remarks), particularly as Fujisawa is directed to a different invention. Examiner respectfully disagrees with applicant’s assessment. Examiner respectfully submits that to establish a prima facia case of obviousness against a particular claim, the teachings of the secondary reference (in this case, Fujisawa) must suggest a potential modification of the primary reference system (in this case Inoue, as modified by Kajino and Kato) which would have been obvious at the time of invention absent the benefit of the instant application's disclosure such that the combination system teaches the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim. Fujisawa clearly teaches a dichroic separation and recombination system disposed between an illumination module and a prism. Inoue, as modified by Kajino and Kato, discloses a system having a prism and an illumination system, wherein the illumination module comprises a plurality of collimators and a plurality of fluorescent members. Thus as the missing feature, namely a dichroic mirror system comprising three dichroic mirrors with the particular reflection characteristics claimed and which at least combine the light beam in some manner, is fully taught by Fujisawa and the condition exist in the primary reference to accept the missing feature, namely that there be an illumination module and a prism to dispose the dichroic system between, all that remains is the question of obviousness at the time of invention. Examiner respectfully submits, as presented in the preceding office action, that the motivation to one of ordinary skill in the art (pursuant to “[c]ombining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results” as set forth in MPEP 2143 and KSR International Co. v. Teleflex Inc.) would be to predictably improve pixels spacing in the scanning system, thereby improving image sharpness. Accordingly, Applicant’s arguments are not persuasive.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a1 whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1, 3, and 7 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Inoue (U.S. Patent No. 8,038,299 B2) in view of Kajino et al. (Pub. No.: US 2009/0067033 A1; herein referred to as Kajino), Kato (JP 2004-341105 A), and Fujisawa et al. (U.S. Patent No. 7,040,768 B2; herein referred to as Fujisawa).
With respect to Claims 1, 3, and 7, Inoue discloses, in Figs. 1-4, a laser projection system (data projector apparatus 20) comprising a laser module (semiconductor laser 11) having at least a laser device to emit a laser beam (see Col. 2, Lines 21-22), a red fluorescent member (red fluorescent region 13c1) excited by the laser beam from the laser module to emit a red beam (see Fig. 3 and Col. 3, Lines 25-35), a green fluorescent member (green fluorescent region 13c2) excited by the laser beam from the laser module to emit a green beam (see Fig. 3 and Col. 3, Lines 25-35), a blue fluorescent member (blue fluorescent region 13c3) excited by the laser beam from the laser module to emit a blue beam (see Fig. 3 and Col), wherein the laser projection system can produce image light using a DLP optical module (as shown in Fig. 4) or alternatively a scanning optical module (see Col. 6, Lines 39-44).
Inoue does not appear to explicitly teach the particular arrangement of the optical module for the scanning projection embodiment, and thus does not appear to teach that the optical module comprises a first collimator on a path of the red beam from the red fluorescent member to collimate the red beam, a second collimator on a path of the green beam from the green fluorescent member to collimate the green beam, a third collimator on a path of the blue beam from the blue fluorescent member to collimate the blue beam, a prism receiving the collimated beams from the first collimator, the second collimator, and the third collimator to reflect the red beams, the green beam, and the blue beam respectively, and a scanning optical system projecting the red beams, the green beam, and the blue beam from the prism onto an image surface to form an image, wherein a biaxial scan controller controls the scanning optical system to change paths of the red beam, the green beam, and the blue beam projecting onto the imaging surface.
Kajino discloses, in Fig. 23, an illuminator (comprising laser light sources 401) providing red, green, and blue light (see Page 12, [0237]; wherein laser light source 401 emit light beams of three primary [RGB] colors) to the optical module of a scanning projector, wherein the optical modules comprises a first collimator (the one of collimating lenses 402 associated with the red laser light source 401) on a path of the red beam from the red illumination light to collimate the red beam (see Fig. 23 and Page 12, [0237]; wherein collimating lens 402 receives the red illumination light beam from the red laser light source 401 and collimates said light beam), a second collimator (the one of collimating lenses 402 associated with the green laser light source 401) on a path of the green beam from the green fluorescent member to collimate the green beam (see Fig. 23 and Page 12, [0237]; wherein collimating lens 402 receives the green illumination light beam from the green laser light source 401 and collimates said light beam), a third collimator (the one of collimating lenses 402 associated with the blue laser light source 401) on a path of the blue beam from the blue fluorescent member to collimate the blue beam (see Fig. 23 and Page 12, [0237]; wherein collimating lens 402 receives the blue illumination light beam from the blue laser light source 401 and collimates said light beam), a prism (dichroic prism 403) receiving the collimated beams from the first collimator, the second collimator, and the third collimator to reflect the red beams, the green beam, and the blue beam respectively (see Fig. 23 and Page 12, [0237]; wherein dichroic prism 403 receives the collimated red, green, and blue light beams), and a scanning optical system (scan mirror section 406) projecting the red beams, the green beam, and the blue beam from the prism onto an image surface (screen 420) to form an image (see Fig. 23 and Page 12, [0237]; wherein scan mirror section 406 receives the red, green, and blue light beams from dichroic prism 403 and scans said beams together to form an image on screen 420), wherein a biaxial scan controller (mirror driving section 413) controls the scanning optical system to change paths of the red beam, the green beam, and the blue beam projecting onto the imaging surface (see Fig. 23 and Page 12, [0238] - Page 13, [0240]; wherein mirror driving section 413 controls scan mirror section 406 to change the path of the incident light beams to scan them onto screen 420 [wherein the movement of scan mirror section 406 is bi-axial to scan across the entire screen 420]).
It would have been obvious to replace the DLP optical module of Inoue with a scanning optical module as taught by Kajino to predictably improve color saturation and brightness (“[s]imple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results”; see MPEP 2143 and KSR International Co. v. Teleflex Inc. as cited therein).
Inoue, as modified by Kajino, further does not appear to explicitly teach that the laser emits a single wavelength laser beam, wherein the single wavelength laser beam is ultraviolet.
Kato discloses, in Fig. 1, an excitation laser light source (light emitting diode 101; see [0017], wherein light emitting diode can be a semiconductor laser) emitting light to a phosphor layer on a wheel (color wheel 102; see [0012]-[0014]), wherein the excitation light is a single wavelength laser beam in the ultraviolet spectrum (see [0017]-[0018]).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention to replace the generic laser light source 11 of Inoue, as modified by Kajino, with a laser light source emitting light in a single wavelength, particularly in ultraviolet, as taught by Kato, as a matter of routine engineering choice to produce an economical and light projector (see [0008]-[0009] of Kato) and to predictably improve the quantity of light generated by the fluorescent members (“[s]imple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results”; see MPEP 2143 and KSR International Co. v. Teleflex Inc. as cited therein).
Inoue, as modified by Kajino and Kato, further does not appear to teach that the laser projection system further comprises a first dichroic mirror between the fluorescent members and the prism to pass the red beam therethrough and reflect the green beam and the blue beam, a second dichroic mirror between the fluorescent members and the prism to pass the blue beam therethrough and reflect the green beam, and a third dichroic mirror between the blue fluorescent member and the prism to reflect the blue beam, wherein the red beam, the green beam, and the blue beam reflected by the first dichroic mirror, the second dichroic mirror, and the third dichroic mirror respectively are combined to form the image.
Fujisawa discloses, in Fig. 1, a projector (1) having an illuminator (illuminating optical device 3) and a prism (dichroic prism 43) wherein disposed therebetween is a separation unit (color separating optical system) comprising a first dichroic mirror (dichroic mirror 31) between the illuminator and the prism (see Fig. 1) to pass the red beam therethrough and reflect the green beam and the blue beam (see Fig. 1; wherein the red component of the beam is passed through dichroic mirror 31 and the blue and green components are reflected), a second dichroic mirror (dichroic mirror 32) between the illuminator and the prism (see Fig. 1) to pass the blue beam therethrough and reflect the green beam (see Fig. 1; wherein the green component of the beam is reflected by dichroic mirror 32 and the blue component is passed therethrough), and a third mirror (either of reflecting mirrors 37, 39) between the illuminator and the prism (see Fig. 1) to reflect the blue beam (see Fig. 1; wherein reflecting mirrors 37, 39 reflect the blue component of the beam), wherein the red beam, the green beam, and the blue beam reflected by the first dichroic mirror, the second dichroic mirror, and the third dichroic mirror respectively are combined to form the image (see Fig. 1).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, as a matter of routine engineering choice, to provide a separation unit, as taught by Fujisawa, between the illuminator (which includes the fluorescent members) and prism of Inoue, as modified by Kajino and Kato, to predictably improve pixels spacing in the scanning system, thereby improving image sharpness (“[c]ombining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results”; see MPEP 2143 and KSR International Co. v. Teleflex Inc. as cited therein).
Claim 2 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Inoue in view of Kajino, Kato, and Fujisawa as applied to Claim 1 above, and further in view of Kurosaki et al. (Pub. No.: US 2010/0328632 A1; herein referred to as Kurosaki).
With respect to Claim 2, Inoue, as modified by Kajino, Kato and Fujisawa, discloses all limitations of Claim 1, as cited above.
Inoue, as modified by Kajino, Kato, and Fujisawa, does not appear to explicitly teach an arrangement where the laser projection system further comprises at least a collimator between the laser module and the fluorescent members to collimate the laser beam from the laser module.
Kurosaki discloses, in Fig. 5, an illuminator for a projector (light source device 63) having laser module (comprising light sources 72; see Page 2, [0027], wherein light sources 72 are lasers) and a fluorescent member (fluorescent wheel 71), wherein at least a collimator (collimator lenses 150) is disposed therebetween to collimate the laser beam from the laser module (see Fig. 5 and Page 6, [0069]).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention to provide the illuminator of Inoue, as modified by Kajino, Kato, and Fujisawa, with at least a collimator between the laser module and the fluorescent members as taught by Kurosaki to predictably minimize optical artifacts, such as astigmatisms, in the projected image (“[c]ombining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results”; see MPEP 2143 and KSR International Co. v. Teleflex Inc. as cited therein).
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a). A shortened statutory period for reply to this final action is set to expire THREE MONTHS from the mailing date of this action. In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action. In no event, however, will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the date of this final action.

The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.

DETAILED ACTION
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Applicant’s amendments and remarks filed on 9/26/2014 have been fully considered.
Claims 343-356, 358-360, and 362-375 are pending for examination. Claims 1-342, 357, and 361 are cancelled.
Claim Objections
Claims 343, 345 and 367 is objected to because of the following informalities: In regard to claim 345, the term “for” should be deleted. In regard to claim 367, line 2, “:” should be set forth after “comprising”. Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112 – First paragraph
AIA
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112:
The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.
Claims 344 and 358 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement. The claim(s) contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the relevant art that the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the inventor(s), at the time the application was filed, had possession of the claimed invention. Claim 344 recites the microarray further comprises “a device for a laparoscopic, endoscopic, arthroscopic, or catheter-based procedure for separately extracting, sampling or analyzing the tissue or cells at the sites of administration”. The claimed limitations cover all possible types of “device(s)” for the cited procedure(s) and function(s). Paragraphs [0010] and [0097] of the specification merely disclose a couple examples of the “device” but fail to provide sufficient supports for all possible “device(s)”. Similar deficiencies can be found in claim 358 regarding “one or more device”. The specification does not provide sufficient supports for all possible devices of performing the function of sampling or analyzing.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112 – Second paragraph
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 344, 346, 354, 358, 364, and 371-375 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention. Claims that depend directly or indirectly from claim(s) 344, 346, 354, 358, 364, and 371-375 is/are also rejected due to said dependency.
Claim 344 recites “a device for a laparoscopic, endoscopic, arthroscopic, or catheter-based procedure for separately extracting, sampling or analyzing the tissue or cells at the sites of administration”. First, the limitations recited after terms “for” are considered as intended use(s) which contain insufficient patentable weight(s). Second, the structure of the “device” is not recited in the claims. It is unclear what positive structural limitation(s) is/are intended by the limitation to further limit the claim(s) it depends.
Claim 346 recites “each of the reservoirs may be loaded… which can be released…”. The limitations contain conditional/ optional languages which do not positively claim the limitations (“Language that suggests or makes optional but does not require steps to be performed or does not limit a claim to a particular structure does not limit the scope of a claim or claim limitation”, see MPEP 2103 C and 2111.04). Therefore, the recited limitations are given insufficient patentable weight(s).
Claims 354 and 364 recite “may be indicative…” which do not positively claim the limitation. Therefore, the recited limitations are given insufficient patentable weight(s).
Claim 358 recites “one or more device for separately sampling or analyzing...”. The limitations recited after “for” are considered as intended use(s) which have insufficient patentable weights. The structure of the “ one or more devices” is/are not recited in the claims. It is unclear what positive structural limitation(s) is/are intended by the limitation to further limit the claim(s) it depends.
Claim 371 recites “the method of claim 367 for administration to tissue or cells to determine sensitivity of the tissue or cells to a therapeutic agent”. It is unclear what positive step(s) is/are intended by the limitations. First, it is unclear if the “administration” is a positive step for administrating of anything to the tissue or cells. The parent claim 367 merely recites “at the sites of administration”. Second, the limitation of “to determine” is considered as intended use(s) which contain insufficient patentable weight(s). Third, the relationship(s) between the administration and determination are not recited in the claim. Clarification is requested.
Claim 372 recites “extracting cells or tissue at the site of each release sites within an individual”. First, it is unclear “each release sites” indicates a single site or multiple sites. Second, claim 367, which claim 372 depends from, recites “the sites of extraction”. It is unclear if the “release sites” are the “sites of extraction” or other sites. Clarification is requested.
Claim 373 recites “a device for controlling…”. The limitations recited after “for” are considered as intended use(s) which contain insufficient patentable weight(s). It is suggested that the limitation should be set forth “ a device configured to control…” in order to more positively claim the limitations.
Claims 374 and 375 recite “one or more pump assemblies for delivery of …”. The limitations recited after “for” are considered as intended use(s) which contain insufficient patentable weight(s). It is unclear whether the microarray comprises structure(s) including a carrier fluid, a fluid outlet, a fluid pathway, a reservoir, and distal ported outlet. If the structures are essential to the invention, it is suggested that they should be incorporated in the claims. In addition, claims 374 and 375 recite “…which is implanted at a target tissue site”. It is unclear what portion(s)/ element(s) is/are implanted because the term “which” might indicate one of the recited elements. Clarification is requested.

Claim 344 recites “a device for a laparoscopic, endoscopic, arthroscopic, or catheter-based procedure for separately extracting, sampling or analyzing the tissue or cells at the sites of administration”. First, the limitations recited after terms “for” are considered as intended use(s) which contain insufficient patentable weight(s). Second, the structure of the “device” is not recited in the claims. It is unclear what positive structural limitation(s) is/are intended by the limitation to further limit the claim(s) it depends.
Claim 346 recites “each of the reservoirs may be loaded… which can be released…”. The limitations contain conditional/ optional languages which do not positively claim the limitations (“Language that suggests or makes optional but does not require steps to be performed or does not limit a claim to a particular structure does not limit the scope of a claim or claim limitation”, see MPEP 2103 C and 2111.04). Therefore, the recited limitations are given insufficient patentable weight(s).
Claims 354 and 364 recite “may be indicative…” which do not positively claim the limitation. Therefore, the recited limitations are given insufficient patentable weight(s).
Claim 358 recites “one or more device for separately sampling or analyzing...”. The limitations recited after “for” are considered as intended use(s) which have insufficient patentable weights. The structure of the “ one or more devices” is/are not recited in the claims. It is unclear what positive structural limitation(s) is/are intended by the limitation to further limit the claim(s) it depends.
Claim 371 recites “the method of claim 367 for administration to tissue or cells to determine sensitivity of the tissue or cells to a therapeutic agent”. It is unclear what positive step(s) is/are intended by the limitations. First, it is unclear if the “administration” is a positive step for administrating of anything to the tissue or cells. The parent claim 367 merely recites “at the sites of administration”. Second, the limitation of “to determine” is considered as intended use(s) which contain insufficient patentable weight(s). Third, the relationship(s) between the administration and determination are not recited in the claim. Clarification is requested.
Claim 372 recites “extracting cells or tissue at the site of each release sites within an individual”. First, it is unclear “each release sites” indicates a single site or multiple sites. Second, claim 367, which claim 372 depends from, recites “the sites of extraction”. It is unclear if the “release sites” are the “sites of extraction” or other sites. Clarification is requested.
Claim 373 recites “a device for controlling…”. The limitations recited after “for” are considered as intended use(s) which contain insufficient patentable weight(s). It is suggested that the limitation should be set forth “ a device configured to control…” in order to more positively claim the limitations.
Claims 374 and 375 recite “one or more pump assemblies for delivery of …”. The limitations recited after “for” are considered as intended use(s) which contain insufficient patentable weight(s). It is unclear whether the microarray comprises structure(s) including a carrier fluid, a fluid outlet, a fluid pathway, a reservoir, and distal ported outlet. If the structures are essential to the invention, it is suggested that they should be incorporated in the claims. In addition, claims 374 and 375 recite “…which is implanted at a target tissue site”. It is unclear what portion(s)/ element(s) is/are implanted because the term “which” might indicate one of the recited elements. Clarification is requested.

DETAILED ACTION
AIA
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 22 and 23 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention.
Claim 22, it is unclear if "the elongate member" is referring to "the elongate holding element" or if it is referring to a different member.
Claim 23, “a length of floss” should be - -the floss string- -. Furthermore, it is unclear if "the elongate member" is referring to "the elongate holding element" or if it is referring to a different member.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 13-18, 22, and 24 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over U.S. Patent No. 4,852,728 to Court in view of Charatan (US 4,519,408).
Court discloses a flossing device that includes a segment of dental floss 208 with a sheet 200 rolled around the ends of the floss segment to form two paper sticks separated by a section of exposed floss (see Figures 8 and 9; column 3, lines 56-68; and column 4, lines 1-9), the ends of the floss segment being secured to the paper sticks (see column 3, lines 64-67). The elongate holding member has a frangible section being a score to separate the two paper sticks (202) (see Figure 7). The elongate holding element is formed by rolling a sheet of material wherein the sheet of material is paper (col. 3, lines 60-70). Court does not disclose the floss string having two ends and extending through the bore the ends of the floss string having a greater diameter than the first diameter of the bore. Charatan teaches a flossing device with handles 14, 36 and 16, 38 where the dental floss segment 18 is threaded through the holes 40, 42 of the handles and the floss segment secured thereto (see column, lines 8-33 and Figures 1-3). It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to thread a floss segment onto the handles of a flossing device as disclosed in Charatan in the teaching of Court in order to attach and secure the handles to the floss segment. While Court does not specifically disclose the sheet being T shaped, one of ordinary skill in the art would find it obvious to provide a sheet of different shapes as Court contemplates use of various shapes which may be rolled onto the floss segment (see, for example, column 2, lines 3-6). Court and Charatan disclose the claimed invention except for a graphic or printed character. It further would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to provide visual indicia on elongate element, since it has been held that when the claimed printed matter (graphic or character) is not functionally related to the substrate it will not distinguish the invention from the prior art in terms of patentability. In re Gulack, 217 USPQ 401, (CAFC 1983). The fact that the content of the printed matter placed on the substrate may render the device more convenient by providing an individual with a specific type of character does not alter the functional relationship. Mere support by the substrate for the printed matter is not the kind of functional relationship necessary for patentability. Thus, there is no novel and unobvious functional relationship between the printed matter e.g. visual indicia and the substrate e.g. dental assembly which is required for patentability.
Claims 20 and 23 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Court and Charatan as applied to claim 13 -18, and 24 above, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,234,182 to Berglund.
Court and Charatan disclose the invention as claimed as discussed above. Court also discloses the length of the floss being short (see, for example, column 1, lines 33-40). These references do not specifically disclose the dimensions recited by Applicant. Berglund discloses a flossing device with two handles where each handle may have a length within the range of 20 mm and 60 mm or 1.5 inches and a diameter within the range of between 2mm and 8mm or 1/8 of an inch (see column 3, lines 36-51). It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to include the dimensions of the flossing device disclosed in Berglund in the teaching of Court and Charatan in order to provide a flossing device that may be conveniently handled by a user.
Claim 21 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over U.S. Patent No. 4,852,728 to Court and Charatan as applied to claims 13 -18, 22 and 24 above, and further in view of Published U.S. Patent Application No. 2011/0265811 to Lorch.
Court and Charatan disclose the invention as claimed as discussed above. These references do not specifically disclose the use of a sealant coating. Lorch discloses a flossing device with handles 14, 16 that may be coated in wax (see paragraph 79). It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to include the use of a wax coating as disclosed in Lorch in the teaching of Court and Charatan in order to allow a user to better grip the handles when the handles become wet during use of the device.
Claim 19 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over U.S. Patent No. 4,852,728 to Court and Charatan as applied to claims 13-18, 22 and 24 above, and further in view of Charatan (US 5,174,314).
The combination of Court and Charatan disclose the claimed invention except for the elongate holding element including a plurality of frangible sections. Charatan '314 teaches an elongate holding element including a plurality of frangible sections (14a, 14b) (see Figure 3). It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to have the elongate holding element of the combination of Court and Charatan to have a plurality of frangible sections as taught by Charatan '314 in order to allow for extra cleaning space.
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments filed February 2, 2016 have been considered but are moot because the arguments do not apply to any of the references being used in the current rejection.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

In considering patentability of the claims under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a), the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered therein were made absent any evidence to the contrary. Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and invention dates of each claim that was not commonly owned at the time a later invention was made in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) prior art under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
Claims 6, 8 and 9 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Choi et al. (US 2011/0242468), of record, in view of Sonoda et al. (US 7,859,625).
Regarding claim 6, Choi et al. disclose a liquid crystal display panel (see Figs. 3-4) comprising:
a pair of substrates (100 and 200); and
a liquid crystal layer (3) between the pair of substrates, wherein
at least one of the pair of substrates includes a photo-alignment film (35 or 36),
the photo-alignment film aligns liquid crystal molecules horizontally to a main surface of the at least one of the pair of substrates (para. [0530]),
the liquid crystal display panel includes photospacers (250; paras. [0213-0214]) between the pair of substrates,
the photospacers are on the at least one of the pair of substrates and project toward the liquid crystal layer (see Fig. 4A),
the at least one of the pair of substrates includes a groove (185h) in at least a portion of an area between the photospacers (see Fig. 4A), and
the groove is in a light-shielding region (i.e., region with 220, Fig. 4A).
Choi et al. do not explicitly disclose the liquid crystal layer at a position corresponding to the groove has a thickness substantially equal to or larger than the liquid crystal layer in an active area which is not shielded from light.
However, Sonoda et al. disclose a liquid crystal display panel (see Figs. 1 and 4), wherein a liquid crystal layer (LC) at a position corresponding to a groove (e.g., contact hole at pixel electrode PX) has a thickness substantially equal to or larger than the liquid crystal layer in an active area (i.e., LC at color filter FIL region) which is not shielded from light (i.e., not at black matrix BM region) (see Figs. 1 and 4).
It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the applicant’s invention was made to incorporate wherein the liquid crystal layer at a position corresponding to the groove has a thickness substantially equal to or larger than the liquid crystal layer in an active area which is not shielded from light, as in Sonoda et al., into the LCD panel of Choi et al. to form the color filter layer in an equal or greater thickness than the black matrix layer, and not overlapping, for ease in manufacturing while using less materials.
Regarding claim 8, Choi et al. disclose wherein the at least one of the pair of substrates further includes a polymer layer on a liquid crystal layer side of the photo-alignment film (see Figs. 15 and paras. [0522, 0531, 0534, 0539 and 0541]).
Regarding claim 9, Choi et al. disclose wherein an electrode (191) is on a lateral side and base of the groove, and
the groove is a contact hole (185h) for connecting electrodes (191 and 175h) in layers above and below an interlayer insulation film (181 and/or 182) including the groove to a same potential (see Fig. 4A and paras. [0130-0133]).
Claim 7 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Choi et al. (US 2011/0242468) in view of Sonoda et al. (US 7,859,625) as applied to claim 6 above, and further in view of Andrews et al. (US 2009/0174855), of record.
Regarding claim 7, Choi et al. and Sonoda et al. disclose the limitations of claim 6 above, but fail to explicitly disclose wherein each of the photospacers has a diameter of 14 µm or less as measured on its surface in contact with the at least one of the pair of substrates.
However, Andrews et al. disclose a liquid crystal display panel (see Fig. 3), wherein each of photospacers (303) has a diameter of 14 µm or less as measured on its surface in contact with at least one of a pair of substrates (301 and 302) (paras. [0049, 0051 and 0076]).
It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the applicant’s invention was made to incorporate wherein each of the photospacers has a diameter of 14 µm or less as measured on its surface in contact with the at least one of the pair of substrates, as in Andrews et al., into the LCD panel of Choi et al. and Sonoda et al. to use a small-sized spacer which increases aperture ratio.
Claim 20 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Choi et al. (US 2011/0242468) in view of Sonoda et al. (US 7,859,625) as applied to claim 6 above, and further in view of Kurasawa (US 2011/0187981).
Regarding claim 20, Choi et al. and Sonoda et al. disclose the limitations of claim 6 above, but fail to explicitly disclose wherein the groove has a depth that is not less than half the thickness of the liquid crystal layer at the position corresponding to the groove.
However, Kurasawa discloses a liquid crystal display panel (see Figs. 1-4), wherein a groove (19a) has a depth that is not less than half a thickness of a liquid crystal layer (35) at a position corresponding to the groove (i.e., G2, Fig. 4).
It would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the applicant’s invention was made to incorporate wherein the groove has a depth that is not less than half the thickness of the liquid crystal layer at the position corresponding to the groove, as in Kurasawa, into the LCD panel of Choi et al. and Sonoda et al. to provide a relief area for excess liquid crystal material in a non-display area.
Furthermore, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the applicant’s invention was made to incorporate the depth being not less than half the thickness of the liquid crystal layer at the position corresponding to the groove, since it has been held that where the general conditions of a claim are disclosed in the prior art, discovering the optimum or workable ranges involves only routine skill in the art. See MPEP 2144.05.
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments with respect to claim 6 have been considered but are moot because the arguments do not apply to the secondary reference being used in the current rejection.
Applicant has amended independent claim 6 to include the limitations “the groove is in a light-shielding region, and the liquid crystal layer at a position corresponding to the groove has a thickness substantially equal to or larger than the liquid crystal layer in an active area which is not shielded from light,” and has argued that this distinguishes over Choi et al. These arguments are persuasive; therefore, the previous grounds of rejection have been overcome. However, this is not a patentable distinction since Sonoda et al. disclose these features as discussed above. Therefore, the new grounds of rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) over Choi et al. in view of Sonoda et al. are considered appropriate.
Conclusion
Applicant’s amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
DETAILED ACTION
Information Disclosure Statement
The listing of references in the specification is not a proper information disclosure statement. 37 CFR 1.98(b) requires a list of all patents, publications, or other information submitted for consideration by the Office, and MPEP § 609.04(a) states, "the list may not be incorporated into the specification but must be submitted in a separate paper." Therefore, unless the references have been cited by the examiner on form PTO-892, they have not been considered.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 27-45 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention.
Examiner notes that the claims are replete with indefinite language, non-limiting examples are listed below.
With regard to claim 27: Line 4 of the claim, it’s unclear as to how columns are inserted between separated columns (emphasis added). It appears the hydraulic machine is used to --insert a column module between the lower column module and upper column module--?. Line 5 of the claim, it’s unclear if the recited limitation of “columns” is referencing the previously recited columns. It appears the limitation was meant to be directed to--the column modules--? Further, the limitation "the column" found in line 5 of the claim lacks sufficient antecedent basis. Line 8 of the claim, it’s unclear if the “steel platforms” if referencing the previously steel framework platforms. Line 12 of the claim, the limitation “the columns" lacks sufficient antecedent basis.
With regard to claim 28: Line 1-2 of the claim, it’s unclear how the “process of building vertical column structure” is different from the step of "building a multi-stacked column" as both involve the upper and lower column module. Further, it's unclear as to how the upper column module is hoisted above a cable hoist (3) and the hydraulic machine (6). As shown in figure 2, the upper module being hoisted is initiated by a mobile crane unit (5).
With regard to claim 29: It’s unclear as to what “top end” the claim is referring to, a top end of the low column module or cable hoist? Does applicant means to recite the hydraulic machine is linked or attached to at top end of the lower column module such as shown in figure 3? The limitation "the bottom end" found in line 3 of the claim lacks sufficient antecedent basis.
With regard to claim 30: The scope the front slash in the limitation "module/unit" is unclear. It's unclear if the front slash is equivalent to the word "and" or the word "or". Further, it’s unclear if the "new column module/unit" is the same as the columns to be inserted as recited in claim 1. Last line of the claim, it’s unclear if the limitation “vertical columnar structure” is the same vertical columnar structure recited in claim 29.
With regard to claim 34: It’s unclear as to how the column modules can be configured to be square and cylindrical in shape (emphasis added). Further, it’s unclear as to how the column modules being cylindrical shape can include a four side steel templates casing.
With regard to claim 38: The limitation “the outer surface” found in line 1 of the claim lacks sufficient antecedent basis. It’s unclear if the "lift elevator" recited in the claim is the same as the hydraulic machine recited in claim 27. Note that pg. 12, lines 3-10 of the original specification recites the lift elevator comprises the hydraulically power arms.
With regard to claim 39: It’s unclear if the "lift elevator" recited in the claim is the same as the hydraulic machine recited in claim 27. Note that pg. 12, lines 3-10 of the original specification recites the lift elevator comprises the hydraulically power arms. The limitation “both sides of the columns” lacks sufficient antecedent basis.
With regard to claim 41: Line 3 of the claim, the limitation "each newly erected column" lacks sufficient antecedent basis. Line 3 of the claim, it’s unclear as to what “top end” the claim is referring to, a top end of one of the modules or the column? Examiner notes that it appears the cable hoist is only present at a top end of the multi-stacked column (see figs. 2-3). It’s unclear if the "lift elevator" recited in the claim is the same as the hydraulic machine recited in claim 27. Note that pg. 12, lines 3-10 of the original specification recites the lift elevator comprises the hydraulically power arms. The limitation “both sides of the columns” lacks sufficient antecedent basis. Further, it's unclear as to how the lower module is moved up and down. Examiner submits that it appears that the lower column module is erected and stationary (see fig. 5). Line 6 of the claim, the limitation "the process of multi-stacking column" lacks sufficient antecedent basis. Line 6-7, It's unclear if the recited "vertical columnar structure” is referencing the previously recited "multi-stacked column”. Examiner notes that they appear to be the same. Lines 8-9 of the claim, the limitation "the vertical columnar structure" lacks sufficient antecedent basis.
With regard to claim 42: The limitation "the centre" found in line 2 of the claim lacks sufficient antecedent basis. It's unclear was what centre is being referred to, is applicant referring to the centre of the of building? It’s unclear if the central hydraulic machine and vertical columnar structure is referencing the previously recited machine and column modules found in claim 27.
With regard to claim 43: The limitation "the alternating opening and closing of gateway zone gates" found in line 5 of the claim lacks sufficient antecedent basis. Last line of the claim, the limitation “the gateway zone" lacks sufficient antecedent basis. It’s unclear if the central hydraulic machine and vertical columnar structure is referencing the previously recited machine and column modules found in claim 27. Further, it’s unclear if the "lift elevator" recited in the claim is the same as the hydraulic machine recited in claim 27. Note that pg. 12, lines 3-10 of the original specification recites the lift elevator comprises the hydraulically power arms.
With regard to claim 44: The limitations "the floor platforms”; “the columnar structure" and the “the top” lacks sufficient antecedent basis.
With regard to claim 45: It's unclear as to what top and bottom the claim is referring to. Is applicant referring to the top and bottom of the building?
Response to Amendment
The objection to the drawings has been withdrawn in view of the amendment filed 9/3/15.
The objection of claim 27 has been withdrawn in view of the amendment filed 9/3/15
The rejection of claim 46 under 112 2nd paragraph and 35 USC 103 has been withdrawn in view of the amendment filed 9/3/15.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

DETAILED ACTION
Applicant's amendment filed on 12/28/2016 is acknowledged. Claims 1-7 have been amended. Claims 1-7 are presented for examination on the merits.
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Terminal Disclaimer
The terminal disclaimer filed on 12/28/2016 disclaiming the terminal portion of any patent granted on this application which would extend beyond the expiration date of Patent No. US 8,639,947 B2 respectively have been reviewed and is accepted. The terminal disclaimer has been recorded.
Response to Arguments
1. In light of the Terminal Disclaimer filed on 12/28/2016, the Examiner hereby withdraws the Non-Statutory Double Patenting rejection of the claims.
2. With regards to the rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 112 Applicant’s amendment to the claims is acknowledged. In light of the amendments and applicant’s remarks in page 4 filed on 12/28/2016 have been fully considered and are persuasive. The rejections to the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) are hereby withdrawn.
3. Applicant's arguments see pages 7-9 filed on 12/28/2016 with respect to the rejection under 35 USC § 103(a) have been fully considered but is moot because newly added limitation to the claim (s) requires a new ground of rejection necessitated by amendments. In light of the aforesaid amendments and upon further search/consideration the new ground of rejection to the respective claims is presented below. The reasons of obviousness are included below in this office action.
4. With regards to claims 1-7 rejected under 35 USC § 101, Applicant’s amendments to the claims are acknowledged. However, after careful review, the rejection under 35 USC §101 of the claims is maintained as the claimed limitations do not meet the subject matter eligibility under Alice analysis. The applicant argues that present invention does not merely deal with manipulating information using mathematical relationships, but rather with a new architecture that is based on placing an encryption module inside the database management software (DBMS), just above the database cache, and using a dedicated technique to encrypt each database value together with its coordinates. These two properties allow the proposed new architecture to achieve a high level of data security, while offering enhanced performance and total transparency to the application layer. Further, Applicant argues that claim 1 contains an inventive concept sufficient to transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
The examiner respectfully disagrees and notes that the amended claims fall under one of the four main categories, namely an idea of itself (for example, manipulating information using mathematical operations). The claims include additional elements (e.g., placing a dedicated encryption module in a layer belonging to a layered application architecture and being above a database cache, said dedicated encryption module is being transparent to the application layer) that are insufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception because the limitations are merely instructions to implement the abstract idea on an application architecture that are well-understood, routine and conventional activities previously known to the industry (e.g. mere placement of an encryption module in an application layer which appears to have no significance in encrypting database values). In other words, the encryption module being above a database cache does nothing in encrypting data that might be traversing a network or temporarily residing in the server's memory (i.e. data-in-motion, data-in-use, data-at-rest). Furthermore, encrypting a value using coordinates can be performed by human activities using pen and paper and/or mental operations without requiring any computer-controlled automated systems. This is similar to other concepts that have been identified as abstract by the courts, such as organizing information through mathematical correlations (Digitech).
Further, the mechanism of mere placement of an encryption module just above the database cache and separately encrypting database values using coordinates is a generic computer operation that does not enhance the functionality of the computer.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 101
5. 35 U.S.C. 101 reads as follows:
Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
6. Claim 1 is directed to encrypting a value with its coordinates. The claimed steps, “placing a dedicated encryption module inside a Database Management Software above a database cache; b. encrypting each value of said database together with the coordinates of said value using a dedicated encryption method” are merely directed to encrypting data, are therefore abstract (e.g. an idea of itself – encrypting data using a dedicated encryption method).
The claims do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the abstract idea (because the limitations are merely instructions to implement the abstract idea and require no more than a generic computer to perform generic computer functions that are well-understood, routine and conventional activities previously known to the industry (e.g. placing a dedicated encryption module inside a Database Management Software.. encrypting each value of said database together with the coordinates of said value).
The features claimed are generic and ancillary to the purpose of the invention which is encrypting a value together with its coordinate – this is not novel, but neither is its subject matter as would be understood by those skilled in the art. Further, the claim does not recite an improvement to another technology or technical field, an improvement to the functioning of the computer itself, or meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of an abstract idea to a particular technological environment or field of use.
Further, the claimed functions such as “encrypting each value of said database together with the coordinates of said value” (Claim 1) and “…wherein said encryption method is implemented according to: E.sub.nc k(V.sub.trc)=E.sub.k(.mu.(t,r,c).sym.V.sub.trc); wherein V.sub.trc--is a plaintext value located in a table t, row r and column c..” (Claim 2) are mathematical and thus directed towards an abstract idea.
The examiner notes that the invention appears to stop short of meaningful limitations by simply “encrypting each value….together with the coordinate”.
7. Dependent claims 2-7 do not represent significantly more and are too directed to non-statutory subject matter.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
8. In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status
9. The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
10. The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims under 35 U.S.C. 103(a), the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered therein were made absent any evidence to the contrary. Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and invention dates of each claim that was not commonly owned at the time a later invention was made in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
11. Claims 1 and 5-7 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Sutter (US 6446092 B1) in view of Damiani et al. (Article: Balancing Confidentiality and Efficiency in Untrusted Relational DBMSs, hereinafter, Leppanen) and further in view of Pham et al. (US 7143288 B2, hereinafter, Pham).
Regarding claim 1, Sutter discloses a method for encrypting a database, comprising the steps of: a. placing a dedicated encryption module inside a Database Management Software (DBMS), (Col. 36, lines 5-25: key must be derived using a different algorithm; Col. 63, lines 43-49; Col. 6, lines 43-67: Database Management System) and
[in a layer belonging to a layered application architecture]
and being above a database cache (Col. 44, lines 20-35: dGroup Table: Cached number of related records in dPermissionGroup to prevent record-deletion attacks in that table);
[said dedicated encryption module is being transparent to the application layer]; and
b. encrypting each value of said database together with the [coordinaes of said value] using a dedicated encryption method (Col. 82, lines 33-37, Col, 76, lines 20-25: the encryption `different` in each possible table position, so that even using the same cryptographic key and the same stamp column, the same value will encrypt to a different result in one row than in another; Col. 87, lines 45-50).
Sutter does not explicitly states but Damiani from the same or similar fields of endeavor teaches coordinates of said value (Damiani, Page 94, Left Col. 1st Paragraph: cartographic coordinates; Page 95, left Col; Fig. 2 & associated texts).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention wherein encrypting a value together with the coordinates as taught by Damiani in the teachings of Sutter for the advantage of ensuring an adequate level of protection to databases’ content through database encryption and preventing exposure of sensitive information even if the database server is compromised (Damiani, Page 93, introduction).
The combination of Sutter and Damiani does not explicitly states but Pham from the same or similar fields of endeavor teaches a layer belonging to a layered application architecture (Pham, Figs. 5A, 6 and associated texts: Encryption Driver 208; Col. 11, lines 53-60, Col. 21, lines 10-29: application layer in extended software architecture; Col. 19, lines 45-55: operating at the TCP layer and above; Fig. 4 & associated texts” Block 122 and 114)…
dedicated encryption module (Pham, abstract, Col. 9, lines 27-32, Col. 20, lines 50-51: dedicated or proprietary file systems where a file access controller, implemented independent of the operating system kernel, is coupled to the security file system layer and supports the file access control function by defining permitted file data transfers through the file system; Fig. 5A: Dedicated File System 136)
is being transparent to the application layer (Pham, Col. 5, lines 1-12, Col. 17, lines 7-12, Col. 18, Table I: file data encryption maintains the logical file-oriented structure of the data and is thus transparent to the persistent storage resources where initial seed value are used for encryption and encryption seeds are a function of Init_Vector + LAB Offset i.e. data values are encrypted with coordinates; Col. 2, lines 6-19, Fig. 2 and associated texts,: kernel space buffer cache wherein platform conventionally includes an operating system kernel 42 supporting execution of applications, such as a database management system (DBMS) 44 and other server applications 46, in a user mode execution space).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to place a dedicated encryption module in a layer belonging to a layered application architecture….said dedicated encryption module is being transparent to the application layer as taught by Pham in the teachings of Sutter and Damiani in order to ensure that any security breach of the platform operating system kernel cannot compromise the function of the security file system layer as a file access controller, implemented independent of the operating system kernel, is coupled to the security file system layer and supports the file access control function by defining permitted file data transfers through the file system (Pham, Abstract).
Regarding claim 5, the combination of Sutter, Damiani, and Pham discloses the method according to claim 1, wherein the coordinates of a value are a table, row and column (Col. 2, lines 23-25, 51-54; Col. 82, lines 33-37, Col, 76, lines 20-25: table, row and column).
Regarding claim 6, the combination of Sutter, Damiani, and Pham discloses the method according to claim 1, wherein indexes of said database are constructed on encrypted columns in the exact same way that said indexes were constructed on non-encrypted columns (Pahe 94, right col., Page 95, right col.).
Regarding claim 7, the combination of Sutter, Damiani, and Pham discloses the method according to claim 1, wherein database backup operations at the database file granularity level are performed without the need to encrypt or decrypt data (Col. 87, lines 40-50, Col. 2, lines 48-65: fine granularity at the column level; Col. 3, lines 4, Col. 60, lines 46-50).
Allowable Subject Matter
12. Claims 2-3 would be allowable if rewritten or amended to overcome the rejection(s) under 35 U.S.C. §101, 112(b) and double patenting, set forth in this office action and to include all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Conclusion
13. Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action. In no event, however, will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the mailing date of this final action.

A nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting rejection is appropriate where the conflicting claims are not identical, but at least one examined application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because the examined application claim is either anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s). DETAILED ACTION
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
Claim 3 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Edmond et al. (US 5,539,217 of record).
The rejection is maintained as of record and repeated herein.
With reference to Fig. 1, Edmond teaches a p-type SiC single crystal 11 containing no inclusions (interpreted as containing no n-type dopant) and having resistivity of 100 to 200 mΩ.cm (col. 5, lines 35-36).
Note that although the reference does not specifically disclose the p-type SiC substrate 11 is a single crystal SiC, col. 4, lines 17-22 discloses that the substrate is formed of a SiC having polytype of 4H, 6H, or 15R, and such polytype SiC is known in the art as single-crystal SiC (see para. [0036] in Ohtani et al. (US 2010/0289033), which is cited herein merely for the purpose of showing this fact).
The resistivity range disclosed in the prior art overlaps with that of the claim ( 35 to 120 mΩ.cm). However, the determination of the resistivity range as claimed would have been obvious to one skilled in the art because it is well settle that, absent a showing of criticality or unexpected result by applicant, where the general conditions of a claim are disclosed in the prior art, it is not inventive to discover the optimum or workable range by routine experimentation. See In re Aller, 220 F.2d 454, 456, 105 USPQ 233, 235 (CCPA 1955); In re Hoeschele, 406 F.2d 1403, 160 USPQ 809 (CCPA 1969); Merck & Co. Inc. v. Biocraft Laboratories Inc., 874 F.2d 804, 10 USPQ2d (Fed.cir), cert. denied, 493 U.S. 975 (1989); In re Kulling, 897 F.2d 1147, 14 USPQ2d 1056 (Fed. Cir. 1990); and In re Geisler, 116 F.3d 1465, 43 USPQ2d 1362 (Fed. Cir. 1997). Furthermore, the specification contains no disclosure of either the critical nature of the claimed resistivity range or any unexpected results arising therefrom. Where patentability is said to be based upon particular chosen resistivity range or upon another variable recited in the claim, the applicant must show that the chosen resistivity range is critical. In re Woodruff, 919 F.2d, 1575, 1578, 16 USPQ2d, 1936 (Fed. Cir. 1990).
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 1-2 are allowed over prior art of record.
The following is an examiner’s statement of reasons for allowance:
Prior art of record does not teach or suggest the claimed method for producing a SiC single crystal which utilizes the temperature gradient y in the surface region of the Si-C solution satisfy formula (1) recited in claim 1.
Any comments considered necessary by applicant must be submitted no later than the payment of the issue fee and, to avoid processing delays, should preferably accompany the issue fee. Such submissions should be clearly labeled “Comments on Statement of Reasons for Allowance.”
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 4/5/2016 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
In page 3 of the Remarks, applicant argues that the p-type SiC single crystal of Edmond contains inclusion, hence Edmond does not teach the claimed limitation “"a p-type SiC single crystal containing no inclusions and having resistivity of 35 to 120 mΩ.cm. " This is found unpersuasive because the claim does not specify or define the types of inclusions, hence the absence of any substances, for example n-type dopant, in the substrate 11 is broadly interpreted as being no inclusions, i.e., the substrate does not contain n-type dopant.

In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
