Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 10/24/2016 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
The applicant argues that the limitations record play information including a location of each stroke taken by the particular golf player and an orientation of the particular golf player relative to a golf ball the particular player is using to execute a particular shot while playing the particular hole as the golf player is executing the particular shot are differentiating over the prior art. However, as noted above, the examiner views the golf ball tracking system and user tracking system as being capable of achieving such function. Tracking of a user relative to a golf ball can render information that could be considered the orientation of the golf player relative to the golf ball. Furthermore, such tracking systems would be capable of tracking as the golf player is executing the particular shot.
The applicant argues that Leech does not teach using the set of computerized eyewear to record an orientation of a golf player relative to a golf ball as the player is executing a particular shot. However, the examiner views such finding as being a narrow interpretation of the Leech reference. Leech does teach tracking a user and golf ball and further teaches tracking the trajectory of a golf ball and a signal emitter in a golf ball wherein such location tracking capabilities wouldn't be limited to only inflight data.
The applicant argues that the motivation to combine the Forest reference with the Leech reference as they address entirely unrelated golf problems. However, the examiner does not agree. Although the detailed specifics of Leech may not have the exact same intent as that of Forest both prior art disclosures are directed towards improving a user’s experience during playing golf. Furthermore, one can reference MPEP 2144 IV where the courts held that “The reason or motivation to modify the reference may often suggest what the inventor has done, but for a different purpose or to solve a different problem. It is not necessary that the prior art suggest the combination to achieve the same advantage or result discovered by applicant.” (See, e.g., In re Kahn, 441 F.3d 977, 987, 78 USPQ2d 1329, 1336 (Fed. Cir. 2006)) As such, although the specifics of the two reference may vary such a variance is not seen to render the combination non-obvious. Furthermore, the Forest reference provides some great motivations to combine that one of ordinary skill in the art would readily find beneficial. For example, one can look at paragraph [0009] of Forest to see that one of the goals of Forest is to "level the playing field between the average player of a sport such as golf and the richer players and professions.” The paragraph goes on to explain how professional golfers and people with enough money have caddies that accompany them on the golf course and provide additional assistance (along with other benefits) which a golfer of a lower income level would not be able to utilize. This problem is addressed by Forest through trying to bring this assistance within the range of lower income golfers. The examiner views this rationale as a great reason to combine Forest with Leech. Any person skilled in the art would see the benefit of bringing such advantage to all golfers independent of their personal income levels.
The applicant argues that the limitations in claim 2 are not met by the citations in Forest. Specifically the limitations directed to “using the information regarding the golf player’s past play on the particular hole to determine a recommendation as to where the golf player should aim when executing the particular shot while playing the particular hole" are argued as not being met by the "get and enter GPS data for position of ball", "retrieve and display stored course data", and "determine recommended actions". However, the examiner considers "retrieve and display stored course data” and “determine recommended actions" as encompassing these attributes. For example, one could retrieve and display stored course data which could include past shots by the player on the particular hole wherein such past data may show multiple occurrences of slicing the ball which could then recommend the player to offset their aim to counter the effects of slicing the ball.
The applicant argues that the limitations of " generating a visual hole summary for the particular hole that visually indicates the player’s respective physical position as the player took each of a plurality of strokes on the particular hole, the visual hole summary comprising, for each respective stroke on the hole, a visual indication of the player’s respective physical position and orientation as the player took the respective stroke along with the visual representation of the particular hole’s fairway, green, and current pin position so that the visual indication and the visual representation communicate each of the respective player physical positions as the player played the hole” are not met by the Forest reference. However, in review of the citations the examiner views such limitations as being met. For example, the argued limitations of “a visual hole summary that indicates a visual representation that communicates each of the respective player positions as the player played the hole” can be seen through the utilization of the "current ball position 402" along with the recitation of “preferably recorded and associated with the hole depiction…further the date and time may be shown and are preferably also recorded” wherein a review of the flow chart in Figure 21 wherein “retrieve and display stored course data” can be interpreted as retrieving and displaying the recorded ball positions on the hole that can be organized by previous dates and times. Furthermore, the citations reference the utilization of reference distances which can include current ball position wherein such an attribute could be considered an orientation as the player took a stroke.

Response to Arguments
10/24/2016
The applicant argues that the limitations record play information including a location of each stroke taken by the particular golf player and an orientation of the particular golf player relative to a golf ball the particular player is using to execute a particular shot while playing the particular hole as the golf player is executing the particular shot are differentiating over the prior art. However, as noted above, the examiner views the golf ball tracking system and user tracking system as being capable of achieving such function. Tracking of a user relative to a golf ball can render information that could be considered the orientation of the golf player relative to the golf ball. Furthermore, such tracking systems would be capable of tracking as the golf player is executing the particular shot.
The applicant argues that Leech does not teach using the set of computerized eyewear to record an orientation of a golf player relative to a golf ball as the player is executing a particular shot. However, the examiner views such finding as being a narrow interpretation of the Leech reference. Leech does teach tracking a user and golf ball and further teaches tracking the trajectory of a golf ball and a signal emitter in a golf ball wherein such location tracking capabilities wouldn't be limited to only inflight data.
The applicant argues that the motivation to combine the Forest reference with the Leech reference as they address entirely unrelated golf problems. However, the examiner does not agree. Although the detailed specifics of Leech may not have the exact same intent as that of Forest both prior art disclosures are directed towards improving a user’s experience during playing golf. Furthermore, one can reference MPEP 2144 IV where the courts held that “The reason or motivation to modify the reference may often suggest what the inventor has done, but for a different purpose or to solve a different problem. It is not necessary that the prior art suggest the combination to achieve the same advantage or result discovered by applicant.” (See, e.g., In re Kahn, 441 F.3d 977, 987, 78 USPQ2d 1329, 1336 (Fed. Cir. 2006)) As such, although the specifics of the two reference may vary such a variance is not seen to render the combination non-obvious. Furthermore, the Forest reference provides some great motivations to combine that one of ordinary skill in the art would readily find beneficial. For example, one can look at paragraph [0009] of Forest to see that one of the goals of Forest is to "level the playing field between the average player of a sport such as golf and the richer players and professions.” The paragraph goes on to explain how professional golfers and people with enough money have caddies that accompany them on the golf course and provide additional assistance (along with other benefits) which a golfer of a lower income level would not be able to utilize. This problem is addressed by Forest through trying to bring this assistance within the range of lower income golfers. The examiner views this rationale as a great reason to combine Forest with Leech. Any person skilled in the art would see the benefit of bringing such advantage to all golfers independent of their personal income levels.
The applicant argues that the limitations in claim 2 are not met by the citations in Forest. Specifically the limitations directed to “using the information regarding the golf player’s past play on the particular hole to determine a recommendation as to where the golf player should aim when executing the particular shot while playing the particular hole" are argued as not being met by the "get and enter GPS data for position of ball", "retrieve and display stored course data", and "determine recommended actions". However, the examiner considers "retrieve and display stored course data” and “determine recommended actions" as encompassing these attributes. For example, one could retrieve and display stored course data which could include past shots by the player on the particular hole wherein such past data may show multiple occurrences of slicing the ball which could then recommend the player to offset their aim to counter the effects of slicing the ball.
The applicant argues that the limitations of " generating a visual hole summary for the particular hole that visually indicates the player’s respective physical position as the player took each of a plurality of strokes on the particular hole, the visual hole summary comprising, for each respective stroke on the hole, a visual indication of the player’s respective physical position and orientation as the player took the respective stroke along with the visual representation of the particular hole’s fairway, green, and current pin position so that the visual indication and the visual representation communicate each of the respective player physical positions as the player played the hole” are not met by the Forest reference. However, in review of the citations the examiner views such limitations as being met. For example, the argued limitations of “a visual hole summary that indicates a visual representation that communicates each of the respective player positions as the player played the hole” can be seen through the utilization of the "current ball position 402" along with the recitation of “preferably recorded and associated with the hole depiction…further the date and time may be shown and are preferably also recorded” wherein a review of the flow chart in Figure 21 wherein “retrieve and display stored course data” can be interpreted as retrieving and displaying the recorded ball positions on the hole that can be organized by previous dates and times. AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(b) the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country, more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States.
Claims 1, 5-6, and 8-10 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by Yamaguchi WO 2008099611.
As per claim 1, Yamaguchi discloses an operating device comprising:
a casing (71),
at least one input unit (20) for inputting input relating to an instruction to drive movement of an object (7);
a detection unit (9) for detecting the input from the at least one input unit,
the detection unit including a plurality of the individual detection units (74-79, 84-89) which are arranged over a partial or entire range of a circumference of the casing, the individual detection units corresponding to inherent movement directions of the object; and
a jacket member (10) which covers the plurality of individual detection units,
wherein the jacket member is rotatable around the circumference of the casing at least within the range in which the plurality of individual detection units are arranged, and
the at least one input unit is provided on or as part of the jacket member (through cable 8).
As per claim 5, Yamaguchi discloses an adjustment input detection unit (81-83) for detecting input relating to an instruction to correct the movement direction of the object.
As per claim 6, Yamaguchi discloses an interior casing (71) having a surface on which the individual detection units are provided; and
an exterior casing (10) that accommodates the interior casing, is formed to be free to rotate relative to the interior casing on an outer side thereof, and thereby serves as the jacket member; and the exterior casing has an inner surface on which a reference member (73) that serves as ON means relative to the detection units on the interior casing is provided.
As per claim 8, Yamaguchi discloses a display unit (106) for displaying, in a visually comprehensible manner, information relating to a displacement amount when an orientation of the object is modified, in at least a region excluding an outer surface of the casing.
As per claim 9, Yamaguchi discloses a traveling body (5) used to move an object; and an operating device for manipulating an operation of the traveling body, wherein the operating device is the operating device according to claim 1.
As per claim 10, Yamaguchi discloses a traveling body (5) used to move an object; and
an operating device for manipulating an operation of the traveling body,
wherein the operating device is the operating device according to claim 3.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 7 and 11 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Yamaguchi WO 2008099611.
As per claim 7, Yamaguchi discloses the claimed invention except that an illuminating device for forming a light spot is disposed in a location exposed to the exterior of the casing on a surface that corresponds to an opposite side to an operator, as a notification unit for providing notification of a travel direction of a traveling body that travels together with the object.
However, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to have modified the invention of Yamaguchi since it was known in the art to have an illuminating device for forming a light spot is disposed in a location exposed to the exterior of the casing on a surface that corresponds to an opposite side to an operator, as a notification unit for providing notification of a travel direction of a traveling body that travels together with the object for the purpose of allowing operators to see the travel direction more easily from a remote position.
As per claim 11, Yamaguchi discloses a traveling body (5) used to move an object; and
an operating device for manipulating an operation of the traveling body,
wherein the operating device is the operating device according to claim 1; and
a display unit (106) for displaying, in a visually comprehensible manner, information relating to a displacement amount when an orientation of the object is modified or information relating to an advancement direction of the object, in at least a region excluding an outer surface of the casing.
Yamaguchi does not disclose a display unit (106) for displaying, in a visually comprehensible manner, information relating to a displacement amount when an orientation of the object is modified or information relating to an advancement direction of the object is fixed to the traveling body.
However, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to have modified the invention of Yamaguchi since it was known in the art to have a display unit (106) for displaying, in a visually comprehensible manner, information relating to a displacement amount when an orientation of the object is modified or information relating to an advancement direction of the object is fixed to the traveling body for the purpose of allowing operators to see the travel direction more easily from a remote position.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 2/11/2014 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.

DETAILED ACTION
This action is pursuant to the claims filed on May 5, 2014. Claims 1-14 and 17-30 are pending. Claims 1-10 and 25-30 are withdrawn from consideration. Claims 15 and 16 are cancelled. A final action on the merits of claims 11-14 and 17-24 are as follows.
Priority
Applicant’s claim for the benefit of a prior-filed application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) is acknowledged. Applicant has complied with conditions for receiving the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) for provisional application number 61/323,796, 61/323,801 and 61/323,816 filed on April 13, 2010.
AIA
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
AIA
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 11-14 and 17 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hooven et al. (hereinafter ‘Hooven’, U.S. PGPub. No. 2005/0187545), in view of Grabek (in IDS filed 5/5/2014, U.S. PGPub. No. 2004/0064138) as evidenced by Stewart et al. (hereinafter ‘Stewart’, U.S. PGPub. No. 2006/0020271).
In regards to claim 11, Hooven discloses a method of affecting tissue within a body (Fig 1) comprising: advancing a first device comprising tissue-affecting elements to a first surface of a target tissue, wherein the first tissue-affecting device is positioned against a portion of the first surface of the target tissue (epicardial surface; [0031], [0093]-[0094]); advancing a second device comprising tissue-affecting elements to a second surface of the target tissue, wherein the second surface is opposite the first surface of the tissue (endocardial surface; [0031], [0094]); positioning the first and second devices such that ablation energy passes through the target tissue between the tissue-affecting elements of the first and second devices; operating the tissue-affecting elements of the first and second devices simultaneously such that a lesion is formed in the target tissue (paragraph [0095]: "the electrodes can be activated for ablation by the ablation activation device. The tissue layer is ablated by the electrical connection between the electrodes disposed on opposite sides of the tissue layer"; shown in Figs. 12 and 14). However, Hooven fails to disclose advancing a closure device comprising a snare loop and a suture loop to an external surface of a left atrial appendage; and isolating the left atrial appendage with the closure device.
Grabek teaches a method of advancing a closure device (electrocautery tool 60 in Fig. 4) comprising a snare loop (distal loop 64) and a suture loop (suture 90 in Fig. 7) to an external surface of a left atrial appendage (appendage 18 in Figs. 6 and 7); and isolating the left atrial appendage with the closure device ([0021]: “application of electrical energy (RF)... can either remove or close the atrial appendage"). This process would provide essentially a bloodless procedure for removal of left atrial appendage ([0021]). As evidenced by Stewart, a removal of left atrial appendage is a concomitant procedure during other cardiac surgeries. For example, in almost all atrial fibrillation (AF) patients suffering from embolic stroke, a thrombus clot forms in the appendage of the left atrium and removal of left atrial appendage during other cardiac surgery will prevent strokes in AF patients (Stewart, [0003]-[0004]).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to have modified the method of affecting tissue, specifically the cardiac tissue, as disclosed by Hooven to incorporate the steps of advancing a closure device and isolating the left atrial appendage as taught by Grabeck, given that a removal of left atrial appendage is considered a concomitant procedure during other cardiac surgeries.
In regards to claim 12, Hooven/Grabek combination further discloses advancing the first device comprising inserting a curved sheath at a location beneath a sternum and advancing the first device through the sheath (guiding facility (GF) in Fig. 1; paragraph [0099] and [0150]: “ a guide facility which is shaped or curved to follow the surface of the heart...the guide facility is preferably capable of shape retention and may be manually shaped by the operator in a desired orientation prior to insertion into a patient’s body…guiding facility may be introduced into the patient with an aid of a guiding catheter...").
In regards to claim 13, Hooven/Grabek combination further discloses the positioning the first and second ablation devices using one or more magnetic components (paragraph [0095]: “the magnetically attraction between the distal ends also supplies clamping pressure to the tissue layer so as to effectively clamp the tissue layer between the distal ends").
In regards to claim 14, Hooven/Grabek combination further discloses the target tissue is cardiac tissue (paragraph [0081]).
In regards to claim 17, Hooven/Grabek combination further discloses verifying that the formed lesion spans between the first and second tissue-affecting devices (paragraph [0098]: "various viewing instruments may be inserted into the intrapericardial space for visual monitoring of the selected ablation site, before, during and/or after ablation").
Claim 18 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hooven in view of Grabek as applied to claim 17/11 above, and further in view of Robinsky et al (hereinafter 'Robinsky’, U.S. PGPub 2008/0015571).
In regards to claim 18, Hooven/Grabek combination discloses the invention substantially as claimed. However, Hooven does not disclose verifying step comprising assessing a lesion using electrical impedance tomography.
Rubinsky teaches the use of electrical impedance tomography, an imaging technique in which a tissue’s electrical impedance characteristics are reconstructed by applying a current across the tissue and measuring electrical currents and potentials (paragraph [0049]) to precisely locate a tumor (target tissue), to confirm the placement of electrodes relative to the tumor and create images of the currents of irreversible electroporation which increases the electrical conductivity and permeability of the cell plasma membrane caused by an externally applied electrical field in real time (paragraph [0059]) .
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skilled in the art at the time the invention was made to have modified Hooven/Grabek combination to incorporate the teachings of Rubinsky and incorporated a verifying step comprising assessing a lesion using electrical impedance tomography. Even though Rubinsky teaches the use of electrical impedance tomography for real time imaging of electroporation, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skilled in the art to have used it for real time imaging during ablation of target tissue. Doing so would aid in precisely locating a target tissue and confirm the placement of electrodes relative to the target site and create real time images to determine the extent of target site affected by the ablation.
Claim 19 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hooven in view of Grabek as applied to claim 17/11 above, and further in view of Halperin et al (hereinafter 'Halperin’, U.S. PGPub 2008/0058635).
In regards to claim 19, Hooven/Grabek combination discloses the invention substantially as claimed. However, Hooven does not disclose verifying step comprising assessing a lesion using thermal imaging techniques.
Halperin teaches the use of thermal imaging technique for guidance (and visualization during catheter ablation (e.g., ablation of atrial fibrillation) and the resulting ablation lesions, thereby greatly simplifying production of continuous linear lesions (abstract and paragraph [0059]).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skilled in the art at the time the invention was made to have modified Hooven/Grabek combination to incorporate the teachings of Halperin to incorporate verifying step comprising assessing a lesion using thermal imaging techniques. Doing so would aid in guidance (and visualization during catheter ablation (e.g., ablation of atrial fibrillation) and the resulting ablation lesions, thereby greatly simplifying production of continuous linear lesions.
Claims 20-23 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hooven in view of Stewart.
In regards to claim 20, Hooven discloses a method of forming a lesion in the tissue of a left atrium comprising: advancing a first tissue-affecting device (second body 14 in Fig. 3) into the left atrium, wherein the first tissue-affecting device is positioned against the atrial wall (endocardium ‘EN’, preferably within the left atrium, [0094]); advancing a second tissue-affecting device (first body 12) to an external atrial wall, wherein the second tissue-affecting device is positioned against the external atrial wall opposite the first tissue-affecting device ([0094]: “positioned within the intrapercardinal space adjacent the epicardium", [0095]: “clamp the tissue layer [left atrium] between the distal ends [of first and second body]”); positioning the first and second tissue-affecting devices such that ablation energy may pass between them ([0096]: "the electrodes can be activated for ablation by the ablation activation device. The tissue layer is ablated by the electrical connection between the electrodes disposed on opposite sides of the tissue layer”); operating the first and second tissue-affecting devices simultaneously such that a lesion is formed in the atrial wall at least partially therebetween (paragraph [0094]: “preferably within the left atrium, for ablating of a portion of the heart wall or myocardium”); and isolating the left atrial appendage ([00980, labeled as ‘left appendage’ in Fig. 34).
However, Hooven fails to teach advancing said first tissue-affecting device into the left atrium is through a puncture in the left atrial appendage. Rather, Hooven teaches positioning said first tissue-affecting device into the left atrium through insertion into a femoral or subclavian vein to the right atrium and piercing a thin opening through the septum to access the left atrium.
Stewart teaches positioning and placement of a catheter into the left atrium through a puncture in a left atrial appendage during a cardiac surgery ([0161]) is preferred over a left atrium access via a catheter placed through a femoral vein access as taught by Hooven. Furthermore, Stewart discusses that Hooven’s method is more difficult to reach transvenously, requiring first, right atrial access followed by a transseptal puncture through the fossa ovalis of the inter-atrial septum into the left atrium and only a small diameter catheters can be passed through the vasculature ([0132]-[0133]).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to have substitute positioning said first tissue-affecting device into the left atrium through insertion into a femoral or subclavian vein to the right atrium and piercing a thin opening through the septum to access the left atrium as taught by Hooven to incorporate the steps of advancing said first tissue-affecting device into the left atrium is through a puncture in the left atrial appendage. Doing so would provide easier and more controlled access to the left atrium.
In regards to claim 21, Hooven/Stewart combination further discloses advancing the first tissue-affecting device further comprises advancing a first guide wire through a puncture in the left atrial appendage into the left atrium, and advancing the first tissue-affecting device over the first guide wire (paragraph [0099]: “several types of guide facilities are possible including but not limited to a wire, a tube, surgical tape or the like..."; paragraph [0151]: " a first or epicardially disposed body, generally indicated at 312.... may further cooperatively receive the guide facility to assist in guiding the body to the selected tissue location").
In regards to claim 22, Hooven/Stewart combination further discloses advancing the second tissue-affecting device further comprises advancing a second guide wire to the external atrial wall, and advancing the second tissue-affecting device over the second guide wire (paragraph [0093] and [0099])
In regards to claim 23, Hooven/Stewart combination further discloses positioning step comprising positioning the first and second ablation devices using one or more magnetic components (paragraph [0095]: “the magnetically attraction between the distal ends also supplies clamping pressure to the tissue layer so as to effectively clamp the tissue layer between the distal ends").
Claim 24 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hooven as applied to claim 17/11 above, and in view of Jovois et al (hereinafter 'Jovois’, U.S. PGPub 2007/0083230).
In regards to claim 24, Hooven/Stewart combination discloses the invention substantially as claimed. However, Hooven does not disclose isolating a left atrial appendage comprising positioning an occlusion device comprising a rounded disc with one or more grooves circumscribing the outer perimeter of the disc, wherein the disc is sized and shaped to be constrained in base of the left atrial appendage.
Jovois teaches isolating a left atrial appendage comprising positioning an occlusion device (left atrial appendage occlusion device 10 in Fig 1; paragraph [0012]) comprising a rounded disc with one or more grooves circumscribing the outer perimeter of the disc (sheet 60 covers the wire coil 20 in Fig 2; paragraph [0029]: “wire coil 20 may be cylindrically shaped such that wire orbits at the proximal end), wherein the disc is sized and shaped to be constrained in base of the left atrial appendage (paragraph [0012]: “one anchor adapted to attach the device [10] to left atrial appendage tissue) to reduce clotting and embolization leading to stroke (paragraph [0002]-[0003]).
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skilled in the art at the time the invention was made to have modified Hooven to incorporate the teachings of Jovois and incorporated a step where isolating a left atrial appendage comprising positioning an occlusion device comprising a rounded disc with one or more grooves circumscribing the outer perimeter of the disc, wherein the disc is sized and shaped to be constrained in base of the left atrial appendage. Doing so would reduce clotting and embolization leading to stroke.
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments, filed May 5, 2014, have been fully considered and are persuasive. Applicant argues on pages 7 and 8 of the Remarks, with respect to the rejection of claims 11-14, 17 and 20-23 under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated over Hooven et al. (hereinafter ‘Hooven’, U.S. PGPub. No. 2005/0187545) that Hooven fails to provide for each of the limitations set forth in amended independent claim 1 and 20.
With regards to amended independent claim 1, Applicant takes issue that Hooven fails to teach “advancing a closure device comprising a snare loop and a suture loop to an external surface of a left atrial appendage; and isolating the left atrial appendage with the closure device”. This has been found persuasive and the rejection of claims 11-14, 17 under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated over Hooven has been withdrawn. However, upon further consideration, a new ground of rejection with respect to claims 11-14 and 17 under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hooven in view of Grabek (in IDS filed 5/5/2014, U.S. PGPub. No. 2004/0064138) has been made in above Office Action. It is the Examiner’s position that Grabek, in teaching advancing a closure device and isolating the left atrial appendage, would aide in curing the deficiency of Hooven. It is for at least the reasoning set forth above that the Examiner believes that the rejection of claims 11-14, and 17 under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hooven in view of Grabek is tenable.
With regards to Applicant's arguments on pages 8 and 9, Applicant takes issue that Hooven fails to teach “advancing a first tissue-affecting device into the left atrium through a puncture in a left atrial appendage” as claimed in independent claim 20. This has been found persuasive and the rejection of 20-23 under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated over Hooven has been withdrawn. However, upon further consideration, a new ground of rejection with respect to claims 20-23 under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hooven in view of Stewart et al. (in IDS filed 5/5/2011, hereinafter ‘Stewart’, U.S. PGPub. No. 2006/0020271) has been made in above Office Action. It is the Examiner’s position that Stewart, in teaching advancing an ablation device into the left atrium through a puncture in a left atrial appendage, would aide in curing the deficiency of Hooven. It is for at least the reasoning set forth above that the Examiner believes that the rejection of claims 20-23 under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hooven in view of Stewart is tenable.
With regards to claims 18, 19 and 24, see pages 13 and 14 of Remarks, the Examiner notes that Applicant's arguments therein are solely directed towards the secondary references failure to cure the above-noted deficiency of amended claims 1 and 20. Given this lack of additional arguments against these rejections, it is the Examiner’s position that each of the rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are tenable for the new grounds of rejection presented above or are moot in view of new grounds of rejection.
Conclusion
Applicant's submission of an information disclosure statement under 37 CFR 1.97(c) with the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(p) on May 5, 2014 prompted the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 09/22/2016 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Notably, Applicant argues that the prior art does not teach the newly-amended language of independent claim 1. However, as best as these limitations may be understood, they do appear to be taught by the prior art of record.
Regarding the claimed “setting a boundary condition,” the combination of Spruce and Kusiak does disclose setting a boundary condition for the rotor speed of the wind turbine at the second moment in time (see Kusiak: p. 770, col. 1: maximum rotor speed is set to 23 r/min).
Regarding the “cost function” comprising “electrical energy,” the combination of Spruce and Kusiak does disclose that the cost function to be optimized may be the electrical energy generated (Spruce: see, e.g., [0028]: optimal power [i.e., electrical energy] may be generated).
Regarding the “cost function” comprising both “electrical energy” and “kinetic energy,” the combination of Spruce and Kusiak does disclose that the cost function to be optimized may be the electrical energy generated plus a kinetic energy of the rotor at the second moment in time (Kusiak, see p. 766: maximizing energy captured from the wind to increase competitiveness of wind energy production—i.e., both kinetic energy capture as well as power/electrical energy generated are being optimized; see also p. 767: Table 1 [listing wind turbine power output and rotor speed—representative of kinetic energy of the rotor—as parameters for optimization]; dynamic equations (1) and (2) for both power output and rotor speed).
Regarding “optimizing” a “converted aerodynamic energy,” the combination of Spruce and Kusiak does disclose optimizing a converted aerodynamic energy from the wind (Kusiak, see p. 766: col. 1: “Maximizing energy captured from the wind”).
Thus, the prior art of record does appear to teach the claimed limitations.
Additionally, in response to applicant's arguments against the references individually, one cannot show nonobviousness by attacking references individually where the rejections are based on combinations of references. See In re Keller, 642 F.2d 413, 208 USPQ 871 (CCPA 1981); In re Merck & Co., 800 F.2d 1091, 231 USPQ 375 (Fed. Cir. 1986).
Furthermore, Applicant’s amendments have served to highlight a more serious issue—that of possession of the claimed invention, as required under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). This issue is addressed in the appropriate section hereinbelow.
Title
The title of the invention is not descriptive. A new title is required that is clearly indicative of the invention to which the claims are directed.
Whereas Applicant's amendment to the title in order to expedite prosecution is appreciated, it is kindly noted that modifying “Wind Turbine” to include “Variable Speed Wind Turbine” does not distinguish the claimed invention in any significant manner. Certainly, wind turbines generally operate at variable speeds, since winds—which provide motive force for turbines—are, typically, variable in speed.
Drawings
The drawings are objected to because of the following informalities.
Appropriate correction is required.
The examiner notes that the following may not be an exhaustive list of informalities. It is suggested that the applicant thoroughly review the drawings.
Regarding Figures 2b, 2c, 2d, 2e, 3b, the drawings are objected to as they fail to provide appropriate labels, including values and units of measured variables, for their respective ordinate (“Y”) axes.
Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. The figure or figure number of an amended drawing should not be labeled as “amended.” If a drawing figure is to be canceled, the appropriate figure must be removed from the replacement sheet, and where necessary, the remaining figures must be renumbered and appropriate changes made to the brief description of the several views of the drawings for consistency. Additional replacement sheets may be necessary to show the renumbering of the remaining figures. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Claim Objections
Claims 1, 18 are objected to because of the following informalities. Appropriate correction is required.
Regarding claim 1, the limitations “the wind,” “the kinetic energy of the rotor” are recited. There is insufficient antecedent basis for these limitations in the claim.
Regarding claim 18, the limitation “the longitudinal axis” is recited. There is insufficient antecedent basis for this limitation in the claim. For the purpose of examination, the phrase “for rotating the blades around the longitudinal axis of the blades” will be read as —for rotating each the blade[[s]] around a longitudinal axis thereof—.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph:
The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.
Claims 1-7, 10, 12, 14-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement. The claim(s) contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the relevant art that the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the inventor(s), at the time the application was filed, had possession of the claimed invention.
Regarding claim 1, the claim requires “using a control strategy to optimize a cost function […] by controlling the torque of the generator and the pitch angles of the blades […] wherein the cost function to be optimized is converted aerodynamic energy […], electrical energy generated plus the kinetic energy of the rotor […], or electrical energy generated while setting a boundary condition […].”
However, the specification does not appear to describe the claimed subject matter in such a way as to reasonably convey that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
Notably, the specification does not describe the manner by which a “cost function” including the claimed limitations may be “optimized.” It is understood that a solution to the optimization problem is desired, but it is not indicated how the solution is achieved—whether, e.g., a closed form solution is obtainable or whether numerical analysis is to be used.
To resolve this issue, reference to the following passages from the specification is made.
[0030] In some embodiments, the control strategy may be a Model Predictive Control (MPC) strategy, and optionally a non-linear Model Predictive Control. MPC aims at effectively solving problems of control and automation of processes that are characterized by having a complicated, multivariate and/or unstable dynamic behaviour. The control strategy underlying this type of control uses a mathematical model of the process to be controlled to predict the future behaviour of that system and, based on this future behaviour, it can predict future control signals.
[0046] In this example, a (non-linear) MPC strategy is implemented to optimize the cost function:

[0049] In the MPC strategy, this cost function may be optimized within certain constraints. These constraints may include maximum and minimum generator torque, generator rotor speed, maximum and minimum pitch angles and maximum and minimum generator output power: […]
Thus, whereas the specification does discuss that a “cost function may be optimized” in general terms, it does not discuss how the cost function may be “optimized.” The specification indicates certain “constraints” associated with the optimization problem, which “may include maximum and minimum generator torque, generator rotor speed, […] pitch angles and […] generator output power” (see [0049]) but the specification does not explicitly state how the “optimization” may be carried out. The specification also makes mention that “the control strategy underlying this type of control uses a mathematical model” but does not make clear which specific “model” is to be used and, more importantly, how to solve such a “model” in order to carry out the claimed invention.
The lack of specific information on how to calculate or “optimize” the “cost function” is further exacerbated by the multitude of variables that the specification indicates may be used—see, e.g., [0035], [0049].
Therefore, without indication of how to specifically “optimize” the “cost function” or even a general indication of what form a solution may take—e.g., whether a solution in closed form may be obtained or whether numerical analysis would be required—one skilled in the relevant art would not be sufficiently apprised that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(B) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 1-7, 10, 12, 14-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention.
Regarding claim 1, the newly-amended limitation “wherein the cost function to be optimized is converted aerodynamic energy […] or electrical energy generated while setting a boundary condition […] in time” is vague and indefinite. It is unclear whether additional steps are required for “optimiz[ing]” the “aerodynamic energy,” “electrical energy,” and/or “kinetic energy.” Furthermore, it is unclear whether “setting a boundary condition” comprises an additional, active step for the claimed method or not; and, if so, what may or may not be comprised by “setting a boundary condition.” Clarification is requested.
Regarding claims 2-7, 10, 12, 14-20, they are dependent on claim 1.
Regarding claim 4, the limitation “estimating […] based on empirical statistical information of the wind” is vague and indefinite. The claim fails to make clear what is comprised by “empirical statistical information of the wind,” the manner by which such “information” is obtained, and the manner by which the “estimating” is “based on” such information. For the purpose of examination, the limitation “wherein estimating representative future wind speed values […] or estimated instantaneous representative wind speed values” will be interpreted as —wherein estimating future wind speed values comprises measuring or estimating instantaneous wind speed values and estimating future wind speed values—. This was previously noted in the Office Action of 06/23/2016, but neither amended nor addressed by Applicant in the Response of 09/22/2016.
Regarding claim 6, the limitation “assuming the wind speed value” is vague and indefinite due to its dependency on claim 4. In claim 4, both “instantaneous representative wind speed values” and “future wind speed values” are recited. Thus, the recitation of “assuming the wind speed value” is indefinite since the claim does not make clear to which, if any, of the previously-recited “wind speed values” (i.e., “instantaneous” or “future”) reference is possibly being made. This was previously noted in the Office Action of 06/23/2016, but neither amended nor addressed by Applicant in the Response of 09/22/2016.
Regarding claims 6, 7, the limitation “assuming the wind speed value to be constant over a rotor swept area” is vague and indefinite. The claim fails to make clear if a) an additional method step (e.g., a step of “assuming …”) is being required; or, if no additional step is being recited, b) the manner by which a previously-recited method step is being further limited. Furthermore, the claim does not make clear the manner by which “a rotor swept area of the wind turbine” is used in any previously-recited method step. This was previously noted in the Office Action of 06/23/2016, but neither amended nor addressed by Applicant in the Response of 09/22/2016.
Regarding claim 10, it is dependent on claim 9. However, claim 9 has been cancelled. Therefore, the metes and bounds of patent protection sought have not been made clear.
Regarding claims 15, 16, the limitations “Model Predictive Control strategy,” “non-linear Model Predictive Control strategy” are vague and indefinite. The claims fail to make clear what the claimed “strategy” method steps may or may not comprise. For the purpose of examination, the limitation “wherein the control strategy is a Model Predictive Control strategy or a non-linear Model Predictive Control strategy” will be interpreted as —wherein the control strategy utilizes either a linear or a non-linear model—. This was previously noted in the Office Action of 06/23/2016, but neither amended nor addressed by Applicant in the Response of 09/22/2016.

(a) at a first moment in time estimating representative future wind speed values from the first moment in time up to a second moment in time, the second moment in time being equal to the first moment in time plus a predetermined finite period of time (see, e.g., [0043], [0046], [0047]: sensor 15, including LIDAR system 26, is used to predict future wind speed values for a future time window—i.e., from a first moment in time to a second moment in time—of a predetermined finite time period, the period depending on average wind speed and LIDAR capabilities: the exemplary value is a predetermined time period of approximately 3 seconds);

substantially continuously repeating steps (a) and (b) (method operates continuously; see, e.g., Figure 8 and [0084]: method will be repeated for next time instant and time series will be updated).

optimizing a converted aerodynamic energy from the wind (Kusiak, see p. 766: col. 1: “Maximizing energy captured from the wind”);

setting a boundary condition for the rotor speed of the wind turbine at the second moment in time (see Kusiak: p. 770, col. 1: maximum rotor speed is set to 23 r/min).

Regarding claim 5, the combination of Spruce and Kusiak further discloses that estimating representative future wind speed values comprises measuring representative wind speeds upstream of the wind turbine (Spruce: see, e.g., [0026] as discussed hereinabove regarding claim 4).

Regarding claim 19, the combination of Spruce and Kusiak further discloses a LIDAR (Spruce: LIDAR 26) for measuring wind speed values upstream (Spruce: see, e.g., [0026]) from the wind turbine (Spruce: wind turbine 1)
s 17, 20 are
Spruce et al. (US 2013/0106107 A1) in view of Kusiak et al. (IEEE Transactions: Anticipatory Control) and further in view of Hammerum (WO 2010/060772 A2)

DETAILED ACTION
The present action is in response to Applicant’s submission dated March 28, 2017. Claims 1-20 are pending in the current application.
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA. In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
Claims 1-11 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Patel (U.S. Pat. No. 9,455,530) in view of Pearson et al. (Int. Pat. No. WO 2014/209325 A1, hereinafter “Pearson”).
Specifically, regarding Claim 1, Patel discloses a neutral connector assembly (Abstract), comprising: a neutral connector (40; FIG. 4) including a first side (1S) configured to make an electrical connection with a neutral bar (120) on a top of the neutral bar (120), a shield (122; col. 6, ll. 35-37) of an insulating material having a connector side (CS) abutting a second side (2S) of the neutral connector (40) opposite the first side (1S), and a bias spring (46A, 46B) abutting a spring side of the shield (122) opposite the connector side (CS) and configured to bias the neutral connector (40; col. 8, ll. 11-18). Patel does not discloses that the neutral connector assembly is for a circuit breaker.
PNG media_image1.png 884 1162 media_image1.png Greyscale
However, Pearson discloses a neutral connector assembly for a circuit breaker (Abstract, FIG. 4B). Thus, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to combine the assembly of Pearson with the assembly of Patel to easily and securely establish a neutral connection without a degradation in electrical performance.
Regarding Claim 2, Patel discloses that the neutral connector (40) comprises a first prong (46A; FIG. 4) and a second prong (46B), each of the first prong (46A) and the second prong (46B) being spaced from the first side (1S) to form a gap configured to receive the neutral bar (120) therein (an area between 46A, 46B, and 40).
Regarding Claim 3, Patel discloses a first extension stop (a first one of 60; FIG. 4) of the neutral connector (40) configured to engage with a first limit stop (a first one of 52; FIG. 4).
Regarding Claim 4, Patel discloses that the first limit stop (52) is included in a housing (between 16 and 20) of a circuit breaker (FIG. 4).
Regarding Claim 5, Patel discloses a second extension stop (a second one of 60; FIG. 4) of the neutral connector (40) configured to engage with a second limit stop (a second one of 52; FIG. 4).
Regarding Claim 6, Patel discloses a neutral conductor wire (26) fastened to the neutral connector (40).
Regarding Claim 7, Patel discloses that the neutral connector (40) comprises a first upright (46A) and a second upright (46B), wherein the first upright (46A) and the second upright (46B) extend alongside of the shield (122; FIG. 4).
Regarding Claim 8, Patel discloses that the bias spring (46A, 46B) is received in a recess or on a post of the shield (122; when 122 is provided between the gap discussed at col. 6, ll. 35-37).
Regarding Claim 9, Patel discloses that the neutral connector (40) comprises a first extension stop (a first one of 60) coupled to a first end (a first one of 52; FIG. 4) and a second extension stop (a second one of 60) coupled to a second end (a second one of 52; FIG. 4).
Regarding Claim 10, Patel discloses that the shield (122) comprises an alignment feature (122 itself0 configured to engage and align the neutral connector (40) to the shield (122).
Regarding Claim 11, the combination of Patel and Pearson does not disclose that the shield includes a groove that receives the neutral connector. However, it would have been obvious to utilize a groove on a top surface of 122 to establish a secure relationship between the shield and neutral connector since Applicant has presented no explanation that this particular configuration of the shield significant or are anything more than one of numerous configurations a person of ordinary skill in the art would find obvious for the purpose of coupling a shield and a connector. A change in shape is generally recognized as being within the level of ordinary skill in the art. In re Dailey, 149 USPQ 47 (CCPA 1976).
AIA

AIA
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
DETAILED ACTION
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments filed 02/06/2017 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
The applicant argues none of the cited references teaches the limitation as amended in claims 1, 14, and 20. The examiner respectfully disagrees. Hayashi et al. (figures 1A-1B) discloses a light controlling apparatus as claimed but is silent regarding a transparent display panel including a transmissive area and an emissive area, the emissive area having pixels displaying an image; dichroic dyes and a second alignment film including an adhesive material. Jin et al. (figure 3) teaches a transparent display panel including a transmissive area and an emissive area, the emissive area having pixels displaying an image. Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to combine the emissive panel as taught by Jin et al. in order to achieve a double-sided light emitting display capable of displaying different images on different sides of a panel. Zang (figures 4a-4c) teaches a first alignment film covering the dams and the plurality of liquid crystal area; and a second alignment film including an adhesive material, wherein the first and second alignment films are attached to each other on the dams for sealing the plurality of liquid crystal areas encompassing the second liquid crystals and the dichroic dyes (see at least paragraphs 0065 and 0098). Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to combine wall as taught by Zang in order to keep the top and bottom substrates apart at a fixed distance and improve the mechanical properties and structural integrity of the film structure. The claim language therefore does not patentably distinguish over the applied reference[s], and the previous rejections are maintained.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1-4, 7-10, 20 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hayashi et al. (US 2008/0094551) in view of Zang (US 2008/0020007).
Regarding claim 1, Hayashi et al. (figures 1A-1B) discloses a light controlling apparatus, comprising:
first and second substrates facing each other (30);
a first electrode on the first substrate (see at least paragraph 0037);
a second electrode on the second substrate; and
a polymer dispersed liquid crystal (PDLC) layer including first liquid crystals having droplets, and a guest-host liquid crystal (GHLC) layer (10 and 20) including second liquid crystals, between the first electrode and the second electrode;
a first alignment film covering the wall; and
a second alignment film.
Hayashi et al. (figures 1A-1B) discloses the limitations as shown in the rejection of claim 1 above. However, Hayashi et al. is silent regarding dichroic dyes and a second alignment film including an adhesive material. Zang (figures 4a-4c) teaches a guest-host liquid crystal (GHLC) layer including second liquid crystals, dichroic dyes and a wall having concavo-convex shape, a second alignment film including an adhesive material, wherein the first and second alignment films are attached to each other for encompassing the second liquid crystals and the dichroic dyes (see at least paragraphs 0065 and 0098). Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to combine wall as taught by Zang in order to keep the top and bottom substrates apart at a fixed distance and improve the mechanical properties and structural integrity of the film structure.
Regarding claim 2, Hayashi et al. (figures 1A-1B) discloses the limitations as shown in the rejection of claim 1 above. However, Hayashi et al. is silent regarding wherein wall has dams and a plurality of liquid crystal areas between the dams, and the first and second alignment films are attached to each other on the dams. Zang (figures 4a-4c) teaches wherein wall has dams and a plurality of liquid crystal areas between the dams, and the first and second alignment films are attached to each other on the dams (see at least paragraph 0070). Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to combine wall as taught by Zang in order to keep the top and bottom substrates apart at a fixed distance and improve the mechanical properties and structural integrity of the film structure.
Regarding claim 3, Zang (figures 4a-4c) teaches the second liquid crystals and the dichroic dyes are disposed in the plurality of liquid crystal areas, and the first and second alignment films seal the plurality of liquid crystal areas
Regarding claim 4, Zang (figures 4a-4c) teaches ratios of the second liquid crystals to the dichroic dyes between the plurality of liquid crystal areas have a difference within 1% (see at least paragraph 0070).
In the case where the claimed ranges “overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art” a prima facie case of obviousness exists. In re Wertheim, 541 F.2d 257, 191 USPQ 90 (CCPA 1976); In re Woodruff, 919 F.2d 1575, 16 USPQ2d 1934 (Fed. Cir. 1990) (The prior art taught carbon monoxide concentrations of “about 1-5%” while the claim was limited to “more than 5%.” The court held that “about 1-5%” allowed for concentrations slightly above 5% thus the ranges overlapped.). Similarly, a prima facie case of obviousness exists where the claimed ranges and prior art ranges do not overlap but are close enough that one skilled in the art would have expected them to have the same properties. Titanium Metals Corp. of America v. Banner, 778 F.2d 775, 227 USPQ 773 (Fed. Cir. 1985) (Court held as proper a rejection of a claim directed to an alloy of “having 0.8% nickel, 0.3% molybdenum, up to 0.1% iron, balance titanium” as obvious over a reference disclosing alloys of 0.75% nickel, 0.25% molybdenum, balance titanium and 0.94% nickel, 0.31% molybdenum, balance titanium.). See MPEP § 2144.05.
Regarding claim 6, Zang (figures 4a-4c) teaches the first alignment film on the PDLC layer to arrange the second liquid crystals and the dichroic dyes.
Regarding claim 7, Hayashi et al. (figures 1A-1B) discloses the PDLC layer and the GHLC layer are realized in a transparent mode for transmitting incident light when no voltage is applied to the first and second electrodes or when a voltage difference between a first voltage applied to the first electrode and a second voltage applied to the second electrode is smaller than a first reference voltage (see at least paragraphs 0059-0061).
The limitation, “the PDLC layer and the GHLC layer are realized in a transparent mode for transmitting incident light when no voltage is applied to the first and second electrodes or when a voltage difference between a first voltage applied to the first electrode and a second voltage applied to the second electrode is smaller than a first reference voltage” is functional in nature. Such a functional limitation is only given patentable weight insofar as it imparts a structural limitation. Here, Hayashi et al. discloses the structural limitations required to perform the function as claimed. It is further noted that apparatus claims must be structurally distinguishable from the prior art and that the manner of operating the device does not differentiate the apparatus claim from the prior art (see e.g. MPEP 2114). In other words, the prior art need not perform the function, but must merely be capable of doing so.
Regarding claim 8, Hayashi et al. (figures 1A-1B) discloses the first liquid crystals, the second liquid crystals and the dichroic dyes are arranged in a vertical direction when no voltage is applied to the first and second electrodes or when a voltage difference between a first voltage applied to the first electrode and a second voltage applied to the second electrode is smaller than a first reference voltage (see at least paragraphs 0059-0061).
The limitation, “the first liquid crystals, the second liquid crystals and the dichroic dyes are arranged in a vertical direction when no voltage is applied to the first and second electrodes or when a voltage difference between a first voltage applied to the first electrode and a second voltage applied to the second electrode is smaller than a first reference voltage” is functional in nature. In other words, the prior art need not perform the function, but must merely be capable of doing so.
Regarding claim 9, Hayashi et al. (figures 1A-1B) discloses the PDLC layer and the GHLC layer are realized in a light shielding mode for shielding incident light when a voltage difference between a first voltage applied to the first electrode and a second voltage applied to the second electrode is greater than a second reference voltage (see at least paragraphs 0059-0061).
The limitation, “the PDLC layer and the GHLC layer are realized in a light shielding mode for shielding incident light when a voltage difference between a first voltage applied to the first electrode and a second voltage applied to the second electrode is greater than a second reference voltage” is functional in nature. Such a functional limitation is only given patentable weight insofar as it imparts a structural limitation. Here, Hayashi et al. discloses the structural limitations required to perform the function as claimed. It is further noted that apparatus claims must be structurally distinguishable from the prior art and that the manner of operating the device does not differentiate the apparatus claim from the prior art (see e.g. MPEP 2114). In other words, the prior art need not perform the function, but must merely be capable of doing so.
Regarding claim 10, Hayashi et al. (figures 1A-1B) discloses the first liquid crystals, the second liquid crystals and the dichroic dyes are arranged in a horizontal direction when a voltage difference between a first voltage applied to the first electrode and a second voltage applied to the second electrode is greater than a second reference voltage (see at least paragraphs 0059-0061).
The limitation, “the first liquid crystals, the second liquid crystals and the dichroic dyes are arranged in a horizontal direction when a voltage difference between a first voltage applied to the first electrode and a second voltage applied to the second electrode is greater than a second reference voltage” is functional in nature. Such a functional limitation is only given patentable weight insofar as it imparts a structural limitation. Here, Hayashi et al. discloses the structural limitations required to perform the function as claimed. It is further noted that apparatus claims must be structurally distinguishable from the prior art and that the manner of operating the device does not differentiate the apparatus claim from the prior art (see e.g. MPEP 2114). In other words, the prior art need not perform the function, but must merely be capable of doing so.
Regarding claim 20, Hayashi et al. (figures 1A-1B) discloses a transparent display device, comprising:
a transparent display panel a lower substrate and an upper substrate; and
a light controlling apparatus below the lower substrate of the transparent display panel,
wherein the light controlling apparatus includes:
first and second substrates facing each other (30);
a first electrode on the first substrate (see at least paragraph 0037);
a second electrode on the second substrate; and
a plurality of liquid crystal layers including a polymer dispersed liquid crystal (PDLC) layer and a guest-host liquid crystal (GHLC) layer between the first electrode and the second electrode (10 and 20),
a first alignment film;
