DETAILED ACTION
This action is in response to amendment filed on 9/20/2016. Claim 2 has been cancelled. Claims 1, 7, 10, 13, and 18 have been amended. Claims 39-41 are newly added claims. Claims 1, 3-24 and 39-41 are pending examination.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 13-19 are rejected under under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Namngani (US 5594414) in view of Karandikar (US 20130184979).
Regarding claim 13, Namngani disclose a communication method for a vehicle comprising:
a. calculating a distance of the vehicle from an object (determining distance from the vehicle to an object in field of view, col. 2, lines 55-57);; and
b. recording the event if the vehicle is an unsafe distance from the object (wherein the controller includes a memory for storing input signals from said distance and velocity sensors, claim 3 which depends to claim 1 which discloses said distance to be measured for an object in acceleration and magnitude of the acceleration) but does not explicitly disclose the operation state of the vehicle if the vehicle enters a safe-zone threshold with respect to the object. However, Karandikar disclose the limitation, at least see Fig. 6, steps 604 and 605, and paragraph 33, lines 3-18. It would have been obvious to modify the teaching of Namngani to include the operation state of the vehicle if the vehicle enters a safe-zone threshold with respect to the object to obtain vehicle current operation while vehicle is within threshold distance from an object.
Regarding claim 14, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the event is saved (storing initial distance and velocity input signals, col. 8, lines 15-17).
Regarding claim 15, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein a plurality of different recorded events recorded at different times are saved (col. 10, lines 15-22).
Regarding claim 16, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the saved event is retrievable (col. 11, lines 7-9).
Regarding claim 17, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the saved event is automatically retrievable (col. 11, lines 7-9).
Regarding claim 18, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the unsafe distance is a programmable value (col. 8, lines 4-5).
Regarding claim 19, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further further comprising adjusting the speed of the vehicle based upon the distance of the vehicle from the object (col. 1, lines 40-43).
Claims 1-9, 11-12 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Namngani (US 5594414) in view of Dunne (US 5617199) and Karandikar (US 20130184979).
Regarding claim 1, Namngani disclose a communication system for a vehicle comprising:
a. a pointable range finder (range finders, col. 1, line 32) to calculate a distance between the vehicle and an object (determining distance from the vehicle to an object in field of view, col. 2, lines 55-57);
b. a recorder for recording an operation status of the vehicle (storing input signals from said distance and velocity sensors, claim 3); and
c. wherein the range finder sends a signal to the control device corresponding to a distance of the vehicle from the object and the control device operates the recorder in a manner dependent upon the signal from the range finder (electric device obtaining input signal of distanced from the vehicle to a stationary or moving object, col. 1, lines 1-3). But does not explicitly disclose wherein a control device coupled to the rangefinder and the recorder. However, Dunne discloses a control device coupled to the rangefinder and the recorder, at least see Fig. 1, #16, #30, #34). It would have been obvious to modify the teaching of Namngani wherein a control device coupled to the rangefinder and the recorder to promptly process signals obtained from range finders, but does not explicitly disclose the operation state of the vehicle if the vehicle enters a safe-zone threshold with respect to the object. However, Karandikar disclose the limitation, at least see Fig. 6, steps 604 and 605, and paragraph 33, lines 3-18. It would have been obvious to modify the teaching of Namngani to include the operation state of the vehicle if the vehicle enters a safe-zone threshold with respect to the object to obtain vehicle current operation while vehicle is within threshold distance from an object.
Regarding claim 2, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the control device sends a signal to the recorder to record the operation status of the vehicle if the vehicle is an unsafe distance from the object (wherein the controller includes a memory for storing input signals from said distance and velocity sensors, claim 3 which depends to claim 1 which discloses said distance to be measured for an object in acceleration and magnitude of the acceleration).
Regarding claim 3, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein a recorded operation status is saved (storing initial distance and velocity input signals, col. 8, lines 15-17).
Regarding claim 4, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein a plurality of different recorded operation statuses recorded at different times are saved (col. 10, lines 15-22).
Regarding claim 5, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the saved operation status is retrievable (col. 11, lines 7-9).
Regarding claim 6, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the saved operation status is automatically retrievable (col. 11, lines 7-9).
Regarding claim 7, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the unsafe distance is a programmable value (col. 8, lines 4-5).
Regarding claim 8, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the range finder is actively pointable (col. 7, lines 21-23).
Regarding claim 9, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the rangefinder is pointable in the direction of the object as the vehicle is making a turn (col. 7, lines 21-32). .
Regarding claim 11, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein comprising a speed control system coupled to the control device, wherein the control device operates the speed control system in a manner dependent upon the distance between the vehicle and the object (col. 2, lines 55-65).
Regarding claim 12, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the object comprises a leading vehicle (col. 1, lines 9-13).
Claim 10 and 39 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Namngani (US 5594414) in view of Dunne (US 5617199) and Karandikar (US 20130184979), as applied to claim 1 above, and in further view of Breed et al (US 20090140887).
Regarding claim 10, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above but does not explicitly disclose wherein the rangefinder comprises an accelerometer to determine the direction and degree of turn. However, Breed disclose the limitation, at least see paragraph 103, lines 3-7. It would have been obvious to modify the teaching of Namngani to include wherein the rangefinder comprises an accelerometer to determine the direction and degree of turn.
Regarding claim 39, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above but does not explicitly disclose wherein the recorded operation status comprises a GPS location of the vehicle. However, Breed disclose the limitation, at least see Fig. 4, #46. It would have been obvious to modify the teaching of Namngani to include wherein the recorded operation status comprises a GPS location of the vehicle.
Claim 40 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Namngani (US 5594414) in view of Karandikar (US 20130184979), as applied to claim 13 above, and in further view of Breed et al (US 20090140887).
Regarding claim 40, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above but does not explicitly disclose wherein the recorded operation status comprises a GPS location of the vehicle. However, Breed disclose the limitation, at least see Fig. 4, #46. It would have been obvious to modify the teaching of Namngani to include wherein the recorded operation status comprises a GPS location of the vehicle.
Claims 20-24 and 41 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Namngani (US 5594414) in view of Dunne (US 5617199) in view of Breed et al (US 20090140887).
Regarding claim 20, Namngani disclose a communication system for a vehicle comprising:
a. a system located within a vehicle to calculate and record an unsafe distance encroachment event by the vehicle (determining distance from the vehicle to an object in field of view, col. 2, lines 55-57); and
b. a database for saving the encroachment event, (storing input signals from said distance and velocity sensors, claim 3) But does not explicitly disclose wherein the database is not located within the vehicle. However, Breed et al discloses a remote memory, at least see 127, lines 4-6. It would have been obvious to modify the teaching of Namngani wherein a control device coupled to the rangefinder and the recorder to include wherein the database is not located within the vehicle to obtain external information maintained externally.
Regarding claim 21, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the unsafe distance is based upon the traveling speed of the vehicle (col. 1, lines 40-43).
Regarding claim 22, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the unsafe distance is programmable (col. 8, lines 4-5).
Regarding claim 23, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the encroachment event is automatically saved within the database (storing initial distance and velocity input signals, col. 8, lines 15-17).
Regarding claim 24, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above and further disclose wherein the encroachment event is automatically saved when the vehicle returns to its starting point (storing initial distance and velocity input signals, col. 8, lines 15-17).
Regarding claim 41, Namngani disclose the limitations indicated above but does not explicitly disclose wherein the system records a GPS location of the vehicle with the encroachment event. However, Breed disclose the limitation, at least see Fig. 4, #46. It would have been obvious to modify the teaching of Namngani to include wherein the system records a GPS location of the vehicle with the encroachment event..
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments in regards to claims 1, 3-19 and 39-41 have been considered but are moot in view of the new ground(s) of rejection.
Applicant’s arguments in regards to claims 20-24 have been fully considered but are not persuasive. In particular the applicant argues prior arts do not disclose or suggest "recording an operation status of a vehicle if the vehicle enters a safe-zone threshold with respect to the object". Examiner respectively disagrees. Claim 20 was NOT amended to incorporate "if the vehicle enters a safe-zone threshold" and prior art does teach existing limitations as indicated in rejection above.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).
A shortened statutory period for reply to this final action is set to expire THREE MONTHS from the mailing date of this action. In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action. In no event, however, will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the date of this final action.

If attempts to reach the examiner by telephone are unsuccessful, the examiner’s supervisor, Thomas Tarcza can be reached on 571-272-6979. The fax phone number for the organization where this application or proceeding is assigned is 571-270-8406.

An applicant's duty of disclosure of material information is not satisfied bypresenting a patent examiner with "a mountain of largely irrelevant data from which heis presumed to have been able, with his expertise and with adequate time, to have found the critical data. It ignores the real world conditions under which examiners work." Rohm & Haas Co. v. Crystal Chemical Co., 722 F.2d 1556, 1573, 220 U.S.P.Q. 289 (Fed. Cir. 1983), cert. denied, 469 U.S. 851 (1984). An applicant has a duty to not just disclose pertinent prior art references but to make a disclosure in such way as not to "bury" it within other disclosures of less relevant prior art. See Golden Valley Microwave Foods Inc. v. Weaver Popcorn Co. Inc., 24 U.S.P.Q.2d 1801 (N.D. Ind. 1992); Molins PLC v. Textron Inc., 26 U.S.P.Q.2d 1889, 1899 (D. Del. 1992); Penn Yan Boats, Inc. v. Sea LarkBoats, Inc. etaL, 175 U.S.P.Q. 260, 272 (S.D. FI. 1972). It is unreasonable for Examiner to review all of the cited references thoroughly. By initialing the accompanying 1449 forms, Examiner is merely acknowledging the submission of the cited references and indicating that only a cursory review has been made.

AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Amendment, filed 3/21/15, has been entered. Claims 1-14 remain pending.
Priority
Applicant’s claim for the benefit of a prior-filed application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c) is acknowledged. Applicant has not complied with one or more conditions for receiving the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 as follows:
The later-filed application must be an application for a patent for an invention which is also disclosed in the prior application (provisional application). The disclosure of the invention in the parent application and in the later-filed application must be sufficient to comply with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or the first paragraph of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, except for the best mode requirement. See Transco Products, Inc. v. Performance Contracting, Inc., 38 F.3d 551, 32 USPQ2d 1077 (Fed. Cir. 1994)
The disclosure of the prior-filed application, Application No. 61/635,092, fails to provide adequate support or enablement in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph for one or more claims of this application.
The provisional application comprises no support for the claim 1 limitations directed to messages conforming to different protocols, forming of protocol specific queues or correlation IDs.
Therefore, the filing date 04/12/2013 of the current application is the priority date of the application.
Drawings
The drawings were received on 3/21/15. These drawings are not approved, because they introduce NEW MATTER by deleting Fig. 3 and changing the scope of the disclosed invention .
Specification
The amendment filed 3/21/15 is objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132(a) because it introduces new matter into the disclosure. 35 U.S.C. 132(a) states that no amendment shall introduce new matter into the disclosure of the invention. The added material which is not supported by the original disclosure is as follows: deleted text portions on [0005] and [0022], deleted Fig. 3 and added text on [0005] and [0028].
Applicant is required to cancel the new matter in the reply to this Office Action.
Claim Objections
Claims 1-14 are objected to because of the following informalities: abbreviations “ID” should be explained in the claim 1 limitations, abbreviations “FIFO”, “SIP”, “HTTP”, etc. should be explained in the corresponding claims limitations. Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
Claim 1-14 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the enablement requirement. The claim(s) contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to enable one skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and/or use the invention.
The specification does not provide sufficient details to enable a skilled in the art to make and use the invention because it does not adequately describe the following:
Regarding claim 1, how to use a protocol specific identifier to identify the protocol to which the message conforms.
Regarding claim 4, how to combine SIP, HTTP, MGCP, Diameter, CAP, MAP, INAP, SMTP or SMPP protocols.
The specification does not provide enough details about the structure and operation of the elements associated with the above identified claimed features to enable one skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation.
Other claims are rejected as the claims depending on the claim 1, which is rejected above.
Claims 1-14 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention.
Claim 1 limitations, directed to “a plurality of messages conforming to different protocols and associated with a common communication call” are unclear in light of the disclosure,
protocols are described as set of treatments and tests prescribed by a medical practitioner on [0005], protocols are also described as formats for medical records (HL7, Dicom, etc.) on [0005], and telecommunication protocols (SIP, SS7 or HTTP) on [0004].
Therefore, it is unclear, which types of protocols are identified in the claim 1, as the meaning of “protocols” have numerous and contradictory interpretations, as any of the “protocols” can be used with a communication call/session in a communication network.
Claim 1 limitations, directed to “a common communication call” are unclear in the light of the disclosure, as “a call” is described as telephone connection between a use and another telephone on [0004] and as a plurality of messages from different sources/network using different protocols on [0006], directly contradicting the telephone call description above.
Therefore, it is unclear, if the claimed “common communication call” is a telephone call or an event comprising multiple sources/networks with multiple messages.
In addition, it is unclear which elements can be considered belonging to the “same common communication call”, as the “same call” comprising multiple sources/networks, does not have a clear definition of the call uniting/common/same criteria.
Other claims are rejected as the claims depending on the claim 1, which is rejected above.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
Claims 1 and 3-14 are rejected (as best understood) under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hammer (US 8, 045,473) in view of Martin (US Pub. 2009/0125332).
Regarding claim 1, Hammer substantially teaches a method for correlating a plurality of messages conforming to different protocols (communication between nodes in a packet-switched network, as described on 1:44-2:3) and associated with a common communication call in a communication network (setting up a call or session in the network, as described on 2:4-15), comprising the steps of:
- extracting an information from a message (inherently separating the header of the message from the message payload, because this step is essential for the header analysis, as described on 1:44-60);
-extracting a protocol specific identifier to identify the protocol to which the message conforms, such that all the messages conforming to the same protocol have the same protocol specific identifier (extracting the message header and analyzing the header to determine the message protocol, as described on 1:44-60, and using the headers to combine and store all the messages by the same protocol, as shown on Fig. 2 and described on 8:27-43);
- forming a plurality of protocol specific queues, such that messages having same
protocol specific identifier are in same queue (forming separate queues for specific protocols, shown as 223a and 223b on Fig. 2, described on 8:27-43);
- forming a correlation ID using the information extracted from the message and the protocol specific identifier of the message, (forming/creating call application threads, extracted from the received packets, which are organized in the protocol specific queues, as shown on Fig. 2 and described on 8:37-9:27); and
- forming a call specific queue comprising of messages extracted from the plurality of protocol specific queues (forming call application threads queues, as shown on Fig. 2 and described on 8:53-9:27).
Hammer does not teach forming a correlation ID/threads associated with the same communication call/event.
Martin teaches receiving multiple messages, associated with medical information events, as described on [0028]-[0031], wherein the messages are organized in queues with a particular event name, as described on [0031], and using multiple threads to process the messages, as described on [0110] and [0111].
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to add forming a correlation ID/threads associated with the same communication call/event of Martin to the system of Hammer to improve the system operation in managing medical records application.
Regarding claim 3, Hammer teaches a telecom network exchanging messages/packets, as described on 1:14-43.
Regarding claim 4, Hammer teaches the network using SIP or HTTP protocols, as described on 5:39-56.
Regarding claim 5, Hammer teaches the messages to contain payload/data, as described on 1:44-57.
Regarding claim 6, Hammer teaches the messages protocols to comprise a trailer to identify the end of the data and other protocols/formats, as described on 1:44-2:3.
Regarding claims 7 and 8, Hammer teaches using the message/packet header and OSI model/set of rules for the payload extraction, as described on 1:44-2:1, and using other rules, like tunnel encapsulation, for the payload extraction, as described on 2:1-3.
Regarding claims 7 and 8 (under different claims interpretations), Martin teaches using rules based events, comprising different protocols, as described on [0039]-[0045].
Regarding claims 9 and 10, Martin teaches using sets of methods/rules for organizing messages into events with corresponding threads and using different medical protocols, as described on [0028]-[0031].
Regarding claims 11-14, Martin teaches plural events identifiers, as described on [0039], saving the events in the system memory, as described on [0039], mapping the events with different protocols, as described on [0041]-[0045], and identifying a particular source, including IP address, or type of messages for the messages mapping, as described on [0045]-[0047].
Claim 2 is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Hammer in view of Martin.
Regarding claim 2, Hammer in view of Martin substantially teaches the claim limitations (see claim 1 rejection above for details), comprising use of queues for the packets, as shown on Fig. 2 and described on 8:17-43.
Hammer in view of Martin does not teach using FIFO for the queues.
Official notice is taken that use of FIFO for queues is well known in the art..
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made to add using FIFOs to the system of Hammer in view of Martin to implement a widely used FIFO criterion for the system queues.
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 3/21/15 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
On page 8 and 9 of the Response, Applicant argues that claim 1 limitations are supported by the Provisional Application 61/635,036.
Examiner respectfully disagrees.
Applicant citations are directed to the later filed disclosure, without citing any mention of queues and correlation IDs in the Provisional Application, which “are present in the provisional application at broader level”.
Examiner could not locate cited portions of the Provisional Application 61/635,036 with “This procedure marks related call from different protocols...”, “The proposed solution solves this problem cleanly because it utilizes the index…” and “Protocol connectors have provided specific thread pool…”.
On pages 9 and 10 of the Response, Applicant argues that the provide objections to the Drawings and Specification are overcome by the current Amendment.
Examiner respectfully disagrees.
The submitted Drawings and text amendments are introducing NEW MATTER into the Application by excluding the medical interpretation of the protocol. See deleted portions of [0005] and [0022] and deleted Fig. 3, which changes the scope of the Application.
Added text on [0005], [0022] and [0028] introduces NEW MATTER into the Application.
On pages 10 and 11of the Response, Applicant argues that enablement and clarity problems of the claims, indicated in the previous Office Action, are overcome by amending the Specification.
Examiner respectfully disagrees.
Examiner indicated that the cited text introduces NEW MATTER and Applicant is required to cancel the new matter in the reply to this Office Action.
On pages 12-15 of the Response, Applicant argues that claim 1 is allowable, because the there is no motivation to combine teachings of Hammer and Martin.
Examiner respectfully disagrees.
Hammer clearly teaches correlating a plurality of packets, which belong to a call or a session, by organizing the packets in specific queues based on their protocol and application threads (see rejection above for details).
Martin teaches organizing multiple packets associated with medical information applications in queues for a particular event name, as described on [0031], using multiple threads to manage medical records.
The Supreme Court opinion in KSR case ( 04-1350, U.S. Apr. 30, 2007), rejected the rigid application of the test, requiring “teaching, suggesting or motivation” in the prior art which would lead one of the ordinary skills in the art to combine the prior art teachings.
In current case, combining known methods of Hammer and Martin yield predictable result.
In addition, current Application is clearly directed to medical record keeping, as indicated on [0005] and Fig. 3, the fact, which cannot be erased by the current Amendment to fit different interpretation of the claimed subject, as suggested by Applicant.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action. In no event, however, will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the date of this final action.

DETAILED ACTION
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Priority
AIA
Applicant’s claim for the benefit of a prior-filed application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) is acknowledged. Applicant has not complied with one or more conditions for receiving the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120 as follows:
The later-filed application must be an application for a patent for an invention which is also disclosed in the prior application (the parent or original nonprovisional application or provisional application). The disclosure of the invention in the parent application and in the later-filed application must be sufficient to comply with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or the first paragraph of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, except for the best mode requirement. See Transco Products, Inc. v. Performance Contracting, Inc., 38 F.3d 551, 32 USPQ2d 1077 (Fed. Cir. 1994)
In communications filed 9/29/2015, Applicant claims priority to:
US provisional application 61/314370
Application No. 12/337554, now U.S. 8,118,754
Application No. 11/957988, now abandoned
Application No. 11/940673, now U.S. 8,060,179
As to item (1), Applicant's provisional application, US 61/314370 appears to provide adequate written description support for the claimed invention.
As to item (2), the disclosure of the prior-filed application, Application No. 12/337554, now U.S. 8,118,754, fails to provide adequate support or enablement in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph for one or more claims of this application. Application No. 12/337554 does not disclose using a superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) to detect a residual magnetic field produced by antibody-labeled magnetic nanoparticles injected into the patient for specific binding to T-cells for the purposes of determining organ transplant condition. As such, the prior-filed application fails to provide adequate written description support at least for the system of claim 1 and the method of claim 3. While the prior-filed application cites the Flynn reference (see col. 11, lines 21 - 24) relied on by the examiner in the previous Office Action to reject the instant claims, the mere citation of Flynn journal article is insufficient to provide adequate written description support of the claimed subject matter. Examiner notes that the Flynn journal article is not incorporated by reference into the prior-filed application; and even if it were, essential subject matter necessary to provide written description support for the claimed invention may be incorporated by reference, but only by way of an incorporation by reference to a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication, which patent or patent application publication does not itself incorporate such essential material by reference. See “37 C.F.R. 1.57 Incorporation by reference” and MPEP 608.01(p).
As to item (3), the disclosure of the prior-filed application, Application No. 11/957988, now abandoned, fails to provide adequate support or enablement in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph for one or more claims of this application. Application No. 11/957988 does not disclose using a SQUID to detect a residual magnetic field produced by antibody-labeled magnetic nanoparticles injected into the patient for specific binding to T-cells for the purposes of determining organ transplant condition. As such, the prior-filed application fails to provide adequate written description support at least for the system of claim 1 and the method of claim 3.
As to item (4), the disclosure of the prior-filed application, Application No. 11/940673, now U.S. 8,060,179, fails to provide adequate support or enablement in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph for one or more claims of this application. Application No. 11/940673 does not disclose using a SQUID to detect a residual magnetic field produced by antibody-labeled magnetic nanoparticles injected into the patient for specific binding to T-cells for the purposes of determining organ transplant condition. As such, the prior-filed application fails to provide adequate written description support at least for the system of claim 1 and the method of claim 3. While the prior-filed application cites and incorporates by reference the Flynn journal article (see col. 5 lines 42 - 47 and col. 10, lines 51 - 54), this incorporation is insufficient to provide adequate written description support of the claimed subject matter at least because:
Essential subject matter necessary to provide written description support for the claimed invention may be incorporated by reference, but only by way of an incorporation by reference to a U.S. patent or U.S. patent application publication, which patent or patent application publication does not itself incorporate such essential material by reference. See “37 C.F.R. 1.57 Incorporation by reference” and MPEP 608.01(p); and
Claimed subject matter must have support continuously all the way back to the earliest claimed filing date to get benefit of that date. The claimed subject matter was not supported at least in applications 12/337554 and 11/957988.
Accordingly, claims 1 - 5 and 7 - 15 are not entitled to the benefit of items (2) - (4) discussed above. For the purposes of art, claims 1 - 5 and 7 - 15 are afforded benefit of the filing date of item (1), which is 3/16/2010.
Specification
The specification is objected to as failing to provide proper antecedent basis for the claimed subject matter. See 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and MPEP § 608.01(o). Correction of the following is required: “providing an indication of the organ transplant condition.”
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
AIA
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112:
The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.
Claims 2 - 5 and 7 - 15 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement. The claim(s) contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the relevant art that the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the inventor(s), at the time the application was filed, had possession of the claimed invention.
Claim 2 recites that “the remnant magnetic field detector comprises a processor configured to provide an image …”
Applicant’s specification discloses that the “remnant magnetic field detector” may comprise an “array of gradiometers” ([0007], [0021], as published). Applicant’s specification does not disclose that “the remnant magnetic field detector comprises a processor configured to provide an image …” While Applicant suggests a method including providing an image ([0019], inter alia), Applicant fails to disclose any structure that is configured to provide the image. Applicant's specification makes no mention of a processor or computer configured to provide an image. Moreover, one of ordinary skill in the art would not understand a gradiometer array (that is, a “remnant magnetic field detector”) as being a structure that comprises a processor that is configured to provide an image.
Claim 2 is therefore deemed to present new matter. For the purposes of art, Examiner interprets the limitation as attempting to set forth the intended use of the gradiometers to provide an image.
Claim 3 recites “(b) injecting a plurality of magnetic nanoparticles, each labeled with a targeting agent that specifically binds to cells whose presence is indicative of organ transplant condition.” The scope of this claim limitation is not commensurate with the disclosure.
Applicant’s specification discloses injecting antibody-labeled magnetic nanoparticles that comprise CD antibodies, which are disclosed to be T-cell specific (original claim 15; and specification at [0007]; CD8 and CD4, [0019]; CD3, [0024]; CD2, [0026], as published). Applicant's specification would therefore reasonably convey to one of ordinary skill in the art that Applicant was in possession, at the time the invention was made, of a method comprising injecting magnetic nanoparticles labeled with CD antibodies.
However, claim 3, as amended, is not specific to injecting magnetic nanoparticles labeled with CD antibodies. Rather, amended claim 3 reads on injection of magnetic nanoparticles labeled with any targeting agent, either known only by others or yet to be invented, “whose presence is indicative of organ transplant condition,” wherein the relationship between the targeting agent's presence and organ transplant condition is either known only by others or yet to be discovered. Applicant’s specification briefly discusses that in addition to CD antibodies, “other antibodies specific to organ transplant acceptance can be attached to the biocompatible surface through conjugation methods” ([0023]). However, this statement is not deemed to reasonably convey to one of ordinary skill in the art that Applicant was in possession, at the time the invention was made, of a method commensurate in scope with the method of claim 3. Specifically, this statement in [0023] does not convey that Applicant was in possession of a method comprising injecting magnetic nanoparticles labeled with any targeting agent, either known only by others or yet to be invented, “whose presence is indicative of organ transplant condition,” wherein the relationship between the targeting agent's presence and the organ transplant condition is either known only by others or yet to be discovered.
Step (b) of claim 3 is therefore deemed to present new matter. Examiner suggests overcoming this rejection by amending claim 3 to recite subject matter that is more clearly commensurate in scope with Applicant’s disclosed invention.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(b) the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country, more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States.
Claims 1 - 5 and 7 - 15 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as being anticipated by Flynn et al. (“Use of a SQUID array to detect T-cells with magnetic nanoparticles in determining transplant rejection.” J Magn Magn Mater. 2007 April; 311(1): 429–435; hereinafter Flynn).
Regarding claim 1, Flynn shows a superconducting quantum interference device sensor system, comprising a magnetic pulser, adapted to apply a uniform magnetizing pulse field to a transplanted organ of a patient (“magnetizing pulse from the Helmholtz coils produces a uniform field at the subject of 38 G”, pg. 4, top par.); and a remnant magnetic field detector, adapted to detect at a plurality of regions in space the residual magnetic field produced by a plurality of antibody-labeled magnetic nanoparticles injected into the patient for specific binding to T-cells (magnetic nanoparticles are conjugated to specific T-cell antibodies and the SQUID array detects the decaying remanence fields from labeled cells, pg. 2, bottom par.; fig. 3).
Regarding claim 2, the remnant magnetic field detector may be used to provide an image of the nanoparticles bound to the T-cells on the transplanted organ of the patient (array of SQUIDs used to detect and image the targeted cells, pg. 3, top par.) Examiner interprets this as meeting the limitations of claim 2, as discussed in the written description rejection above.
Regarding claim 3, Flynn shows a method for nonsurgical determination of organ transplant condition (title, abstract, inter alia), comprising:
a) providing a superconducting quantum interference device sensor system comprising a magnetic pulser, adapted to apply a uniform magnetizing pulse field to a transplanted organ of a patient (“magnetizing pulse from the Helmholtz coils produces a uniform field at the subject of 38 G”, pg. 4, top par.); and a remnant magnetic field detector, adapted to detect and measure the residual magnetic field produced by the applied pulsed field (magnetic nanoparticles are conjugated to specific T-cell antibodies and the SQUID array detects the decaying remanence fields from labeled cells, pg. 2, bottom par.; fig. 3);
b) injecting a plurality of magnetic nanoparticles, each labeled with a targeting agent such as an antibody or peptide, into the patient for specific binding to the transplanted organ (particles would be injected into the subject where they would specifically target activated T-cells, pg. 3, top par.);
c) using the magnetic pulser, applying the uniform magnetizing pulse field to magnetize the nanoparticles injected into the patient (“magnetizing pulse from the Helmholtz coils produces a uniform field at the subject of 38 G”, pg. 4, top par.); and
d) using the remnant magnetic field detector, detecting and measuring the residual magnetic field of the magnetized nanoparticles (array of SQUIDs is then used to detect and image the targeted cells, pg. 3, top par.) An image of the nanoparticles bound to the transplanted organ of the patient is provided. The image provides an indication of the organ transplant condition.
Regarding claim 4, the magnetic pulser comprises a pair of Helmholtz coils (“magnetizing pulse from the Helmholtz coils produces a uniform field at the subject of 38 G”, pg. 4, top par.)
Regarding claim 5, the remnant magnetic field detector comprises an array of gradiometers (sensors are second-order gradiometers, pg. 6, second full par.)
Regarding claim 7, the transplanted organ comprises a kidney (inter alia, abstract; pg. 4, bottom par.; pg. 7, second full par.)
Regarding claim 8, the magnetic nanoparticles are labeled with an antibody that specifically binds to T-cells present in or near the transplanted organ (specifically target activated T-cells, pg. 3, top par.)
Regarding claims 9 - 15, the magnetic nanoparticles comprise an iron oxide core that is 25 nm in diameter coated with a biocompatible coating comprising carboxyl and the T-cell specific antibody comprises a CD antibody (pg. 4, second to last par.)
Response to Arguments
Applicant's arguments filed 12/12/2014 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
As to Applicant's arguments that the “priority documents teach magnetization and measurement as in the present claims,” examiner respectfully disagrees. The claims are specifically directed towards the use of a SQUID to detect the residual magnetic field produced by antibody-labeled magnetic nanoparticles injected into the patient for specific binding to T-cells for the purposes of determining organ transplant condition. While the prior applications suggest certain aspects of the claimed SQUID system and the use of nanoparticles conjugated to targeting agents, these features do not provide full written description support for the claimed invention at least because the prior applications do not disclose systems and methods specific to transplanted organs, as recited in the instant claims. As such, Examiner is unable to afford the claimed invention a priority date that precedes the Flynn journal article.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).

Claim 3 is indefinite because it is unclear how the recited method steps relate to the claim’s preamble, as the steps do not include any determination of any condition of an organ.
Claim 3 is indefinite because it recites "a remnant magnetic field detector, adapted to detect, measure, image, or a combination thereof, the residual magnetic field …” It is unclear how a detector may be adapted to “image”. For the purposes of examination, the limitation was interpreted as being directed towards providing a detector or a processor configured to produce an image generated from the detected magnetic field.
Claim 3 is indefinite because it recites “injecting a plurality of magnetic nanoparticles, each labeled with a targeting agent such as an antibody or peptide.” It is unclear whether the targeting agent comprises an antibody or peptide, or whether “such as an antibody or peptide” is merely a list of examples and not a claimed feature of the invention.
Claim 3 is indefinite because it is unclear how steps c) and d) relate to the SQUID provided in step a). For example, it is unclear if the uniform magnetizing pulse field applied in step c) is the field that the magnetic pulser is adapted to apply. Similarly, it is unclear how the whether the detection step relates to the claimed provided detector.
Claim 3 is further indefinite because it is unclear how detecting the residual magnetic field of the magnetized nanoparticles provides an image of the nanoparticles, as detection and image construction are interpreted as distinct steps.
Claim 3 is further indefinite because there is insufficient antecedent basis for "the residual magnetic field" in line 6.
Claim 6 is indefinite because claim element “imaging means that solves an electromagnetic inverse problem” is a limitation that invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph. However, the written description fails to disclose the corresponding structure, material, or acts for the claimed function.
Applicant may:
(a) Amend the claim so that the claim limitation will no longer be interpreted as a limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph; or
(b) Amend the written description of the specification such that it expressly recites what structure, material, or acts perform the claimed function without introducing any new matter (35 U.S.C. 132(a)).
If applicant is of the opinion that the written description of the specification already implicitly or inherently discloses the corresponding structure, material, or acts so that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize what structure, material, or acts perform the claimed function, applicant should clarify the record by either:
(a) Amending the written description of the specification such that it expressly recites the corresponding structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function and clearly links or associates the structure, material, or acts to the claimed function, without introducing any new matter (35 U.S.C. 132(a)); or
(b) Stating on the record what the corresponding structure, material, or acts, which are implicitly or inherently set forth in the written description of the specification, perform the claimed function. For more information, see 37 CFR 1.75(d) and MPEP §§ 608.01(o) and 2181.

DETAILED ACTION
AIA
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
AIA
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
Claim Objections

Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA

As pertaining to Claim 1, Funahashi discloses (see Fig. 1, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, and Fig. 7) a mobile terminal (1), comprising:
a touchscreen (see (10) in Fig. 1) having touch sensors and a fingerprint sensor (see (10); and see Page 2, Para. [0024]-[0025]); and
a controller (see (12) in Fig. 1) configured to:
receive a touch input (i.e., finger or pen input) via the touch sensors (see (10)) of the touchscreen (see (10) in Fig. 1);
determine whether the touch input (i.e., finger or pen input) is intended to include first fingerprint information (i.e., a finger input; see (S21) in Fig. 7);
activate the fingerprint sensor (see (10)) of the touchscreen (10) and receive second fingerprint information (i.e., fingerprint authentication information; see (S22, S23, S24, S25) in Fig. 7) via the fingerprint sensor (see (10)); and
execute a locked application (i.e., a locked processing function) when the second fingerprint information (i.e., fingerprint authentication information; see (S22, S23, S24, S25) in Fig. 7) matches stored fingerprint information (i.e., a stored fingerprint template; see Page 1, Para. [0003] and Page 3, Para. [0035]-[0037]; and, more specifically, see Page 3 through Page 4, Para. [0038]-[0039], Para. [0040]-[0044] and [0046], and Para. [0048]-[0055] for a description of the fingerprint, password, and signature registration process of Fig. 3; and see Page 4 through Page 5, Para. [0058]-[0077] for a description of the fingerprint, password, and signature authentication process of Fig. 7).
Funahashi discloses that a user may select between a fingerprint registration and authentication process, a password registration and authentication process, and a signature registration and authentication process using a graphical user interface and/or a switch (see Page 3, Para. [0036]-[0037] and see (S1) of Fig. 3 and (S21) of Fig. 7). Funahashi further discloses that the separate registration and authentication processes are separately adapted for finger touch input and pen touch input. However, Funahashi does not explicitly disclose that the controller is configured to determine whether a touch input is an input using a finger of a user or a pen input device, and that the prescribed user interfaces for authentication are provided based on that determination. In this regard, Funahashi does not explicitly disclose that the controller is configured to determine whether the touch input includes first fingerprint information when the touch is applied, and activate the fingerprint sensor of the touchscreen when the touch input includes the first fingerprint information.
However, in the same field of endeavor, Kennedy discloses (see Fig. 1, Fig. 2, and Fig. 3) a mobile terminal (200) comprising a touchscreen (see (210) in Fig. 2) and a controller (see (220, 230, 240) in Fig. 2) configured to determine whether a touch input (i.e., a finger input or a pen input) is an input using a finger of a user (see (310, 320, 350, 360) in Fig. 3) or a pen input device (see (310, 320, 330, 340) in Fig. 3), and a prescribed interface (see (330, 340) and (350, 360) in Fig. 3) is provided based on that determination (see Page 3 through Page 4, Para. [0031], [0033]-[0035] and [0040]-[0041]; and Page 5, Para. [0044]-[0047]). Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments with respect to Claims 1, 5, 10-12, 15, 17-19, and 21-26 have been considered but are moot because the arguments do not apply to the combination of references being used in the current rejection. The applicant has argued that none of the references relied upon by the examiner in the prior Office Action, namely Funahashi and Kennedy, teach or fairly suggest the limitations of the amended independent claims including the display of "a first icon" wherein the controller determines "whether the touch input includes first fingerprint information when the touch input is applied to the first icon." The examiner respectfully asserts that the limitations of the independent claims are plainly suggested by the combined teachings of Funahashi, Kennedy, and Moy as newly relied upon above. The applicant is reminded that one cannot show nonobviousness by attacking references individually where the rejections are based on combinations of references. See In re Keller, 642 F.2d 413, 208 USPQ 871 (CCPA 1981); In re Merck & Co., 800 F.2d 1091, 231 USPQ 375 (Fed. Cir. 1986). In this regard, and with respect to the teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy relied upon by the examiner in the prior Office Action, the applicant appears to assert that Funahashi does not teach or fairly suggest a controller to “activate the fingerprint sensor… that differs from a touch sensor used to receive first fingerprint information... and receive second fingerprint information via the fingerprint sensor..." (see Remarks at Page 10). Likewise, the applicant further appears to assert that Kennedy does not teach or fairly suggest a controller to “activate the fingerprint sensor… that differs from a touch sensor for receiving the first fingerprint information... and receive second fingerprint information via the fingerprint sensor..." (see Remarks at Page 12). The examiner respectfully points out that the rejection of the pending claims is based, at least in part, on the combination of the teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy, and the suggestion that those teachings would make to one of ordinary skill in the art. In this regard, the combined teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy plainly suggest a controller to “activate the fingerprint sensor… that differs from a touch sensor used to receive first fingerprint information... and receive second fingerprint information via the fingerprint sensor..." as Funahashi plainly discloses a controller disposed to activate a fingerprint sensor, that differs from a touch sensor, in response to a selection made by a user, and Kennedy plainly suggest the automation of the controller such that the touch sensor receives first fingerprint information prior to automatically activating a finger input mode. In this regard, the combined teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy plainly suggest the activation of the fingerprint sensor disclosed by Funahashi based on whether a touch input includes first fingerprint information as suggested by Kennedy. As such, the rejection of Claims 1, 5, 10-12, 15, 17-19, and 21-26 is maintained.

Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments with respect to Claims 1, 5, 10-12, 15, 17-19, and 21-26 have been considered but are moot because the arguments do not apply to the combination of references being used in the current rejection. The applicant has argued that none of the references relied upon by the examiner in the prior Office Action, namely Funahashi and Kennedy, teach or fairly suggest the limitations of the amended independent claims including the display of "a first icon" wherein the controller determines "whether the touch input includes first fingerprint information when the touch input is applied to the first icon." The examiner respectfully asserts that the limitations of the independent claims are plainly suggested by the combined teachings of Funahashi, Kennedy, and Moy as newly relied upon above. The applicant is reminded that one cannot show nonobviousness by attacking references individually where the rejections are based on combinations of references. See In re Keller, 642 F.2d 413, 208 USPQ 871 (CCPA 1981); In re Merck & Co., 800 F.2d 1091, 231 USPQ 375 (Fed. Cir. 1986). In this regard, and with respect to the teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy relied upon by the examiner in the prior Office Action, the applicant appears to assert that Funahashi does not teach or fairly suggest a controller to “activate the fingerprint sensor… that differs from a touch sensor used to receive first fingerprint information... and receive second fingerprint information via the fingerprint sensor..." (see Remarks at Page 10). Likewise, the applicant further appears to assert that Kennedy does not teach or fairly suggest a controller to “activate the fingerprint sensor… that differs from a touch sensor for receiving the first fingerprint information... and receive second fingerprint information via the fingerprint sensor..." (see Remarks at Page 12). The examiner respectfully points out that the rejection of the pending claims is based, at least in part, on the combination of the teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy, and the suggestion that those teachings would make to one of ordinary skill in the art. In this regard, the combined teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy plainly suggest a controller to “activate the fingerprint sensor… that differs from a touch sensor used to receive first fingerprint information... and receive second fingerprint information via the fingerprint sensor..." as Funahashi plainly discloses a controller disposed to activate a fingerprint sensor, that differs from a touch sensor, in response to a selection made by a user, and Kennedy plainly suggest the automation of the controller such that the touch sensor receives first fingerprint information prior to automatically activating a finger input mode. In this regard, the combined teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy plainly suggest the activation of the fingerprint sensor disclosed by Funahashi based on whether a touch input includes first fingerprint information as suggested by Kennedy. As such, the rejection of Claims 1, 5, 10-12, 15, 17-19, and 21-26 is maintained.

However, in the same field of endeavor, Perski discloses (see Fig. 1A, Fig. 2, and Fig. 3) a mobile terminal comprising a touchscreen (see (20) in Fig. 2) and a controller (i.e., see (6) in Fig. 1A) configured to determine whether a touch input (i.e., a finger input or a pen input) is an input using a finger of a user or a pen, wherein the touchscreen (see Fig. 2 and Fig. 3) comprises a touch IC including a plurality of Tx lines (24, 28), a plurality of Rx lines (24, 28) intersecting the Tx lines (24, 28) and touch sensors (see Fig. 3) formed at intersections of the Tx lines (24, 28) and the Rx lines (see (24, 28); and see Page 5 through Page 6, Para. [0118]-[0119] and [0139]-[0140]; Page 7, Para. [0147]-[0148]; and Page 8 through Page 9, Para. [0165], [0168]-[0169], and [0172]-[0174]). It is a goal of Perski to provide a natural, seamless, and intuitive means of operating a touchscreen that is capable of discriminating between finger inputs and pen inputs using the single touchscreen (see Page 5, Para. [0113]-[0114]). Further, Perski discloses a touchscreen structure that is known in the art and suggested by the teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy.
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to combine the teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy with the teachings of Perski in order to support a natural, seamless, and intuitive means of operating a touchscreen that is capable if discriminating between finger inputs and pen inputs using a structure that is known in the art.
As pertaining to Claim 4, Funahashi discloses (see Fig. 1, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, and Fig. 7) that the controller (see (12) in Fig. 1) is configured to recognize coordinates of a touch input (i.e., finger or pen input) corresponding to the touch input and to acquire the fingerprint image through the touch IC when fingerprint authentication (see (S22, S23, S24, S25) in Fig. 7) is necessary to execute an application (i.e., processing function) corresponding to the recognized coordinates (again, see Page 3, Para. [0035]-[0039]; and see Page 4, Para. [0058]-[0063] of Funahashi in combination with Page 3 through Page 4, Para. [0031], [0033]-[0035] and [0040]-[0041]; and Page 5, Para. [0044]-[0047] of Kennedy; and also see Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 of Perski)
5 is
Funahashi in view of Kennedy and further in view of Semba et al. (hereinafter “Semba” US 7,359,534)
As pertaining to Claim 5, neither Funahashi nor Kennedy explicitly discloses that the controller is configured to provide, on the touchscreen, a notification indicating that acquisition of the fingerprint information of the user through the fingerprint sensor is in progress.
However, in the same field of endeavor, Semba discloses (see Fig. 1, Fig. 2, and Fig. 11) a fingerprint sensor (170) associated with a display screen (150), wherein a controller (see (120) in Fig. 2) is configured to provide, on the display screen (150), a notification (see (SB1) and (SB3) in Fig. 11) indicating that acquisition of the fingerprint information of the user through the fingerprint sensor (170) is in progress (see Col. 3, Ln. 31-58; and Col. 11, Ln. 39-57; and Col. 2, Ln. 33-46). It is a goal of Semba to provide a device and method for fingerprint identification that is capable of implementation in a portable device (see Col. 1, Ln. 12-17). Further, the teachings of Semba with regard to the display of notifications indicating fingerprint acquisition suggest the obvious benefit of improved user interfacing and user friendliness.
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to combine the teachings of Funahashi and Kennedy with the teachings of Semba in order to support fingerprint identification in a portable device with improved user interfacing and friendliness
s 6 and 7 are
Funahashi in view of Kennedy and further in view of Hinoue et al. (hereinafter “Hinoue” US 6,879,710)

However, in the same field of endeavor, Hinoue discloses (see Fig. 1 and Fig. 2) a touchscreen display device (see (34) in Fig. 2) comprising a controller (see Fig. 1) and a fingerprint sensor (see (32, 33, 35, 40) in Fig. 1) wherein the controller is configured to display a fingerprint input window (see (60) in Fig. 2; also see Fig. 9 and Fig. 11, for example) on the touchscreen (34) and to acquire fingerprint information of the user through the fingerprint sensor (32, 33, 35, 40) when a finger of the user touches the fingerprint input window (60; see Col. 7, Ln. 58-67 through Col. 8, Ln. 1-49; also see Col. 11, Ln. 47-62 and Col. 12, Ln. 27-42). s 13 and 20 are
Funahashi in view of Kennedy and further in view of Hinckley et al. (hereinafter “Hinckley” US 9,244,545)
As pertaining to Claim 13, neither Funahashi nor Kennedy explicitly discloses that when the touch input is recognized as including a touch by the user’s finger and a part of the user’s body other than the finger, the controller is configured to process the touch input for only the touch by the user’s finger as a normal touch input.
However, in the same field of endeavor, Hinckley discloses (see Fig. 5) a touchscreen (200) configured to sense touch inputs from a finger and a pen, and a contact discriminator (see Fig. 3) implemented such that when a touch input (see (500, 520)) is recognized as including a touch by the user’s finger (520) and a part of the user’s body (see (500)) other than the finger (520), a controller is configured to process the touch input for only the touch by the user’s finger (520) as a normal touch input (i.e., as a valid touch input; see Col. 16, Ln. 34-54). Hinckley further discloses that user fatigue can be reduced by discriminating between finger touch input and input associated with a part of the user's body other than the finger (see Col. 16, Ln. 49-54).
