Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 1-4, 10-12 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being un patentable over PG Publication US Publication US 20050259629 A1 Oliver et al. (here in after "Oliver"), in view of US 20070263570 A1 Alapuranen et al. (Hereinafter “Alapuranen”).
As per claim 1, Oliver teaches an access node for digital subscriber line (DSL) communication comprising: a transceiver configured to couple a subscriber line (Fig 1, transceiver at the network is couple to subscribers); and a control entity coupled to the transceiver, wherein the control entity is configured to: receive a request to switch to a nominal asymmetry ratio between an upstream data rate and a downstream data rate after initialization of the subscriber line (Para [0014-0016], [0025-0029], fig, 4, network side control device determine the TDD frame and determine the TDD in asymmetrical ratio for uplink and downlink transmission); determine a flexible time period value based on the nominal asymmetry ratio, wherein the flexible time period is used to define a time division duplexing (TDD) frame structure (Para [0014-0016], [0025-0029], fig, 4, determining the frame in TDD asymmetrically based on the information for uplink and downlink for transmitting the information to the subscriber); and forward a message that comprises the flexible time period value to the transceiver, wherein the transceiver is configured to: transmit an downstream transmission using the TDD frame structure over the subscriber line (Para [0014-0016], [0025-0029], fig, 1&4, network is transmitting the information towards the subscriber side ); and receive a upstream transmission using the TDD frame structure over the subscriber line (Para [0014-0016], [0025-0029], fig, 4, receiving the information from the subscriber device in the uplink frame side of the TDD).
Oliver is silent but Alapuranen teaches wherein the plurality of subscriber lines comprise wired connections (Para [0019], the communication between source node and destination node in TDM network is either wired or wireless).
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, to modify the system of Oliver by wherein a downstream transmitter of the first subscriber line is powered off after the transmission of the active symbols during the downstream transmission portion of the TDD frame as shown by Alapuranen. This modification would benefit the system of Oliver for enabling to access the network having multiple access technologies from subscriber side.
As per claim 2, Oliver, Alapuranen teaches the access node of claim 1, wherein the transceiver is further configured to transmit the message to a remote site located at the opposite end of the subscriber line, and wherein the transceiver is further configured to transmit the message multiple times within a TDD frame (Para [0014-0016], [0025-0029], fig, 4, transmitting to opposite side of the subscriber information and is able transmit multiple times).
As per claim 3, Oliver, Alapuranen teaches the access node of claim 1, wherein the transceiver is further configured to switch to the nominal asymmetry ratio at a predefined TDD frame (Para [0014-0016], [0025-0029], asymmetry is defined in time slot).
As per claim 4, Oliver, Alapuranen teaches the access node of claim 1, wherein the TDD frame structure comprises a fixed downstream time period and a fixed upstream time period, wherein the fixed downstream time period may indicate the minimum time period allocated for the downstream transmission, and wherein the fixed upstream time period may indicate the minimum time period allocated for the upstream transmission (Para [0014-0016], [0025-0029], fig 2,4, comprise a fixed time period for uplink and downlink period for transmission and period for uplink transmission).
As per claim 10, Oliver, Alapuranen teaches the access node of claim 1, wherein the control entity is further configured to determine the flexible time period value according to the nominal asymmetry ratio (Para [0021] , fig. 4, determines transmission based on the ration), a fixed downstream time period value, and a fixed upstream time period value, wherein the fixed downstream time period value is based on a minimum data rate for the downstream transmission, and wherein the fixed upstream time period value is based on a minimum data rate for the upstream transmission (Para [0021] , fig. 4, comprise a fixed time period for uplink and downlink period for transmission and period for uplink transmission).
As per claim 11, Oliver, Alapuranen teaches the access node of claim 10, wherein the flexible time period value, the fixed downstream time period value, and the fixed upstream time period value remain the same until the control entity receives another request to switch to a different nominal asymmetry ratio (Para [0021] , fig. 4, entity receives information comprise a fixed time period for uplink and downlink period for transmission and period for uplink transmission)..
As per claim 12, Oliver, Alapuranen the access node of claim 1 further comprising a management information base (MIB), wherein the MIB provides the nominal asymmetry ratio to the control entity (fig. 4, frame structure information base provides information to the control entity).
6. Claims 13, 16 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being un patentable over PG Publication US 20090245093 A1 Rangan et al. (Hereinafter “Rangan”), US 20080232286 A1 Habetha et al. (Hereinafter “Habetha”), in view of US 20070263570 A1 Alapuranen et al. (Hereinafter “Alapuranen”).
As per claim 13, Rangan teaches an access node for digital subscriber line (DSL) communication over a plurality of subscriber lines comprising: a control entity; a transceiver coupled to the control entity, wherein the transceiver is configured to: determine a number of active symbols to be transmitted within a time division duplexing (TDD) frame (Para [0051-0052], determining the number active symbols based on active flag on the symbol for the TDD operation); and transmit a downstream transmission portion of the TDD frame via a first subscriber line using the number of active symbols to be transmitted (Para [0024],[0032], transmitter is meant for transmitting plurality of symbols in a downstream packets in TDD operation ), wherein the TDD frame comprises a plurality of symbols, wherein the number of active symbols to be transmitted is no more than a total number of symbols allocated for the downstream portion of the TDD frame (Para [0030], plurality of symbols in a frame to be transmitted and active symbol with flag is less than the total number of symbol in a frame).
Rangan is silent but Habetha teaches wherein a downstream transmitter of the first subscriber line is powered off after the transmission of the active symbols during the downstream transmission portion of the TDD frame (Para [0028], transmitter of the device list is power off when the active information is passed no more there to pass).
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, to modify the system of Rangan by wherein a downstream transmitter of the first subscriber line is powered off after the transmission of the active symbols during the downstream transmission portion of the TDD frame as shown by Habetha. This modification would benefit the system of Rangan for efficient power management in a wireless communication network for a better power management.
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, to modify the system of Rangan by wherein a downstream transmitter of the first subscriber line is powered off after the transmission of the active symbols during the downstream transmission portion of the TDD frame as shown by Alapuranen. This modification would benefit the system of Rangan for enabling to access the network having multiple access technologies from subscriber side.
As per claim 16, Rangan, Habetha, Alapuranen teaches the apparatus of claim 13, Rangan teaches wherein the control entity is configured forward information to a second subscriber line that the downstream transmitter of the first subscriber line will power off after the transmission of the active symbols during the downstream transmission portion of the TDD frame (Para [0024],[0032], subscriber line that the downstream transmitter of the first subscriber line will power off after the transmission).
Claims 14 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being un patentable over Rangan, Habetha, Alapuranen in view of US 20110058468 A1 Singh et al. (Hereinafter “Singh”).
As per claim 14, Rangan, Habetha, Alapuranen teaches the apparatus of claim 13, combination is silent but Singh teaches wherein the number of active symbols to be transmitted in a TDD frame are set during the showtime state of the first subscriber line, wherein the show time state references the time period after initializing the first subscriber line, and wherein a vectoring mechanism is used to cancel crosstalk between the first subscriber line and a second subscriber line (Para [0068], [0035], vectoring mechanism is used to cancel crosstalk between the first subscriber line and a second subscriber line and subscriber initializing wherein the show time state references the time period after initializing the first subscriber line).
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, to modify the system of Rangan, Habetha by number of active symbols to be transmitted in a TDD frame are set during the showtime state of the first subscriber line, wherein the show time state references the time period after initializing the first subscriber line, and wherein a vectoring mechanism is used to cancel crosstalk between the first subscriber line and a second subscriber line as shown by Singh. This modification would benefit the system of Rangan, Habetha for efficient signal control mechanism in transmission mechanism.
8. Claims 15 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being un patentable over Rangan, Habetha, Alapuranen in view of US 20110274056 A1 Sampath et al. (Hereinafter “Sampath”).
As per claim 15, Rangan, Habetha teaches the apparatus of claim 13, Sampath teaches wherein each of the symbols comprise a plurality of bits, and wherein the number of active symbols to be transmitted within a time division duplexing (TDD) frame is determined according to the traffic volume of the subscriber line, the total length of the TDD frame, the number of bits per symbol, and the number of symbols transmitted per second (Para [0071], The length of a particular time slot may be determined by the access point 1E based upon previous communications with the one or more stations, channel conditions, traffic usage, or other indications). US 20110274056 A1
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, to modify the system of Rangan, Habetha by wherein each of the symbols comprise a plurality of bits, and wherein the number of active symbols to be transmitted within a time division duplexing (TDD) frame is determined according to the traffic volume of the subscriber line, the total length of the TDD frame, the number of bits per symbol, and the number of symbols transmitted per second as shown by Sampath. This modification would benefit the system of Rangan, Habetha for improved capabilities for subscriber line characterization.
9. Claims 18-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being un patentable over Oliver, Habetha, in view of Alapuranen .
As per claim 18, Oliver teaches a method for digital subscriber line (DSL) communication over a plurality of subscriber lines in the show time state, wherein the method comprises: receiving a message that sets a number of active symbols within a TDD frame (Para [0014-0016], [0025-0029], fig, 4, fig. 1, network transmitter is connected to distribution system for transmitting the information to the clients and ); and transmitting an upstream transmission portion of the TDD frame over a first subscriber line (Para [0014-0016], [0025-0029], fig, 4, fig. 1, transmitting the information towards the subscribers through TDD using downlink towards the subscribers ),
Oliver is silent but Habetha teaches wherein the upstream transmission portion of the TDD frame comprises an awake window and a sleep window (para [0011- [0012], comprises sleep windows and awake windows), wherein the length of the awake window and the sleep window are set by the number of active symbols (para [0011- [0012], length is determined by the active information to be transmitted ), and wherein a transmitter of the first subscriber line powers off during the sleep window (para [0011- [0012], transmitter turns of the power off during the sleep window).
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, to modify the system of Rangan by wherein a downstream transmitter of the first subscriber line is powered off after the transmission of the active symbols during the downstream transmission portion of the TDD frame as shown by Habetha. This modification would benefit the system of Rangan for efficient resource management in a wireless communication network for a better resource management.
Oliver is silent but Alapuranen teaches wherein the plurality of subscriber lines comprise wired connections (Para [0019], the communication between source node and destination node in TDM network is either wired or wireless).
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, to modify the system of Oliver by wherein a downstream transmitter of the first subscriber line is powered off after the transmission of the active symbols during the downstream transmission portion of the TDD frame as shown by Alapuranen. This modification would benefit the system of Oliver for enabling to access the network having multiple access technologies from subscriber side.
As per claim 19, Oliver, Habetha, Alapuranen teaches the method of claim 18, Oliver teaches further comprising transmitting an acknowledgement message after receiving the message that sets the number of active symbols within the TDD frame (Para [0031], acknowledge messages are received for setting active period in the time slots).
As per claim 20, Oliver, Habetha, Alapuranen teaches the method of claim 19, Oliver teaches wherein the message maps the location of the awake window and the sleep window within the upstream transmission portion of the TDD frame (para [0011- [0012], awake window and the sleep window are within transmission portion).
Allowable Subject Matter
Claim 5-9, 17 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and any intervening claims.
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments with respect to claims 1-20 have been considered but are moot because the arguments do not apply to any of the references being used in the current rejection.

AIA
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA.
DETAILED ACTION
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments, see Remarks page 8, filed 20 November 2015, with respect to the invocation of 35 USC 112(f) for limitations in claims 1-10 have been fully considered, but are not persuasive. Examiner respectfully disagrees that sufficient structure has been added to claim 1 in order to necessitate withdrawal of the invocation of 35 USC 112(f). Further specifying the “interest aware disparity mapping component” to “define a multiplicity of camera regions…for a target device” merely adds additional description of the function of the “interest aware disparity mapping component” without further specifying the structure for performing its claimed function.
Applicant’s arguments, see Remarks page 8, filed 20 November 2015, with respect to the rejection of claim 16 under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) have been fully considered and are persuasive; the rejection has been withdrawn.
Applicant’s arguments, see Remarks page 9, filed 20 November 2015, with respect to the rejection of claims 11-18 under 35 U.S.C. 101 have been fully considered and are persuasive; the rejection has been withdrawn.
Applicant's arguments, see Remarks pages 9-12, filed 20 November 2015, with respect to claim rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive. On page 10, Applicant argues “Kannan, in describing “…step 102 a depth map of a scene is processed” (as quoted in the Office Action), refers to edges of objects and texture edges, but does not mention, disclose, or suggest a depth edge, or a “depth edge frame” as recited in claim 1.” Examiner respectfully disagrees. Kannan discloses processing a depth map of a scene in order to identify objects in the scene via their edges and corresponding set of pixels (See paragraphs 0018-0020). If pixels corresponding to edges of objects are identified from a depth map, then the set of pixels is “a depth edge frame” as recited in claim 1.
On pages 10-11, Applicant further argues that “Kannan does not disclose performing edge detection on the depth frame.” Claim 1 merely recites “generate a depth edge frame form the depth frame” and does not recite “performing edge detection on the depth frame.” As stated above, Kannan does generate a “depth edge frame” from the depth frame.
AIA
CLAIM INTERPRETATION
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f):
(f) Element in Claim for a Combination. – An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph:
An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
Claim limitation “interest aware disparity mapping component” has been interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, because it uses a generic placeholder “component” coupled with functional language “generate a depth edge frame from the depth frame...” without reciting sufficient structure to achieve the function. Furthermore, the generic placeholder is not preceded by a structural modifier. The structure for performing the function of the "interest aware disparity mapping component" is not necessarily the "processor" in line 2 of claim 1.
Since the claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, claims 1-10 have been interpreted to cover the corresponding structure described in the specification that achieves the claimed function, and equivalents thereof.
A review of the specification (27 December 2013) shows that the following appears to be the corresponding structure described in the specification for the 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph limitation: paragraph 0118 discloses the embodiments of the invention being implemented by “hardware elements” which include “microprocessors.”
A review of the specification (27 December 2013) shows that the following appears to be the corresponding algorithm described in the specification for the 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph limitation: Fig. 9 and paragraphs 0060-0069.
If applicant wishes to provide further explanation or dispute the examiner’s interpretation of the corresponding structure, applicant must identify the corresponding structure with reference to the specification by page and line number, and to the drawing, if any, by reference characters in response to this Office action.
If applicant does not intend to have the claim limitation treated under 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 , sixth paragraph, applicant may amend the claims so that they will clearly not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, or present a sufficient showing that the claims recite sufficient structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function to preclude application of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
For more information, see MPEP § 2173 et seq. and Supplementary Examination Guidelines for Determining Compliance With 35 U.S.C. 112 and for Treatment of Related Issues in Patent Applications, 76 FR 7162, 7167 (Feb. 9, 2011).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.

Kannan et al., hereafter “Kannan” teaches generating a depth edge frame (Kannan, 0020, “At step 106, significant edges associated with the objects in the depth map of the scene are identified”) from a depth frame (Kannan, 0018, “At step 102, a depth map of a scene is processed”) and generating a depth distribution diagram for the depth frame based on the depth edge frame (Kannan, 0020, “At step 110, a foreground region, a background region and a mixed pixel region associated with each of the identified edges are identified based on the identified set of pixels using morphological operations”), the depth distribution diagram defining a multiplicity of regions (Kannan, 0020, “a foreground region, a background region and a mixed pixel region”).
It would have been obvious for one having ordinary skill in the art, before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, to modify a depth scaling process, such as taught by Suh, such that the received depth map is used to generate a depth edge frame and corresponding depth distribution diagram, such as taught by Kannan, in order to achieve the predictable result of identifying mixed pixel regions associated with the identified edges in the depth edge frame, to thereby "preserve soft edges of the objects in rendered 3D views" (Kannan, 0003).
Suh in view of Kannan does not explicitly teach an S3D game and an S3D frame comprising a red-green-blue (RGB) frame.
Cruz et al., hereafter “Cruz” teaches an S3D gaming device (Cruz, Abstract, “Kinect is a device introduced in November 2010 as an accessory of Xbox 360.”) that creates an S3D frame comprising a red-green-blue (RGB) frame and depth frame (Cruz, page 5, “The most natural data representation obtained with Kinect is an RGBD Image, i.e., a combination of three color channels (one for each color: red, green and blue) and another for the depth data… The different nature of colors (visual) and depth (geometric) allow us to use the RGB data to do some tasks that were difficult before, when not impossible. For instance, real time object segmentation, pose recognition (marker-free), etc.").
It would have been obvious for one having ordinary skill in the art, before the effective filing date of the claimed invention, to modify an S3D frame and corresponding depth frame used as inputs to a depth-scaling process, such as taught by Suh in view of Kannan, such that the S3D frame and depth frame are created with a gaming device, such as taught by Cruz, in order to achieve the predictable result of generating RGBD image data for subsequent image processing, to thereby increase the number of applications of the apparatus (See section V of Cruz).
Regarding claim 2, Suh in view of Kannan, and in further view of Cruz teaches the apparatus of claim 1, the viewing parameters of the target device including screen size and expected viewing distance for the target device (Suh, 0044, “The viewing distance is a parameter for indicating a distance between a user and a display screen. The screen size is a parameter for indicating the size of a display screen.” Suh 0047, “A unit established for actual values among a variety of information represented by fields shown in FIG. 2 may be changed to another unit according to display conditions (for example, a device type, a transmission system, and the like).”).
Regarding claim 3, Suh in view of Kannan, and in further view of Cruz teaches the apparatus of claim 1, the depth frame comprising a two dimensional representation of depth information as a function of pixel position for objects depicted in the S3D frame (Suh, 0172, “FIG. 12 shows a method for compensating for a 3D effect being reduced in response to a display screen of the receiving unit in the same manner as in FIG. 10. In more detail, FIG. 12 shows a method for scaling a depth map. The depth map is a kind of data table having depth values of individual pixel coordinates of a real image.”).
Regarding claim 4, Suh in view of Kannan, and in further view of Cruz teaches the apparatus of claim 1, the depth edge frame comprising a set of pixels (x,y) (Suh, 0172, “FIG. 12 shows a method for compensating for a 3D effect being reduced in response to a display screen of the receiving unit in the same manner as in FIG. 10. In more detail, FIG. 12 shows a method for scaling a depth map. The depth map is a kind of data table having depth values of individual pixel coordinates of a real image.”) and values u(x,y) where u(x,y) is proportional to a change in depth in pixels adjacent to pixel (x,y) (Kannan, 0020, “At step 110, a foreground region, a background region and a mixed pixel region associated with each of the identified edges are identified based on the identified set of pixels using morphological operations.” The “mixed pixel region” is adjacent the foreground and background regions. Kannan, 0023, “At step 116, transparency values for the pixels in each of the identified mixed pixel regions are estimated using the alpha model based on depth value and depth jump at each of the identified mixed pixel regions… After each iteration, new pixels are assigned a corresponding transparency value from the alpha model.”).
The rationale for obviousness is the same as provided in claim 1.
Regarding claim 8, Suh in view of Kannan, and in further view of Cruz teaches the apparatus of claim 1, the interest aware disparity mapping component to calculate a camera parameter (Suh, 0177, “the relative position of a recognized object”) for each of the multiplicity of camera regions.
Regarding claim 9, Suh in view of Kannan, and in further view of Cruz teaches the apparatus of claim 1, the interest aware disparity mapping component to generate a mapped left frame L and right frame R for presentation of the S3D frame on the target device, where L and R are a sum of respective left camera views and right camera views of the multiplicity of camera regions (Suh, 0167, “In order to compensate for a reduced depth range in which a depth value of Zw is reduced to another depth value of Zx, the left image is shifted to the right, and the right image is shifted to the left, such that the reduced depth value of Zx can be compensated in the range of Zc. In the case where the display screen of the receiving unit becomes larger than the intended screen size of the manufacturer, individual images are shifted in opposite directions, such that a changed 3D effect can be compensated for. It is also possible that with considering various display conditions, one of the left image and the right image can be shifted.” The mapped left and right images each contain multiple depth layers, which each provide a different view to the viewer. Each image therefore contains a “sum” of the respective camera views for each region with the image because each image contains the total amount of the different camera views.).
Regarding claim10, Suh in view of Kannan, and in further view of Cruz teaches the apparatus of claim 1, comprising a display to present the S3D video (Suh, 0166, “display screen of the receiving unit”), a network interface (0171, “broadcast receiver”) and a radio (Suh, Fig. 9, “RF channel.” The input to the Tuner & Demodulator 9010 is a radio frequency signal, which requires a radio in order to be transmitted in the first place.).
Claims 11-14, 17 and 18 correspond to claims 1-4, 8 and 9, further reciting at least one computer-readable storage medium comprising instructions that when executed by a computing device, cause the computing device to receive viewing parameters of a target device and perform the corresponding functions of the apparatus from claims 1-4, 8 and 9. Suh teaches such a medium (Suh, 0184, “random access memory (RAM)”). Therefore, claims 11-14, 17 and 18 are rejected for the same reasons of obviousness as claims 1-4, 8 and 9.
Claims 19-21, 24 and 25 correspond to claims 1-4, 8 and 9, further reciting a computer implemented method comprising receiving viewing parameters of a target device and performing the corresponding functions of the apparatus from claims 1-4, 8 and 9. Suh teaches such a method (Suh, 0184, “The method disclosed in the present invention may be implemented in the form of program commands executable by a variety of computer means, and recorded on a computer-readable recording medium”). Claim 20 corresponds to claims 2 and 3 considered as a whole. Claim 25 depends from claim 21, whereas corresponding claim 9 depends from claim 1; this difference would not require further rationale beyond that provided to reject claim 4 (which corresponds to claim 21). Therefore, claims 19-21, 24 and 25 are rejected for the same reasons of obviousness as claims 1-4, 8 and 9
Allowable Subject Matter
Suh in view of Kannan, and in further view of Cruz do not explicitly teach the specific grayscale diagram in claims 5, 15, and 22
Conclusion
Chauvier et al. (“DOES SIZE MATTER? THE IMPACT OF SCREEN SIZE ON STEREOSCOPIC 3DTV” - 2010) discuss methods of depth correction in order to address the issues caused by different screen sizes displaying 3D content.
Lambooij et al. (“Visual Discomfort and Visual Fatigue of Stereoscopic Displays: A Review" - 2009) discuss the state of the art with respect to stereoscopic displays including a discussion on the "Zone of Comfortable Viewing."

DETAILED ACTION
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
This Office Action is taken in response to Applicant’s Amendment and Remarks filed on 4/3/2015 regarding application 13/484,627 filed on 05/31/2012.
Claims 7, 12, and 16 have been canceled. Claims 1, 6, 8, 10, 11 and 13 have been amended. Claims 1-16 are currently pending for consideration.
Response to Amendment and Remark
The applicant’s amendments and remarks have been fully and carefully considered, with Examiner’s response set forth below.
Applicant’s amendments to the “Claims 11-16 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101” in claim 11 have overcome each previously set forth in the Non-Final Office Action mailed 11/05/2014.
As to applicant’s amendments to the “Rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)" and “Rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a)”, refer the Office Action as below
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1-6, 7-11, 13-15 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Cohen-Martin (US 2010/0023863 A1, hereinafter as “Cohen-Martin”) in views of Ramamurthy et al. (US 2011/0219308 A1, hereinafter as “Ramamurthy”).
As to claim 1, Cohen-Martin in view of Ramamurthy discloses a method of producing a personalized script for asynchronous video creation, comprising:
establishing a template video format having a generic framework including generic data components; ([0282], the template is designed differently to offer a particular style in the generation of a video. A template include a plurality of items, including one or more placeholders (i.e. framework), multimedia assets (i.e. data components), e.g., visual and/or audio assets such as, images, video clips, texts, animations, soundtracks, sound effects, narration, and further include placeholders that may be linked and populated with dynamic data objects, e.g., universal resource locator (URL), path, database connection link, or any other reference provided by the user or selected from data content of the user).
scripting said template for dynamic merging of said generic data components; ([0283], template is implemented using any suitable textual or binary format, for example an XML string containing XML tags presentation of the different objects, layers and placeholders of multimedia assets. [0122], the customized template has a "placeholder" for insertion of dynamic personalized components, e.g. audio, text, images … etc. The content in the place holders is variable and can be changed dynamically for a variety of media usages and a variety of targets).
said scripting defines alteration of said generic data components; ([0122], changing the info in the place holders is called personalization for different clients, different products, different outlets, etc).
said scripting comprises standard information having parameters for said alteration of said generic data components for incorporating personalized data components into said framework; ([0122], The content is variable and can be changed endlessly in the placeholder for personalization with a variety of media usages and a variety of targets. Each instantiation over the Internet can be targeted to each individual user. [0207], FIG. 5e the customized content is personalized by changing one or more of the variable parameters for a multiplicity of ad purposes).
wherein said parameters include script variables for said alteration of said template with said personalized data components; and, ([0069], the template with various sources of media content to be integrated is available for personalization and customization by the user and also personalize the individual fields in the template to match the distribution list with features such as names, pictures. [0207], the customized content is personalized by changing one or more of the variable parameters for a multiplicity of ad purposes).
merging said personalized data components into said generic framework to form a personalization framework for creating the personalized script for synchronous video creation. ([ABS], FIG. 12, 13 video processor generates a composite video by using the created template based on the XML string including the media asset, wherein the dynamic content objects are replaced with respective extracted data and presented in association with the media asset based on their respective layouts (i.e. framework)).
Cohen-Martin does not explicitly disclose the template framework and script variables are used to dynamically construct a personalized script in real time with personalized data components.
However, Ramamurthy discloses a personalized script with variables as AVST (Applied Voice $ Speech Technique) Template Editor to allow user to build and modify the template files easily. This feature provides assistance with generating scripting (e.g. AviSynth – a script language) code as detail scripts of various tags illustrates in Table A (see [0065]).
Cohen-Martin does not explicitly disclose the scripting automatically set script variables as function of generic data components.
However, Ramamurthy discloses Auto Fade In/Out feature allows for an automatic setting fade in/out from black to be placed at the beginning and/or end of the final generated output (i.e. script variables) deliverable, with the option to specify fade duration (see [0067]).
Thus, one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention have recognized that when Ramamurthy’s personalized script with the setting variables was combined with Cohen-Martin’s personalization framework, the claimed limitation on the constructing a personalized script in real time with setting script variables automatically would be obvious. The motivation to combine Cohen-Martin and Ramamurthy is to provide the capability to easily, efficiently, and economically generate a deliverable video (see [0004]).
As to claim 2, Cohen-Martin in view of Ramamurthy discloses the method of claim 1, wherein said parameters include said script variables for inserting of said personalized data components using said personalization framework for creating said personalized script. ([0122], the content is variable and can be changed endlessly in the placeholder for personalization with a variety of media usages and a variety of targets. This is in response to Applicant’s application 13/484627 filed on 05/31/2012.
Claims 1 - 16 are currently pending with the application.
The information disclosure statement (IDS) submitted on 05/31/2012 was filed before the mailing date of the non-final office action. The submission is in compliance with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97. Accordingly, the information disclosure statement is being considered by the examiner.
Claims 11-16 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
Claim 11 is a system type claim that recite, “[a] system for generating a personalized script, comprising a template including an established format … including generic data components; … template includes functional scripts". However, it does not recite any computer hardware or processor associated with such system. And so, it lacks the necessary physical articles or objects to constitute a machine or a manufacture within the meaning of 35 USC 101. The means to implement the system may be regarded as software per se. Therefore, it fails to fall within a statutory category.
Claims 12-16 depends on claim 11 and all are rejected under 35 USC 101 as well.

AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
DETAILED ACTION
Response to Arguments
Applicant's amendment filed 11 July 2014 has been fully considered. Claims 1-14, 19 and 20 are pending. Applicant has amendment independent claims 1 and 19 to recite a plurality of flexible adapter components. This new limitation is not discloses in either Standish or van der Bos. However, upon undated search and further consideration the Examiner relies on Riddell et al. (2011/0142637) to teach segmenting noise reduction components on the on the trailing edge of the blade. As such the rejection under 35 USC 103(a) has been modified to include Riddell et al.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1-7, 9-15 and 17-20 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Standish et al. (7,918,653) in view of van der Bos et al. (7,909,576) in further view of Riddle et al. (2011/0142637). Standish discloses a blade 22 comprising: an aerodynamic blade body comprising a leading edge 34 and a trailing edge 50; at least one flexible adaptor component 28 having a first side coupled to the trailing edge.
In regards to claim 2, the trailing edge comprises a truncated trailing edge (See Figure 5).
In regards to claim 3, the at least one flexible adaptor component is shaped to fit over at least a portion of the truncated trailing edge (See Figure 5).
In regards to claim 7, the blade comprises a wind blade.
In regards to claim 9, the at least one flexible adapter component comprise plastic materials or rubber materials (Column 5, lines 51-55).
In regards to claim 12, Standish discloses at least one mechanical fastener coupling the adaptor component to the trailing edge (Column 4, lines 23-29).
In regards to claim 13, the at least one fastener comprises an electrically insulative or insulated material.
In regards to claim 14, the at least one fastener is sized to match an aerodynamic shape of the blade body.
In regards to claim 15, Standish discloses a flexible trailing edge adapter component for a wind blade; the trailing edge adapter component comprising: a first side portion shaped for attachment to a truncated airfoil trailing edge of the wind blade.
In regards to claim 19, Standish discloses A method comprising: positioning a first side of at least one adaptor component over at least a portion of a trailing edge of a wind turbine blade and fastening or bonding the at least one adaptor component to the trailing edge of the wind turbine blade.
Standish further discloses providing the trailing edge assembly with a noise attenuating shape (Figures 7, 10 and 12) however the noise attenuating features are not separate components and therefore Standish does not explicitly disclose at least one rigid acoustic segment attached to an opposing second side of the at least one flexible adapter component for mitigating noise during fluid flow over the blade. Further Standish does not teach a plurality of flexible adaptor components segments of a length of two meters or less.
van der Bos teaches at least one rigid acoustic segment 110 attached to an opposing second side of the at least one flexible adapter component for mitigating noise during fluid flow over the blade.
In regards to claim 4, the at least one rigid acoustic segment extends beyond the second side of the flexible adapter component (See Figure 4).
In regards to claim 5, the at least one rigid acoustic segment comprises a serration 112.
In regards to claim 6, van der Bos further discloses an adhesive material 150 for attaching the at least one rigid acoustic segment to the second side of the at least one adapter component (Column 8, lines 49-55).
In regards to claim 10, van der Bos teaches the component comprises a plurality of raised protrusions 122 for positioning of the plurality of serrated segments.
In regards to claim 11, the component comprises a plurality of recessed portions 130 for further positioning the plurality of serrated segments.
In regards to claim 17, the component comprises a plurality of protrusions towards the second side portion for locating the rigid acoustic segments.
In regards to claim 18, the component comprises a plurality of recess portions for attaching the rigid acoustic segments.
In regards to claim 19, van der Bos discloses attaching at least one rigid acoustic segment to an opposing second side of the component.
In regards to claim 20, since the rigid acoustic segment is attached to the trailing edge of the component it would be obvious to attach the segment to the component prior to attaching the component to the trailing edge.

DETAILED ACTION
Response to Amendment
Applicant's arguments filed 8/18/16 have been fully considered but they are not persuasive.
Applicant argues that DeSalvo fails to teach determining if the request to save the call information is an update to existing information in an existing contact card or a request to create a new contact card in the contact database". The Examiner disagrees. DeSalvo discloses four elements 505, 507, 509 and 511 in figure 5 to determine whether the incoming call is new or already existing in the phonebook or not (par.029 “Various other known matching/correlation techniques may be employed to identify a matching entry", "the name and phone number may be added to the address book program (e.g. in response to the user configuring the wireless device store all unlisted callers").
Applicant argues that DeSalvo fails to teach the above subject matter when discussing the allowable subject matter of claim 10. The Examiner disagrees. Claim 1 doesn't have the determine steps after to determine whether the contact card is existing or new to the database by further disclose when the request is to update existing information. DeSalvo fails to teach when the request is to update existing information; display a contact list of contact cars stored in the contact database; in response to displaying the contact list, as cited in claim 10.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(e) the invention was described in a patent granted on an application for patent by another filed in the United States before the invention thereof by the applicant for patent, or on an international application by another who has fulfilled the requirements of paragraphs (1), (2), and (4) of section 371(c) of this title before the invention thereof by the applicant for patent.
Claims 1, 3-7 and 29-32 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) as being anticipated by DeSalvo (US Pub. 2003/0091173, IDS dated 7/01/15).
Regarding claim 1, DeSalvo discloses a computer implemented method comprising:
receiving a request to save call information (fig.5 element 503);
determining if the request to save the call information is an update to existing information in an existing contact card (fig.5 element 505) or a request to create a new contact card in the contact database (fig.5 element 507); and when the request is to update existing information:
receiving a selection of a contact card to be updated (par.023 “to access call information, such as the caller’s name 207”, par.026 “an embodiment of the invention is shown in the form of a phone log for a data processing device”);
updating the selected contact card with the call information related to the phone call (par.030-031) and
storing the updated contact card (par.020 “update and/or supplement the phone number in the address book”, 029).
Regarding claim 3, DeSalvo discloses the call information comprises a phone number (par.015).
Regarding claim 4, DeSalvo discloses the call information further comprises a name of a caller (par.015).
Regarding claim 5, DeSalvo discloses the call information comprises a date of the phone call (par.016).
Regarding claim 6, DeSalvo discloses the call information comprises a time of the phone call (par.016).
Regarding claim 7, DeSalvo discloses the call information comprises a duration of the phone call (par.016).
Regarding claim 29, DeSalvo discloses everything as claim 1 above. More specifically, DeSalvo disclose at least one processor and memory encoding computer executable instructions (par.032, 034).
Regarding claim 30, DeSalvo discloses when the request to create a new contact card:
Automatically populating at east on data field of the new contact card with a least a subset of the call information (par.029 “The user may subsequently be given the option to classify the unknown number under a certain type heading, e.g., home, cell phone... etc.”);
receiving, via a user interface, contact data to be associated with the new contact card (par.029 “The user may subsequently be given the option to classify the unknown number under a certain type heading, e.g., home, cell phone... etc.”);
modifying at least on additional data field in the new contact card with the receive contact data (par.029 “The user may subsequently be given the option to classify the unknown number under a certain type heading, e.g., home, cell phone... etc.”); and storing the new contact card (par.029 “For example, the number stored in the address book may be the caller’s work number and the current call may have been placed from the caller’s home or cell phone”).
Regarding claim 31, DeSalvo discloses the call information comprises a phone number (par.015).
Regarding claim 32, DeSalvo discloses the call information further comprises a name of a caller (par.015).
Allowable Subject Matter
Claims 10-18 are allowed.
The following is an examiner’s statement of reasons for allowance:
Regarding claim 10, the prior art fails to teach “determining if the request to save the call information is an update to existing information in a contact card stored in the contact database or a request to create a new contact card in the contact database”, as cited in the claim.
Conclusion

DETAILED ACTION
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Response to Amendment
The amendment filed 07/22/15 has been entered. Claims 1-18 are pending in the application.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 1-18 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention.
The term "fixed tangentially" in claim 1 is a relative term which renders the claim indefinite. The term "tangentially" is not defined by the claim, the specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree, and one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of the scope of the invention. The specification recites “loose guidance is carried out such that component 4, 5 is displaceable in the radial direction, but tangentially a flat or the like stop prevents a rotation of the element, so that feeder 4, as it were "floating" on drilling tool holder 1, follows the radial displacement thereof” [0034] which is not clear what “tangentially” is limited to since there are an infinite number of tangential points/lines/abutments possible. The drawings do not make up for this deficiency either.
Claim 18 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential structural cooperative relationships of elements, such omission amounting to a gap between the necessary structural connections. See MPEP § 2172.01. The omitted structural cooperative relationships are: the transfer part “interacting” with drill tool holder is structurally unclear what "interacting" is limited to and how it is linked structurally with the tool holder and the housing with fixing ring, holding part, and feeder are all unclear structurally what members they connected to and how they are linked with the tool holder. Since the parts/elements are not structurally linked in the claim, it is unclear how they are connected and what the structural cooperative relationships are.
Drawings
The drawings are objected to under 37 CFR 1.83(a) because they fail to show how component 4, 5 is displaceable in the radial direction, but tangentially a flat or the like stop prevents a rotation of the element, so that feeder 4, as it were "floating" on drilling tool holder 1, follows the radial displacement thereof as described in the specification. It is not clear how the component 4,5 is displaced. It is also not clear if “guide belt 41” is a belt made of fabric or a more rigid material. Any structural detail that is essential for a proper understanding of the disclosed invention should be shown in the drawing. MPEP § 608.02(d). Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. The figure or figure number of an amended drawing should not be labeled as “amended.” If a drawing figure is to be canceled, the appropriate figure must be removed from the replacement sheet, and where necessary, the remaining figures must be renumbered and appropriate changes made to the brief description of the several views of the drawings for consistency. Additional replacement sheets may be necessary to show the renumbering of the remaining figures. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
In addition to Replacement Sheets containing the corrected drawing figure(s), applicant is required to submit a marked-up copy of each Replacement Sheet including annotations indicating the changes made to the previous version. The marked-up copy must be clearly labeled as “Annotated Sheets” and must be presented in the amendment or remarks section that explains the change(s) to the drawings. See 37 CFR 1.121(d)(1). Failure to timely submit the proposed drawing and marked-up copy will result in the abandonment of the application.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102/103
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(b) the invention was patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country or in public use or on sale in this country, more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States.
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), that are applied for establishing a background for determining obviousness under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 1-18 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) as anticipated by Bongers-Ambrosius et al. (US 6575254 B2) or, in the alternative, under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over Bongers-Ambrosius et al. (US 6575254 B2) in view of Watanabe et al. (US 5129467 A).
Regarding claims 1-18, Bongers-Ambrosius et al. discloses a device (9) for supplying a rinsing medium (8) to a tool (16) of a hammer drill (1), comprising:
at least one of a rotatable and axially displaceable drilling tool holder (16) having at least one supply channel ducts (10, 11, 12, 13) for the rinsing medium (col. 1, lines 8-25);
a transfer part (17) interacting with the drilling tool holder;
a housing (7);
a feeder (17) structured and shaped essentially in an axially symmetrical manner; and
a holding part (15) with a rinsing medium inlet (10) and seals for pump 14;
the feeder and the holding part being arranged as a permanently connected component (17 is connected to 15 via housing 7);
friction bearings (bearing collars shown in figure 2 next to outlet 13 and bearing collar at distal end portion of 17) being arranged on both sides of the feeder and arranged toward the drilling tool holder (figure 2 shows the bearing collars toward the drilling tool holder on both sides of 17),
wherein the holding part (housing 7 is a double housing connected by ring member shown in fig. 1 or the holding arm handle member shown in fig. 2 that holds 17 to the power tool) is structured to be radially displaceable with respect to at least one of the housing and a fixing ring connected to the housing, but rotationally fixed and is displaceable within limits via bending with respect to at least one of the housing (7) and a fixing ring connected to the housing, but positively fixed tangentially (housing 7 is a double housing with a interconnecting ring element showing in figure 1 and/or there is a holding arm handle member shown in fig. 2 that holds 17 to the power tool) wherein the holding part is adjustable and
In the alternative, if it can be argued that Bongers-Ambrosius et al. does not disclose or teach having friction bearings being arranged on both sides of the feeder and arranged toward the drilling tool holder and having belts and seals on each side of the feeder and the holding part is not have adjustment capability, Watanabe et al. teaches a hammer drill (fig. 1) having a drilling tool holder (chuck, fig. 1) includes a dust collector (22) on the side of the holder with a bearing bushing hood/collar 27 adjacent a feeder nozzle 28, with a slideable pipe 29 in a pipe 30, where the pipes 29/30 extends parallel to an longitudinal axis of the drill bit 21 and 30 is fixedly mounted on the body 20 by means of the holder 26 and further including hoods 27 with an adjustment knob shown in fig. 1 and bearing collar around 26 in fig. 2 and a flexible hose seal 31 that surrounds all sides.
Therefore, given the teachings of Watanabe et al. of having a vacuum collector extending parallel to the tool axis and housed adjacent the tool with a sliding and radial releasing means with belts and seals, it would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention to modify Bongers-Ambrosius et al. cleansing means 17 with having a bearing attachment which allows sliding and rotating/bending the cleansing means from the tool holder for removal needs/purposes as taught by Watanabe et al.
Response to Arguments
Applicant’s arguments, see Remarks, filed 07/22/15, with respect to the specification reciting “a tool of a hammer drill, and in particular a tool of a taphole power drill” have been fully considered and are persuasive via correction to the specification. The 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection for the specification has been withdrawn and the objection of the specification for not having antecedent basis for the taphole power drill and comma has been withdrawn.
In response to applicant's argument that the references fail to show certain features of applicant’s invention, it is noted that the features upon which applicant relies (i.e., the holding part being structurally linked to the housing and the other structural members) are not recited in the rejected claim(s). Although the claims are interpreted in light of the specification, limitations from the specification are not read into the claims. See In re Van Geuns, 988 F.2d 1181, 26 USPQ2d 1057 (Fed. Cir. 1993). The phrase "positively fixed tangentially" does not clearly recite the essential structural cooperative relationships and specific structural connection of the holding part to the other structure members. Therefore, as claimed in the text, Bongers-Ambrosius et al. discloses a device (9) with a tool holder having a supply channel for a rinsing medium.
Examiner suggests structurally linking all the elements being claimed.
Conclusion
Applicant's amendment necessitated the new ground(s) of rejection presented in this Office action. Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL. See MPEP § 706.07(a). Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).
