DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA or AIA Status
AIA
The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA first to invent provisions.
Claim Status
Claims 7, 8, 13, 15, and 16 have been canceled. Claims 1-6, 9-12, 14, and 17-22 are pending. Claim 5 is withdrawn without traverse. Claims 1-4, 6, 9-12, 14, and 17-22 are being examined on the merits.
Election/Restrictions
Applicant’s election without traverse of SEQ ID NO:40 in the reply filed on 24 May 2016 is acknowledged.
The sequence of SEQ ID NO:40 has been searched and art applied as found below. Accordingly, claim 5 is withdrawn as being directed to species (SEQ ID NOs:1 to 39) non-elected without traverse.
Priority
Applicant’s claim for the benefit of a prior-filed application under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) or under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c) is acknowledged.
I. New Rejection:
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 1-4, 6, 9-12, 14, and 17-23 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA the applicant regards as the invention.
Claim 1 (from which all other claims depend) recites several amino acid positions where the amino acid can be selected from "B” or "X". "B" and "X" are not single letter amino acid codes with a common definition, i.e. the recitation of each within the claims does not allow one of ordinary skill to readily ascertain what amino acids should be present at each position. It appears that the "B" or "X" amino acid codes are meant to refer to norleucine and a stapling amino acid, respectively, but this is not clear from the claims or the specification. It is suggested that to overcome this rejection the explicit definition of each amino acid be included in the claims, as long as support is found within the specification for each specific definition.
II. Modified Rejection:
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The text of those sections of Title 35, U.S. Code not included in this action can be found in a prior Office action.
Claims 1-4, 6, 9-12, 14, and 17-23 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Han et al. (Structure 15:1306-1315, published October 2007, hereafter referred to as Han) and Verdine G and Kim Y (WO 2008/121767 A2, published 9 October 2008, hereafter referred to as ‘767).
Han teaches recognition of EZH2 by EED via a crystal structure (see e.g. Figure 4). Han teaches that a fragment of EZH2 from residues 39-68 was able to bind to full-length EED (see e.g. Figure 1C). In particular, Han teaches that the EBD of EZH2 comprises a sequence of FSSNRQKILERTETLNQEWKQRRIQPV (see e.g. Figure 4D). The F42 residue at the beginning of the EBD of EZH2 is taught to make extensive van der Waals contacts with EED (see e.g. p.1309 Col.1), and a F42E mutant is taught to lose affinity for EED (see e.g. Figure 4C), indicating that F42 is critical for binding. This suggests to one of ordinary skill in the art that a region of EZH2 from 42-68 would be sufficient for binding to EED. The Han art teaches that in EZH1, the residue at position 55 is an Ile, not Thr as in EZH2 and ENX1 (see e.g. Figure 4D). The Han art concludes that EED can be a cancer target by designing small molecules to interfere with binding of EZH2 to EED (see e.g. p.1314 Col.1 ¶1). This suggests to one of ordinary skill in the art that disruption of EZH2 binding to EED in general is a desirable goal, which one of ordinary skill in the art would conclude could be done with a fragment of EZH2 blocking receptor binding.
The difference between Han and the claimed invention is that Han does not explicitly teach that the polypeptide is SEQ ID NO:40 (i.e. where residue 55 is a Ile), nor does Han teach stapling or stitching of the polypeptide.
The ‘767 application generally teaches stitching of polypeptides (see e.g. Abstract). In particular, ‘767 teaches that alpha helical peptides are prone to unraveling, leading to decreased biological activity and increased proteolytic degradation (see e.g. ¶[0002]). ‘767 teaches peptide stapling using an all-hydrocarbon cross-link to maintain natural secondary structure in peptides (see e.g. ¶[0004]-[0005]), including multiple staples to reach a “stitch” (see e.g. ¶[0004]). Included in the ‘767 patent are pharmaceutical compositions of the stapled and/or stitched polypeptides (see e.g. ¶[0006]). Generic peptide having at least three staples to form an internal stitch are presented (see e.g. Formula (II-a) on p.56). Pharmaceutical compositions can include additional biologically active substances (see e.g. ¶[00267]), which includes treatments for cancer (see e.g. ¶[00311]).
It would be obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention based on the teachings of Han that the EZH2 peptide from residues 42-68 (FSSNRQKILERTETLNQEWKQRRIQPV) is an alpha helix that could be isolated and used to bind to EED and block binding of full-length EZH2. Furthermore, given the teachings in Han that residue 55 in other isoforms is Ile, one of skill would be motivated to investigate such a mutation in EZH242-68, and arrive at the instantly claimed and elected SEQ ID NO:40. Given the highly all-alpha helical nature of the EZH2 fragment of Han, one of skill in the art would find it obvious to then introduce peptide stitches as guided by '767 in order to stabilize said helix and ensure its ability to bind to EED and maintain biological activity, and would seek to target residues on one helix face not interacting with EED. The motivation to do so comes explicitly from '767, which has guided that peptide stapling and/or stitching is useful to stabilize peptide secondary structure to maintain biological activity and prevent proteolytic degradation. The teachings of '767 provide motivation to examine staples at a minimum between residues in a helix such as EZH2 to stabilize the secondary structure, and compounds such as formula (IIa) of '767 provide motivation to place multiple staples therein and arrive at a stitched polypeptides. The invention could be reproduced with a reasonable expectation of success, given that Han provides for the all-helical EZH2 domain and its interaction with EED, and '767 provides guidance as to stabilization of helical peptides by introducing peptide staples and/or stitches. The invention would be prima facie obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention.
With respect to claim 2, as set forth supra the Han art provides for a peptide that matches SEQ ID NO:40 with the exception of residue 55 being Thr instead of Ile. The Han art provides motivation to make such a mutation to match SEQ ID NO:40 by comparing EZH2 to related peptides from the family.
With respect to claim 3, the SEQ ID NO:40 as provided by Han is a species reading upon the more generic SEQ ID NO:2 as claimed.
With respect to claim 4, the ‘767 art provides motivation to prepare peptide staples and/or stitches in the helix of Han. The length of the peptide is highly limited (27 amino acids) such that one of skill in applying the staples of ‘767 to the peptide of Han would arrive at the internal staples as claimed. For instance, a combinatorial approach to introducing a single staple from '767 to the peptide of Han would arrive at the i+3, i+4, and i+7 staples at a minimum.
With respect to claim 6, again applying the staples of ‘767 in a combinatorial fashion (given the highly limited 27 amino acid-long fragment to utilized), one of skill would likely seek to place the staples in the same face of the helix (i.e. away from EED interaction domain), and in doing so would by necessity arrive at compounds having at least two staples at i and i+3, i+4, i+7, i-3, i-4, and i-7 as claimed.
With respect to claim 9, as set forth supra, at a minimum the combinatorial approach to stapling as provided by ‘767 would lead to introduction of stitching at multiple amino acids along one face of the EZH2 fragment helix, which by necessity would have to be separated by two, three, or six amino acids.
With respect to claim 10, as set forth supra, the combinatorial examination of the EZH2 peptide of Han and replacement of residues along one helix face with staples would result in the production of two staples connecting three amino acids.
With respect to claims 11 and 12, again the combinatorial examination of the EZH2 peptide of Han and introduction of internal staples as suggested by '767 would result in production of two distinct internal staples encompassing four amino acids, with the first and second pairs of amino acids being internally separated by two, three, or six
amino acids.
With respect to claim 14, again the Han art provides for the same peptide as encoded by SEQ ID NO:40., and the teachings of '767 would allow for internal staples including substitutions of at least two residues to allow for incorporation of the staple.
With respect to claim 17, the '767 art provides for use of multiple staples in a single polypeptide, resulting in a stitch (see e.g. ¶[00133]). Accordingly, this would result in an "internal staple" and an "internal stitch", as by the Applicant's own definition of "peptide stitching" merely indicates the presence of multiple and tandem stapling events in a single polypeptide chain (see e.g. p.18 lines 21-24).
With respect to claims 18 and 19, as set forth supra the ‘767 art provides for preparation of at least one internal staple, which could be separated by two, three, or six amino acids. The '767 art also demonstrates preparation of internal stitches where a first amino acid is connected to two other amino acids where the first and second are separated by three amino acids and the first and third are separated by six amino acids (see e.g. Abstract, Figure 10). One of ordinary skill would reasonably apply these structures to the EZH2 peptide of Han (and avoiding those residues critical for EED interactions) to arrive at the instantly claimed polypeptide.
With respect to claims 20 and 21, as set forth above the ‘767 application allows for pharmaceutical compositions comprising the crosslinked peptides, including those where a medicament for treatment of cancer is included.
With respect to claim 22, a systematic evaluation of the peptide of Han and introduction of staples per '767 would result in production of a staple between A1 and E1, especially given that Han teaches that neither residue A1 (Gln47) or E1 (Glu51) are important residues for interaction with EED (see e.g. Figure 4D).
With respect to claim 23, as set forth above a systematic evaluation of EZH2 as provided by Han, and ignoring those positions known to be important for EED binding, would result in staples as claimed being produced using the teachings of '767. Again, as set forth above the linkage between A1 and E1 would be investigated since neither is important for EED binding, and are found in the helix, resulting in a i+4 staple.
Response to Arguments:
The Applicants argue that no teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine the references exists, and that there is no reasonable expectation of success. The Applicants argue that Han teaches an EZH2 peptide of residues 39-68, with residues F42, N45, I49, L50, L56, P67, and V68 being key residues targeted for mutation. The Applicants argue that all but L50 art critical for interaction with EED, such that the skilled artisan would not target residues for mutation as they would "likely result in loss of affinity for EED". The Applicants argue there is no motivation to alter the EZH2 of Han, and that the altered "loss of affinity" would lead to a loss of any reasonable expectation of success. The Applicants argue that ‘767 is silent with respect to EZH2 and does not provide any motivation to modify EZH2 as claimed or reasonable expectation of success. The Applicants argue that EZH2 is not all alpha-helical, such that residues following E3 would adopt a rigid coil as secondary structure. The Applicants argue this combination of secondary structure is not addressed by '767 to allow for stitching of anything other than an alpha helix. The Applicants’ arguments have been considered but are not persuasive.
First, the requirement for a specific teaching, suggestion, or motivation was rejected by the Supreme Court as too rigid of a test for obviousness. See MPEP 2141:
The Supreme Court in KSR reaffirmed the familiar framework for determining obviousness as set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), but stated that the Federal Circuit had erred by applying the teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) test in an overly rigid and formalistic way. KSR, 550 U.S. at 404, 82 USPQ2d at 1391.
The Court in KSR reaffirmed the framework of Graham v. Deere, and the instant application utilizes what is essentially rationale (A) for concluding obviousness (combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results). In the instant case, the Examiner has identified the relevant teachings in Han, providing for where mutations should and should not be made in EZH2, as well as a reasonable teaching from Han that provides for production of SEQ ID NO:40 as claimed via introduction of Ile instead of Thr at position 55. Again, since Han teaches this residue is not critical for interaction with EED and that at least one homolog in the family possesses an Ile at this position, it is reasonable that one of ordinary skill would apply such a mutation to EZH2 of Han. Furthermore, the ‘767 art provided the staples and/or stitches utilized and demonstrated that they could be used to stabilize secondary structure in a peptide, particularly in an alpha helix. Even assuming arguendo that EZH2 possesses both alpha helical and rigid coil structure, the skilled artisan would still seek to stabilize the alpha helix of EZH2 (ignoring critical residues for EED interaction) in order to provide a stabilized EZH2 analog. MPEP 2143 I. A. does not require any other findings beyond those presented in the rejection, nor does it require a specific TSM to be present in order to conclude obviousness. Respectfully, the Examiner submits that the Office’s burden in concluding obviousness has been met.
As to the arguments that Han teaches critical residues for EED interaction, such that those would not be targeted for mutation via staples/stitches owing to a potential loss of EED affinity, the Examiner has not indicated that any of these residues should be targeted. Rather, the Examiner has indicated that (1) residue 55 should be mutated to Ile as found in at least one other family member (and is not a critical residue for interaction with EED) and (2) even considering these residues as important, Han has set forth that blocking interaction of EZH2 with EED could be an important cancer target. Doing so via designing of a stabilized EZH2 fragment (i.e. one that might interact but not activate EED) would be desirable. Even ignoring this, the Han art clearly sets forth the critical residues for interaction, which the skilled artisan would ignore as a first step in applying the staples and/or stitches of '767 to EZH242-68.
As to the supposed lack of motivation to alter EZH2, again the Examiner submits that Han sets forth a goal of disrupting EZH2 and EED interaction. This could be accomplished by utilizing fragments of EZH2, i.e. the SEQ ID NO:40 as provided by Han and altered by helix stabilization of ‘767. Even ignoring this, the Examiner has already set forth the ‘767 application as providing motivation to alter Han, as it sets forth ways of stabilizing helical structure via polypeptide staples and/or stitches.
The Applicants have provided nothing more than a statement that there is no reasonable expectation of success. Given that the instant claims require nothing other than a stapled or stitched EZH2 of SEQ ID NO:40, the Examiner sees no reason why the skilled artisan would not expect to be able to produce such a molecule using Han and ‘767. Again, Han provides for production of SEQ ID NO:40, and provides guidance on residues to avoid for critical interactions with EED. The ‘767 art provides for stabilizing of alpha helices via stapling and/or stitching, which could readily be applied to EZH2 having the same alpha helical structure. Since the critical residues for EED interaction are highlighted by Han, one of skill would have a reasonable knowledge where and how to target SEQ ID NO:40 for stapling and/or stitching, and arrive at the claimed invention. Since no particular features are required of the final peptide, Examiner fails to see how the expectation of success is lacking (i.e. the only real effort required is stapling, which is already known in the art).
As set forth supra, the ‘767 art provides a base motivation to alter Han by disclosing the stabilization of alpha helical structure with peptide staples and/or stitches. Since Han demonstrates the same structure is present, the skilled artisan would reasonably apply the same stabilization techniques of ‘767 to the same type of secondary structure.
The Examiner agrees after further consideration that EZH2 is not all alpha helical. However, nothing in the claims requires E3 to be involved in any staples and/or stitches. The '767 art combined with Han still allows for staples and/or stitches to occur in the alpha helical structure of EZH2, and thus stabilize the secondary structure. Nothing in the instant claims requires the stapling to occur specifically between the helical portion of EZH2 and the rigid coil region. Even were this the case, there is nothing from the '767 art indicating that a link cannot be made between residues in disparate secondary structures.
The rejection is maintained.

The objection to claims 1, 4, 6, 9, 10, and 14-16 for informalities is withdrawn in light of the amendment filed 18 October 2016.
The rejection of claims 1, 4, 6, 9-13, and 15-21 under 35 U.S.C. 112, 1st paragraph for written description is withdrawn in light of the amendment filed 18 October 2016.
The rejection of claims 15-19 under 35 U.S.C. 112, 2nd paragraph is withdrawn in light of the amendment filed 18 October 2016.

The F42 residue at the beginning of the EBD of EZH2 is taught to make extensive van der Waals contacts with EED (see e.g. p.1309 Col.1), and a F42E mutant is taught to lose affinity for EED (see e.g. Figure 4C), indicating that F42 is critical for binding. This suggests to one of ordinary skill in the art that a region of EZH2 from 42-68 would be sufficient for binding to EED. The Han art teaches that in EZH1, the residue at position 55 is an Ile, not Thr as in EZH2 and ENX1 (see e.g. Figure 4D). The Han art concludes that EED can be a cancer target by designing small molecules to interfere with binding of EZH2 to EED (see e.g. p.1314 Col.1 ¶1). This suggests to one of ordinary skill in the art that disruption of EZH2 binding to EED in general is a desirable goal, which one of ordinary skill in the art would conclude could be done with a fragment of EZH2 blocking receptor binding.
The difference between Han and the claimed invention is that Han does not explicitly teach that the polypeptide is SEQ ID NO:40 (i.e. where residue 55 is a Ile), nor does Han teach stapling or stitching of the polypeptide.
The ‘767 application generally teaches stitching of polypeptides (see e.g. Abstract). In particular, ‘767 teaches that alpha helical peptides are prone to unraveling, leading to decreased biological activity and increased proteolytic degradation (see e.g. ¶[0002]). ‘767 teaches peptide stapling using an all-hydrocarbon cross-link to maintain natural secondary structure in peptides (see e.g. ¶[0004]-[0005]), including multiple staples to reach a “stitch” (see e.g. ¶[0004]). Included in the ‘767 patent are pharmaceutical compositions of the stapled and/or stitched polypeptides (see e.g. ¶[0006]). Generic peptide having at least three staples to form an internal stitch are presented (see e.g. Formula (II-a) on p.56). Pharmaceutical compositions can include additional biologically active substances (see e.g. ¶[00267]), which includes treatments for cancer (see e.g. ¶[00311]).
It would be obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention based on the teachings of Han that the EZH2 peptide from residues 42-68 (FSSNRQKILERTETLNQEWKQRRIQPV) is an alpha helix that could be isolated and used to bind to EED and block binding of full-length EZH2. Furthermore, given the teachings in Han that residue 55 in other isoforms is Ile, one of skill would be motivated to investigate such a mutation in EZH242-68, and arrive at the instantly claimed and elected SEQ ID NO:40. Given the highly all-alpha helical nature of the EZH2 fragment of Han, one of skill in the art would find it obvious to then introduce peptide stitches as guided by '767 in order to stabilize said helix and ensure its ability to bind to EED and maintain biological activity, and would seek to target residues on one helix face not interacting with EED. The motivation to do so comes explicitly from '767, which has guided that peptide stapling and/or stitching is useful to stabilize peptide secondary structure to maintain biological activity and prevent proteolytic degradation. The teachings of '767 provide motivation to examine staples at a minimum between residues in a helix such as EZH2 to stabilize the secondary structure, and compounds such as formula (IIa) of '767 provide motivation to place multiple staples therein and arrive at a stitched polypeptides. The invention could be reproduced with a reasonable expectation of success, given that Han provides for the all-helical EZH2 domain and its interaction with EED, and '767 provides guidance as to stabilization of helical peptides by introducing peptide staples and/or stitches. The invention would be prima facie obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention.
With respect to claim 2, as set forth supra the Han art provides for a peptide that matches SEQ ID NO:40 with the exception of residue 55 being Thr instead of Ile. The Han art provides motivation to make such a mutation to match SEQ ID NO:40 by comparing EZH2 to related peptides from the family.
With respect to claim 3, the SEQ ID NO:40 as provided by Han is a species reading upon the more generic SEQ ID NO:2 as claimed.
With respect to claim 4, the ‘767 art provides motivation to prepare peptide staples and/or stitches in the helix of Han. The length of the peptide is highly limited (27 amino acids) such that one of skill in applying the staples of ‘767 to the peptide of Han would arrive at the internal staples as claimed. For instance, a combinatorial approach to introducing a single staple from '767 to the peptide of Han would arrive at the i+3, i+4, and i+7 staples at a minimum.
With respect to claim 6, again applying the staples of ‘767 in a combinatorial fashion (given the highly limited 27 amino acid-long fragment to utilized), one of skill would likely seek to place the staples in the same face of the helix (i.e. away from EED interaction domain), and in doing so would by necessity arrive at compounds having at least two staples at i and i+3, i+4, i+7, i-3, i-4, and i-7 as claimed.
With respect to claim 9, as set forth supra, at a minimum the combinatorial approach to stapling as provided by ‘767 would lead to introduction of stitching at multiple amino acids along one face of the EZH2 fragment helix, which by necessity would have to be separated by two, three, or six amino acids.
With respect to claim 10, as set forth supra, the combinatorial examination of the EZH2 peptide of Han and replacement of residues along one helix face with staples would result in the production of two staples connecting three amino acids.
With respect to claims 11 and 12, again the combinatorial examination of the EZH2 peptide of Han and introduction of internal staples as suggested by '767 would result in production of two distinct internal staples encompassing four amino acids, with the first and second pairs of amino acids being internally separated by two, three, or six
amino acids.
With respect to claim 14, again the Han art provides for the same peptide as encoded by SEQ ID NO:40., and the teachings of '767 would allow for internal staples including substitutions of at least two residues to allow for incorporation of the staple.
With respect to claim 17, the '767 art provides for use of multiple staples in a single polypeptide, resulting in a stitch (see e.g. ¶[00133]). Accordingly, this would result in an "internal staple" and an "internal stitch", as by the Applicant's own definition of "peptide stitching" merely indicates the presence of multiple and tandem stapling events in a single polypeptide chain (see e.g. p.18 lines 21-24).
With respect to claims 18 and 19, as set forth supra the ‘767 art provides for preparation of at least one internal staple, which could be separated by two, three, or six amino acids. The '767 art also demonstrates preparation of internal stitches where a first amino acid is connected to two other amino acids where the first and second are separated by three amino acids and the first and third are separated by six amino acids (see e.g. Abstract, Figure 10). One of ordinary skill would reasonably apply these structures to the EZH2 peptide of Han (and avoiding those residues critical for EED interactions) to arrive at the instantly claimed polypeptide.
With respect to claims 20 and 21, as set forth above the ‘767 application allows for pharmaceutical compositions comprising the crosslinked peptides, including those where a medicament for treatment of cancer is included.

Again, as set forth above the linkage between A1 and E1 would be investigated since neither is important for EED binding, and are found in the helix, resulting in a i+4 staple.
Response to Arguments:
The Applicants argue that no teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine the references exists, and that there is no reasonable expectation of success. The Applicants argue that Han teaches an EZH2 peptide of residues 39-68, with residues F42, N45, I49, L50, L56, P67, and V68 being key residues targeted for mutation. The Applicants argue that all but L50 art critical for interaction with EED, such that the skilled artisan would not target residues for mutation as they would "likely result in loss of affinity for EED". The Applicants argue there is no motivation to alter the EZH2 of Han, and that the altered "loss of affinity" would lead to a loss of any reasonable expectation of success. The Applicants argue that ‘767 is silent with respect to EZH2 and does not provide any motivation to modify EZH2 as claimed or reasonable expectation of success. The Applicants argue that EZH2 is not all alpha-helical, such that residues following E3 would adopt a rigid coil as secondary structure. The Applicants argue this combination of secondary structure is not addressed by '767 to allow for stitching of anything other than an alpha helix. The Applicants’ arguments have been considered but are not persuasive.
First, the requirement for a specific teaching, suggestion, or motivation was rejected by the Supreme Court as too rigid of a test for obviousness. See MPEP 2141:
The Supreme Court in KSR reaffirmed the familiar framework for determining obviousness as set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1, 148 USPQ 459 (1966), but stated that the Federal Circuit had erred by applying the teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) test in an overly rigid and formalistic way. KSR, 550 U.S. at 404, 82 USPQ2d at 1391.
The Court in KSR reaffirmed the framework of Graham v. Deere, and the instant application utilizes what is essentially rationale (A) for concluding obviousness (combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results). In the instant case, the Examiner has identified the relevant teachings in Han, providing for where mutations should and should not be made in EZH2, as well as a reasonable teaching from Han that provides for production of SEQ ID NO:40 as claimed via introduction of Ile instead of Thr at position 55. Again, since Han teaches this residue is not critical for interaction with EED and that at least one homolog in the family possesses an Ile at this position, it is reasonable that one of ordinary skill would apply such a mutation to EZH2 of Han. Furthermore, the ‘767 art provided the staples and/or stitches utilized and demonstrated that they could be used to stabilize secondary structure in a peptide, particularly in an alpha helix. Even assuming arguendo that EZH2 possesses both alpha helical and rigid coil structure, the skilled artisan would still seek to stabilize the alpha helix of EZH2 (ignoring critical residues for EED interaction) in order to provide a stabilized EZH2 analog. MPEP 2143 I. A. does not require any other findings beyond those presented in the rejection, nor does it require a specific TSM to be present in order to conclude obviousness. Respectfully, the Examiner submits that the Office’s burden in concluding obviousness has been met.
As to the arguments that Han teaches critical residues for EED interaction, such that those would not be targeted for mutation via staples/stitches owing to a potential loss of EED affinity, the Examiner has not indicated that any of these residues should be targeted. Rather, the Examiner has indicated that (1) residue 55 should be mutated to Ile as found in at least one other family member (and is not a critical residue for interaction with EED) and (2) even considering these residues as important, Han has set forth that blocking interaction of EZH2 with EED could be an important cancer target. Doing so via designing of a stabilized EZH2 fragment (i.e. one that might interact but not activate EED) would be desirable. Even ignoring this, the Han art clearly sets forth the critical residues for interaction, which the skilled artisan would ignore as a first step in applying the staples and/or stitches of '767 to EZH242-68.
As to the supposed lack of motivation to alter EZH2, again the Examiner submits that Han sets forth a goal of disrupting EZH2 and EED interaction. This could be accomplished by utilizing fragments of EZH2, i.e. the SEQ ID NO:40 as provided by Han and altered by helix stabilization of ‘767. Even ignoring this, the Examiner has already set forth the ‘767 application as providing motivation to alter Han, as it sets forth ways of stabilizing helical structure via polypeptide staples and/or stitches.
The Applicants have provided nothing more than a statement that there is no reasonable expectation of success. Given that the instant claims require nothing other than a stapled or stitched EZH2 of SEQ ID NO:40, the Examiner sees no reason why the skilled artisan would not expect to be able to produce such a molecule using Han and ‘767. Again, Han provides for production of SEQ ID NO:40, and provides guidance on residues to avoid for critical interactions with EED. The ‘767 art provides for stabilizing of alpha helices via stapling and/or stitching, which could readily be applied to EZH2 having the same alpha helical structure. Since the critical residues for EED interaction are highlighted by Han, one of skill would have a reasonable knowledge where and how to target SEQ ID NO:40 for stapling and/or stitching, and arrive at the claimed invention. Since no particular features are required of the final peptide, Examiner fails to see how the expectation of success is lacking (i.e. the only real effort required is stapling, which is already known in the art).
As set forth supra, the ‘767 art provides a base motivation to alter Han by disclosing the stabilization of alpha helical structure with peptide staples and/or stitches. Since Han demonstrates the same structure is present, the skilled artisan would reasonably apply the same stabilization techniques of ‘767 to the same type of secondary structure.
The Examiner agrees after further consideration that EZH2 is not all alpha helical. However, nothing in the claims requires E3 to be involved in any staples and/or stitches. The '767 art combined with Han still allows for staples and/or stitches to occur in the alpha helical structure of EZH2, and thus stabilize the secondary structure. Nothing in the instant claims requires the stapling to occur specifically between the helical portion of EZH2 and the rigid coil region. Even were this the case, there is nothing from the '767 art indicating that a link cannot be made between residues in disparate secondary structures.
The rejection is maintained.
III. Withdrawn Objections/Rejections:
The objection to claims 1, 4, 6, 9, 10, and 14-16 for informalities is withdrawn in light of the amendment filed 18 October 2016.
The rejection of claims 1, 4, 6, 9-13, and 15-21 under 35 U.S.C. 112, 1st paragraph for written description is withdrawn in light of the amendment filed 18 October 2016.
The rejection of claims 15-19 under 35 U.S.C. 112, 2nd paragraph is withdrawn in light of the amendment filed 18 October 2016

These include "level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention. A claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient descriptions of a representative number of species or disclosure of relevant, identifying characteristics such as functional characteristics coupled with known or disclosed correlation between function and structure (MPEP 2163(3)a(II)). The number of species that describe the genus must be adequate to describe the entire genus; if there is substantial variability, a large number of species must be described.
The analysis for adequate written description considers (a) actual reduction to practice, (b) disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas, (c) sufficient relevant identifying characteristics in the way of complete/partial structure or physical and/or chemical properties or functional characteristics when coupled with known or disclosed correlation with structure, and (d) representative number of samples.

The claims at their broadest are drawn to a peptide of SEQ ID NO:1. SEQ ID NO:1 encodes a generic 29 amino acid-long peptide where each of the 29 positions can additionally be "a conservative substitution".

Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
AIA
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
AIA
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claims 1-5, 7, and 9-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Baleine et al. U.S. Patent Application Publication 2012/0200698.
With respect to claims 1, 11, 12, and 20, Baleine teaches receiving, by a processor, realtime data from a camera (IR camera 14) monitoring one or more hot gas path components of the gas turbine (turbine 15) while the gas turbine is in operation (paragraph 12); comparing, by the processor (processor 30), the realtime data to reference data (images from spots 181, 182, and 183, are compared to previous images from the same spots, paragraphs 19-20); based at least in part on the comparison, determining, by the processor, that a difference between the realtime data and the reference data exceeds a predetermined threshold (processor 30 and image recognition module can compare images to determine a physical change, the change in the image is interpreted as being a threshold as the threshold can be the data from the "first" image); and based at least in part on the determination, selectively notifying of an anomaly in the one or more hot gas path components (paragraph 21).
With respect to claim 2, Baleine teaches wherein the receiving the realtime data comprises receiving a thermographic map (paragraph 26).
With respect to claim 3, Baleine teaches wherein the comparing comprises measuring a distance between the one or more hot gas path components on the thermographic map and comparing the measured distance to a reference distance between the one or more hot gas path components (images are compared to previous images and a change between these images in determined, this change is interpreted as a distance, paragraphs 19-23).
With respect to claims 4 and 17, Baleine teaches wherein the comparing comprises counting pixels between the one or more hot gas path components on the thermographic map and comparing the counted pixels to a reference number of pixels between the one or more hot gas path components (paragraphs 19-23).
With respect to claims 5 and 18, Baleine teaches wherein the comparing comprises subtracting an image associated with the one or more hot gas path components from a reference image associated with the one or more hot gas path components (paragraphs 19-23).
With respect to claim 7, Baleine teaches wherein the notifying comprises one or more of the following: issuing an alert to operators of the gas turbine, providing a maintenance advisory to the operators of the gas turbine, issuing a signal to a protective system associated with the gas turbine, providing operation recommendation to the operators of the gas turbine, and providing a visualization of abnormality trends to the operators of the gas turbine (paragraph 21).
With respect to claim 9, Baleine teaches storing the realtime data to a database to be used as historical data at a later time (paragraphs 19-23).
With respect to claims 10 and 14, Baleine teaches wherein the determining that the difference between the realtime data and the reference data exceeds the predetermined threshold is indicative of one or more of migration, liberation, shrouding, and cracking of the one or more hot gas path components (paragraphs 19-22).
With respect to claim 13, Baleine teaches wherein the camera comprises a video camera (14, figure 1).
With respect to claim 15, Baleine teaches wherein the camera comprises a thermographic camera (14, figure 1).
With respect to claim 16, Baleine teaches wherein the reference data comprises reference temperature values associated with the one or more hot gas path components and the realtime data comprises realtime temperature values associated with the one or more hot gas path components (paragraphs 19-23).
With respect to claim 19, Baleine teaches wherein the one or more hot gas path components comprise one or more of a bucket, a nozzle, and a rotor (figure 1).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
AIA
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
AIA
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
AIA
Claim 6 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Baleine et al. U.S. Patent Application Publication 2012/0200698 in view of Telfer U.S. Patent Application Publication 2013/0202192.
With respect to claim 6, Baleine teaches the claimed invention except wherein the comparing comprises comparing 3D images of adjacent one or more hot gas path components, the 3D images being created by mapping images generated by the camera onto preexisting 3D models.
Telfer teaches an apparatus and method for measuring strain on a turbine component wherein 3D images are compared to determine component damage (paragraph 26).
Accordingly, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art turbine component analysis at the time the invention was made to modify the system of Baleine with the 3D image processing as taught by Telfer in order to more accurately determine changes to the turbine during operation.
AIA
Claim 8 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Baleine et al. U.S. Patent Application Publication 2012/0200698 in view of Narcus U.S. Patent 7,925,454.
With respect to claim 8, Baleine teaches the claimed invention except wherein comprising performing a shutdown of the gas turbine based at least in part on the determination.
Narcus teaches a process for determining the remaining life of a component wherein the engine is shut down after it is determined the component is damaged (step 21).
Accordingly, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art turbine engine analysis at the time the invention was made to modify the system of Baleine with the shutdown procedure as taught by Narcus in order to protect the engine from further damage before the component will suffer critical damage or the engine will suffer unacceptable performance (abstract, Narcus).

With respect to claims 2-4, 15-16, and 20, Telfer teaches a gas turbine including a plurality of hot gas path components (74); a camera (88) operable to monitor the plurality of hot gas path components; and a processor (controller 90) communicatively coupled to the camera and operable to: receive realtime images from the camera monitoring the plurality of hot gas path components of the gas turbine (S102); compare the realtime images to reference images (S108); based at least in part on the comparison, determine that a difference between the realtime images and the reference images exceeds a predetermined threshold (S110); and based at least in part on the determination, selectively notify of an anomaly in the plurality of hot gas path components (S114, paragraphs 23-30). Further, Telfer teaches wherein the dimension between the images are compared (paragraph 26) and the change (difference/distance) between the images is used determine an anomaly.
But Telfer fails to teach the camera being an IR camera and the images, both stored and received, being thermal images or a thermographic map.
Baleine teaches an apparatus and method for temperature mapping a turbine wherein a processor (30) is coupled to a thermal imager (14) for processing imaging data of a turbine. The processor generates a map of the component based on the image data (paragraph 26-32).
Accordingly, it would have been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art of gas turbine testing at the time the invention was made to modify the system of Telfer with the IR camera and thermal data gathering as taught by Baleine in order to consistently provide accurate absolute temperature measurements of the component (Baleine paragraph 5)
